The FSM Extraction Engine
The FSM recognition engine provides benefits such as accurate FSM extraction,
diagnostic messages, support for FSM reset filtering, and compile-time performance. The
engine improves the analysis of FSMs split across module boundaries. It also improves
the analysis of FSMs with code in functions.
The FSM engine identifies when there are multiple signals used to hold the next-state
value as it is being computed. There are some cases where signals are not considered to
be FSMs. If you see differences you do not understand, it is recommended that you use
the -diag fsm switch on the VCS command line at compile time. This produces messages
explaining why signals are or are not recognized as FSMs.
The FSM extraction engine finds some impossible state-to-state changes. Also, you can
see that the order, in which states and transitions is reported, helps in identifying the
source line numbers for states and transitions. Note that VCS uses a strict ordering for
both states and transitions.

Introduction
Partition compile flow allows you to compile portions of the design and get significantly
faster turnaround time during the iterative process of compile and recompile. There are
two modes of using partition compile flow. They are as follows:
• Autopartitioning
• Manual Partitioning
Autopartitioning
Autopartitioning is the default mode in partition compile flow where partitioning is decided
by VCS by simply enabling the partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time
option. Autopartitioning automatically partitions the design and the testbench. You do not
need to specify yourself what parts of the design and testbench are in which partitions.
VCS creates optimal number of partitions to get better performance and the typical
compile time of each partition is 3-4 minutes. Further, the partitioning is regularly updated
based on the incremental changes done in the design to get optimal recompile time.
Autopartitioning automatically takes care of the cross-partition limitations across partitions
and re-adjusts the partitioning to avoid any cross-partition errors.
The use model for autopartitioning is easy to adopt partition compile flow.
To use partition compile flow with autopartitioning, use the following command in VCS two-
step flow:
% vcs -partcomp top <other vcs elaboration options>

Chapter 1: Overview
Managing Cross-Module References
You can change the autopartitioning threshold using the following option:
-partcomp=autopart_[low|medium|high]
The option applies autopartitioning to both modules and packages with a low, medium
and high threshold. By default, the option applies autopartitioning to both modules and
packages with a medium threshold.
Manual Partitioning
When you want to create a separate partition for a specific block that is under debugging
or development, then you can use the manual partition to create a separate partition along
with autopartitioning.
You can specify manual partition using the following command:
% vcs -partcomp top +optconfigfile+pc.cfg <other vcs elaboration options>
Here, +optconfigfile is a simple text file. You can specify a partition in the
+optconfigfile files with a line beginning with the partition keyword. The cell keyword
specifies that the partition is for all instances of the module name or the program block
name that follows.
For example:
// +optconfigfile configuration file cfg.txt
partition cell test;
partition cell dut;
This configuration file specifies:
• one partition for program block test.
• one partition for both instances of module dut.
VCS honors manual partitioning mentioned in the configuration file as well as enables
autopartitioning for the remaining portion of the design.
Managing Cross-Module References
When your design is partitioned, there is a chance that there are cross-module references
(XMRs) across partitions. That is, signals and variables from one partition are accessed
from another partition.

Chapter 1: Overview
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
You can manage XMRs using the partition compile flow as follows:
• If there is no change in XMRs, you do not need any extra option or any change in
configuration file for the partition compile flow.
• If the XMR changes, use the -partcomp=noxmrconfig option, so that only the
changed partition is recompiled or it might cause some runtime slowdown. If you do not
use any option, both the referrer and the referee partitions are recompiled.
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
The following scenarios causes recompilation of a partition:
• ◦ ▪ Changes in module definition.
▪ Changes in vcs command-line option or in the synopsys_sim.setup or
+optconfigfile configuration file.
▪ Changes to the global design property, such as adding $dumpvars to a partition.
This retriggers recompilation of all the partitions.
▪ Changes to the $unit scope: Any change (addition of new signal, type, module,
interface) to the $unit results in recompilation of all the partitions associated
with this $unit scope.
▪ Changes to an interface require the recompilation of all modules connected to
that interface.
▪ Changes to a shared package. In this case, recompilation is required for all the
partitions sharing this package.
Note:
Complete list of scenarios that triggers recompilation of a partition is available in
the Partition Compile section of the VCS/VCS MX LCA Features Guide.

Introduction
When you are debugging or developing a block in the design, then you end up spending
lot of time compiling the entire design for a small piece of change in the block in your
design.
To improve compile-time performance in VCS/VCS MX, you can use the default
incremental compilation method or enable the partition compilation method and save
on the overall compile turnaround time (TAT) during the process of debugging or
development.
Incremental compilation is the default method in VCS/VCS MX. During incremental
compilation, VCS/VCS MX analyzes and compiles only those design units that are
changed since last compilation.
However, when the design is complex and you want further optimized compile
performance, then you can use the partition compile flow. Partition compile flow allows you
to decide on how to partition your design so that you can fine tune the recompile behavior.
The partition compile can significantly reduce the compilation turnaround time by allowing
you to recompile only the changed partitions (portions of the design) and reuse the
partitions for the unchanged portions of the design that are already compiled earlier. You
can enable partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time option.

Incremental Compile Flow
Incremental compile flow works for both two-step and three-step flows and it recompiles
only the modified files. It is enabled by default to give optimized compile-time performance.

Stable Endpoint MCPs: When Protocol Meets Timing
Figure 2 shows the canonical stable MCP pattern. The dvalid signal strobes every three
cycles, creating a microarchitectural protocol that enforces the multi-cycle relationship.
Even in zero-delay simulation, the design functions correctly because dvalid controls
when FF2 samples.
Figure 2 MCP With Stable Endpoint
What the Figure Shows:
• FF1/Q changes data when dvalid pulses (every three cycles).
• FF2/D samples only when dvalid is high.
• The combinational logic between them has a three-cycle MCP declared in SDC.
• At zero delay, dvalid ensures correct operation, independent of SDC .
Potential Issue: What if the SDC specifies four cycles but dvalid implements three
cycles?

Figure 3 MCP With Stable Endpoint: Design Bug Missed
Figure 3 illustrates the critical failure case:
• RTL Reality: dvalid strobes every three clock cycles
• SDC Declaration: set_multicycle_path -setup 4 (timing team relaxed to ease
convergence)
• Zero-Delay Simulation: Passes completely—dvalid protocol ensures correct three-
cycle sampling
• Silicon Failure: Timing tools optimized assuming four-cycle capture. On cycle 4, FF2
samples while FF1 is transitioning → metastability
Why Traditional Simulation Misses This: The functional protocol dvalid is correct. The
timing assumption (four-cycle) is never tested because zero-delay simulation treats all
paths as instantaneous.

Figure 4 MCP With Stable Endpoint - Bug Detected Using VCS SDC

What VCS SDC Adds:
• Setup Checker (Red Marker): Triggers at the point where the source changes within
four cycles of the destination sampling.
◦ What it detected: FF1/Q changed at cycle 3, but FF2 sampled at cycle 0 (only
three cycles prior; SDC requires ≥4)
◦ Message:
MCP Setup Violation: Source changed 3 cycles after destination
captured (expected ≥4)
• X-Injection (Purple Shaded Region): Shows where VCS SDC injected X-values at
the input of FF2
◦ Duration: Cycles 1–3 (modeling the uncertainty window)
◦ Purpose: Forces downstream logic to prove it does not depend on early data arrival

logged

parts of the design. This option compiles your design to collect
profile data.

testbench for collecting both CPU time and machine memory profile
information. Then at runtime specifies collecting CPU time profile

testbench for collecting both CPU time and machine memory profile
information. Then at runtime, specifies collecting machine memory

-simprofile
The unified simulation profiler reports the amount of CPU time and machine memory used
by the Verilog, SystemVerilog, SystemC, and VHDL parts of the design. Compile your
design using the -simprofile compile-time option.
%> vcs <file_name> -simprofile <=optional_argument>

%> vcs source.v -simprofile
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=time
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=mem
-simprofile=time
This compile time option specifies compiling the design and testbench for collecting both
CPU time and machine memory profile information. Then at runtime specifies collecting
CPU time profile information.
With the time argument, you can omit the -simprofile runtime option if you want to
collect the profile time information that you have specified at compile time.
If at runtime you want VCS to collect the profile memory information, you can specify the
mem argument with the runtime option.
%> vcs -simprofile=time
%> vcs -simprofile=time
In the following example, the mem argument is specified with the runtime option for the VCS
to collect the profile memory information:
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=time
%> simv -simprofile mem
-simprofile=mem
This compile time option specifies compiling the design and testbench for collecting both
CPU time and machine memory profile information. Then at runtime, specifies collecting
machine memory profile information.
With the mem argument, you can omit the -simprofile runtime option if you want to
collect the profile memory information that you have specified at compile time.
If at runtime you want VCS to collect the profile time information, you can specify the time
argument with the runtime option.

%> vcs -simprofile=mem
%> vcs -simprofile=mem

Enables monitoring toggle coverage for modport when specified along with the -cm_tgl
fullintf option. For each modport in an array, VCS reports toggle coverage for each of the
signal members of the modport.
% vcs <design_file> <other_compile_options> -cm tgl -cm_tgl fullintf
+modportarr
% vcs -sverilog -cm tgl -cm_tgl fullintf+modportarr test.v
-cm_tgl signalsort
Enables you to sort the signals of toggle coverage in alphabetical order.
% vcs <design_file> <other_compile_options> -cm tgl -cm_tgl signalsort
% vcs -sverilog -cm tgl -cm_tgl signalsort test.v
-cm_tgl portsonly
Instructs VCS to compile and monitor only the ports in your design for toggle coverage, so
that the coverage reports that URG writes contain information only about the ports. These
reports do not contain information about either the variables and nets that are not ports in
your Verilog modules or the variables and signals declared in your VHDL architectures.
% vcs <design_file> <other_compile_options> -cm tgl -cm_tgl portsonly
% vcs -sverilog -cm tgl -cm_tgl portsonly test.v

unencrypted_signals

-cm_tgl_unpacked_limit <value>

What’s New In This Release
This section describes the new features and improvements in VCS Intelligent Coverage
Optimization (ICO). The following points introduce the new and enhanced features of ICO
and provide pointers to additional information:
• ICO improves error detection by analyzing failure history-including unique signatures,
total failures, and failure rates to accelerate error detection through the following two
mechanisms:
◦ Predictive Bug Hunting: Learns from the past regression runs and applies that
knowledge to stress the observed failure spaces for adjacent failures and to explore
new failure spaces.
◦ Adaptive Bug Hunting: Uses the new bugs mode to automatically adjust bug
modes (such as bug, bug2, and so on) based on a prescribed methodology as
testing progresses and failure rates stabilize.
For more information, refer to Predictive and Adaptive Bug Hunting.
• Starting with this release, ICO can record Important Signal Predictor (ISP) data during
simulation as a compressed binary file named record.isp under the store record
directory. You can then use the crg command to translate this file into a readable form
(for example, CSV) and to generate an ID map that links each recorded value back to
its source location and variable name. The recorded data can be used for downstream
analysis, debug, and machine-learning flows.
For more information, refer to Identifying and Recording Important Signal Predictors
(ISP).
• Starting with this release, ICO can dump failure signatures during simulation when
you run it in bug-finding mode. A failure signature is a normalized form of an error
message in which dynamic content , such as simulation time and data values, has
been removed. As a result, multiple error messages that report the same underlying
problem collapse to a single signature.
For more information, refer to Dumping Failure Signatures.
• Starting with this release, ICO supports functional context aware class naming for
learning. Use +ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt to enable function or task context in
class instance names and +ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt_depth to control context

paths and improves learning precision.
For more information, refer to Functional Context for Class Naming.
• Starting with this release, you can run the bugs strategy without the -l <log_file>
option when you enable an internal log by setting a positive log chunk size. This feature
is enabled using the +ntb_solver_bias_log_chunk_size runtime option.
For more information, refer to Manage Log Files for Bug and Failure Prediction.

effective in improving coverage. For more information on prognosis feature, see ICO

simv \

Viewing Root Cause Constraints
Figure 12 shows the sample RCA report. This report shows hyperlink actions (red arrows)
from a variable to the Coverage Category window. You can click ILLEGAL hyperlink to
identify the root cause constraints shown in the pop-up window. This window shows the
potential over constraint possibilities. It takes you to one of the constraints that could be a
potential reason why the bin is illegal.
Figure 12 RCA Detail Report
In this example, as highlighted in the pop-up window, variable a cannot take the negative
values such as range [-26:-25-1] because of the constraint a > 0 .

ICO Runtime Options
This chapter describes the runtime options available to enable the ICO features in the

Mode Add-ons
+256 Enables biasing of variables

Option for Using Bias for Randomization
Mode Description
+512 Enables collect always (ignore ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit)
+1024 Enables alternating between bias/no bias
+2048 Enables bias after a threshold number (=32) of randomization
+4096 Enables Binary Decision Diagram (BDD) biasing
+8192 Enables bin biasing
+16384 Enables part-select. For more information, see Biasing of the Part-Select
Variables.
+32768 Enables edge biasing. For more information, see Edge Biasing to Improve
Coverage of Corner Values.
The following is an example for enabling multiple modes using the
+ntb_solver_bias_mode option:
+ntb_solver_bias_mode = 1289 (= 9 + 256 + 1024)
This option does the following:
• Enable both record and bias modes. The variable values are biased with varying
weights across randomization in both intra- and inter runs (9).
• Enable bias variables ( +256)
• Enables alternate biasing/no biasing ( +1024)
Option for Using Bias for Randomization
+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit
+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit=N
Uses bias for randomization when count <=N. There is no randomization limit if N <= 0 .
Option to Specify Scope Variables
+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file
+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=<file>
Specifies a file with scope variables for record/bias. (Format of scope is discussed in

Option to Store Information
Option to Store Information
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path>
Specifies the cdb database to be stored. If this option is not specified, the database is
stored in simv.cst/stimuliDb/record.
Option to Load Records
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<path>
If used in shared mode, path specifies the cdb database to be stored as a backup load
from the shared record. If this option is not specified, the database is stored in simv.cst/
stimuliDb/load_record.
Backup load is required to debug simv failures.
If used for replaying simulation failures of the runs in shared mode, the
path should be pointing to the same cdb database that is specified with the
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record option during the shared mode.
If not used in shared mode, then the path specifies the cdb database to be loaded from
a previous run for chaining. If this option is not specified, then there is no chaining.
If used for replaying simulation failures of the runs in non-shared mode,
the path should be pointing to the same cdb database that is specified with the
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record option during non-shared mode.
Option to Specify Shared Database
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared>
Specifies the cdb shared database stored/updated by all concurrent simv runs. If this
option is not specified, then distributed sharing is disabled.

Options for Dumping Failure Signatures
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_strategy=<bugs>

Options for Dumping Failure Signatures
Selects the ICO biasing strategy for the run. Use the bugs value to enable the bug-finding
strategy that triggers failure signature dumping.
Enables failure prediction. Specify a non-zero value to trigger failure signature dumping
independently of the strategy mode.
For more information, refer to Dumping Failure Signatures.

CRG Options
ICO produces stimuli distribution in a coverage database (cdb)of the TB during the
simulation run using the following command:
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<record>
A post simulation utility, crg is used to generate the reports from a cdb generated from
simv run. The crg utility can also be used to manage both shared and non-shared cdb
databases.
% crg -dir <dir> [-f <filelist>][-report report_dir][-format <text|
html|both>][-text <flat|hier|summary|brief>][-merge merge_dir]
[-elfile <elFile>][-purge <pFile>][-purgeX <xFile>][-purge_key <uvm
+rca+sbin>][-purgeX_key <uvm+rca+sbin>][-sbin_merge <add+reuse+modify>]
[-part_select][-work <wdir>][-wdiv][-shared <init|init_sfs|check|
snap|update|save|restore>][-reset_tag <biased|scope>][-purge_untag
<biased|scope>][-auto_purge][-exclude <uncovered|illegal>][-isp_in
<path_to_record.isp>][-isp_out <output_file>] [-isp_format <bin|csv>]
[-diff][-show <tests|records>][-zip <level>][-base_merge <level>][-incr]
[-prognosis][-stat][-illegal_attr][-illegal_group][-rca_effort_attr]
[-check_db][-q, -quiet][-l, -log <logfile>][-v, -version][-sdb <dir>]
[-shared_save_period <sec>]
-auto_purge
Purges the stale information from the given CDBs, saves it in <shared_cdb_new> (when
specified with the -merge option), and initializes it for sharing.
For more information, refer to Reusing Shared CDB Across Changing Models.
-base_merge <level>
Specifies the base class merge <level>. It should be 1 or more. For more information,
refer to Base Class Merging Based on User-Defined Level.
-check_db

Checks each input cdb and output cdb (if specified). Prints check db output in <wdir>/
check_db.txt. For more information, refer to Integrity Check of CDB.
-dir <record_dir>
Specifies the directory to record data. You can specify this option multiple times.
-diff
Displays and highlights the delta difference between two coverage databases in the
coverage report. For more information, refer to Delta Difference Between Two CDBs.
-elfile <elFile>
Exclude all the bins specified in the file. For example, you can use the text report file
bininst_status.csv to keep the lines you want to exclude. For more information, refer to
Excluding Uncoverable Bins From Reports.
-exclude <uncovered|illegal>
Specifies bin coverage type to exclude. Default is uncovered. You can specify multiple
-exclude options. This option is applicable only on bins specified with -elfile. The
-exclude illegal option excludes illegal

-purge_key uvm+rca+sbin
Purges variables depending on the keys uvm, rca, and sbin. The ‘+’ sign denotes the
disjunction of the keys. For more information, refer to RCA Noise Reduction.
-purgeX_key uvm+rca+sbin
Purges variables excluding those captured with the key uvm, rca, or sbin. The ‘+’ sign
denotes the disjunction of the keys. For more information, refer to RCA Noise Reduction.
-purge_untag <biased|scope>: [Input]
Specifies the tag to purge all the information of untagged biased or scope variables from a
coverage database. For more information refer to Reusing Shared CDB Across Changing
Models.
If both the tags are specified as follows, then the variable information is purged if it is not
tagged by either biased or scope. -purge_untag biased -purge_untag scope
-q,-quiet
Suppress all messages.
-rca_effort_attr
Annotates RCA effort attributes for bins with no RCA information. For more information,
refer to Incremental RCA Support for Auto Bins.
-reset_tag <biased|scope>: [Flag]
Specifies the tag to reset (default: none). If scope, then scope tag of all the variables are
reset. If biased, then biased tag of all the variables are reset. For more information refer to
Reusing Shared CDB Across Changing Models.
During simv runs, if a variable is biased, it is tagged as biased, and is not untagged
until reset_tag is invoked. Similarly, if a variable is tagged as scope, it is not untagged
until reset_tag is invoked. You can use both the tags as follows: -reset_tag biased
-reset_tag scope
-report <report_dir>: [output]

Generates the coverage report in the report_dir directory in either HTML or text format.
The reports are generated with tagged biased and scope variables. The following files are
generated, which contain list of variables that are scope or biased:
varinst_scope.txt, varclass_biased.txt
The varinst_scope.txt file contains a line denoting a variable var for the randomization
object identified by the randomize site file:line and class name as follows:
file:line:class:var
Example: test.sv:10:foo:x
The varclass_biased.txt file contains a line denoting a variable var for the
randomization object identified by a class name as follows:
*:*:class:var
Example: *:*:foo:x
Both varinst_scope.txt and varclass_biased.txt files can be used as scope file
(+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=scope.txt) in simv run or as pFile in crg -purge
<pFile>.
-show <tests|records>
Shows the names of the tests in the coverage reports. For more information, refer to
Coverage Option.
-stat
Prints cdb statistics in <work_dir>/stat.txt. For more information, refer to Reporting
Recommendation to Purge the Shared CDB or Use New DB.
-sbin_merge add+reuse+modify
Enables merging of the user-defined sample bins (sbins). For more information, refer to
Custom Diversification.
-shared init
Initialize <dir> for shared recording. For more information, refer to Shared Regr

ICO Auto Configuration
ICO supports shortcut options for auto bias that combines most of the runtime options with
their default values. These options allow you to selectively overwrite the default values,
thereby, enabling you to harness the full value. Also, you to quickly make the changes in
the legacy scripts and easily track optimal configuration.
Following is the syntax for shortcut to auto bias:
simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=<0|1|2>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record>
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=<0|1>
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=<0|1|2>
0: Disables auto configuration

1: Enables auto configuration
2: Enables auto configuration with enhanced set (recommended)
Specifies the work directory.
Default location: ./simv.cst/stimuliDb/
• When +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=1 is specified, the following options are
set:
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=5
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<work_dir>/<tname>_<seed>.store_record
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<work_dir>/<tname>_<seed>.load_record

ICO Auto Biasing
There are multiple bias modes (+ntb_solver_bias_mode) to configure ICO depending
on the choice of constraint solver (+ntb_solver_mode), part selects, bin biasing, inter and
intra learning.
ICO is enhanced to learn and automate bias mode using the Auto Bias feature for
improved usability and ease of usage. You must use the +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto
runtime option to enable this feature.
The +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto option takes a value from 1 to 10 corresponding
to the most conservative biasing to aggressive biasing, respectively. For example,
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=5 is the most balanced biasing mode allowing equal
proportion of simv runs with various biasing modes such as 16649, 24841, 20745, and
28937. For each bias mode, the solver mode is automatically selected under the hood.
You can also track the test name for each bias using the +ntb_solver_bias_test_name
runtime option. Auto biasing can exploit the test names such that proportion is
applied to the reseeded run set of each unique test separately. To enable this,
you can use the +ntb_solver_bias_test_name=<uniqTestName>_<Id> or
-cm_test <uniqTestName>_<Id> option. Id can be a random seed (specified using
+ntb_random_seed). If Id is a random seed, then ‘_’ separator is not needed. Preference
is given to +ntb_solver_bias_test_name over the -cm_test option.

Following is the Auto Bias use model:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<auto_bias_mode>
+ntb_enble_fast_solver=0 +ntb_solver_bias_test_name=<uniqTestName>_<Id>
-cm_test <uniqTest><Id>
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<auto_bias_mode>
auto_bias_mode: 0 to 10 (default: 0).
0: Disable auto bias

Key Points to Note
• If auto bias is enabled, the +ntb_solver_bias_mode option is ignored if specified.
• The following options are not needed and are internally set by the auto bias feature:
+ntb_solver_mode
However, if they are specified, then the values of these options are honored overriding
the internal value set by the auto bias feature.
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name=<uniqTestName>_<Id>
Tracks the test name in the coverage reports. Id can be a random seed (specified
using +ntb_random_seed). If Id is a random seed, then ‘_’ separator is not needed.
Preference is given to +ntb_solver_bias_test_name over -cm_test.
Support for Changing Bias Mode During Simulation
ICO allows you to change the bias modes intra-simv, that is, across
randomization within a single simv run. This feature is enabled using the
+ntb_solver_bias_auto_intra_enable=1 simulation option. This feature improves the
diversity of the bias modes and stimuli coverage.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<autoBias>
+ntb_solver_bias_auto_intra_enable=<0|1>

+ntb_solver_bias_auto_intra_enable=<0|1>
0: Default value. Disables auto bias for intra simv
1: Enables auto bias for intra simv
Example 1 test.sv
class myClass;
rand bit[4:0] x,y,z,w;
constraint c {
x<y && y<z && z<w;
w dist {[0:9] := 10,
[10:19] := 4,
[20:31] := 1};
}

myClass t=new;
repeat (1000) begin
t.randomize();
end
end

Extracting Test Names Using Filters Based on Regular
Expressions
ICO uses test names to identify tests that belong to the same template test. The biasing
engine uses this inference to determine the optimal auto-biasing parameters. If the
correct template test is not inferred, the setting is sub-optimal, and desired outcome is not
observed.
You can use the runtime options +ntb_solver_bias_test_name and
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type to specify test names. However, ICO does not infer the
UVM template test name in the following cases:
• The suffix of the template test name does not match the random seed.
Example: +ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm +UVM_TESTNAME=mytest_ 1234
+ntb_random_seed=300

Extracting Test Names Using Filters Based on Regular
Expressions
ICO uses test names to identify tests that belong to the same template test. The biasing
engine uses this inference to determine the optimal auto-biasing parameters. If the
correct template test is not inferred, the setting is sub-optimal, and desired outcome is not
observed.
You can use the runtime options +ntb_solver_bias_test_name and
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type to specify test names. However, ICO does not infer the
UVM template test name in the following cases:
• The suffix of the template test name does not match the random seed.
Example: +ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm +UVM_TESTNAME=mytest_ 1234
+ntb_random_seed=300
• Only suffix check is supported even when the prefix of the template test name matches
the random seed.
Example: +ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm +UVM_TESTNAME=300_mytest
+ntb_random_seed=300
• Using the hash value of random seed as a suffix.

Example: +ntb_solver_bias_test_type=cm_name -cm_name mytest-<hashValue
of random seed> +ntb_random_seed=300
• Updating the test name of the +ntb_solver_bias_test_name runtime option in the
script due to legacy reasons.
To overcome the above mentioned limitations, ICO allows you to specify filters
based on regular expressions to include/exclude part of test names using the
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name_filter=<regex> runtime option.
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type=<uvm|ovm|cm_test|cm_name>
+UVM_TESTNAME=<uvm>
+OVM_TESTNAME=<ovm>
-cm_test <cm_test>
-cm_name <cm_name>
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name_filter=<regex>
You can specify the test type to override the default order by using
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type with one of the cm_name|cm_test|ovm|uvm strings.
• Only POSIX regular expressions are supported.
• The test name filter is applicable for both auto and prognosis runs.
Examples
Example-1:
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type=cm_name -cm_name test-a1234
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name_filter="[[:alpha:]]+" +ntb_random_seed=12
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record
% crg -dir record -json -WORK; grep tnames WORK/record.cdb.json

"utnames":["test_"]

+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record
% crg -dir record -json -WORK; grep tnames WORK/record.cdb.json

+ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm +UVM_TESTNAME="test_1234_xyz_1245"

)_" +ntb_random_seed=14 +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record
% crg -dir record -json -WORK; grep tnames WORK/record.cdb.json

Scoping Random Variables and Constraint Blocks for Biasing
Use the scoping feature to control which random variables and constraint classes ICO
(Intelligent Coverage Optimization) targets for biasing during simulation. Specify your
selection in a scope file using the +ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=<scopeFile> option,
allowing you to focus biasing on specific variables or classes and improve simulation
efficiency and coverage quality. Use wildcards and escaped names in the scope file to
match multiple variables or parameterized classes as needed.
By default, all random variables are targeted by ICO during runtime. You can selectively
choose certain random variables, constraint classes, and class instances to target for
biasing using a scope file. This file is specified as a runtime option during simulation using
the +ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=<scopeFile> option.
The scope file is a text file with one or more lines. You should follow the following format,
that is, four fields separated by ‘:’, representing one or more instances of random variables
to be included, as follows:
<filePath>:<lineNum>:<className>:<varName>
Where, <varName> corresponds to a random variable of the constraint class <className>
whose instance is randomized at source file <filePath> and line <lineNum>, respectively.
Example: test.sv:10:foo:x
This corresponds to the variable instance with name x of the constraint class foo which is
randomized at line 10 of the file test.sv.
Support for Wildcard '*'
There is a limited support with wildcard to include more variables per line. A field can have
a wildcard '*'. It represents all possible names with prefix match to the field upto '*'.

Following are some examples:
• test.sv:*:foo:xyz — Match all variables with name xyz of the randomized class foo
instantiated anywhere in file test.sv.
• *:*:foo:xy* — Match all variables with prefix xy of the randomized class foo
instantiated anywhere.
• *:*:foo:* — Match all variables of

Simv Runtime Options
To enable functional context for class naming, add the following runtime options to your
existing ICO simv command:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_strategy=<ico_strategy> \
+ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt=<fcxt_enable> \
+ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt_depth=<0:31>
Where:
+ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt=<fcxt_enable>
Controls which types of randomization calls include functional context in the class instance
name. Specify one of the following values:
• 0 — Disables functional context. This is the default.
• 1 — Enables functional context for std::randomize only.
• 2 — Enables functional context for non-std::randomize only.
• 3 — Enables functional context for both std::randomize and non-std::randomize.
+ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt_depth=<0:31>
Controls how many levels of the call path ICO captures. Specify a value between 0 and
31:
• 0 — Disables context collection. This is the default when functional context is not
enabled.
• 1 — Captures one level of context. This is the default when functional context is
enabled.
• 2 to 31 — Captures deeper call paths up to the specified level.
Guidelines
Follow these guidelines when you enable functional context:
• Start with +ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt=3 and
+ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt_depth=1 if your testbench uses helper functions or
tasks around randomization calls. This gives you the new behavior with minimal path
depth.
• Increase the depth only when nested helper calls represent distinct learning scenarios
that you want ICO to track separately.
• Keep the depth value small unless you need deeper call-path separation. Smaller
values keep instance names shorter and easier to interpret.

Consider a testbench where a packet object gets randomized through multiple tasks and
functions:
class pkt;
rand bit [7:0] addr;
constraint c_addr { addr < 200; }

task automatic gen_pkt_task(ref pkt p, int max_addr);
p.randomize() with { addr < max_addr;};
endtask

task automatic gen_pkt_task2(ref pkt p, int max_addr);
gen_pkt_task(p, max_addr);
endtask

function automatic gen_pkt_fn (ref pkt p, int min_addr);
p.randomize() with { addr > min_addr;};
gen_pkt_task(p, min_addr);
endfunction

pkt p = new();
int i=80;

gen_pkt_task(p, i);
gen_pkt_task2(p, i);
gen_pkt_fn(p, i);
end
Without functional context, ICO records only two learning instances because it identifies
them by randomization location and class name alone:
test6a.sv:9:pkt
test6a.sv:17:pkt
With functional context enabled, ICO records four distinct instances because it includes
the call path:
test6a.sv:25:gen_pkt_task.pkt:addr
test6a.sv:26:gen_pkt_task2.gen_pkt_task.pkt:addr
test6a.sv:27:gen_pkt_fn.pkt:addr
test6a.sv:27:gen_pkt_fn.gen_pkt_task.pkt:addr

Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of the Uncovered Bins
Enable Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to identify and mark bins as illegal when constraints
block them, using the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 runtime option. This feature helps you
improve coverage and diversity scores by automatically detecting which bins cannot be
covered due to constraints. Review RCA results in the coverage report to understand and
address coverage gaps efficiently.
ICO is enhanced to search the blocking constraints for the uncovered bins and mark them
as illegal. You must use the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 runtime option to enable this
feature. This feature helps to improve the overall O-SCOREs of coverage and diversity.
This feature requires additional computation. You can use the
+ntb_solver_rca_cpu_time_limit=<nsec> runtime option to increase the
CPU time allocated for RCA. Where, <nsec> is the time limit of RCA.
Use the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 and +ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=<nsec>
options as follows to enable RCA of the uncovered bins:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<mode>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record> +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=100
To generate reports, use the crg utility on the <record> directory after the run as follows:
% crg -dir <record> -report crgReport
% firefox crgReport/index.html

Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of the Uncovered Bins
Enable Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to identify and mark bins as illegal when constraints
block them, using the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 runtime option. This feature helps you
improve coverage and diversity scores by automatically detecting which bins cannot be
covered due to constraints. Review RCA results in the coverage report to understand and
address coverage gaps efficiently.
ICO is enhanced to search the blocking constraints for the uncovered bins and mark them
as illegal. You must use the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 runtime option to enable this
feature. This feature helps to improve the overall O-SCOREs of coverage and diversity.
This feature requires additional computation. You can use the
+ntb_solver_rca_cpu_time_limit=<nsec> runtime option to increase the
CPU time allocated for RCA. Where, <nsec> is the time limit of RCA.
Use the +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2 and +ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=<nsec>
options as follows to enable RCA of the uncovered bins:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<mode>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record> +ntb_solver_bias_rca=2
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=100
To generate reports, use the crg utility on the <record> directory after the run as follows:
% crg -dir <record> -report crgReport
% firefox crgReport/index.html

Support for Ignoring Soft Constraints
Soft constraints allow you to specify default values for random variables. These
constraints must be honored if possible; otherwise, they are disregarded or dropped if no
solution is possible. Soft constraints are applied only to individual constraint expressions
and provide control for each constraint expression.
Example: soft x < 10;
If there are no other constraints on x, then x must take a value less than 10 as per the
SystemVerilog LRM. You may want to drop x, so that it is free to take any value. When
a design is close to tape out, you may want to drop the soft constraints and check if the
blocked scenarios can expose some real bugs.
ICO provides a set of +ntb_solver_bias_soft_ignore* runtime options to ignore (that
is, drop) soft constraints. These options allow you to:

Incremental RCA Support for Auto Bins
When performing Root Cause Analysis (RCA), you can limit the CPU time allocated for
RCA run using the runtime option such as
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=300
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=300.
Due to this time limit, it is possible that some RCA information may not get generated. For
uncovered bins, it is not clear if they are potentially coverable or cannot be covered at all
(not tried or timed-out).
VCS ICO provides effort attributes for the uncovered/illegal categories. These attributes
provide information on whether the unresolved problem:
• is hard and requires more time, or
• does not have sufficient time allocated and no time left to try, or
• is coverable, that is, not blocked, and sufficient randomization is needed.

VCS ICO provides the following runtime options to specify the kind of problem to target or
not for RCA and specify the time effort for each problem:
• The
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_incr=1
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_incr=1 option to track the effort attributes of each RCA
problem.
• The
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_focus=nt+to
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_focus=nt+to option to focus on the not tried ‘nt’ and
timed out ‘to’ RCA problems.
• The
ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=totalminmax
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=total:min:max option is enhanced to
control the CPU time.
Simulation Runtime Options
simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 ; //recommended
+ntb_solver_bias_clean=0 ; //recommended
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<sharedDb>
+ntb_solver_bias_rca=<0|1|2|3>
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_incr=<0|1>
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_focus=<nt|to|nt+to>
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=total:min:max
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_incr=<0|1>
0: No tracking of incremental RCA effort (default).
1: Enables tracking of incremental RCA effort.
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_focus=<nt|to|nt+to>
nt: Target not-tried RCA unsolved problems.
to: Target timed-out RCA unsolved problems.
nt+to, to+nt: Target both not-tried and timed-out RCA problems.
+ntb_solver_bias_rca_cpu_limit=total:min:max
total: Total CPU time (in sec) for solving the RCA problem.
min: Minimum CPU time (in sec) allocated for solving an RCA problem. When a problem is
attempted for the first time, this time is allocated. Default min time is 60 sec.
max: Maximum CPU time (in sec) allocated for solving an RCA problem. Default max time
is twice the min value.
When a problem is timed-out, then the time allocated to it the next time is doubled until it
reaches max or gets solved. Maximum time can be up to 2 hours.

Singleton Bins for Enum Types
You can use the +ntb_solver_bias_enum_bin=1 simulation option to create singleton
bins for each enum value. This option is supported only for the variables of enum type.
This feature does not change the behavior of auto-binning for non-enum type variables.

+ …

When set to 1, this option creates singleton bins for all enum values.

If any cdb_record is created with +ntb_solver_bias_enum_bin=1, then the coverage
report for enum bin changes.
If the number of enum values of any given enum type is greater than 65536, default
binning is used.
The bin values are shown in HEX format, that is, h_XXX. Non-enum values are not
displayed.

Tracking and Diversifying Higher Values as Singleton Bins
For signed/unsigned rand variables, the +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=16,17,18
runtime option allows you to create singleton bins for each value in the range [-512,511]
and [0,1023] respectively. However, this option does not support the following:
• Track higher values individually
• Track values/intervals in the constraints which are more relevant for coverage
You can use the following runtime options to track and diversify the higher values (that
appear in the constraints) as singleton bins. This feature also addresses the scalability
issue that may arise for tracking all possible higher values. Additional bins tracked are
shown in the coverage reports.
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=16,17,18,19
+ntb_solver_bias_interval_size_limit=<interval_size_limit>

Limitations
The following are the limitations for the creation of singleton bins from a given user-defined
interval for a given rand variable:
• All values of intervals should be in the range [-231,231-1], that is, should be an
integer. For example, for an interval L:H, where L has an integer value and H has a
value larger than the integer value, then that interval is not considered for singletons.
• The size of each contiguous interval cannot exceed 65000. For example, if there
is a contiguous interval [L:i][i+1:h], such that [L:H] size exceeds 65000, then
singletons are not created for this interval even if [L:i] or [i+1:H] could have size
more than 65000. If there are intervals such that [L:i] size is less than 65000 but [i
+1:h]size is more than 65000, then singletons are created for the first one.
• RCA for additional singletons is not computed.
Incremental Recording and Merging
ICO supports incremental (non-accumulating) recording of each run in the cdb using the
+ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode simulation option. Incremental recording allows you to
bias the contribution of some tests differently than others during merging, which can also
improve the overall diversity.

% simv +ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode=<0|1|2>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared> …
+ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode=<0|1|2> (default: 0)
0: No incremental recording
1: Enables incremental recording
2: Enables incremental recording and biased merging
You can use the following command to generate runtime report:
% crg -dir <dir1> -dir <dir2> -incr -merge <mdir> -report <rpt>
-incr
Specifies to use incremental information for merging, report generation, and get the
difference between two coverage databases.
% crg -dir inc_store -incr -merge mergedCdb -report crgReport -diff

Non-Shared Regression Mode: Manual Merging and Chaining
Each simv run stores cdb at a specified unique location
(+ntb_solver_bias_store_record). Merging of the store records is done by
the crg utility as shown in Figure 33. Chaining is done by loading the merged cdb
(+ntb_solver_bias_load_record) in the following regression.

Figure 33 Merging and Chaining
Regression 1 (possibly concurrently):
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=265
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_265_1_1 +ntb_solver_mode=2
+ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=265
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_265_2_1 +ntb_solver_mode=2
+ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=4361
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_4361_1_1
+ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=4361
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_4361_2_1
+ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
+ntb_solver_bias_mode=265 (= 9 + 256)
+ntb_solver_bias_mode=4361 (= 9 + 256 + 4096)

The bias modes 265 and 4361 enable the following:
Both record and bias modes. The variable values are biased with varying weights across
randomization in both intra- and inter-simv runs (9).
Biasing of variables (+256)
The bias mode 4361 also enables the following:
BDD biasing (+4096)
You can use the following command to merge the cdb:
% crg -f cdb.lst -merge cdbMerged_1 -report crgReport_1
% cat cdb1.lst
./record_265_1_1
./record_265_2_1
./record_4361_1_1
./record_4361_2_1
Chain the merged cdb to next regression as highlighted:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=265
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_265_1_2 +ntb_solver_bias_load_rec
ord=./cdbMerged_1 +ntb_solver_mode=2 +ntb_enable_fast_solver=0
+ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=265
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_265_2_2 +ntb_solver_bias_load_rec
ord=./cdbMerged_1 +ntb_solver_mode=2 +ntb_enable_fast_solver=0
+ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=4361
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_4361_1_2 +ntb_solver_bias_load_re
cord=./cdbMerged_1 +ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=4361
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record_4361_2_2 +ntb_solver_bias_load_re
cord=./cdbMerged_1 +ntb_enable_fast_solver=0 +ntb_random_seed_automatic
% crg -f cdb2.lst -merge cdbMerged_2 -report crgReport_2
% cat cdb2.lst
./record_265_1_2
./record_265_2_2
./record_4361_1_2
./record_4361_2_2

For example, to disable BDD biasing (+ntb_solver_bias_mode =+4096 ) and Slot biasing
(+ntb_solver_bias_mode=+8192), you can add the following options:
+ntb_solver_bias_disable_opt=9,10
Prognosis-Aware Auto Biasing
To select an appropriate autobias mode, you must run a prognosis step on the entire
design. The autobias mode is recommended based on the prognosis scores. The following
are the drawbacks of this approach:
• The prognosis scores are typically aggregate scores among all tests and may not truly
represent a single test accurately. Partitioning a regression into groups of similar kinds
of prognosis scores and applying a suitable autobias mode is not very practical.
• Running prognosis as a first step is not always desirable. It can be used for evaluation
purposes, but not for production usage as you would like to avoid one extra regression
for prognosis.
This feature overcomes the above mentioned drawbacks using the runtime optimization
option +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103. This option allows a test to start with a given
autobias mode (default is 5), and then the subsequent reseeds of the same test are run
with an appropriate autobias mode learned on-the-fly.
In addition, you can use the runtime option +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=20 to track
additional constraint density metrics to be used for the determination.
Runtime Options
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=20,103
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103
Enables prognosis-aware autobias mode selection.
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=20
Enables a new constraint density metric for prognosis analysis.
The above options are enabled only when the autobias feature is enabled.

The following note is highlighted when Prognosis is enabled:
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103 +ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=./
shared_record
Prognosis + DistMerge feature(s).
Example 18 test1.sv
class packet;
rand int a,b;
constraint cst {
a inside {[0:10]};
a < b; b == 100; }

module constr_iteration;
packet pkt;
pkt = new();
pkt.randomize();
end
end
Example 19 test2.sv
class packet;
rand int a,b;
constraint cst {
2*b < a; a < b; }

module constr_iteration;
packet pkt;
pkt = new();
pkt.randomize();
end
end

For the example test1.sv, the following are the dynamically computed prognosis scores
with +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=20,103:
Cstr2VarRatioAvg=1.20 (0.5 without option 20)
VarFreeAvg=50.00
For the example test2.sv, the following are the dynamically computed prognosis scores
with +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=20,103:
Cstr2VarRatioAvg=0.80 (0.5 without option 20)
VarFreeAvg=100.00
ValFreeAvg=100.00
When you use the option +ntb_solver_bias_enable=103 (with and without 20),
AutoBias 2 is picked for example test1.sv. For example test2.sv, Autobias 5 is
picked.
When
Cstr2VarRatioAvg <= 0.2
VarFreeAvg <= 20
ValFreeAvg <= 20
then AutoBias=1 is selected.
Improving Coverage and Diversity in Autobias
You can specify the +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=201 runtime option with the
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=1 option to improve coverage and diversity in
autobias.
The +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=201 option enables the corresponding optVal=201.
This option enables new autobias setting. If previous setting is needed, then specify
optVal=200 or don’t specify +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt.
For example, use the following options to enable the new autobias setting:
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=201
Identifying the Illegal Bins of the Part-Select Variables
ICO allows you to identify the illegal bins of the part-select variables. You can use the
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=25 runtime option to enable this feature. This feature
improves the diversification and stimulus coverage.

% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=25
where,
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=25
Enables illegal determination of the part-select variable values.
This option does not have an effect if the -part_select option is disabled
using +ntb_solver_bias_disable_opt=11.
Example 20 test.sv
rand bit [31:0] addr_tmp;
constraint cons{
addr_tmp[31:28] inside {[4:15]};
addr_tmp[27:16] inside {[12'h700:12'h800]};
addr_tmp[15:0] inside {[16'h0000:16'h0100]};
}
endclass initial begin
repeat(20) begin
end
end
% vcs -sverilog test.svp
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=108,25
% crg -dir simv.cst/stimuliDB/record -report rpt -part_select

-sbin_merge add+reuse+modify (default is add+reuse)
Enables merging of the user-defined sample bins (sbins) as per ICO Simulation Details.
The left and right cdbs are determined by the order of specifying the -dir options in the -f

-purge_sbin <file>
Purges the sbins of the variables specified in <file>.
-purgeX_sbin <fileX>
Purges the sbins of the variables excluding those specified in <fileX>.
The format for <file> and <fileX> is same as the varinst_scope.txt file.

Format for the User-Defined Sample Bin File
Following is the format of the user-defined sample bin (sbin) file:
<File>:<line>:<randomization_class_name>:<class_variable_name>:<focus_bins>
The five records in the above format are separated by ‘:’. The first four are same as the
scope file format. The format for the last record <focus_bins> is as follows:
<focus_bins> ::= <single>|<interval>|<range>|<focus_bins>","<focus_bins>
<single> ::= <integer>
<range> ::= <integer>_<integer>
<interval> ::= <integer>:<integer>
<range> - Allows you to specify singleton value bins for each value between two numbers.
<interval> - Allows you to specify an interval value bin defined by two numbers.
<integer> - A value within the bound of a signed 64-bit integer.
For example:
<focus_bins> = 1_10,11:20,-21:-100
There are 10 singleton bins from 1 to 10, and two interval bins [11:20] and [-100:-21].
• The singleton and interval bins are sorted internally. White space is allowed.
• If two lines have the same first four records, the <focus_bins> are accumulated.
• If the bins overlap in the increasing sort order (sorted on the lower interval value), then
the overlapping bins are not merged, however the next higher adjacent overlapping
bins are dropped. This rule is applied recursively while dropping minimum bins to
obtain a sorted list of non-overlapping bins.
• The value can be prefix with ‘ h_’ or ‘0x’ for hex.

Examples:
• *:*:myClass1:abc.line*:1:100
Includes all variables of myClass1 with prefix abc.line and creates a single interval
bin [1:100].
• test.sv:*:myClass2:*:1_10
Includes all variables of myClass2 for randomization in test.sv and creates 10 bins
with values 1 to 10 for the variables.
• test.sv:23:myClass3:xyz:10,12
Includes variable myClass3::xyz for randomization in test.sv at line 23, and create
bins 10 and 12
CRG Report
Variables with custom bins have ‘C’ appended to the name in separate rows. The report
displays two rows, one for the variable for the auto bins, and another for the variable for
the custom bins.

This section describes the following performance features:
• Reducing Disk Footprint of CDB
• Auto Clean at Runtime

Reducing Disk Footprint of CDB
The learn information is accumulated in the coverage database (cdb) memory during
runtime (simv runs) and is later saved in the disk before the run is finished. For later simv
runs, the learn information in the cdb is loaded from the disk and an updated cdb with
additional learning is stored back in the disk. For example:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_store=<recordStore>
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<recordLoad> +ntb_solver_bias_mode=2
By default, the stimuli distribution history is loaded from the record <recordLoad> (if
specified), and the updated history is stored in the record <recordStore>. Each cdb
loaded during the run must be saved for reproducing the run during debugging. This can
lead to a requirement of large disk space and possibly management of disk cleaning.

Runtime Performance Features
ICO allows you to reduce the size of a cdb with lossless compression technique enabled
at runtime using the simulation option +ntb_solver_bias_zip.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_zip=<level>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared> …
The cdb databases are compressed and stored in the disk based on the compression
level.
Compression level: 0 to 9 (default: 0).
0: No compression
1: Fastest compression

9: Best compression
Compression level greater than 0 compresses the local store record (specified
with +ntb_solver_bias_store_record), local load record (specified
with +ntb_solver_bias_load_record), and share record (specified with
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record).
During generation of the merge database using crg, you can use compression to reduce
the size of the merge database.
% crg -dir <dir1> -dir <dir2> -zip <level> -merge <mdir> -report <rpt>
-zip <level>
Compression level: 0 to 9 (default: 0).
0: No compression
1: Fastest compression

9: Best compression
Compression level greater than 0 compresses the local store record (specified
with +ntb_solver_bias_store_record), local load record (specified
with +ntb_solver_bias_load_record), and share record (specified with
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record).
During generation of the merge database using crg, you can use compression to reduce
the size of the merge database.
% crg -dir <dir1> -dir <dir2> -zip <level> -merge <mdir> -report <rpt>
-zip <level>
Compression level: 0 to 9 (default: 0).
0: No compression
1: Fastest compression

9: Best compression
Based on the zip level, the merge output <mdir> is compressed.
To load a cdb compressed with +ntb_solver_bias_zip at runtime or with -zip using the
crg utility, there is no need to specify additional options. ICO automatically decompresses
the coverage database on-the-fly during loading if needed.

Runtime Performance Features
Following are the advantages of this feature:
• Reduces the need for large disk space and/or frequent disk cleaning
• Improves the performance by reducing the disk input/output data
Auto Clean at Runtime
You can reduce the disk footprint by removing the local records from the run directory
using the +ntb_solver_bias_clean=<cleanupLevel> runtime option with various levels
of cleanup for the records created by the runs.
Following is the use model in shared mode:
simv +ntb_solver_bias_clean=<cleanupLevel>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared> …
+ntb_solver_bias_clean=<cleanupLevel>
Cleanup level: 0 to 3 (default: 0).
0: No cleanup
1: Removes local store coverage database
2: Removes local store and local load coverage databases
3: Enables 2 and removes local store cdb failed to be merged. When the store cdb is
not merged to the shared cdb, it is not deleted to allow later merge. You can use the
+ntb_solver_bias_clean=3 runtime option to remove the local store record that failed to
be merged to the shared cdb.
Following is the use model in the non-shared mode:
simv +ntb_solver_bias_clean=<cleanupLevel>
+ntb_solver_bias_clean=<cleanupLevel>
Cleanup level: 0 to 3 (default: 0).
0: No cleanup

Runtime Performance Features
1: Removes store cdb
2: Removes store cdb (no impact on load cdb)
3: Removes store cdb. No impact on load cdb (same as 2).
The record.cdb.diag file is not removed. Use +ntb_solver_bias_diag=0 to
not generate diagnosis file.

Disabling Load Record Overwrite
In the shared mode, the learned information is loaded from the shared record cdb. During
the run, the learned information is accumulated in cdb in memory. Just before the run is
finished, the updated information is saved in a local store cdb and the information is then
pushed into the shared record cdb. For example:
simv +ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_Record>
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<load_Record>
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<store_Record> …
The <load_Record> is required to replay the simulation during the debugging
of failed tests. You must pass <load_Record> generated during the original run
to the +ntb_solver_bias_load_record option of the replay run and add the
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=1 (enables replay mode) to replay the simulation.
If you skip to enable the replay mode, the simulation run overwrites the backup
<load_Record> which was generated during a regression run. If <load_Record> is
overwritten, you may not be able to reproduce simulation behavior.
If <load_Record> already exists, then ICO issues the following error and exits the
simulation:
The distributed backup load record directory
'/remote/…/VCS_TEST/TB/cdb_load'
could not be initialized: File exists.
Please make sure the distributed backup load record directory is
creatable and accessible.
This feature prevents the <load_Record> from getting overwritten when you try to replay
the simulation.

Saving the Load Record Information of All Simulations Running
Serially
You can specify the <loadRecord> location explicitly using the
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<loadRecord> option. By default, it is created
automatically with a name based on test name and random seed in the work directory
specified using the option +ntb_solver_bias_wdir=<wdir> (default work directory is
simv.cst/stimuliDB).
When multiple simulations run in sequence with the same test name and random seed,
each generating and feeding DUT/test configuration information to the next simulation run,
all the <loadRecord> records are created with the same name under work directory at
simulation stage, and therefore gets overwritten. This prevents replay of a specific stage.
To save the load record for all the simulations running serially, ICO renames or
saves (backed up) the existing <loadRecord> instead of overwriting it when it is
specified implicitly using work directory. However, when specified explicitly using
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record, the simulation aborts if there exists a <loadRecord>
specified with +ntb_solver_bias_load_record.
If both +ntb_solver_bias_load_record and +ntb_solver_bias_wdir are
specified, then +ntb_solver_bias_load_record takes precedence.
Case Scenarios:
• Case-1: A note is issued if <loadRecord> already exists and is renamed with suffix
<#>. Following is the sample note:
Note-[CNST-SBDBLRB] Solver bias distributed backup load record
renamed. The existing distributed backup load record directory
'/remote/vgch2rnd/VCS_TEST/REGR/TD.new/newTestCases/loadback/wdir/test
_100.load_record'
is renamed to
'/remote/vgch2rnd/VCS_TEST/REGR/TD.new/newTestCases/loadback/wdir/test
_100.load_record.10'.
• Case-2: A warning message is issued if <loadRecord> already exists and there are
already >= 65336 backups. Following is the sample warning message:
Warning-[CNST-SBDBLRBF] Solver bias distributed backup load record
rename failed
The existing distributed backup load record directory

'/remote/vgch2rnd/VCS_TEST/REGR/TD.new/newTestCases/loadback/wdir/tes
t_100.load_record'
failed to be renamed: Too many existing backups (>= 65536).
That load record directory may get overwritten.

• Case-3: A warning message is issued if <loadRecord> already exists and cannot be
renamed due to any system error. Following is the sample warning message:
Warning-[CNST-SBDBLRBF] Solver bias distributed backup load record
rename failed
The existing distributed backup load record directory
'/remote/vgch2rnd/VCS_TEST/REGR/TD.new/newTestCases/loadback/./simv.c
st/stimuliDB/test_100.load_record'
failed to be renamed: Permission denied.
That load record directory may get overwritten.
If <loadRecord> is specified explicitly with
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record and is existing, then it will not be backed
up. The simulation aborts.
Exiting the Simulation Gracefully when Interrupted With
Terminate Signal
When simulation run is terminated, synchronization locks are not released if the
terminating signal arrives while the locks are held. This does not crash the regression runs
but degrades distributed merging and hence the optimization of ICO.
To address this issue, ICO supports graceful exit when SIGTERM and SIGINT signals
arrive. During exiting, ICO releases any synchronization lock acquired for smooth
functioning of distributed merging.This helps to keep the distributed merging from
degrading. You can run the simulation using timeout as follows:
$timeout -k 10 3600 ./simv <runtime_options>
After 3600s, simv receives SIGTERM. This gives ICO 10s to perform critical tasks (disk IO,
lock release) to finish, after which SIGKILL is sent to kill the application if it has not ended
yet.
Generating Prognosis Report for Prognosis-Aware Autobias
ICO reports prognosis scores in the prognosis.csv file for the prognosis information
computed during runtime. This file is generated along with the other CRG reports.
+ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103
Where, +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103 enables prognosis-aware autobias mode
selection.

These options are enabled only when autobias is enabled.
Use the following command:
% crg -dir cdb_shared -report rpt
The -report rpt option generates the prognosis.csv file. This file has the same format
as generated with the -prognosis option. The only difference is that this prognosis file
contains the prognosis information if the +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103 option is
specified for the autobias runs. Also, not all information is available like regular prognosis
runs to reduce the runtime and memory overhead. Unavailable information is reported as
‘0’ as shown in the following example.
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=./shared +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=103
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name=test

Shared CDB Update Notification
Each run at the end of the simulation updates the shared cdb. This database contains the
merged information of each run. ICO issues a message about the shared cdb update at
the end of the simulation when the distributed merge feature is enabled. This message
includes the path of the ICO database that was written/updated. Following is the sample
message:
Note-[CNST-SBDRM] Solver bias distributed record merged
The distributed shared record
'/remote/check/log/shared_record' is merged with this run data.
If the merge fails due to some resource contention or system failure, then a warning
message is issued. The following is the sample warning message:
Warning-[CNST-SBDRMF] Solver bias distributed record merge failed
The distributed shared record
'/remote/check/log/shared_record' is not merged with this run data.
Please save store record '/remote/check/log/wdir/test_7.store_record' for
a deferred 'auto' merge.

• Deferred ‘auto’ merge indicates that when you run crg later, it is merged
automatically. Note that the shared cdb contains the information that failed to
be merged.
% crg -dir shared_cdb -merge snap_cdb
• If the message contains the keyword ‘manual’ instead of ‘auto’, then you
must provide the location of the store record for merging. If multiple such
store records are failed to be merged, you can use the -f <filelist>
compile option or specify multiple -dir options for each store record that
failed to be merged.
% crg -dir shared_cdb -dir <store_record> -merge snap_cdb
Controlling the Shared CDB

estore
-shared_save_period <sec>
-shared save
Enables backup of shared cdb.
-shared restore
Restores from the backup (must exist).
-shared_save_period <sec>

Takes periodic backup every <sec> seconds (default 0) of the shared cdb. If the value is 0,
the command quits immediately after creating a backup.
• The save option can run only in one process, whereas the regression using
the same shared db can run concurrently with the process running the save
option.
• The restore option can run only in one process, whereas the regression
using the same shared db must notrun concurrently with the process
running the restore option.

Controlling Merging of Class Instances in Repeat Randomization
By default, class instances in repeat randomization are merged. When the covergroups
are declared for each class instance, then the recording and biasing of each
class instance per repeat randomization can improve coverage. You can use the +ntb_solver_bias_inst_merge
+ntb_solver_bias_inst_merge=<0|1> runtime option to control the merging of class
instances in repeat randomization.
+ntb_solver_bias_inst_merge=<0|1>
Allows you to enable or disable the merging of class instances in repeat randomization.
0: Disables the merging of class instances in repeat randomization.
1: Enables the merging of class instances in repeat randomization (default behavior).
Consider the following testcase:
Example 22 test.sv
class foo;
rand bit signed [31:0] x;
constraint con{
x inside {[-550:-400], [400:550]};
}

module tb();
foo f;
integer i;
repeat(5) begin
f = new();
f.randomize();
end
end
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=./shared +ntb_solver_bias_inst_merge=0

Smart Error Detection
You can use the +ntb_solver_bias_enable_opt=105 and 106 runtime options for the
following:
• Automatically enable error detection mode when coverage is disabled
• Prognosis-aware error detection
This feature helps to automatically detect errors when coverage is disabled to speed up
the simulation.
These runtime options allow a test to start wi

detection by analyzing failure history-including unique signatures,
total failures, and failure rates to accelerate error detection through the following two
mechanisms:
• Predictive Bug Hunting: Learns from the past regression runs and applies that
knowledge to stress the observed failure spaces for adjacent failures and to explore
new failure spaces.
• Adaptive Bug Hunting: Uses the new bugs mode to automatically adjust bug
modes (such as bug, bug2, and so on) based on a prescribed methodology as testing
progresses and failure rates stabilize.
This feature helps in early bug detection and coverage convergence, and also
improves verification efficiency.

Use the following runtime options to enable this feature:
• +ntb_solver_bias_mode_strategy=bugs
• +ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex=<regex>
• +ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex_file=<regex_file>
• +ntb_solver_bias_fail_predict=<0-101>
The following is the syntax:
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_strategy=bugs
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record>
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=<0|1|2>
+ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex=<regex>
+ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex_file=<regex_file>
-l <simv.log>
Where:
+ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex=<regex>
Specifies the regular expressions (regex) for identifying failure messages. By default, it
looks for various failure patterns, including common ones such as UVM_ERROR, offending,
and ASSERT FAILED .
You can use ‘|pattern1|pattern2’ if you intend to expand the regex scope to include
the default patterns as well as both pattern1 and pattern2.
You can use ‘pattern1|pattern2’ if you intend to expand the regex scope to include
only pattern1 and pattern2 (and not the default pattern).
+ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex_file=<regex_file>
Specifies a list of regexes, with one entry per line in an external file. If you specify
this option along with +ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex, the regex scope of
+ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex is expanded to include the expressions specified within
the file.
If +ntb_solver_bias_fail_regex=|, then regex scope is expanded to include
the default and the expressions specified in the file.

Identifying and Recording Important Signal Predictors (ISP)
An Important Signal Predictor (ISP) is a random variable that is randomized only once
during a simulation. Such variables often gate large regions of stimulus or coverage
behavior, so capturing their values gives you a compact, high-signal view of the run.
ICO can record ISP data during simulation as a compressed binary file named
record.isp under the store record directory. You can then use the crg command to
translate this file into a readable form (for example, CSV) and to generate an ID map that
links each recorded value back to its source location and variable name. The recorded
data can be used for downstream analysis, debug, and machine-learning flows.
This feature is an addition to the existing ICO flow. It does not change any other ICO
behavior. You enable it through a new set of simv runtime options and access the
recorded data through new crg options.
• Use Model
• Simv Runtime Options
• Include and Exclude File Format

Include and Exclude File Format
The ISP include and exclude files use the same format as other ICO scope-style files (for
example, scope and focus files). Each entry occupies one line in the following format:
file:line:class:var
Where:
• file: Source file name.
• line: Line number of the variable declaration.
• class: Class name in which the variable is declared.
• var: Variable name.
ISP Recording Behavior
ISP records variables that are randomized only once, based on the selected ISP mode.
A variable can be randomized once at t=0 and once again at t>0. In that case, ICO
records the variable when the ISP mode is 1 or 2, but not when the mode is 3 (because
the variable is no longer randomized only once across all time).

The following table summarizes this behavior:
Table 16 ISP Recording Behavior
Variable Behavior isp_mode=1 isp_mode=2 isp_mode=3
Randomized only once at t=0 Recorded Not recorded Recorded
Randomized only once at t>0 Not recorded Recorded Recorded
Randomized once at t=0 and
once at t>0
Recorded Recorded Not recorded
Translating ISP Data Using crg
The record.isp file is a compressed binary file. Use the crg command to translate this
file into a readable format. You can write the translated output to standard output (default)
or to a file.
The following is the syntax:
% crg -isp_in <path_to_record.isp> [-isp_out <output_file>]
[-isp_format <bin|csv>] [-q] [-l <log>]
The following table describes the ISP-related crg options:
Table 17 crg Options for ISP Translation
Option Description
-isp_in <file> Specifies the path to the ISP file to translate.
-isp_out <file> Specifies the output file path. If you omit this option, crg
writes the output to standard output.
-isp_format <bin|csv> Specifies the output format. The default format is bin.
The translated ISP data reports pairs of values where the first field is the 64-bit variable ID
and the second field is the recorded value.
Generating an ID Map for ISP Data
Each ISP record stores a 64-bit variable ID rather than the variable name. Use the -idmap
option with crg to generate a mapping file that links each ID to the corresponding source
location, variable name, and module.
The following is the syntax:
% crg -dir <cdb> -idmap [-work <wdir>]

This command generates <wdir>/idmap.csv based on the specified CDB. If you do not
specify -work, the default work directory is WORK.
The idmap.csv file contains space-separated columns for the following fields:
Table 18 idmap.csv Fields
Field Description
file:line:class:var Source location and variable name.
id 64-bit hexadecimal variable ID.
module Module or package name. If module information is not available,
this field is -.

• line: Line number of the variable declaration.
• class: Class name in which the variable is declared.
• var: Variable name.
ISP Recording Behavior
ISP records variables that are randomized only once, based on the selected ISP mode.
A variable can be randomized once at t=0 and once again at t>0. In that case, ICO
records the variable when the ISP mode is 1 or 2, but not when the mode is 3 (because
the variable is no longer randomized only once across all time).

The following table summarizes this behavior:
Table 16 ISP Recording Behavior
Variable Behavior isp_mode=1 isp_mode=2 isp_mode=3
Randomized only once at t=0 Recorded Not recorded Recorded
Randomized only once at t>0 Not recorded Recorded Recorded
Randomized once at t=0 and
once at t>0
Recorded Recorded Not recorded
Translating ISP Data Using crg
The record.isp file is a compressed binary file. Use the crg command to translate this
file into a readable format. You can write the translated output to standard output (default)
or to a file.
The following is the syntax:
% crg -isp_in <path_to_record.isp> [-isp_out <output_file>]
[-isp_format <bin|csv>] [-q] [-l <log>]
The following table describes the ISP-related crg options:
Table 17 crg Options for ISP Translation
Option Description
-isp_in <file> Specifies the path to the ISP file to translate.
-isp_out <file> Specifies the output file path. If you omit this option, crg
writes the output to standard output.
-isp_format <bin|csv> Specifies the output format. The default format is bin.
The translated ISP data reports pairs of values where the first field is the 64-bit variable ID
and the second field is the recorded value.
Generating an ID Map for ISP Data
Each ISP record stores a 64-bit variable ID rather than the variable name. Use the -idmap
option with crg to generate a mapping file that links each ID to the corresponding source
location, variable name, and module.
The following is the syntax:
% crg -dir <cdb> -idmap [-work <wdir>]

This command generates <wdir>/idmap.csv based on the specified CDB. If you do not
specify -work, the default work directory is WORK.
The idmap.csv file contains space-separated columns for the following fields:
Table 18 idmap.csv Fields
Field Description
file:line:class:var Source location and variable name.
id 64-bit hexadecimal variable ID.
module Module or package name. If module information is not available,
this field is -.
It is recommended to generate the ID map from the shared record CDB so
the output includes mappings for all variables. If you generate the map from a
narrower CDB, the

Limitations
The following is the limitation of this feature:
• ISP supports only variables whose values fit within the range of a signed 64-bit integer.

CSV Text Reports
ICO can generate a text format report equivalent to the HTML report generated by
coverage. The text reports (in csv formats) allow you to enable post-processing scripts
where sorting can be done easily. You can also directly use these reports for exclusion and
purging.
You can use the following option in the crg command line to enable this feature:
-format text
This option generates the following files:
bininst_status.csv, binclass_status.csv, varinst_status.csv,
varclass_status.csv, inst_status.csv, class_status.csv, total_status.csv
% crg -dir <dir> -report <report_dir0> -format <text>
In the following, the format for each of the csv files is explained in detail:
• Format: bininst_status.csv
Following is the format of the bininst_status.csv file:
id file line class var bin freq category rca comment

10@10 test.sv 10 foo x [10:10] 1.00 ILLEGAL - -

Excluding Uncoverable Bins From Reports
When running a TB with ICO, you may encounter some uncovered bins due to user-
specified constraints such as state variable or inlined constraints. To generate meaningful
reports, bins that are not covered due to user-specified constraints can be considered for
exclusion.
You can use the -elfile option in the crg command line to exclude selected uncoverable
bins based on the user-specified constraints in the input bias mode.
The following steps describe the use model:
1. Use the runtime options +ntb_solver_bias_mode=265 and
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path_to_record> during simv using the
following command:
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path_to_record>
+ntb_solver_bias_mode=265
2. Generate the report using the following command:
% crg -dir <dir> -report <report_dir0> -format text
3. Keep the lines with UNCOVERED bins from the report_dir0/bininst_status.csv file
and save it in a file (for example, excl0.txt).
4. Generate the exclusion report using the following command:
% crg -dir <dir> -report <report_dir1> -format text -elfile
<excl0.txt>

or,
% crg -dir <dir1> -dir <dir2> -merge <mdir> -report <report_dir1>
-format text -elfile <excl0.txt>
The report_dir1 contains the excluded UNCOVERED bins, which are specified in the file
excl0.txt with potentially improved coverage and diversity scores.
-elfile <elFile>
Exclude all the bins specified in the file. For example, you can use the text report file
bininst_status.csv to keep the lines that you want to exclude.
-merge <mdir>
If one or more database directories are specified, this option creates a merged database
in the output directory merge_dir after optional operations such as -purge, -reset_tag,
-purge_untag, and -zip.
Example to exclude all uncovered bins
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode=1 +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record0
% crg -dir record0 -report crgReport0 -format text
% grep -v UNCOVERED ./crgReport0/bininst_status.csv > excl0.txt// to
exclude all UNCOVERED bins from the report.
% crg -dir record0 -report crgReport1 -format html -elfile excl0.txt
Exclusion Report
In the HTML report, a separate column for exclusion and category “Excluded” is included,
as shown in Figure 41. The red rectangle shows the additional column corresponding to
exclusion.
