Calculation of Glitch Delay and Pulse Width:
By default, the glitch delay and pulse width are supported as a fraction of the clock cycle.
VCS-SBF Glitch Delay and Pulse Width by Clock Period
The following switch defines the fraction of clock cycle after which a glitch check should be
performed:
-sdc= glcapdel:<N(in float)>
-sdc=glcapdel:.3
clk_period = 10 ns
The glitch check is performed at the destination after 3 ns of the source change.

The following switch defines the fraction of clock period for which a glitch is inserted in the
destination:
-sdc= glxdelta:<N(in float)>
Ex: -sdc=glxdelta:.3
Clk_period = 10ns
Glitch is inserted for 3ns.
Virtual clocks are also supported in VCS-SBF, Glitch violation is as per the time
period of a virtual clock.
The VCS-SBF Clock Glitch identifies all potential post-simulation clock glitches during
the RTL-level phase. The goal is to inject glitches in RTL simulation to cause simulation
failures, enabling designers to detect and address clock glitch circuits earlier in the design
process.
• Detects all possible post-simulation clock glitches during RTL simulation.
• Ensures glitches are injected and cause simulation failures, so issues are not missed.
• Avoids injecting false glitches that could cause incorrect simulation failures.
Clock glitch check in VC Static
The following scenario explains how to detect glitches in a clock path when the select pin
of a multiplexer (MUX) changes, such as during clock mode selection.

Figure 15 Example 1
VC Static generates the following glitch command for all clock merging cases:
SETUP_SYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*,
SETUP_ASYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*
set_glitch_path -from <sig_list> -to <gate_output> -type clock
Here,
sig_list: All first-level RTL signals in the fan-in of the MUX select pin.
gate_output: Output of the MUX. If the MUX output is an internal net, the first RTL net in
the fanout is reported.
• If async or sync clock overlap occurs on a combinational gate other than a
MUX, VC Static does not generate a set_glitch_path command for that
overlap.
Generated SDC Example:
Glitch paths are generated at the VC Static stage, and the SDC includes an
extra field to mark it as a clock path glitch:
set_glitch_path -from {d} -to {clk_mux1/O} -to_clock {clk} -type
clock

Glitch Identification in VCS SBF
When the select pin toggles, X propagates to the MUX output following the X-propagation
mechanism. A glitch violation is reported at the MUX output. The gli

• A new runtime switch -sdc=glclkdel:<N> is added, where N is the fraction
of the clock period for which the glitch needs to be injected at mux output.
• The use of -sdc=glxdelta:<N> for clock glitches has been eliminated, as
long-duration delay injection is not needed for propagation to flops.
• X propagation from select to mux output and from mux output to downward
hierarchy follows the Xprop mechanism.
• Verdi marking on mux output is done for the entire -sdc=glclkdel:<N>
duration, regardless of input changes to the mux.
• Clock mux output should not be given as a P2P glitch destination; an error is
reported if the input clocks to this mux, are defined in SDC.
• Only Boolean changes ( 0→1, 1→0) in mux select line are considered for clock
glitch.
• If select changes while mux output is already X, no violation or glitch
injection is reported.
• For UDPs, penultimate module pins going into the UDP instance are
dumped from VC Static.
• Multiplexer outputs have multiple drivers.
• The -sdc=no_x runtime option has no impact on clock glitch paths.
• MDANETs and MDAs as select or mux output are not currently supported.
• For UDP muxes, the X injection time at mux output is for -sdc=glclkdel
value, regardless of any input/select changes.
• Both destination and source of set_glitch_path command should be
present in the same module.

Limiting Glitch Checks on Specific Clock Paths
Figure 18 Limiting Glitch Checks on Specific Clock Paths
To limit glitch detection to specific clock paths going to a particular clock pin, use the
following command in SDC file given as input to VC Static:
set_point2point_glitch -to [get_pins <flop_name>/CP] -type clock
set_point2point_glitch -to [get_pins q_reg/CP] -type clock
The above command limits the glitch checks on clock paths ending at the destination
q_reg/CP.
• With -type clock , only CP pin of the endpoint is supported in
set_point2point_glitch command.
• Other options, except -through <cells> are not supported and are
reported for sanity.
You can also limit glitch checks on clock paths when clock merging happens inside a
specific cell or module. Use the following command in SDC file given as input to VC Static
to specify the cell or module where the clock merging occurs. The -through objects refers
to the muxes involved in the violation
set_point2point_glitch -through [get_cells -hier Module|LibCell] -type
clock

If you give following input to VC Static:
set_point2point_glitch -through [get_cells clk_mux1] -type clock
Then VC Static tool generates the following command:
set_glitch_path -from d2 -to clk_mux1/O -type clock
• When using -type clock with set_point2point_glitch command, only
cells are allowed with the -throughoption. Other values with -through are
not supported.
• If you use both -toand -through options in set_point2point_glitch
command, the tool checks only the paths that satisfy both conditions.
To exclude certain cells from clock glitch checking, use the following command:
configure_glitch_free_cells –path_type CLOCK –ignore_instances
<cell_name>
You must exclude the cell cell_name from clock glitch checking.
If you provide the following input to VC Static:
configure_glitch_free_cells –path_type CLOCK –ignore_instances
<clk_gfree_mux >
VC Static tool generates the following commands:
set_glitch_path -from d2 -to clk_mux1/O -type clock
set_glitch_path -from d3 -to clk_rtlc/O -type clock

Support for -sdc=glmaxdel Option in P2P Glitch Multi-Clock
Scenarios
In VCS, when a point-to-point (p2p) glitch command references multiple clocks, the tool
must select a clock period to compute the glitch delay for checking and injection. By
default, VCS selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock, ensuring conservative glitch
detection. However, for certain validation scenarios—such as worst-case or maximum-
delay analysis—it is desirable to use the largest-period (slowest) clock instead.
The -sdc=glmaxdel simulation-time option changes the clock selection rule for p2p
glitch commands referencing multiple clocks.
When a p2p glitch command uses more than one clock, the tool must choose one clock
period to calculate the glitch delay for checking and injection.
Clock Selection Behavior
• Default Behavior:
◦ The tool selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this period.
◦ No user action required.
• Behavior with -sdc=glmaxdel option:
◦ The tool selects the largest-period clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this maximum period.
◦ Enable this behavior by passing -sdc=glmaxdel at simulation time.

The corruption mechanism follows a sticky approach. In sticky corruption,
each P2P glitch node receives its own independent, deterministic corruption
lifetime. As a result, a fault injected at a node remains visible for its designated
duration, rather than being prematurely cleared or overwritten when logic
paths reconverge or when other nodes are evaluated later in the same time
slice. Corruption is cleared only by a genuine design-driven value change after
injection or when the glxdelta timeout expires.

Top Down Flow in SOC Verification
The top-down flow in SoC verification is a hierarchical approach that improves
performance by excluding paths fully contained within validated IPs during SoC-level
verification. This method prevents redundant validation of IP constraints, saving time and
effort.
In the following example, path5 is entirely within an IP: therefore, it can be excluded from
top-level validation.
Use a configuration file to define IPs as a glassbox, which removes self-contained paths
from SoC-level validation. You can enable the top-down flow for excluding IP-contained
paths during SoC verification. This ensures that all the IP paths, including additional SoC-
level paths, are verified.

• Use the +optconfigfile option to specify such IPs during compilation to include the
file.
Example command: +optconfigfile+<filename>.cfg [Compile Phase]
• When you glassbox an IP by using {sdcGlassboxIp} in the sdc_module.cfg
configuration file, all timing paths that are fully contained within the IP are excluded
from SoC-level validation.
The following is a sample command line:
vcs -sverilog -full64 test.v tb.v -sdc=test.sdc,current_design:top -l
comp.log +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
Both module and instance level exclusions are supported.
• Example configuration File for module-level exclusion:
% +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
sdc_module.cfg
instance {Top.IP1} {sdcGlassboxIp}
• Example configuration File for instance-level exclusion:
% +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
sdc_module.cfg
module {IP1} {sdcGlassboxIp}
All excluded points are dumped in the mcpLogs/sdc_config_diag.txt log file. All paths
inside the IPs are excluded for the IPs specified in the sdc_module.cfg file.
1. The -sdc=only_excluded_path option considers and reports only the paths that
are fully contained within the IPs specified in the configuration file. It is used to report
excluded paths.
2. The -sdc=report_excluded_cmds option reports, in the SDC summary file, both
partially excluded and fully excluded SDC commands.
Comparing IP and SoC Equivalence Check
Occasionally, few constraints are incorporated at the SoC level to account for additional IP
paths that were not present during the IP level verification. This flow helps to compare self-
contained IP paths between IP-level verification and SoC-level verification.
This Unified Report Generator (URG) is a coverage-based solution.

Chapter 7: Top Down Flow in SOC Verification

Follow these steps to perform the equivalence check:
1. Validate IP constraints: Run IP-level verification and generate coverage databases
(simv.vdb) for each IP.
2. Merge Coverage Databases: Use the URG tool to merge coverage databases for all
IPs.
Example command: urg -dir ip1.vdb ip2.vdb -dbname merged.vdb -format
text -dump full_exclusions -show sdcpath
3. Generate Excluded Paths at SoC Level: Mark the IPs as glassboxes during the
SoC-level verification and generate soc_ex.vdb SoC coverage database using the
-sdc=only_excluded_path option.
4. Create Mapping File: Generate map.txt file to map IP paths to the respective SoC
paths.
5. Perform Coverage Analysis: Use the URG tool to compare IP and SoC paths, including
additional paths at the SoC level.
Example command: urg -dir soc_ex.vdb merged.vdb -mapfile map.txt -log
urg.log -format text -sdc level 3 -show sdcpath

For a given module, VCS enables you to report the combined score of specific instances
of the root module in the same location. The list of specific instances that need to be
combined is specified in modtreefile itself.
To enable this feature, use the -modtreefile option as follows:
urg -dir simv.vdb -modtreefile <modtreefile.txt>
or
verdi -cov -covdir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -modtreefile <modtreefile.txt>
where, <modtreefile.txt> contains a module name and the list of all its instances that
need to be merged. For example, the content of <modtreefile.txt> might be as follows:
MODULE: M //modfile module M
INSTANCES: T.X.M1, T.X.M2
//Instances to be combined for the module M
INSTANCES: T.Y.M1, T.Y.M2
//Instances to be combined for the module M
MODULE: N //modfile module N
INSTANCES: A.B.N1, A.B.N2
//Instances to be combined for the module N
MODULE: P //modfile module P
//All its instance

The -modtreefile option can be used to generate a merged VDB without a report using
the following command:
urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -dbname merged -modtreefile mod.txt
-noreport
urg -dir merged.vdb

urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -dbname merged -modtreefile mod.txt
-noreport
verdi -covdir merged.vdb …
The above command can also be written as follows:
urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -dbname merged -noreport
urg -dir merged.vdb -modtreefile mod.txt …

or

urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb -dbname merged -noreport
verdi -covdir merged.vdb -modtreefile mf.txt

Error Handling
VCS skips modtreefile merging and reports syntax errors if the following scenarios are
encountered:
• Keywords other than MODULE and INSTANCES are used in the modtreefile.
• The keyword INSTANCES is used without the keyword MODULE.
• Module name is not specified after the keyword MODULE.
VCS skips modtreefile merging and reports warnings if the following scenarios are
encountered:
• Module name specified with MODULE is not found in the VDB.
• Instance name specified with INSTANCES is not found in the VDB.
Exclusions
When an exclusion is applied on a modtreefile merged instance, then the exclusion
is propagated to all the instances with which this instance got merged. For example,
consider the following configuration file, cfg.txt:
MODULE: M
INSTANCES: T.X.M1, T.X.M2
INSTANCES: T.Y.M1, T.Y.M2
If objects in T.X.M1 and T.Y.M2 are excluded, then the same object is excluded in the other

Support for LRM-Compliant Escaped Identifiers
Similarly, as per modtreefile merge rules, any exclusion on:
• T.X.M1.P1 is propagated to T.X.M2.P1 and vice versa
• T.X.M1.P2 is propagated to T.X.M2.P2 and vice versa
• T.Y.M1.P1 is propagated to T.Y.M2.P1 and vice versa
• T.Y.M1.P2 is propagated to T.Y.M2.P2 and vice versa
Following are the limitations specific to this feature:
• Wildcard is not supported with the keywords MODULE and INSTANCES.
• A merged VDB created with -modtreefile having instance configurations cannot be
reverted to being a VDB with non-modtreefile scores. The merging of instance data
cannot be undone.

Coverage Computation for Glitch
VCS computes coverage per glitch assertion. For an n-source glitch, multiple (n) glitch
paths are generated.
For each glitch assertion, VCS monitors the following coverage metrics for each source:
• Count of toggle for each source
• Count of toggle of each source when any other source is also toggled
• Status (Inactive, Active, Violating)

• Count of Glitch 010 and Glitch 101
Coverage computation is performed only for the probable glitch cases
(multiple sources change, destination does not change.)

Coverage Computation for SDC
Use the VCS
-sdc
-cm sdc switch at compile time to enable coverage computation for SDC. Its
syntax is as follows:
% vcs
-cm sdc
-cm sdc -sdc=<sdc_file>, current_design:<top_design>
-cm sdc is used to enable coverage for SDC.
-sdc=current_design:<top_design> : This option can be specified at the command line
or in an SDC file.
<sdc_file> is the name of an SDC file.
Consider the following code snippet that shows signal connections from ff1-->ff3:
Example 28 SDC Coverage
module mult2x(input[3:0] in, input clk, input clk2, output[3:0] out,
input rst);
reg[3:0] ff1,ff2,ff3;
wire[3:0] mout;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff1 <= 0;
else ff1 <= in;
assign mout = ff1*ff1;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff3 <= 0;
else ff3 <= mout;
always @(posedge clk2 or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff2 <= 0;
else ff2 <= ff3;
assign out = ff2;
The sample content of the .sdc file is shown in Example 29:
Example 29 test.sdc
create_clock -period 20 -name sys_clk [get_ports clk]
create_clock -period 60 -name sys_clk2 [get_ports clk2]
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from ff1* -to ff3*
set_clock_group -asynchronous -group sys_clk -group sys_clk2
In the example, create_clock, set_multicycle_path, and set_clock_group are SDC
commands. SDC commands are the set of rules defined inside the .sdc file.

The compile time and runtime commands for Example 28 are as follows:
%vcs -lca -sverilog -kdb +vcs+fsdbon -full64 tb.v dut.v -cm
sdc -sdc=test.sdc, current_design:mult2x, print_violation,
verify_clock_group
%simv -sdc=max_destination_violation:10000 -cm sdc
The URG report of this example is shown in Figure 42.
Merging
VCS enables you to create a report by merging the paths from multiple simulation runs.
The simulation data can be merged whether it was produced from the same compilation or
from different compilations. Here is the reporting command for SDC:
%urg -show sdcpath -dir simv1.vdb [simv2.vdb] -format text
It is possible to give one or more VDB arguments to the -dir option.
Example 30 demo.v
module mult2x(input[1:0] in, input clk, output[1:0] out, input
rst);

assign out = ff2;
Here is the .sdc file for Example 30:
current_design mult2x
create_clock -period 20 -name sys_clk [get_ports clk]
set_multicycle_path 3 -from ff1* -to ff2*
In the example, current_design, create_clock, and set_multicycle_path are SDC
commands.

The URG report for SDC coverage report covers the following:
• Total paths relevant for an SDC command
• Categorization of the paths per “Violating”, “Inactive”, “Active”
• Details of the paths (start and end point)

Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
This feature has the following limitation:
• The urg -dbname command of union merge is not supported for SDC.
Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
VCS supports monitoring Finite-State Machine (FSM) coverage for FSMs modeled in
multi-dimensional arrays (MDAs), that is, an array of arrays or an array of arrays of arrays.
• URG Report
• Support for Arrays With Constant Index Value
• Support for Arrays With Unknown Index Values
To monitor FSM coverage for MDAs, use the -cm_fsmopt mda switch at compile time as
vcs
-cm fsm
-cm fsm
-cm_fsmopt
-cm_fsmopt mda
By default, VCS extracts 1000 FSMs from a multi-dimensional array for coverage
computation. To raise this limit, use the -cm_fsm_limit switch at compile time as follows:
vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsmopt mda -cm_fsm_limit 2000
VCS skips the FSMs that are over the limit and displays the following warning message:
Warning-[VCM-FSMMDAMAX] Array of FSMs is too large
file.v, 100
The array 'mybigmda' may be a collection of finite-state
machines, but it contains 6400 elements, which is above the
maximum number 1000 that VCS will create for a single array.
To avoid significant compile-time and runtime overhead, no
FSMs based on this 'mybigmda' will be monitored for coverage.

Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
Consider the following example of an array of arrays of FSMs:
Example 31 An Array of Arrays of FSMs:
typedef enum logic [1:0] {STATE_0 = 2'd0,
STATE_1 = 2'd1,
STATE_2 = 2'd2,
STATE_3 = 2'd3
} fsm_enum_e;

fsm_enum_e [1:0][7:0] cur_st, nxt_st;

for (genvar ii=0;ii<2;ii++) begin
for (genvar jj=0;jj<8;jj++) begin
always_comb begin
case(cur_st[ii][jj])
STATE_0: nxt_st[ii][jj] = sel? STATE_2 : STATE_1;
STATE_1: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_2;
STATE_2: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_3;
STATE_3: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_0;
endcase
end
always @ (posedge clk or negedge rstb) begin
if (!rstb) begin
cur_st[ii][jj] <= STATE_0;
end else begin
cur_st[ii][jj] <= nxt_st[ii][jj];
end
end
end
end
In this example, nested generate loops are used to specify the FSM logic that applies to
all FSMs in the array of arrays of type fsm_enum_e. When the -cm_fsmopt mda switch is
given at compile time, VCS recognizes that this is an array of arrays of FSMs, one each
for cur_st[0][0], cur_st[0][1],, cur_st[0][7]. All of the FSMs have the same list

can be used to generate a merged VDB with a report using the
following command:
urg -dir comp.vdb run*.vdb -modtreefile mod.txt -dbname merged
If a merged VDB is created with the -modtreefile option, the merged VDB saves the
merged coverage scores.
Merged VDBs created with -modtreefile cannot be merged with VDBs that are not
created with -modtreefile. Merged VDBs created with -modtreefile can be combined
if the modtreefile.txt file contains the same list of modules in the same order.

Parameterized Shapes
The instances that belong to the same parameterized versions are merged along with their
sub-hierarchies. However, if there is a mismatch in parameterized shapes of the instances
of a module, the instances are not merged. For example, consider the following figure in
which M1 and M2 are instances of the module mid. The module mid is provided as the input
in the modtreefile.txt file:
Figure 45 Parameterized Shapes
If T1.M1 has a different parameterized shape than T2.M1, then T1.M1 is not merged with
T2.M1. Also, the hierarchies below T1.M1 are not merged with those of T2.M1.

If the metric shape of an instance of a module is not same to another instance
of the module, then both the instances are not merged.
Exclusion Propagation
If exclusions are applied to an object in one instance of a module, its exclusions propagate
to all of its sibling instances. For example, consider three objects, T.M1.P1, T.M2.P1, and
T.X.M1.P1. If T.M2.P1 is excluded, then the exclusion is automatically applied to T.M1.P1
and T.X.M1.P1, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 46 Exclusion Propagation
When an exclusion in a moduletree-merged region is applied, the exclusion is copied
as a separate exclusion object for each instance. A single exclusion is saved that is
automatically propagated to the matching instances when the exclude file is loaded.

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
VCS enables you to define a single hierarchical configuration file to control monitoring of
coverage for both code and assertion coverage. To use this feature, specify your hier file
to the -cm_hier switch (compile time) or the -hier switch (URG) as normal, and add the
-cm_common_hier switch to enable the common hier mode.
For more details on this switch, see the following sections:
• Related Features

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
To specify hierarchical exclusions at compile time, use the following command:
vcs -cm_hier <config_file> -cm_common_hier
-cm line+cond+tgl+fsm+branch+assert
To specify hierarchical exclusions at report time, use the following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -hier <config_file> -cm_common_hier
Consider the following configuration file, config.txt that excludes a module, kp_fsm:
-module kp_fsm

coverage are reported for kp_fsm, as shown in the following figure:
When -cm_common_hier is used with -cm_hier at compile time, both code coverage
and assertion coverage are excluded for kp_fsm, therefore, kp_fsm is not shown in the
following URG report:

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
Related Features
Few important points for consideration:
1. If -cm_hier, -cm_assert_hier, and -cm_common_hier are used at compile time,
-cm_common_hier discards -cm_assert_hier but excludes assertion coverage, as
-cm_hier with -cm_common_hier exclude both code and assertion coverage.
2. There is no change in the existing behavior of -cm_hier or -cm_assert_hier when
they are used separately at compile time.
3. In the unified -cm_common_hier flow, a -tree directive accepts only a hierarchy name
for excluding all assertions of the hierarchy. In the -cm_assert_hier flow, a -tree
directive accepts both a hierarchy name and an assert name. Such assertions cannot
be excluded using the -tree directive in the -cm_common_hier flow. For example, the
following assertion exclusion is not valid in the -cm_common_hier flow:
-tree top.m1.A1
where, A1 is an assertion under the instance, m1.
Alternatively, use an -assert directive to exclude a specific assertion by specifying its
hierarchy and assert name. For example, the following assertion exclusion is valid if
used with -assert:
-assert top.m1.A1
For more details on -assert, see -assert <assertion_name> or
-assert <assertion_hierarchical_name> in the Coverage Technology Reference
4. All directives, such as -module and -moduletree, in the unified hierarchical file are
supported for assertion coverage.
5. Assertions can be excluded or including at report time.
6. Metric-specific rules with begin-end can be applied to assertion coverage.

Excluding Generic Values for Coverage
Excluding Generic Values for Coverage
When generic values are used in conditional expressions, some combinations of values
tracked by VCS for condition coverage may not be possible to cover. You can direct VCS
to try to automatically exclude such condition vectors from coverage monitoring using the
-cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch, as follows:
vcs -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics
Note that the VDBs generated with the -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch are
not merge-compatible with the VDBs generated without this switch.
• URG Report
Consider the following code snippet from a module, mod:
OUT1 <= '1' when (((IN1 = tmp_sig0) and (data_width = 64)) or ((IN1 =
tmp_sig1) and (data_width = 32))) else '0';
end behave;

with the two different generic maps as shown in Table 2.

Coverage merging by default uses a "base" and "input" merging model. The first VDB
specified is the base, or reference VDB, and all other VDBs are called "input" VDBs. In
this flow, when a module's coverage objects are different in an input VDB than in the
base VDB, the coverage data from that input VDB for that module cannot be merged
and is discarded. The -flex_merge code_union switch enables URG to support a flow
where coverage from both the base and input VDBs are combined for a module, even if
the objects are different, as long as the source code itself has not changed. This section
describes how this works.
This flow requires that your merging flow be done in two steps:
1. Merge all of the simulation VDBs from the same design configuration together.
2. Use the -flex_merge code _union switch to merge those merged VDBs.
For example, after the merged VDB is created for each configuration, the merged VDBs
are union merged at reporting time using the -flex_merge code_union switch as follows:
urg -dir simv_base.vdb simv_input.vdb -format both -flex_merge code_union
This section explains the rules used for code coverage union merge.
• Only designs whose source code has not changed can be union merged. This means
differences must arise only from `ifdef and for- and if-generate statements in the
design, not from file edits. If the source file for a module is edited in an input VDB, its
coverage data is merged against the base VDB using the default merging rules.
• Only designs compiled with the same coverage options can be union merged.
At a high level, union merge for code coverage follows these rules:
• Regions (modules and instances) whose shapes are the same in the base and input
designs are merged normally on a metric-by-metric basis. Regions that exist in the
input VDB but not in the base VDB are included in the merged VDB. Regions that
exist in the base VDB but not in the input VDB are not affected by the merge, but are
included in the merged VDB. For details, see Region-Level Merging.
• Coverage data is merged at an object-by-object level from the input VDB to the base
VDB. Even objects that are present only in the input VDB are included in the merged
VDB. For details, see Object-Level Merging.
Region-Level Merging
Using code coverage union merge, even if an instance or a module has a different shape
in the input VDB than in the base VDB, the coverage collected for that instance or module
in the input VDB is included in the merged VDB, as described below. If an instance in the

input VDB exists in the base VDB, the data for the instance in the input VDB is merged
with the data for the instance in the base VDB.
Regions whose shapes are the same in the base and input designs are merged. If a
region's shape is different in the input design than in the base design, the data from the
input design that exists in the base design is merged. Similarly, if a region exists in the
input design that does not exist in the base design, its coverage data is included in the
merged report. For example, consider the following table that shows the input VDB has a
different shape than the base VDB due to different parameters:
Base VDB (p == 4) Input VDB (p == 2) Merged Result
reg a;
reg [7:0] b;
reg [p-1:0] c;

reg d;
reg a;
reg [3:0] b;
reg [p-1:0] c;

wire d;
reg a;
reg [7:0] b;
reg [3:0] c;

reg d;
wire d;
In this example, reg a, reg[3:0] b, and reg[1:0] c exist in both the base VDB and
the input VDB, therefore, these are merged from both the VDBs and are available in the
merged VDB.
reg[7:4] b, reg[3:2] c, and reg d exist only in the base VDB and are included in the
merged VDB.
wire d exists only in the input VDB and is included in the merged VDB.
Note this is an example where union merge can produce designs that are not legal Verilog
or VHDL, but that represent the union of the two configurations.
Object-Level Merging
VCS supports merging data at an object-by-object level from the input VDB to the base
VDB design. Objects that are present only in the input VDB and not in the base VDB are
included in the merged VDB.
Note that if the design source code is changed or is compiled with different coverage
options, merging is not supported. For example, if one VDB was compiled with -cm cond ,
but another was compiled with -cm cond -cm_cond allops , the coverage data from the
two VDBs cannot be merged.

Object-level merging has the following rules:
• If the checksums and signatures of an object in the input VDB are the same as that of
an object in the base VDB, their coverage data is merged.
• If the object exists only in the input VDB, then the object is included in the merged
VDB.
• If the hierarchical path of an instance is in the input VDB but not in the base VDB, then
the coverage data for the instance is included in the merged VDB.
Generates and ifdef Directives
This section explains how union merging works in the presence of the following constructs:
• Generate Loop
• If Generate
• Ifdef and Other Compiler Directives

Generate loops are unrolled to produce a separate iteration of the generate body for each
specified value of genvar. When the unrolled iterations are different in the input and base
VDBs, union merge can still combine the data.
Any iteration from the input VDB is combined with the corresponding iteration in the
base VDB. If an iteration exists only in the input VDB, it is included in the merged VDB.

Plan-Based Grading
A test run is a single execution of simulation. Test runs might be run with different random
seeds, with different input stimulus, or even with different testbench code.
Plan-based grading is the process of accessing the coverage impact of each test run on
a Verification plan or on specific features in the plan. Each feature in a Verification plan
might measure one or more coverage targets. Across a full suite of test runs, some of
those coverage targets might be covered. Plan-based grading computes a minimized set
of test runs for the coverage targets in each feature in the Verification plan that cover all
coverage targets in the features.
To use plan-driven grading, you need a verification plan in an .hvp format and a coverage
database containing the generated coverage data for all the test runs to be graded. Plan-
driven grading annotates the plan from the coverage database and targets the coverage
targets specific in the specified feature. It then produces a list of tests in order for each
feature that measures coverage and for the overall plan.
To enable plan-based grading, use the -grade plangrade switch with URG as follows:
%urg -plan <plan_file> -grade plangrade
For details about grading features, see Chapter, "Grading Tests for Coverage" in the
Coverage Technology User Guide.

Plan-Based Grading
• Managing Feature Grading in Plan-Based Grading
• URG Report
Managing Feature Grading in Plan-Based Grading
By default, the Unified Report Generator (URG) grades tests for each feature individually
and for the entire plan collectively. It results in separate best-first lists of tests for each
feature and an overall list for the plan. These lists are displayed in the feature pages and
the plan-level report files (plan.planname.txt and plan.planname.html).
However, by using the planonly grading suboption, you can suppress feature-level
grading and get only the test list for the plan as a whole. This feature is useful when you
want to focus only on the overall plan grading without the additional granularity of feature-
level grading.
To suppress the feature-level grading in URG reports, use the following option:
% urg -grade planonly …
The plan-level test list is generated in the plan.planname.txt and plan.planname.html
files.

The "real" type in SystemVerilog represents a floating point value equivalent to a double
in the C programming language. Floating point representations are inherently imprecise;
comparing "real" numbers in SystemVerilog is always an approximation. Therefore, to
compare real values and expressions in covergroups, VCS converts real values into
integer values. This comparison is done to a precision automatically determined b y VCS.
VCS matches a coverbin with a given sampled real value if the sampled value matches
the declared bounds of the coverbin to the precision value. For example, consider the
following bin:
bin bin_a = {[0.4:0.5]};
A real value, say 0.5, matches the bin_a bin if it falls within the range (0.4:0.5). As
0.500000 falls in the declared bound, the bin records a hit. However, a value of 0.399999
or 0.500001 does not match this bin.

Ignore and Illegal Bins

VCS allows you to mark a set of real values associated with a coverpoint as ignore or
illegal. All values associated with ignore and illegal bins are excluded from coverage
computation in the following way:
• If the complete range of a regular bin falls in the range of an ignore or illegal bin, then
VCS does not compute coverage of the regular bin.
• If a partial range of a regular bin falls in the range of an ignore or illegal bin, then the
partial range of the regular bin is excluded from
coverage computation
coverage computation.
For example, consider the following two discrete coverpoint definitions:
coverpoint a
{
bins ab[4] = {[1.4 : 1.8]};
ignore_bins ig = { [1.5 : 1.55] };
}
coverpoint b
{
bins bb[4] = {[1.4 : 1.8]};
ignore_bins ig = { [1.5 : 1.6] };
}

The following are the Echo features:
• Support for Procedural Sampling

Support for Procedural Sampling
Echo analyzes procedural context to find targetable coverpoints. Echo supports the
following two aspects of procedural sampling:
• Sampling a non-random variable that is assigned with a targetable random variable.
Echo targets a non-random coverpoint when the non-random variable is assigned with
an expression of random variables.
• Randomizing a sibling class of sampled variables. At runtime, Echo collects targetable
holes from the sibling classes. Echo currently supports only one level of inheritance.
Note that all the variables involved in the expression of a coverpoint must be inherited
from the targeted base class.

Merging of Identical VDBs
When you specify the flex_merge code_union option, VCS Coverage detects the VDBs
that have identical structural constructs and automatically merges them using the basic
merge algorithm. The VDBs with different structural constructs are merged using the
flex_merge code_union option.

Precomputed Scores Mode
The feature is currently under the switch -smart_merge.
The following example has VDBs with identical structural constructs and a different
structural construct.
urg -dir base.vdb/ input0.vdb/ input1.vdb/ input2.vdb/ -format text
-flex_merge code_union -lca
The base, input0, and input2 are identical structural constructs and are merged using
the basic merge algorithm. The input1 is a different structural construct and is merged
using the flex_merge code_union with the default merged VDBs.
The following is the limitation of smart merging of identical VDBs:
• Intermediate VDB names are visible in the reports and warning messages for some of
the usages
Precomputed Scores Mode
When creating a merged coverage database (VDB), you can direct URG to precompute
scores at the region level. This can significantly speed up Verdi startup time for larger
designs.
URG Use Model
To use the precomputed scores mode, add the -dbname_opt precomputescores option
to your URG command line when creating a merged VDB, as shown below:
$VCS_HOME/bin/urg -dbname_opt precomputescores -dbname
<new_database_path> -dir <old_database_path>
$VCS_HOME/bin/urg -dbname_opt precomputescores -dbname simv_lazy.vdb -dir
simv.vdb
This option precomputes the region scores and saves them in the VDB so they can be
quickly loaded later.

UCAPI Use Model
To save the precomputed scores into the merged VDB, use the covdbPrecomputeScores
UCAPI configuration before calling covdb_save from your application, as shown below:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbPrecomputeScores, "true");
covdb_save(designHdl,db_name);
After the merged VDB is generated, the precomputed scores can be used to generate
results with the covdbLazyLoading UCAPI configuration, as shown below:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbLazyLoading, "true");
The following example shows how to load a merged VDB with UCAPI in the precomputed
scores mode:
covdb_qualified_configure(designHdl, covdbLazyLoading, "true");
covdb_save(designHdl,db_name);
covdbHandle designH = covdb_load(covdbDesign, NULL,"merged.vdb");
covdbHandle testH = covdb_load(covdbTest, design,"simv/test");
If the precomputed scores mode is disabled, the normal loading behavior persists.
Updates in Verdi
To use the precomputed scores mode in Verdi after creating a merged VDB with
precomputed scores, use the following command:
verdi –cov –covdir merge.vdb -lazy_load
When you use the -lazy_load option, Verdi starts up faster and allows you to browse top-
level scores without the overhead of loading and computing all of the det

Differences Between Real and Integral Ranges
• Integral Ranges: [1:4] covers discrete values: 1, 2, 3, 4.
• Real Ranges: [1.0:4.0] covers all real values between 1.0 and 4.0, not just discrete
points.
When partitioning real ranges into bins, each bin represents an interval. The last bin is
inclusive of its high value.
Fixed Array Bin
For a fixed number of bins, declared as binname[N], bin names range from binname[0]
through binname[N-1]. The number of items to be distributed is the sum of the number
of intervals of the specified ranges and the number of individual values. If the number of
bins is smaller than the specified number of items, then the items are uniformly distributed
among the specified bins.
If the number of items is not evenly divisible by the number of bins, then the last bin
includes the remaining items. Duplicate items are retained; thus, the same value or
interval can be assigned to multiple bins. Consider the following code, using the default
real interval of 1.0:
bins fixed[4] = {[1.0:4.0], [2.0:5.0], 1.0, 4.0, 7.0};
This example has six intervals: [1.0:2.0), [2.0:3.0), [3.0:4.0], [2.0:3.0), [3.0:4.0), [4.0:5.0],
and three values.
Number of items = 9, number of bins = 4; therefore, number of items per bin = 9/4 = 2.
The items are distributed as follows: <[1.0:2.0), [2.0:3.0)>, <[3.0:4.0], [2.0:3.0)>, <[3.0:4.0),
[4.0:5.0]>, <1.0, 4.0, 7.0>.
If the number of bins exceeds the number of items, then some of the bins are empty. For
example:
bins fixed[5] = {[1.0:3.0], 7.0};

In the above example, number of items = 3 and number of bins = 5; therefore, number of
items per bin = 1. The 3 items are distributed as follows: <[1.0:2.0)>, <[2.0:3.0]>, <7.0>, <
>, < >. Note the empty fourth and fifth bins.
In this case, VCS resizes the array bin to 3 and issues the following runtime warning:
Warning-[FCIABS] Invalid array bin size
test.sv, 4
top, "top::cg"
Number of bins 5 is greater than total number of states 3 in the bin
‘fixed’ of
coverpoint cp in covergroup top::cg. This bin will be resized to 3
bins.
Covergroup instance: inst
Design hierarchy: top
VCS does not report empty bins. This behavior is the same as what VCS does for integral
coverpoint fixed-size array bins.
Default Bin on Real
A default bin for real expressions does not use an array of bins (that is, the [] or [N]
notation is not allowed).
bins others[] = default; // Incorrect
bins others[2] = default; // Incorrect
bins others = default; // Correct
The following warning is issued if incorrect usage is encountered:
Warning-[FCINVDAB] Invalid Default Array Bin
test.sv, 5
top, "others"
Array syntax '[]' has no effect on default bin of coverpoint on real
expression.
Multi-stateness is ignored. Capturing multi-bin data in a single bin.

Backward Compatibility
Support for the real datatype in covergroup is already present in VCS to some extent,
under the compile option -xlrm real_cg . However, there is a difference between the
support VCS has and what the LRM mandates.
• VCS provides option.real_array_bin_max to control the number of bins created
from an open array bin (bins b[] = ). This option must be set at the covergroup
definition level. It cannot be set at the coverpoint or cross level. VCS does not have any
option to control the interval size of range distribution.
• Open array bin names are reported differently in VCS.
For an open array bin, bins b_open[] = {[1.001:1.201]};
Following are the bin names reported by VCS/URG/Verdi:
b_open_1.001:
b_open_1.041:
b_open_1.081:

Accelerating Coverage Database Merging
b_open_1.121:
b_open_1.161:1.201
Whereas bin names for a fixed array bin like bins b_fix[5] = {[1.001:1.201]}; are
as following:
b_fix[0]
b_fix[1]
b_fix[2]
b_fix[3]
b_fix[4]
As seen above, as per LRM, the reporting of open array bin uses close “[” and open “)”
interval range syntaxes. However, the fixed array naming mechanism is the same.
To maintain backward compatibility, if option.real_array_bin_max is found in any
covergroup, then VCS uses the current format (not LRM compliant) to report bin names for
this covergroup. If both option.real_array_bin_max and type_option.real_interval
are set in a covergroup, then a warning is issued, and VCS follows LRM compliant
behavior.
The real expression in covergroup with VCS does not support the following:
• Tolerance taken (+/- and +%-) is not yet supported in VCS. Therefore, it is not
supported in covergroup as well.
• Cross coverage of hierarchical real coverpoints, that is, cross of real coverpoints from
different covergroups.
• Cross coverage user bins.
• User-defined cross coverage bin and select expression.
• CrossQueue type bin in cross of real-valued coverpoints.
• Showing bin values in report.

Constraints Features
This chapter contains the following Constraints feature:
• Constraints APIs for User-Defined ML Flow
• Using Constraints Debug Option for Detecting Conflict Error Caused by Hard
Partitioning
Constraint APIs feature describes the following topics:
• Introduction
• Supported Data Types
VCS provides a callback mechanism to call the API functions before or after each
randomize call to the constraint solver. These API functions influence the constraint solver
(without modifying the SV code) before each randomize call and get feedback after the
randomize task is done.
You must provide SystemVerilog design and C++ files. At compile stage, VCS compiles
the SystemVerilog design to generate simv and compiles the user-provided C++ files to
the shared library.
At runtime, simv imports the generated shared library and triggers callbacks in the shared
library. In your application, constraints and the values of variables can be observed
or modified through the ML C++ Interface topic. This feature allows you to control the
constraint solver through APIs without modifying the SystemVerilog code.

Callback Flow
The following figure illustrate the ML callback flow:
Figure 51 Constraints APIs for User-Defined ML Flow

The following figure illustrates detailed Solver API callback flow:
Figure 52 Solver API Callback Flow
In the Solver API callback flow, an entrypoint is added at the end of randomize() after the
solver is completed, see the highlighted section in Figure 52.
Return Values:
• Retry is true, when the return value is: cumlCBRetryC or cumlCBRetryAndTraceOnC.
• Retry is false, when the return value is: cumlCBFailC or cumlCBSucceedC.

cumlCBSucceedC, // Solve succeeds and will proceed with simulation
without re-try.

trace for constraint inconsistency.

The return status being assigned in the body of callback function is used to decide if
re-randomize is needed when the current callback is triggered at the end of randomize
(means that the mode is EndRandomizeC. Re-randomize occurs until the return value is
changed to cumlCBSucceedC.

• BeginPreRandomizeC/EndPreRandomizeC is for the controller. If constraints and
variables are modified at these two phases, the current randomization is impacted.
You must check the event type in your C++ code. Multiple callbacks could be triggered
in different places for pre_randomize.
• BeginPostRandomizeC/EndPostRandomizeC is only for observation. If constraints and
variables are modified at these two phases, the next randomization is impacted.
You must check the event type in your C++ code. Multiple callbacks could be triggered
in different places for post_randomize.
• EndRandomizeC is used for re-randomize. You can decide if re-try is needed
or not by checking the return status of the current randomize (for example,
Context::get_randomize_return_status()).

Options to Compile User-Defined C++ Code
Following is the use model to compile user-defined C++ files:
vcs <other_options> [ -cumlf=<cpp filelist> |
-cumlc=<c1.cpp>,<c2.cpp>,] [ -cumlr=rulefile ]
-cumlf/-cumlc
Allows you to specify .cpp files.
• User-defined C++ codes are compiled as a shared library.
• Shared library is created as libcumluser.so in the simv.daidir directory.
-cumlr=rulefile
Allows you to apply filter rule at compile time.
Following is the format of rulefile:
class=<class name pattern>
Each class name should be specified in a new line. Glob-wildcards are supported. A glob
wildcard is opposite to regex pattern.
If rulefile is not specified, callbacks are registered on pre_randomize/post_randomize
for all SystemVerilog (SV) classes. If rulefile is specified, callbacks are registered only
for the matched SV classes.
Run Simulation
./simv [other simulation options]
Simv automatically loads the generated shared library.

Compile-Only User-Defined C++ Codes
Following is the command to compile only user-defined C++ code:
vcs [-cumlf=<cpp filelist> | -cumlc=<c1.cpp>,<c2.cpp>, ]
[-cumlr=rulefile] -Mdir=<existing csrc>
If you change C++ code without modifying the SV design, this command allows you to
compile only C++ codes, rebuild the shared library, and avoid recompiling the SV design.

information, see Hard Partition Report.

turned to OFF or STATE by solver, add the comments in ‘notes’ column.

Introduction to Echo and Bias Files
Echo is a technology that automatically analyzes the testbench constraint space and
generates stimuli that significantly reduces the manual effort required to verify a large
number of functional scenarios. In addition, it allows auto-generation of a stimulus
coverage model and uses the bias files to guide the convergence process of either auto-
generated or user-developed stimulus coverage.
In addition, if you have developed your stimulus cover model, then Echo can identify holes
in the stimulus cover model and similarly direct the constraint solver to generate stimulus
such that these cover holes are hit. Echo works at the test level, that is, Echo tries to hit
coverage holes within a test.
Verification tests are mostly run on a regression farm, where multiple copies of the tests
are being executed in parallel on different machines in the farm, with each simulation
being assigned a different random seed. It is desirable that with Echo enabled, each test

be able to target different portions of the coverage space in order to meet coverage goals
in the shortest possible clock time.
What is a “Test”?
A test in the context of Echo is an executable that can be simulated (for example, simv
generated by VCS). The source files, such as testbench files, design files and so on are
compiled by VCS and linked with the simulation engine to create the executable. The
executable can then be invoked multiple times with different runtime options, such as
different random seeds or configuration files and the simulation results can be observed.

The built-in function rand_mode can be used to turn off the randomness of a rand variable.

The coverpoints for variables are called covp_<cover_point_id>. Here,
<cover_point_id> is a unique integer identifier for every coverpoint. The autobins for the
coverpoints are named by the usual naming convention for autobins. The comment for the
cover point indicates details about the variable.
Branch Coverage
Each conditional block has an associated Boolean coverpoint. The coverpoint expression
is the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards. For example:
if (p) {
if (q) {
x == y;
}
}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with the expression p&&q.
The comment for the cover point has the expression string.
Condition Coverage (Sensitized)
Each sensitizing guard condition has a Boolean cover bin associated with it. For example:
if (p || (q && r)) {

}
In the above example, there is a coverpoint with expressions p || (q && r) with one bin
corresponding to the case when expression p is ON (or true) and one bin corresponding
to the case when expression q&&r is true. The idea is to make sure that the conditional
expression becomes true at least once for every implicant in the expression being true.
The coverpoints are guarded by the conjunction of all the enclosing conditional guards.
The subexpressions of the guard expression involving operators other than &&,
||, ! are considered as atomic, and the sensitizing conditions are defined over
these atomic subexpressions.
When the condition expression is a set expression, the condition coverage model is
generated like the set membership coverage model. For example:
if (p in {0:4, 7}) {

}
Here the coverpoint expression is p, and the bins 0, 1-3, 4, 7 are created.
The comment for the coverpoint has the expression string.

Set Membership Coverage
Echo infers a coverpoint for constraints coded using in and dist operations. Equivalent
ways of writing the same constraints using other operators might not result in an inferred
coverage model. For example:
x in {0:5};
results in an inferred cover point, whereas
x >= 0 && x <= 5;
does not result in an inferred cover point. Also, use of set membership in complex
constraints does not result in an inferred cover point.
For membership in sets with constant members:
• A single coverpoint is created. The sample expression is the same as the LHS.
• Value in the set membership constraint.
• A bin is created for the low value of each range.
• A bin is created for the high value of each range, for non-singleton ranges.
• A bin is created for the range excluding low and high values of each range, if the
resulting range is non-empty.
x in {0:5, 7};
In the above example, a cover point with expression x and four bins, 0, 1-4, 5, 7 is
created.

Contribution to Coverage Scoring
The automatically generated coverage model contributes to the coverage score by default
with a weight of 1.0.
Coverage Model Inference for In-line Constraints
As in-line constraints (randomize with {..}) are recommended for use in the
specification of test constraints, a coverage model from such constraints is not inferred. In
fact, the use of test constraints is expected to be minimized after coverage driven stimulus
generation is implemented.
Autogeneration of coverage model is done as part of the VCS compile step. The switch
to enable coverage model generation is -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen . All the coverage
models are written out as text files in the echo_cov_gen directory. The echo_cov_gen
directory is present wherever simv.daidir and simv files are generated by VCS compiler.

Diagnostic Mode
The language in which the coverage model is generated is the same as the syntax of the
testbench.
Example command line for a SystemVerilog testbench.
vcs -sverilog -ntb_opts echo_cov_gen foo.sv
It is expected that the user firstly creates a coverage model using the auto_gen option.
Then, the user includes the coverage model into their testbench (using `include or
#include directives) and then makes sure the coverage model is instantiated in the new
task for the enclosing class (that is, the class where constraints and random variables are
specified). The user is encouraged to view the autogenerated coverage model and make
changes if required.
The VCS compiler does not compile the design when echo_cov_gen is specified (that is,
no simv is created).
Diagnostic Mode
To enable diagnostic mode at compile-time, you need to provide the -ntb_opts

Compile-time Options
To enable Echo flow, use the -ntb_opts echo_new_flow compile-time option along with
the existing compile-time option -ntp_opts echo :
% vcs -ntb_opts echo -ntb_opts echo_new_flow
For procedural sampling where the cover point variable is not directly driven by a rand
variable, Echo attempts to capture the logic using the config-file approach. The compile-
time use model is as follows:
-ntb_opts config-file=<fname>
The config file format is as follows:
<CONS PROP START>
<file> <cls_inheritence.sv:40> //where <filename:line_info> points to the
assignment.
<CONS PROP END>
You can specify a maximum of 10 statements in the configuration file.
Support for Existing Compile-time Options
This use model supports all compile-time options (including compile-time diagnostic
options) except the echo_gen_exclusion_file option. During compile-time, this option
generates an exclusion file for the coverage points (CPs) which cannot be targeted by
Echo. This was primarily supported in Echo to avoid dumping of untargetable CPs in
the generated bias files. In this flow, this is not required since the new engine treats the
untargetable CPs as constants.
Runtime Options
Following are the runtime options:
-echo_hints
Generates positive and negative hints for the CPs targeted by Echo.
-echo_dir
This flow supports only -echo_dir=<>. This option specifies the coverage convergence
database directory.
Example: -echo_dir=<>

The default coverage convergence database directory where reports are generated is
simv.ccdb.
• Conflicting constraint detection is disabled in this flow.
• Targeting transition bins is not supported.
-echo_filter_cov_include
Echo targets all functional coverage points, by default. The -echo_filter_cov_include
switch enables you to limit the functional coverage points by using the following command:
-echo_filter_cov_include=<filter_string>
Here, filter_string may be a bin name or a file name.
-echo_filter_cov_file_include
Enables you to specify multiple filter strings in a single file and pass the file to Echo. The
syntax of this switch is as follows:
-echo_filter_cov_file_include=<filter_file_name>
Replay Options
Following are the replay options:
Argument Description
-echo_replay Specifies the test to replay. Each test targets one or more CPs. All
the tests must be replayed to hit all the targeted CPs.
-echo_dir Specifies the coverage convergence database directory (where
the data was dumped during -echo_hints run). Default is
simv.ccdb dir
-echo_replay_dir Specifies the database directory where replay run data is dumped.
Default is simv.ccdb.replay.
-echo_replay_sym Enables the mode for replaying positive hints for the CPs.
-echo_replay_tests File having information to replay the tests to hit targeted CPs
(case where the test file is present in non-coverage convergence
database directory).
Example,
% ./simv -echo_replay_sym -echo_replay=1 \
-echo_replay_tests=<echo_dir>/cc.tests

Bias Files
Options to Generate Bias Files
Following are the options to generate bias files. You can provide these options during
simulation as well as replay.
-echo_select_cps
Divides the targeted coverage space into multiple ranges, or sets it similar to the Echo
bias file. Each selected range or set can be targeted and replayed separately or in parallel.
-echo_vdb_dir
Specifies the coverage database used to generate the targeted holes.
Examples:
• % ./simv -echo_hints -echo_select_cps=range,<x>,<y>
-echo_vdb_dir=<coverage_database>
Where, x and y are start and end numbers for the range.
• % ./simv -echo_hints -echo_select_cps=set,<x>,<y>
-echo_vdb_dir=<coverage_database>
Where, x is the number of sets into which the targeted coverage space is to be divided,
and y is the number set to the target.

Usage Scenarios
This section discusses Echo usage in various common verification scenarios. In all the
scenarios in this section, it is assumed that the guidelines mentioned in the previous
section are being followed (for example, coverage and constraints are on the same
variables, and so on).
You can load a pre-existing coverage database in every scenario to screen out already-
covered coverage bins. By doing so, the current run can focus only on uncovered bins.
The coverage database must be loaded after all the testbench components have been
instantiated, so that the coverage data from the database can be loaded in the proper (in-
memory) runtime database.

Usage Scenarios
Running a Single Test with Randomized Configurations
This scenario generally applies to multimedia devices, in which the device has many
interfaces and many modes and the device can be configured to select some interfaces
and some modes.
The object of verification is to exercise all the interesting configurations of the device. In
the testbench, configurations are selected, and then data (possibly random) is passed
through the device.
Configurations for a device are typically chosen (through randomize) a few times per
test run. In the extreme case, only one configuration might be selected (for example,
config.randomize is performed only once).
In this scenario, it is important to pre-load the coverage database to ensure that already-
selected configurations are not chosen.
Running a Single Test With Randomized Transactions
This scenario applies to transaction-based verification environments. This scenario is
required for packet-processing devices or instruction-based processor verification.
The device is set in some mode, and then multiple transactions are generated and
passed through the device. You use constraints to generate the transaction objects. In this
scenario, you can use the default arguments for Echo.
If you assume that many transactions are generated (randomized), then it is appropriate
for the convergence heuristics to take over and apply reactive calls as needed.
status = transObj.randomize();
or
repeat (1000) {
transObj = new;
status = transObj.randomize();
}

Methodology and Flow Issues
This section addresses methodology and regression execution issues.
Scenario: All Tests have the Same Constraints and Coverage
Space (Recommended)
When all the tests being executed in parallel have exactly the same coverage space and
the same legal stimulus space (that is, the constraints are exactly the same for all the
tests), then the Echo bias file approach can be used to achieve high efficiency test runs.
Each test should have its own bias file. The input database for the URG utility can be
obtained by running any test and using the output coverage database. The number of test
runs should be used as the value for the echo_gen_bias argument for URG. Once the
bias files are generated, they can be used again and again for repeated regression runs.
It is desirable that the number of times the stimulus objects are randomized in a test be
at least equal to the average number of coverage bins in the bias files. After all the tests
are done running, the coverage database from all the tests can be merged to get the final
coverage number. It is possible but not efficient to use both the random seed and the bias
file for every test.

Methodology and Flow Issues
Scenario: Tests are Grouped into Categories With Each Category
having Specific Test Constraints
In this scenario, tests have test specific test constraints which further constrain the legal
stimulus space and thus also reduce the hittable coverage bins. (Coverage bins whose
value ranges lie outside the space of the test constraints cannot be hit). A bias file can
be created for every category of tests. The bias file should be such that all the coverage
bins in the file are hittable given the test constraints for that category. Each test within
this category can use the same bias file but with a different random seed. The URG bias
generation utility can be used to generate a bias file template. (Note that the URG does
not look at test constraints when generating the bias files). The test writer can then modify
this template to include the hittable coverage bins. As in the previous scenario, assuming
test constraints remain constant across regression runs, then the bias files have to be
generated once and can be used for multiple regression runs. Even if all the bins in a
bias file are not hittable, all it causes is less efficient utilization of resources. Echo may
use some cycles in the test run to try to target unhittable bins, but remaining cycles still
target hittable coverage bins. In this scenario too, the coverage data from all the tests
can be collected and merged. Then a sequential run can be used to target any remaining
coverage holes. For this final sequential run, the merged coverage database can be used
as an input along with the fully open constraints.
Scenario: Coverage Database Being Loaded in the Beginning of a
Test Run
If a coverage database is being loaded as part of the configuration for a test, then there
is no need to use an Echo bias file. Echo only targets coverage bins that are not covered
in the loaded database, so it is already biased in some sense. If the same database
is loaded in multiple tests, then a random seed can be used so that each test targets
different holes. This is useful in a batch mode type of regression environment. Here all
tests have the same constraints and coverage space, but one batch of tests is run at one
time. After the batch is complete, the coverage databases are merged and the merged
database is used as input for the next batch of tests. Note that for repeatability purposes,
the input database associated with a test needs to be preserved in case the test needs to
be run in a stand alone mode. If an Echo bias file is used, then it overrides the bias from
the loaded coverage database, that is, holes in the bias file are targeted even if they are
marked as covered in the loaded coverage database. Hence it does not make sense to
use both coverage database load and Echo bias file approaches for a test.

If you want to dump only specific data, you can use the following options:
• -simprofile=uvm:user- This option allows you to dump data on user classes only.
The option does not dump data on UVM base classes.
• -simprofile=uvm:component - This option allows you to dump data on UVM
component and its derived classes (same as the -simprofile=uvm). This is the default
behavior starting from O-2018.09-SP2 release.
• -simprofile=uvm:all - This option allows you to dump data for all the classes. This
was the default behavior of the -simprofile=uvm option till O-2018.09-SP1-1 release.

Support for UVM Profiler
At Runtime:
No option is required at runtime. Once the simulation is completed, uvm_profiler.db is
generated. This contains the information that can be post-processed to create HTML files.
Post-Processing Utility
uvmprofrpt is the post processing utility that generates the HTML files.
Syntax:
uvmprofrpt -uvm_profiler=db:uvm_profiler.db
When you run this utility, it generates a directory called uvm_profiler. This directory
contains two types of HTML reports, which are hierarchical report and flat report. The
following figures show the sample reports:
Figure 55 UVM Profiler Hierarchical Report
In the above figure, rows with brown background refer to the UVM base class functions
and the rows with purple background refer to the user class functions.

Support for UVM Profiler
Figure 56 UVM Profiler Flat Report
The UVM Profiler Flat report provides the function definition based count and the
respective time consumption. This does not have object based association. The function
calls made from different objects are counted cumulatively based on the definition.
In both the hierarchical view and flat view, when you click on the method name, it shows
the caller-callee list related to that function and the corresponding statistics as shown in
the Caller-Callee report.
Additional Options on UVM Profiler
The following are some of the additional options that can be used to customize the reports:
% simv -uvm_profiler[= num_entries:{value} | ignoreUVMCalls]
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200
% simv -uvm_profiler=num_entries:200+ignoreUVMCalls
These are the descriptions of arguments used in the example:
• num_entries=value - Indicates the number of entries that you need. In the above
example, the top 200 entries that are sorted by Exclusive Wall Time are reported. The
default is 500.
• ignoreUVMCalls - When you specify this option, all UVM functions and tasks called
internally within UVM methods are not reported in detail. Their time consumption is
reported in the first UVM method directly called by user function/task. By default it
includes UVM calls.

Support for UVM Profiler
These options can also be passed to the uvmprofrpt utility.
The feature has the following limitation:
• UVM phase based reporting is currently not supported.
• UVM profiler is applicable only to SystemVerilog.

Support for Unpacked Union
Unpacked union represents a single piece of information that is accessed using one of the
named member data types. VCS supports unpacked union as specified in Section 7.3 of
the IEEE Standards for System Verilog LRM 1800-2012.
The following example shows the usage of unpacked tagged union.
Example 49 Unpacked Union
module test;
typedef union
{
logic [31:0] bitVec;
integer intVar;
}
unionDef;
unionDef unionObj;
unionObj.bitVec32 = 32'habcd;
$display ("unionObj.intVar=%h",unionObj.intVar);

Support for Tagged Unions
end
Following is the output generated when you run the simulation:
unionObj.intVar=abcd
• Unpacked Union is not supported in the following scenarios:
◦ Structural contexts like port connection, continuous assignment and procedural
continuous assign statements.
◦ LHS of Non blocking assignment statements.
◦ $monitor statements.
◦ wait,@ statements.
• Limited debug support. Only UCLI show/get value and Force -deposit is supported.
Support for Tagged Unions
A tagged packed union is a type checked union. Typically for an ordinary (untagged)
union, VCS can write union data values from one type and read the data as another type
of the union. This is a potential loophole because it can write data based on one member
and then by mistake misread the stored data using another type. Consider the untagged
union declaration in Example 50:
Example 50 Untagged Union
union packed {
bit signed [3:0] a;
bit unsigned [3:0] b;
} u;
You specify storing a positive unsigned value in b. According to the SV LRM that value
can be misinterpreted as a negative value if the value is read from a. The SV LRM (IEEE
Standard System Verilog LRM1800-2012) allows this misinterpretation.
Tagged union declarations prevent such accidental misuse of a union by enforcing type-
checking for each read and write on any of the members of the union. If you use a tagged
union instead of an untagged union, VCS does not read or write u

Changing Default Scope of DPI Functions
By default, VCS sets the scope to calling context of DPI function. However, as per
LRM Section H.9.3, scope must be set to declaration context. You can use the
-dpi_lrm_context option at compile time for LRM compliance behavior.
The -dpi_lrm_context option is required only if the declaration context and
the calling context of the DPI function are different.
Use the following option at compile time:
• vcs -sverilog -dpi_lrm_context <filename.sv> <filename.c>
In three step flow, use this option at vcs step.

Assertion Features
This chapter contains the following feature:
• Signature-Based Control
• Enabling Fail-Only Feature
• Support for Dynamic Data Types in Assertions
VCS provides an enhanced way to control unique-case/priority-case violation checks,
deferred assertions (labeled assertions), immediate and concurrent assertions, initial and
final blocks, using the -assert signature compile-time option.
VCS generates a “signature” in addition to the regular assertion message from the
deferred assertions, unique-case/priority-case violation checks, immediate and concurrent
assertions, initial and final blocks, when you use -assert signature .
A signature is a string made up of tokens extracted from the function call stack trace of
assertions, and is separated by dots. Each signature uniquely determines a path from
where the error/warning occurs, as shown in the following example.
Example 67 Function call stack trace
function f(input a, b);
L: assert final(a > b);
endfunction // function is defined in $unit, used by many
callers as
// intellectual property
reg a, b, c, d;
always_comb begin : block1
f(a, b);
end
always_comb begin : block2
f(c, d);

end
The following output contains the signature (highlighted in bold) for function call stack
trace:
"te1.v", 3: \$unit ::f.L: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a > b)'
#0 in f.L at te1.v:3
#1 in top.block1 at te1.v:10
[Warning/Error Signature: "top.block1.f.L"]

"te1.v", 3: \$unit ::f.L: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '(a > b)'
#0 in f.L at te1.v:3
#1 in top.block2 at te1.v:13
[Warning/Error Signature: "top.block2.f.L"]
This feature helps you to locate the exact place where the assertion failure occurs. You
can use signature to control assertions, unique-case/priority-case violation checks, and
initial/final blocks. The following section describes how to use signature to achieve the
required control.
Using Signature to Control Assertions
Existing assertion control tasks, including $assertoff()and $asserton(), accept
signature as an argument to perform the control.
The following topics illustrate how to use signature to control the assertions in various
ways:
• Full-signature control (single control)
• Partial-signature control (group control)
• Static Configuration File
• Runtime Control
Full-signature control (single control)
In Example 68, VCS provides all assertion failures and the corresponding signatures for
them, as shown in Output: run.log.ref:
Example 68 Full-signature Control
reg a;
function reg foo (reg a);
for(int i=1;i<2;i++) begin

to one of the reasons listed in Contexts where no Signature is Generated, they

can still be turned on or off by instance-level control. This is to match legacy
semantics.
Static Configuration File
The signature can be used as an argument for static control. You can use the signature
option with the signature string, as shown in this example, to define signature in static
configuration file.
Example 69 Specifying signature in static configuration file
//----sig.cfg-----------------------------------
+signature M.AL.GenLoop_i_0[0].foo.loopA[0].U1
-signature Top.AL.*.A1
//----------------------------------------------
+signature
Enables all assertions represented by the signature.
-signature
Disables all assertions represented by the signature.
The configuration file (sig.cfg in Example 69) can be used to control either assertions or
unique-case/priority-case violation checks, at compile time or at runtime.
You can use the static configuration file with the -assert hier_uniq option, as described
in Table 10.
Table 10 The -assert hier_uniq option commands
Command Effect
vcs -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg Controls all applicable unique-case/priority-case
violation checks at compile-time.
vcs -assert hier=sig.cfg Controls all applicable assertions at compile-time.
simv -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg Controls all applicable unique-case/priority-case
violation checks at runtime.
simv -assert hier=sig.cfg Controls all applicable assertions at runtime.
-assert hier and -assert hier_uniq runtime options require -assert
enable_hier at compile time.

If you want to control assertions/ unique-case and priority-case violation checks uniformly,
the same configuration file can be passed to different switches, as shown below:
% vcs -assert signature -assert hier_uniq=sig.cfg -assert hier=sig.cfg
In this way, all assertions and unique-case/priority-case violation checks whose signatures
match those defined in configuration file will be disabled/enabled.
• All existing syntax, such as -assert, -tree, and so on continues to work as before.
• You can use the -signature option in the existing file along with legacy -assert,
-tree.
Runtime Control
You can use the call command, as shown below, to call the signature-based control at
runtime.
call {$assertoff(0, "Top.AL.BL1[0].foo.BL[1].GenLoop_j_0[-1].A1")};
All types of control (single or group) presented in sections Partial-signature control (group
control) and Static Configuration File works using the call command.
Generating Warning Message for Invalid Signature Path
VCS generates a warning message, if the static path of the signature is not valid. Consider
the following example testcase:
Example 70 Testcase test.sv
module Test;

logic a;
mod1 m1(a);

$assertoff(0, "Test.m1.m2.blk2.A1");
end

always_comb begin : blk1
A1: assert final (a);
end

VCS generates the following warning message for Example 70:
Warning-[RA-INVSTR] Not found in design
"Test.m1.m2.blk2.A1" not found in design. Ignored in "$assertoff".

"tx.v", 21: Test.m1.m2.blk1.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending 'a'
[Signature: "Test.m1.m2.blk1.A1"]
Key points to note
• An XMR that starts with a module name is not supported. For example, mod1.A1 is not
supported.
• This feature is not supported for designs.
Support for Signature-Based Control in Immediate and
Concurrent Assertions
VCS supports these features for immediate and concurrent assertions:
• Block-level exclusion of assertions.
• Using “*” wildcard character in the regular expressions for exclusion of assertions.
For example, consider Example 71.
Example 71 Testcase test.sv
reg a, b, c, d;

always_comb begin : block
L1: assert (a > b);
L2: assert (a < b);
end
$assertoff(0,"top.block");
$assertoff(0,"top.*");
end
In Example 71, all assertions defined inside the block level top.block are excluded.

In the $assertoff(0,"top.*") command, all the assertions matching the wildcard pattern are
excluded.
Support for Signature-Based Control in Initial and Final Blocks
VCS supports signature-based control for assertions in the initial and final blocks. For
example, consider the following code which contains initial block:
Example 72 test.v

initial begin : INI //Behavioral
for(int i=0;i<1;i++) begin : LOOP
A1: assert final (0);
end
end

This is the simulation output for the above code:
"test.v", 5: top.INI.LOOP.A1: started at 0s failed at 0s
Offending '0'
#0 in top.INI.LOOP.A1 at test.v:5
#1 in loop with i= 0 at test.v:4
[Signature: "top.INI.LOOP[0].A1"]
In the above simulation output, top.INI.LOOP[0].A1 is the signature generated by VCS for
assertion A1 in the initial block.
Key points to note
• Functions having deferred assertions with the named action block, but called from the
final block, are not supported.
• Function calls from the final block are not supported in the partition compile flow.
• Contexts where no Signature is Generated
The signature is introduced to locate the exact place where the assert failure occurs.
Each signature corresponds to a real hardware unit when the design is synthesized.
If an assertion is not placed in a synthesizable code, or if it is not identifiable, no
signature is generated. As a result, such assertions cannot be controlled using
signatures. Example 73, Example 74, , and Example 75 show contexts where
signatures will not be generated.

$assertoff(0,"top.block1.f.L_simple");
end
In Example 76, VCS does not allow you to exclude the assertion for each function call.
This indicates that you cannot exclude top.block1.f.L_simple.

Enabling Fail-Only Feature
VCS supports the -assert failonly compile-time option which enables fail-only mode
for concurrent assertion. The -assert failonly option reports only assertion failures
with their end times. For more information, see the section Fail-Only Assertion Evaluation
Mode in the VCS User Guide. However, VCS also supports
-assert select_failonly
-assert select_failonly
option that can move the selected assertions or covers to fail-only mode. The following are
the options:
• auto
• fastcover
• <filename>
The
failonly
failonly mode improves the runtime performance and decreases the runtime
memory requirement.
The use model is as follows:
• -assert select_failonly=auto
This option automatically identifies the assertions to move to fail-only mode.
• -assert select_failonly=fastcover
This option allows you to move all cover properties to fail-only mode.
• -assert select_failonly=<filename>

Enabling Fail-Only Feature

select_failonly=fastcover
• % vcs -sverilog test.v -assert svaext -assert select_failonly=test.txt
