• Changes in input files like assert hier file, -cm_hier file, UPF file, and XPROP
configuration files.
• The change in a package partition leads to recompilation of its dependent partitions.
• When two or more modules/packages/interfaces are grouped into one partition,
then even if only one module/package/interface is changed, the whole partition is
recompiled.
Achieving the Best Turnaround Time with Partition Compile
To get the maximum gain in turnaround time from the partition compile flow, note the
• Do not create too many partitions
◦ Start with autopartitioning and then tune for performance, if needed.
• Avoid code in $unit
◦ Code changes in the $unit may affect many partitions.
◦ $unit is not sharable across multiple tests.
• Create separate partitions for each top-level design in hierarchy, if more than one top-
level change in subsequent compilation.
◦ All parallel top-level are a single partitions, by default.
◦ Create a separate partition for the top-level that changes frequently compared to
the other parallel top-level that are idle.
• Create separate partitions for each test (program) and only test partition gets
recompiled in this case.
• Make external IP/VIP modules as separate partitions.
• Partitions for mixed HDL designs
◦ Create separate partition for a VHDL entity if it is going to change frequently.
◦ If it is not a separate partition then it is compiled as part of default VHDL top
partition.
• Create one or more partitions for SV packages that are going to change frequently.
• Import packages only where required.
◦ Package changes can cause recompile of multiple partitions (if all packages are
imported in a file and that file is included in many partitions).

The -pcmakeprof compile-time option enables profiling of time spent in each step of a
compilation. The profiling result is tabulated and printed at the end of the compilation log.
The following are usage examples of the option in different compilation flows:
Single Compile, Two-step
vcs -sverilog -pcmakeprof test.sv
Single Compile, Three-step
vlogan -sverilog test.sv
vcs top -pcmakeprof
Partition Compile, Two-step

Partition Compile, Three-step
vlogan -sverilog test.sv

Partition Compile Limitations
The following are the limitations with partition compile:
• Delayed or conditional SDF annotation is not supported.
• The -race option is not supported.
• Utilities like -metadump, -Xrawtokens can be used in regular compile to generate the
• Dynamic Reconfiguration
◦ Dynamic configuration with SDF is not supported.
◦ Dynamic configuration with VHDL
VHDL instance inside dynamic configuration enabled module
Dynamic configuration enabled instance in VHDL
• Interface instances with reference ports inside dynamic configuration enabled module.
• XMR across PE is not supported in partition compile flow.
• XMR referrer in PE module connected as module reference port is not supported in
partition compile flow.

• Cross-partition SDF (VHDL) is not supported.
• Only designs with SystemC on top are supported.
• When using VMC/SWIFT models then the VMC model cannot be a top-level module of
the design.
• Verilog-AMS Mixed Signal Simulation:
◦ Verilog-AMS amsd ie and setd commands are supported.
◦ GenBlock in Verilog-AMS flow is supported.
◦ Mixed Signal Simulation with FINESIM. (No HSIM and Nanosim compatibility with
VCS).
◦ Partition of top-level cell in the Mixed-Signal setup file is not supported in partition
compile flow.
◦ Multiple drivers for wreal net are not supported in partition compile flow.
• Coverage; Constant analysis ( -cm_noconst/-cm_seqnoconst) is more conservative in
partition compile, so some objects which are marked "unreachable" in single compile
are not marked in partcomp.
• The stop -thread <thread_no> command is expected to be different in partition
compile flow due to different thread ID between single compile and partition compile
flow.
• For mixed designs, processing of assertion configuration file (through compile-time
option -assert_hier) occurs at runtime in partition compile flow. This can have some
impact on runtime performance or may capture assertion related errors during runtime
instead of compile-time.
• Cross-partition DPI routine declaration mismatch error is generated at compile-time in
single compile flow for inconsistent declarations of DPI and DPI-C. You can use the
-error=noDPI-DRWIDT compile-time option to workaround this error in single compile
flow.
• Partition Compile does not support the interface port when it is a multi-dimensional
array.
• A compilation error Error-[SV-DOSIF] Delay or synchronization in function
is generated when a time-consuming task is invoked from within a function. For cross-
partition tasks, however, the error is deferred until runtime.

◦ Enclose other tests and sequences derived from the base test classes in separate
dynamic packages. Compile the dynamic packages using the -dynamic_tb option.
% vcs -partcomp test1_pkg -dir= IP_TEST1 -sharedlib=IP_BASE_TEST
-dynamic_tb

-dynamic_tb
-partcomp/-sharedlib/-dir
Enables Partition Compile flow.
-dynamic_tb
Enables dynamic test compile for DTL.
When multiple top packages are provided with -dynamic_tb option, it shows the
following error message. Only one top package is allowed.
Error-[DTL-MULTITOP-ERR] Dynamic Test Load Error
Multiple top packages are not supported with -dynamic_tb. Top
packages found: test2_pkg test1_pkg
The names of the top packages found in the above error message varies
based on the testcase.
This step reuses the partition information as per the -sharedlib option and
simv executable is not generated. You can observe a very fast compilation
for dynamic tests.
3. Simulate base test. Save the Simulation state after the common initial sequence (until
reset_phase in the following example) of the test is executed.
% simv +UVM_TEST_NAME=base_test -ucli -i save.cmds

save.cmds
UCLI command file.
stop -in uvm_component::post_reset_phase -once -continue -command {run
0; save saveddesign; ; run}
◦ You can use VCS save restore feature using UCLI commands or from the $save/
$restore calls from Verilog code.
◦ When the simulation state is restored, the setup and restore portions are executed
in one continuous simulation.
Restored DTL simulations can inherit the simulation log file from the saved base
simulation and continue it. This means that after the restored simulation has ended,
its log file contains the following:
▪ command-line of the base simulation
▪ log output of the base simulation up to the point of the snapshot save
▪ message that indicates that the log file has been inherited by the restored
simulation
▪ command-line of the restored simulation
▪ full log output of the restored simulation
This functionality is supported for DTL flows with $save/-r, native UCLI
(-ucli), and -ucliProc for both Verilog-only and MX designs. The option
-save_options=inherit_log is used for this purpose.
For more information, refer to “-l filename -save_options=inherit_log” in the VCS
Command Reference Guide.
◦ In case of only one UVM run phase in the test and there are no sub-phases:
The test is saved in the middle of the UVM run_phase of base_test, then at

This section describes the programming language interface (PLI) between the C/C++

they execute concurrently. The C/C++ functions in the application use the PLI to read and
write delay and simulation values in the VCS executable. Later during simulation VCS can
call these functions.
VCS supports PLI 1.0 and PLI 2.0 routines for the PLI. Therefore, you can use VPI, ACC,
or TF routines to write the PLI application. See Appendix , .

Writing a PLI Application
When writing a PLI application, you need to perform the following tasks:
1. Write the C/C++ functions of the application calling the VPI, ACC, or TF routines to
access data inside VCS.
2. Associate user-defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions in
your application. VCS calls these functions when it compiles or executes these system
tasks or system functions in the Verilog source code. In VCS, associate the user-
defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions in your application
using a PLI table file (see PLI Table File). In this file, you can also limit the scope and
operations of the ACC routines for faster performance.
3. Enter the user-defined system tasks and functions in the Verilog source code.
4. Compile/Analyze, elaborate, and simulate your design, specifying the table file and
including the C/C++ source files (or compiled object files or libraries) so that the
application is linked with VCS in the simv ex

Reducing Compilation Time in Native Certitude With VCS
Partition Compile Flow
This feature is Limited Customer Availability (LCA). Limited Customer Availability (LCA)
features are features available with select functionality. These features will be ready for a
general release based on customer feedback and meeting the required feature completion
criteria. LCA features do not need any additional license keys.
With the integration of Native Certitude with VCS Partition Compile flow, you can improve
the turnaround time for successive compilations in Native Certitude.
Partition Compile is used primarily to improve the turnaround time in successive
compilations. In Native Certitude, you have various phases of compilation. Therefore,
when you integrate Native Certitude along with the Partition Compile flow, you are able
to reduce the compilation time at each step. This results in improved performance during
compilation time.
The Native Certitude use model remains the same as that of the previous use model. For
information about the use model, see the Native Integration of Certitude and VCS section
in the Certitude User Manual.
Native Certitude consists of three phases in the following order:
• Model
• Activation
• Detection
The three different phases always run in the same order.
The model phase and the activation phase occur in a single compilation. The model phase
analyzes the DUT and creates a list of faults. The activation phase generates the simv
executable, which is used to determine the activated faults. The detection phase performs
the new compilation that generates the simv executable to determine the propagation and
the detection status of the faults. All the phases target the DUT part of the design and they
do not affect the testbench.

Reducing Compilation Time in Native Certitude With VCS Partition Compile Flow
If you want to fine-tune the testbench and recompile the design at activation or detection
phase, you must recompile the entire design including the DUT.
Similarly, after you are completed with the model and activation phases compilation and
you want to perform compilation in the detection phase, you must recompile the entire
design including the testbench that has not changed.
By integrating with Partition Compile, you can avoid the recompilation of unchanged
testbench part of the design. The compilation of testbench partition takes place only when
the testbench is changed.
Consider the following test cases:
//topcfg.v
design top;
partition instance top.dut use dut;

Coverage Directed Solver
Coverage Directed Solver helps you to speed up functional coverage convergence,
identify over-constraints affecting coverage closure, and provide Root Cause Analysis
(RCA) for SystemVerilog Constraint-based Random Verification (CRV) testbenches.
The features of Coverage Directed Solver are as follows:
• Automated Coverage Convergence: Reduces the number of runs required to get to
coverage closure or eliminates manual tests.
• Stimulus and Coverage Diversification: Finds more bugs in the testbench or design
due to a more diverse exploration of the coverage and stimulus space.
• Coverage Hole and Over-Constraint Identification and Root Cause Analysis:
Reduces the debug time to triage coverage holes or to identify over constraints, which
cause coverage holes and can improve testbench quality and reduce the potential for
subtle bugs hidden by testbench over-constraints.
• Improved Coverage Visualization:
◦ Provides URG and Verdi coverage integration of the guided constraint solving
results and analysis when availa

les and options that
are not related to Coverage Directed Solver.
To run Coverage Directed Solver in a three-step (or UUM) flow, use the following
commands:
• % vlogan [vlogan_options] file_list
• % vcs -vso ccex [elab_options] [libname].design_unit
• % simv -vso ccex <run_options>
The <vlogan_options>, <elab_options>, and <run_options> represent files
and options that are not related to Coverage Directed Solver.
Compile Commands
The first step in Coverage Directed Solver is to identify the connections between
covergroups and random variables. Identification of a connection at compile time is
referred to as compile-time connectivity generation.
To generate Coverage Directed Solver compile-time connectivity report, use the following
command:
%vcs -vso ccex -ccex_opts connect_report <compile_options>
• -vso ccex : Enables Coverage Directed Solver in compile-time connectivity mode if
connected covergroups are detected.
-ccex_opts connect_report : Generates the compile-time connectivity report of
Coverage Directed Solver.
User can specify path for connectivity report by specifying an additional argument to the
connect_report option as follows:
-ccex_opts connect_report=<report_path>
To visualize the connections between the coverpoint and crosses in covergroups to
random variables generated by Coverage Directed Solver at compile time, a covergroup-
level summary report of connectivity is available in ccex_summary.json under the same
directory where the compilation is done. This connectivity information is also annotated in
the URG report.

Runtime Commands
By default, Coverage Directed Solver biases the constraint solutions in the direction of
coverage inside a single simulation. This is referred to as intra-simulation biasing.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with intra-simulation biasing, use the following
command:
% simv -vso ccex <other runtime_options>
To enable Coverage Directed Solver to bias the constraint solutions across multiple
parallel simulation jobs running on the simulations, each Coverage Directed Solver-
enabled simulation needs to know the merged coverage state of the simulations which
have completed.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with inter-simulation learning by reading from the
previous VDB, use the following command:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts auto_merge_dir=<inter-sim shared directory>
The <inter-sim shared directory> is the commonly accessible path by all
simulation jobs and has a different path than the one specified with -cm_dir.
The command above performs automated distributed merging of covergroup metrics and
deposits the merged coverage results into the specified directory. Coverage Directed
Solver uses the merged directory as an input to identify covered targets and therefore,
focus efforts on targeting and diversifying over uncovered or rarely covered coverage bins.
Alternatively, if you already have an external method to merge the VDB directories

Change-Based Verification
Change-Based Verification (CBV) is a key component of the VSO.ai smart stress phase,
leveraging its ability to identify changes in the design and its associated Cone of Influence
(COI). CBV optimizes test selection with the goal of catching all the unique failure
signatures around identified area of code changes.
When global ICO phase configuration is used, the recommended tests for
failure recall are impacted.
Installation and Setup
Separate installation or license is not required to enable CBV flow in VSO.ai.
The following are the minimum VCS version requirements to enable this functionality:
• VCS 2023.12-SP2-9
• VCS 2024.09-SP2-3
• VCS 2025.06
• VCS 2026.03
CBV Workflow
The CBV functionality is seamlessly woven into various stages of the VSO.ai workflow.
After design changes are identified, they are mapped to the coverage targets that exist in
the VSO.ai ML model.
Initialization Stage
To use the CBV flow, it is mandatory to enable the line or tgl portonly metric during
the Day0 run of generating the VSO.ai ML model. This is essential because identified
design changes are mapped back to line or tgl portonly coverage targets, allowing
you to stress coverage around those mapped targets in the VSO.ai stress phase.

CBV Workflow
1. Compile Step:
The CBV flow is tightly integrated with VCS compile. Enabling VSO.ai options is
mandatory during the compile step to allow the CBV flow to identify design changes
during the VSO.ai init step.
$VCS_HOME/bin/vcs \
-vso cso \
-vso_opts buildname=<buildname> \
-vso_opts workdir=<workdir> \
[other VCS options]
If multiple builds are used in the project, ensure that a buildname is
associated with each compile, as the CBV flow identifies design changes on
a per-build basis.
2. Init Step:
In the init step, the CBV flow identifies design changes and applies them to the
VSO.ai ML model. This left-shifts coverage closure for code changes and targets
unique failures around the modified areas during the Smart Stress phase. By default,
VSO.ai enables all the following three phases:
◦ Smart Stress
◦ Acceleration
◦ Exploration
If you need to target only the design changes and exit, you can specify --phase
stress[:<N>]. Where, N is an optional value used to specify the number of times the
identified design changes are to be stressed around coverage. By default the value of N
is 1.
On Day0, there are no design changes; therefore, the init step tags only the design-
level information to the vso_workdir.
You must specify the simv location to tag the design information generated during VCS
compile to vso_workdir.
The simv path can be specified to the init step using the simv_location variable for
each build in the configuration file. Alternatively, the simv path can also be specified
using one of the following options:
◦ simv_paths: Comma-separated paths to all the build simvs being targeted by the
regression run.
◦ simv_path_list: File containing simv paths to all the build simvs to be targeted by
re

V-
specific handling during the finalize and merge steps.
Additionally, CBV flow also offers the capability to generate exclusion file for all unchanged
targets identified for current regression run. The generated .el file (exclusion file, typically
with .el extension) can then be used to create an urgReport for the modified portions of
the design, ensuring only the original changed targets are unexcluded. The .el file can
also be consumed by Verdi for interactive exclusion analysis.
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--dump_exclusions_for_changes
--workdir <workdir> \
--vdbdir <vdb_path> \
--target_metric <metrics> \
--elfile_outdir <outdir> \

Analytics and Reporting
where,
• --dump_exclusions_for_changes is a Boolean option that enables the generation of
an exclusion file for unchanged design targets.
• --vdbdir specifies an input vdb to generate an exclusion file compatible with that vdb.
The vdb can be as follows:
◦ vdb for any single build and test
◦ Merged vdb across all tests of a particular build
◦ Merged vdb across all builds
◦ Merged vdb with different flex_merge options
The VDBs generated with flex_merge modules or using –
merge_across_libs as an input may not contain the complete information
on the changes identified.
• --target_metric: If specified, allows to selectively dump the exclusions for the
required metric.
• If specified, --elfile_outdir defines the output directory for generated .el files. If
not specified, these files are generated within the workdir by default. The resulting file
is named excl_for_changes.el.
Analytics and Reporting
For information related to CBV analytics for Smart Stress phase, refer to Visualization in
VSO.ai chapter in the VSO.ai User Guide.
The CBV flow dumps the detailed change report, change_detail_report.txt, for each
build during the init step. This report includes detailed information about the identified
changed elements in the design. The detailed report is saved under workdir/online/
info/builds/<buildname>/change_detail_report.txt.

Limitations
The following are the limitations of the CBV feature:
• Identification of design changes is supported only for Verilog, SystemVerilog, and
VHDL portions of the RTL.
• CBV support for testbench and VHDL is currently a beta feature, which requires
additional options to be specified during the initialization phase of VSO.ai. For more
information, refer to the VSO.ai Beta Features Guide.

This command opens the Interface Browser form.
Figure 79

Interface Browser Form

The Interface Browser form includes the following panes, options, buttons and field.
* Interface Tree: This pane (on the left) lists the interface definitions, interface instances,
modports, and HDL instances in a tree node format. Each interface definition is shown
as a top node with the associated instances listed as underlying nodes. The modports
and HDL instances are listed under the interface instance. The interface instance,
modport and HDL instance nodes may be dragged to the source code frame to show
the associated code, the nSchema window to show the schematic, or the nWave
window to show the waveform.

* Interface Summary: This pane (on the right) lists the ports, variables, and subroutines
of the interface. The contents in this pane are automatically updated when a node in
the Interface Tree pane is double-clicked. Signal node types can be dragged to other
windows.
* Show Active Annotation: This option is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded. When
this option is turned on, the simulation values is displayed in the right-most column for
the variables or ports in the Interface Summary pane. The default value of this option
* Sync Selection to nTrace: When this option is turned on, double-clicking an interface
instance, or HDL instance in the Interface Tree pane displays the associated code
in the source code frame. When this option is turned off, double-clicking an interface
instance, or HDL instance in the Interface Tree pane only updates the Interface
Summary pane. The default value of this option is off.
* By: Click this selection button to specify the search criteria for the value change of a
signal. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Search Backward: Click this button to search backward in time and locate the
previous value change. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Search Forward: Click this button to search forward in time and locate the next value
change. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Cursor Time: This text field displays the current cursor time and also sets the cursor
time. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.

Verdi 2023.12
Starting from this release, you can migrate to NPI Waveform Model/Writer, which is
the latest FSDB Reader/Writer to seamlessly read FSDB. The following data types are
supported only with NPI Waveform Model/Writer:
1. Modport/interface port
2. Virtual file
3. The FSDB which includes power signals
4. Packed mode dumping

Verdi 2019.06
* Starting from this release, by default, Verdi filters the Value Change (VC) of
Value Change Dump (VCD) real signal. To revert the previous behavior, that
is, keeping two duplicates VC in real signal, set the environment variable
FSDB_KEEP_TWO_DUPLICATE_REAL_VC.
* Add ffrGetAPIVersion to get the FSDB Reader API version.
* FSDB is upgraded from version 5.7 to version 5.8.

Verdi 2017.12
* Starting from this release, the FSDB is upgraded from version 5.5 to version 5.6.
* The fsdbVarIdcode is enlarged from int to int64 so that larger designs (over 2G
idcode) can be handled with ease in the future.

Verdi 2023.12
Starting from this release, you can migrate to NPI Waveform Model/Writer, which is
the latest FSDB Reader/Writer to seamlessly read FSDB. The following data types are
supported only with NPI Waveform Model/Writer:
1. Modport/interface port
2. Virtual file
3. The FSDB which includes power signals
4. Packed mode dumping

Verdi 2017.12
* Starting from this release, the FSDB is upgraded from version 5.5 to version 5.6.
* The fsdbVarIdcode is enlarged from int to int64 so that larger designs (over 2G
idcode) can be handled with ease in the future.

Verdi 2016.06
Starting from this release, functions and tasks can be dumped to FSDB. By default, they
are not dumped for performance consideration. You can use one of following methods to
dump them to FSDB during runtime (simulation)
1. Using the FSDB_FUNCTIONS environment variable:
For example: setenv FSDB_FUNCTIONS 1
2. Using the +fsdb+functions runtime option:
For example: simv +fsdb+functions

Safety Specification Format
The Safety Specification Format (SSF) is a file format used in Synopsys functional safety
flows.
It defines safety mechanisms for a design.
An SSF file specifies the safety mechanisms to implement in the design.
This file helps ensure that required safety features are inserted and tracked during the
design process.
After implementation, the tool uses the SSF file to compare the RTL and the physically
implemented netlist.
It performs functional safety (FuSa) equivalence checks. These checks confirm that safety
mechanisms are correctly realized in the final design.

nTrace enables showing or hiding safety virtual cells in the hierarchy tree by using the
Safety Core Cell filter option. This option makes it easy to focus on safety-instrumented
logic as needed. The default status is toggle off.

Figure 3

Safety Core Cell Option

All general features that apply to an RTL instance also apply to a safety virtual cell.
Synchronizing a Safety Virtual Cell with RTL
Double-clicking a safety virtual cell in a hierarchy tree synchronizes the RTL source code
view in nTrace automatically to its module definition. As a result, you can quickly locate
and review the underlying RTL even though the RTL itself is unchanged.

Locating the SSF Source View
The Locate Core Rule Command context menu enables you to locate the SSF source
view for a related safety core rule command.
Figure 4

Context menu of the Locate Core Rule Command

Dragging a Virtual Cell to the RTL Source View
Dragging and dropping a virtual safety cell to the RTL source view changes the active
scope to the scope related to the virtual safety cell. The Data pane and Source view are
updated accordingly.

Safety Instrumental Signal in nTrace
Safety instrumented signals are automatically generated signals that implement or support
safety mechanisms defined by SSF rules. Verdi displays safety instrumented signals by
scope in the Signal pane.
Figure 5

Instrumental Signal in Signal Pane

These signals can be filtered or searched for by using the Safety Inserted option. The
default status is toggle on.

Figure 6

Safety Inserted Filter Option

Synchronizing a Safety Instrumented Signal with RTL
Double-clicking a safety instrumental signal automatically synchronizes the RTL source
code view in nTrace to the original signal declaration. This allows users to quickly locate
and review the underlying RTL, which remains unchanged.
Adding Instrumentation Signals to the Waveform
* To add low-power-related instrumental signals to a waveform by type, choose Add
Instrumented Signals to Waveform > Power.
* To add safety-related signals to a waveform by type, choose Add Instrumented
Signals to Waveform > Safety.
Other than the Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform feature, all general features that
apply to a normal RTL signal also apply to a safety instrumental signal.
If an RTL signal is impacted by a safety rule, the context menus corresponding
to that rule are enabled when you add an instrumented signal to the waveform.
For example, if an RTL signal is impacted by a register rule, the Register
Signals context menu is enabled. If the RTL signal is not impacted by any
safety rule, the Safety submenus remain disabled.

Configuring the Source View of the RTL Signals Impacted by Safety Rules
The Safety Aware page in the Preferences window enables you to specify a color for the
safety aware objects in the source view.

Safety Aware page in the Preference Window

Figure 17

Default Color Table for safety aware objects

If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple types of rule, the colorize priority as follows:
* A safety register object is higher than a safety-fsm object.
* A safety-fsm object is higher than a safety core object.
* A safety core object is higher than an error correction object.
* An error correction object is higher than the compare error object.
The preference option Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) highlights the safety
aware objects in the source view. The default status is toggle on.
The preference option Annotate Safety Aware Design Object(s) enables users to show/
hide the upper annotation for safety aware objects in the RTL source view. The default
status is toggle on. The option status aligns with the top menu command Source > Upper
Annotation > Safety Aware Annotation.

Safety Tree

You can view the applied target right after the safety model name in the <name> (<target>)
format. Safety models and rules are available in the child nodes. Refer to the following
Figure 24

Rules Displayed as Children Nodes

The rule type is displayed in the <name> (<type>) format right after the rule name. The
binding target (HDL signal/instance) lists are available as the child nodes of the rule node
as shown in the following figure:
Figure 25

Binding Target Under the Rule Node

The unused safety-models are available as sibling nodes of the default safety model in the
tree.
Double-clicking a policy node syncs the source view to its declaration and highlights the
policy name in the source view. The Data pane is updated based on the active safety
policy.
Double-clicking the attribute node syncs the source view to its related safety policy
declaration and highlights the attribute in source view.
Double-clicking the nodes that belong to the unused safety models makes the source view
jump to the related command line. However, the related line is inactivated and no actions
are available in the source view. The Data pane does not show any signal for such nodes.
Safety Manager supports search and filter features and unified find search in the safety
tree.

The Safety Specification Format support in nSchema helps users identify, analyze, and
debug safety-related logic in their designs. This is done through safety virtual cells and
safety instrumented signals. These features visually mark cells and signals that are
instrumented for safety. This makes it easier to trace safety mechanisms, understand their
impact, and ensure compliance with safety requirements. By leveraging these features,
users can quickly locate safety-critical elements, view related properties, and add relevant
signals to waveforms for further analysis.

The following topics describe the SSF support available in nSchema:
* Safety Virtual Cells in nSchema
* Safety Instrumental Signals

Safety Virtual Cells in nSchema
Safety virtual cells are instrumented by the set_safety_core_rule command. nSchema
adds the DC label to identify them.

You can identify a virtual cell in a full window highlighted with the DC symbol. The symbol
is positioned on the right top inside the body of the cell in the same color as the color of
the instance name.

Configuring the Source View of the RTL Signals Impacted by Safety Rules
You can use the preference option Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) to color the
safety-aware objects in the source view. The default status is toggle on.
Figure 40

Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) Option in View Menu

If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple types of rule, the colorize priority as follows:
* A safety register object is higher than a safety-fsm object.
* A safety-fsm object is higher than a safety core object.
* A safety core object is higher than an error correction object.
* An error correction object is higher than the compare error object.

Input Format
The following figure provides information about the format that you must follow to provide
the input.
The format of the signal can be signalName#time and signalName#timeWithUnit with
hierarchy delimiter either "/" or ".", for example, /tb/fout1#800, in one signal list. The
target waveform and the reference waveform must be specified in the command line with

Following is an example for the input format:

Input Example
Examples
You must import the design with appropriate Verdi options.
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt -f srcFileList.f
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt -lib work

If you have a design source file named as design.v and list input signals with the
prescribed input format in the signalList.txt signal list, and if you need to save the
output file as reportFile.txt in the parent directory of the current directory, execute the
following command:
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v -out_file ../
reportFile.txt

If you need to trace mismatch fan-ins of each signal listed in the signalList.txt file from
their first mismatch time, execute the following command:
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v -out_file ../
reportFile.txt -jmp_to_earliest

Report Format
After tracing the mismatch for the signal list, the tracediff_report.txt report is
generated in tracediffLog/ under the current directory by default.
As illustrated in the following figure, the configuration settings are recorded at the top
in the report. The root causes are listed and followed by the mismatch signals that they
affect.
Tracediff transforms the given time unit into the time unit used in the target waveform. This
is the reason that in the following figure, tb.fout2#600 instead of tb.fout2#600000ps is
dumped.
The tracediff utility categorizes signals into the following four types and the meaning of
each type is available at the end of the report:
* Root Cause Found
* Root Cause Not Found
* No Mismatch
* Non-Existent Signals
If any duplicated signals are available in the signal list, then these signals are available in
the Duplicated Signals section in the report. However, these duplicated signals are not
counted in report summary. Instead, a warning message is issued which mentions that
some signals with the same tracing times are listed in the input signal list.

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
Starting with this release, if there are any failed tests during regression, Verdi finds the bug
and fixes it before allowing any new changes.
Verdi first takes the file to determine the debug entries. Debug entries are monitored
signals in the DUT that have mismatches between the failing and passed waveform. Then
it traces back to find the root causes, and summarizes it in a text file report. This report is
then loaded into Verdi to see the detail trace path from debug entry to root cause.

The following sub-sections provide the details of the use model:
Determining the Bug Entry
The debug entries are read from a .rc file. There are three types of tags in the .rc file:
* Signal: If the tag is Signal, each line must include the full hierarchical name and
a timestamp. These signals are scanned and they become the debug entries if the
values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two waveform files. For
example,
top.memory.nROutstanding#123
top.mySig1#1000
top.mySig2#50

* Scope: If the tag is Scope, each line must include a list of scope names and a
timestamp. Boundary signals within these scopes are scanned and those signals
become the debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different
within the two waveform files. For example,
top,top.myScope1#200
top.myScope2#300
top#100-200

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

* Assertion: If the tag is Assertion, each line must include an Assertion name and a
timestamp. Signals that are associated to that assertion are scanned and become the
debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two
waveform files. For example,
top.memory.eos#160390000

The follow error message is an example on how to specify an assertion failure as debug
entry:
Error: "token.v", 144439:top.memory.eos : at time 160390000
ALL_DONE_EOS: All write transaction addresses must have been
matched with corresponding write response.
nb_cycles: 16040
Executing Axi End Of Simulation checks

here, ALL_DONE_EOS is the name of the assertion and 160390000 is the time.
Analyzing Root Cause
The root cause is analyzed by running the TraceDiff utility in Verdi. The following are the
enhancements to TraceDiff for root cause:
Trace Multiple Root Cause
For root cause, TraceDiff searches all fanins with mismatch on every level.
Trace Database
For root cause, TraceDiff saves the trace results in a trace result database that can be
efficiently and accurately replayed.
Ignore Mismatches on Waveform Time Boundaries
For root cause, TraceDiff does not trace signals with mismatches on the time boundary
only, because the mismatch may be due to inconsistency in the simulation evaluation
order. This helps to filter out false alarms.
Ignore Shifted Sequence
For root cause, TraceDiff ignores mismatches caused by delay shift.

The nCompare Utility
The nCompare utility compares two FSDB files using a defined rule file and reports the
errors to a file.

Batch Mode Options
Following are the batch mode options in which it is mandatory to specify the -lca option
and set the VERDI_PARALLEL_COMPARISON environment variable.
Options

Explanation

-partition_signal_count Specifies the partition signal count for each
signal_count
comparison. The error report file (*.nce) is updated
each time for each comparison. This option is only
supported without name mapping and with one
cmpSetSignalPair command. The default value is
100,000.
-proc process_number Specifies the multiple process numbers. This option
is only supported with the cmpCompare command.

Utilities for Performance Improvement

Utilities for Performance Improvement
Verdi supports the following two features or utilities for performance improvement:
* Prerequisites
* Trace Cache Utility
* Scan Utility

Prerequisites
To use these functionalities,
1. Set the VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE environment variable as follows:
setenv VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE

2. Specify the -lca option while invoking Verdi.

Trace Cache Utility
Verdi supports the trace cache feature that saves tracing time on the traceX utility. If a
signal is already traced, the trace engine stops at the cached signal and uses cached
traced results. The trace cache feature is enabled by default.You can disable/enable this
feature using the TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE environment variable.
To disable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 0

To enable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 3

Here, the default value is 3.
The trace cache feature is only supported for -cause_count 1. If you set this option with
number greater than 1, trace cache is turned off.

Scan Utility
Verdi provides the scan functionality or utility to scan signals with an X value. The following
options are available to help you to get the X signal list:
[-max_x_per_signal number] [-max_total_x number]
[-max_analysis_level number]

Specifies the maximum number of analysis X levels. If no analysis scope is specified, it
counts from the root scope. When the number is 0, all signals are analyzed. Its default
value is 0.
-max_total_x number

Specifies the maximum number of X for tracing. If the number is 0, it is unlimited. Its
default value is 1000.
-max_x_per_signal number

Specifies the maximum number of X for each signal. When the maximum is reached, the
remaining value changes of the signals are no longer analyzed. Here, 0 signifies no limit.
Its default value is 1.

Verdi supports the following utilities for FSDB:
* Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File Without Gate
* Support for Waveform Utility

Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File
Without Gate
In previous releases, the FSDB Reader takes more memory and CPU time to read an
FSDB file with gate when compared to reading an FSDB file without gate.
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the use of a utility, parallelWaveExpand, to
convert an FSDB file with gate to an FSDB file without gate. You can use this utility to
perform a one-time process to retrieve an equivalent FSDB from an FSDB with gate
enabled. Also, the FSDB Gate in the converted FSDB file is disabled. The FSDB contains
all the value changes so that an FSDB reader does not need to perform any reconstruction
of values.

You can also use the converted FSDB file to replace the original file in the remaining
debug flow. Therefore, you can reduce the consumption of memory and time. You need
to enable the environment variable VERDI_PARALLEL_WAVE_EXPAND for this feature along
with the -lca command line option.

Support for Waveform Utility
Verdi supports a waveform utility tool called waveutils. It enables extracting, reporting,
VCD converting, and converting to SAIF features on waveform file. This utility tool
provides the following:
* Scalability of performance
* Capability of memory usage
* Capacity to handle large designs
Support for Multi-Process for Extract
The waveultis utility supports multi-process (Common Distributed Processing Library
(CDPL)) on extract. This tool uses the multi-process technique for extracting features
to share the jobs with multiple machines, which results in reduced runtime and memory
consumption on each machine.
To enable the multi-process on waveutils in Verdi, you must set up the

CDPL-related environment as follows:
* setenv VERDI_CDPL_ENABLE 1
* setenv VERDI_CDPL_HOST_FILE $HOST_FILE

The waveutils utility has the following limitations:
* Supports only input file version equal or greater than 2.0.
* Supports only fully array/struct/record.
* Does not support formbus.
* Does not filter user interested scope without any signals.
* Does not support information with sequence.
* Does not support "?" in -scope, -exclude_scopeand -sig.
* The unmatched scope/sig/exclude_scope message is printed only on console.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is signal based waveform
file.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is dumped by cheetah
technique.
* The thread number cannot be one when a multi-process is opened.
The memory limit flow cannot work with the multi-process flow.

Strict Exclusions Mode
In strict exclusions mode, excluding a covered object is not allowed. If you load an exclude
file in strict exclusions mode, only the uncovered objects in the exclude file are excluded.
Objects that are covered are not excluded even if they are listed in the exclude file.
When a region such as a module, module instance, or covergroup was excluded in
previous releases and had only uncovered objects in it, the region was excluded and an
exclusion for it could be saved to an exclude file. If a region contained both covered and
uncovered child objects, exclusions for uncovered child objects were not created and
they could not be saved. Starting with this release, when a region is excluded in strict
exclusions mode and it contains both covered and uncovered objects then its uncovered
child objects are excluded properly and those exclusions can be saved to an exclude file.
Note that if annotations are set on the region's exclusion, then those annotations are
automatically propagated to these uncovered child objects when the parent object is
excluded in strict mode.
This feature is now supported for the following exclusions:
* Module/Instance-level exclusions
* Covergroup definitions/instance-level exclusions

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses
Verdi enables you to select any two coverpoints from an n-dimensional cross and project
the cross coverage data into a two-dimensional projection table with those two coverpoints
as the X and Y axis.
This feature helps in identifying coverage holes in the cross, such as when no bins are
covered, when a given coverpoint has a specific value.
For each cross, Verdi provides a list of projection tables and arranges the tables using the
following ranking criteria:
* Rows or columns that are completely uncovered
* Cells that are uncovered in table cells
* Low-coverage cells in table cells
Note that a low-coverage cell is a cell whose score is less than a tenth of the overall score
of a cross.
Also, projections with the same coverage for every cell are considered as least interesting
projections.

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses

To generate two-dimensional projection tables for an n-dimensional cross, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
Consider a cross of the coverpoints: X, Y, and Z in the following figure:

In the table, the red color represents Not Covered and the green color represents
Covered. This table shows the details of entire cross coverage.
It becomes difficult to find coverage holes from the table.
To generate two-dimensional projection tables for a cross of X, Y, and Z, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.
When you click the Cross 2D Proj button, Verdi projects the cross coverage data into twodimensional tables as X x Y, X x Z, and Y x Z using the ranking criteria mentioned above.

Enhancement to Specification Linking

To determine whether a section is linked to a top-plan or a sub-plan, different colors are
allocated to the section. To understand the color coding of the sections, perform the
following steps:
1. Click Tools -> Preferences to open the Application Preferences dialog box and click
Spec Colors in Plan View:

The Application Preferences dialog box shows the default color coding of linked,
ignore, and todo sections of a top plan and its sub-plans. You can change the color
coding as per your preference.
2. Click Save to save your updates.
If an annotation is linked to more than one plan, its color coding is determined by the
planner. You can left-click such annotations to view their linked features. For example, the
following figure shows the text that is linked with both the top plan and its sub-plan:

You cannot create any link or modify any existing link of a sub-plan from a top plan. For
this, you need to directly open the sub-plan and make updates. To reflect the updates of
the sub-plan in the top plan, you need to refresh its linked sections in the top plan.
This feature has the following limitation:
* This feature is not supported when you run a specification review.

In previous releases, Verdi provided a unique feature ID for each plan and feature. This
feature ID is globally unique and supports concurrent edits in the same .hvp file. However,
its length makes it cumbersome for people to read and use in other documents.
Starting with this release, Verdi provides a new built-in string attribute, HVP_FEAT_ID,
which is short, user-friendly, and easy-to-manage ID. Note that this new HVP_FEAT_ID
is not globally unique and is only unique within the HVP file. Moreover, it enables only a
single user to edit any .hvp file at a time to avoid conflicts.

Creating a Custom Compound ID Attribute
As HVP_FEAT_ID conveys information only about feature ID, you can create a custom
compound ID attribute that may convey additional information about a feature, such as
its project number and block number along with HVP_FEAT_ID. This custom attribute, say

FULL_ID, can be created using the HVP file and the Verdi GUI. In the HVP file, use the
following syntax to construct FULL_ID:
attribute string PRJ_ID = "P1";
attribute string BLK_ID = "B1";
attribute string FULL_ID =
"${PRJ_ID}_${BLK_ID}_${HVP_FEAT_ID}";

Verdi enables you to save the current configuration of the panes in the GUI using
bookmarks. Bookmarks provide quick access to these saved views and enable you to
easily toggle between them.
Bookmarks are useful when you need to analyze multiple sections of a design or views of
different coverage results. Consider a scenario in which you perform several operations to
select a particular scope, configure Verdi panes, apply a Plan filter, and so on.
The bookmark feature allows you to save such setups and return to them in the future by
selecting the saved bookmark.
Bookmarks enable you to save pane configurations, pane dock and undock status, scroll
bar locations, expand/collapse status, column configurations, sorting, filtering, and so on.
However, it does not save information such as which database, user data, HVP files,
exclusions/elfiles, specifications, and modifiers files are loaded, so that you can use the
same bookmark for different data sets.
This section discusses the following topics:
* Creating Bookmarks
* Editing Bookmarks
* Saving and Loading Bookmarks

Saving and Loading Bookmarks
You can save bookmarks using File-->Save Bookmarks(see the figure below). A saved
bookmark file has .bk as its default suffix. Bookmarks are independent of the specific
coverage database or design that is loaded when they are created.
Thus, you can create a bookmark while viewing one design and reload that bookmark to
return to the same view/configuration but with different data.
To load a bookmark, use File --> Load Bookmarks(see the figure below).

Consider a scenario in which you load version1 of simv_v1.vdb, navigate to the packet
covergroup, view the bins of a coverpoint z, and scroll both Summary and covDetail
panes.

Then, you notice that certain bins, such that no[0e:0f], are not hit and you decide to
improve the test. Now, you can create a bookmark for this view and save it for future use
(see the figure below).

After improving the test, you collect coverage in simv_v2.vdb, which has the same shape
as that of simv_v1.vdb.
Now, loading the saved bookmark instantly takes you to the bins that were previously not
hit and should be hit with the improved test. For example, the no[0e:0f] bin is now hit
with the improved test (see the figure below):

To load a bookmark file on the Verdi command line, use the -bookmark
<bookmark_file.bk> option as follows:
verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb -bookmark <bookmark_file.bk> &

Bookmarks may not restore the following information correctly:
* Toggle signal vector compressed and expanded bits are not preserved.
* Covergroup expanded bins and the bins shown by "Show More" in crossbin tables are
not preserved.

In Verdi Planner, various functional coverage objects such as covergroups, covergroup
instances, coverpoints, crosses, and bins may be used as sources for data in a plan
feature.
These are connected to plan features by name. As these functional coverage objects were
explicitly created to collect coverage, it is helpful to know if any object was created but left
out of the plan.
Starting with this release, Verdi Coverage provides a new feature that enables you to
find functional coverage objects that are not referenced by any feature in the plan "unmapped" objects - and report them in an .hvp file.

To find unmapped objects in a plan, invoke the Report Unmapped Objects form using the
Plan -> Report Unmapped Objects command.

The following figure shows the Report Unmapped Objects form:
Figure 79

The Report Unmapped Objects Form

In the Report Unmapped Objects form, you can specify the plan to report from the list of
plans.
Also, you can specify the type of unmapped objects that you need to map. The types of
objects are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
* Point/Cross
* Bins
To generate the report for covergroup instances, for example, select the Cover Group
Instance check box in the Report Unmapped Objects form.
In the form, you can select the following different strategies that determine the number of
objects to be reported:
* High
This strategy considers a definition/variant and an instance as separate entities. If a
definition/variant is mapped but its one or more instances are not mapped, then the
instances are considered as unmapped.
For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints, cp1 and cp2, cross
cr1, and instance cg_inst. If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and High
is selected as a strategy to determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is
reported as unmapped.

As the unmapped objects are reported as a complete HVP plan, you can include the

the main verification plan by collating unmapped and newly-created coverage into their
proper meaningful places in the main plan.

Specification Coverage Merge

Specification Coverage Merge
Verdi Coverage provides the specification coverage for each PDF in a plan. Previously, if
the same PDF was linked to different plans, you needed to select each plan separately.
You could view the specification coverage for the PDF in each plan. There was no way to
see the total coverage for a PDF from all linked plans.
The specification coverage feature now provides an overall summary of the specification
coverage for the PDF with the specification coverage from different plans.

To merge the specification coverage for a PDF from different plans, the toggle button
added in the Spec Files view of the HvpDetail pane.

The algorithm provides priority to calculate each plan, which is categorized as Linked,

This section explains how VC Formal coverage is integrated with the Verdi coverage
reporting flow.
The two primary links between Verdi and VC Formal are displaying VCS Formal results in
Verdi, and linking VC Formal results into your verification plan using Verdi Planner.

The section describes how Verdi coverage is used to display and link to VC Formal
results. This sectio

The properties are categorized according to usage fields in VC Formal as:
* assert: The property specifies an assertion to be solved. Its values are proven,
inconclusive, vacuous, and falsified.
* assume: The property specifies as a constraint.
* cover: The property specifies as a cover property. Its values are covered, inconclusive,
and uncoverable.
* unused: The property is disabled.
VC Formal Coverage in Verdi
To load the coverage database generated with VC Formal in Verdi, use the following
command:
verdi -cov -covdir my_covdb.vdb

-cov: Starts Verdi in the coverage mode
-covdir: Opens the coverage database
my_covdb.vdb: The name of the coverage database that gets opened. This is specified in
the test.tcl script with the save_covdb command.

The command generates the following pane:
Figure 83

The Verdi Coverage Assert Pane

The VC Formal information is displayed in the Assert tab in the columns: FVtype,
FVstatus, and FVdepth.
This information should be same as the VC Formal results. The green color represents
Proven or Covered, the red color represents Falsified, Uncoverable, or Vacuous, and the
yellow color represents Inconclusive.
FVtype indicates the usage field. The value in this column can be either Assert, Cover, or

Assume.

FVstatus indicates the run status of VC Formal. Its possible values depend on FVtype:

* If FVtype is Assert, the value of FVstatus can be Proven, Inconclusive, Falsified, or
Vacuous.
* If FVtype is Cover, the value of FVstatus can be Covered, Inconclusive, or
Uncoverable.
The FVdepth column is interpreted as follows:
* If FVstatus is Proven, Vacuous, or Uncoverable and its value is -1, it represents
infinite depth.
* For other FVstatus, N>=0 represents the depth of the trace.

Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP
VC Formal results can be annotated automatically onto features in your verification plan.
Using these results, you can measure your expectations with FVstatus.
The figure below shows VC Formal results in a verification plan with attributes and metrics.
Figure 84

VC Formal Results in HVP

To measure the VC Formal Assert status in HVP, perform the following steps:
1. Set the expected FV Assert status with FV attribute values using
fvassert_expected_status.
feature f_default;
//These values are same as default value, no need
//assignments again here.
//
fvassert_expected_status = proven;
//
fvassert_expected_mindepth = -1;
//
fvcover_expected_status = covered;
//
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 0;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.*";
feature f_expected_assigned;
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive;
fvassert_expected_mindepth = 50;
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 50;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.a2", "property:
fsm.a_loop_break", "property: fsm.c2";

2. Add measures with property type sources and reference the FV Assert metric.
The new FV Assert built-in metric is added to keep the score of the FV Assert status
against users' expectation.
If FVstatus is same as fv

For example, the matching property top.a11: FVtype=assert and
FVstatus=Proven. If the expectation is fvassert_expected_sthe tatus
= Proven, the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1. If the expectation is
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive and fvassert_expected_depth =
60, the FVAssert metric score becomes 0/1.
For example, consider the following figure that shows six cases to measure the VC
Formal Assert status in your verification plan:

Case1: fsm.a2: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is falsified, FVdepth is 6 and it is
excluded. In the top.f_default.m1 feature, the property: fsm.* source matches
the excluded property, therefore, no score is added.
Case2: fsm.a_loop_break: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is inconclusive, and FVdepth
is 70. In the top.f_expected_assigned feature, fvassert_expected_status is
inconclusive and fvassert_expected_mindepth is 50 which are set by users. It is met
with users' expectations and the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1.
Case3: fsm.a_trans: FVtype is assume. In the top.f_assume feature,
fvassume_status is reviewed which is set by users. The FVAssert metric score

becomes 1/1.

Case4: fsm.c_blk_cnt: FVtype is cover, FVstatus is covered, and FVdepth is 1. In
the top.f_default feature, with default attribute values, fvcover_expected_status
is covered and fvcover_expected_maxdepth is 0. Compare FVstatus to expected
attributes values and if the expectation does not meet, the FVAssert metric score
becomes 0/1.
Case5: fsm.c_trans, no FV annotation. In the top.f_default.m_no_fv_ann
measure, matching fsm.c_trans without FV annotation, the FVAssert metric
becomes 0/1 because the FVAssert metric is referred explicated in measure.
Case6: dummy source. In the top.f_default.m_dummy measure, for all metrics for no
matching region, the score becomes all 0.

The background color in the Compare column denotes the result of the comparison.
* Green: Linked section is the same in the new document
* Yellow: Linked section in the old document differs from the new document.
* Red: Linked section is removed in the new document.
Location Column
The location column in the Spec Review Transaction window provides information about
where the linked section can be found in the old document and the new document.
You can double-click on it to open and show the text it points to. Verdi automatically scrolls
the spec viewer to the right position.
Clicking on a Row in Review List View
Clicking on a row in the Review List View, prompts Verdi Coverage to:
* Show diff text in the Old Selection and New Selection text browser.
* HVP Hierarchy List view moves to the corresponding feature to which the section is
linked.

Deleting a Server
You can delete a server using the
icon. When you delete a server, Verdi asks for
confirmation of the operation as follows:
Figure 116

Deleting a Server

Once you click OK to confirm, the related server pane is closed automatically, if currently
open. The plans linked to the server also loose connection to the server and are not able
to link, unlink and sync issues.
Deleting a server breaks the existing association between the server and the plans linked
to it.

Managing Issues in Verdi HVP
Once you have configured and connected to the Redmine servers, you can access the
issue data using the Issue Management pane.
The Issue Management pane is a web page based flexible pane that hosts the third web
page. It provides following extending features besides the capability of hosting the third
party tool:
* List Issues - Shows issues matching a given criterion in the pane.
* Filter Issues - Filters issues based on the filters provided by the third part tool.
* Show Issue Details - Shows the issue details in the Issue Details page.
* Link Issues - Link selected/checked issues to the currently selected feature in the HVP
plan.
* Create an issue and link it to a feature.
This functionality is described in detail in the following sections:
* Finding, Creating, and Filtering Issues
* Displaying Linked Features of an Issue
* Creating Bug Metric and Adding Source Regions From Issues
* Linking a Feature to an Issue
* Unlinking a Feature from an Issue
* Linking the Plan to Projects in Server
* Linking to a Third-Party Issue Server
* Syncing With Issue Server
* Displaying Bug Details
* Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature

Finding, Creating, and Filtering Issues
You can use all the capabilities of the third party tool including finding, creating and filtering
issues in the Issue Management tool.
Displaying Linked Features of an Issue
Verdi planner provides a convenient way to know if the current issue in the Issue
Management plan is linked to any feature. To do that, click the button Show Feature to
find the linked feature in the HVP Plan pane.
Those features linked to the issue are annotated with a small icon <Provide icon>. If you
leave the Issue Details page, the small i

er URL are saved to the
.hvp.bug file.
The server Id is also a part of issue_id whose format is <server_id>:<third party

issue id>.

The server URL in the .bug file is the only key that lets the HVP planner find the correct
server to link in Verdi.
* If you link a plan to an issue server, the server Id and server URL is saved to the .bug
file.
* If open a plan created by another user and if server_URL in plan is not found in the
existing Verdi server list, Verdi prompts you to configure a new server with the server Id
and server URL in the plan.
The new created server configuration is saved in <user.home>/.vedi/
server.config and is listed in the Server pane.
* If server_URL is found in the existing server list, Verdi uses the existing server to
connect to the third party tool. Verdi internally creates a mapping from the server Id of
the existing server to the server Id defined in the .bug file.

However, if you want to replace server_id in the bug file with the one of the existing
server, you can save it as another plan using the Save as option.
In the Save as dialog box, select the Override Server Id option to replace the server Ids
in the .bug file.
Figure 125

Linking to a Third Party Issue Server

It is suggested that you define a server with the same Server Id for a project or
a team.
Syncing With Issue Server
The HVP planner provides a way to automatically link a feature in plan with issues,
provided that these issues have a field named verdi_plan_feature_id and its value
matched feature_id.
If an issue satisfies this above condition, a bug source region is added to the measure
source list of the feature.
You can use the CSM item Sync Issues to refresh these bug source regions once you
add or delete some related issues in the third party issue management tool.
Select the feature(s) for which you want to create bug source regions. If no feature is
selected in the plan, all features in the plan are affected.

Each bug status belongs to one of the two categories Open or Closed. If the category is
not given it is set to Open by default.
Displaying Bug Details
The HVP pane provides the CSM Show Bug Details that shows the issues related to the
current feature or bug measure source in the plan correspondingly.

Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature
Once a plan is connected to the issue servers, you can select a feature in the HVP plan
and use CSM Create an Issue to open the New Issue page in the Issue Management
tool.
If there is more than one server connected to the plan, a sub level menu is available to list
all servers.

Creating a New Issue

After the New Issue page is loaded, you can drag the feature to the desired text field. The
full path of the feature and the feature Id in the plan is appended to the text fields.

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics
Verification Planner for Verdi supports the following additional built-in derived test metrics
to track verification progress:
* Percent Metric for Test Metric
* Test.completion Metric
Using these derived metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status
and test completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
In previous releases, the built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for submetrics test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;

In previous releases, the test metric reports the basic number of tests with status pass,
fail, warn, unknown, and assert in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the
percentage of these scores.

Verification Planner for Verdi reports percentage score for each enum value of the test
metric. This enables you to get the percentage of tests with status pass, fail, warning,
unknown, or assert. The following is the list of the derived percent sub-metrics:
* test.percent.pass
* test.percent.fail
* test.percent.warn
* test.percent.unknown
* test.percent.assert
The score of a percent metric is the percentage of each enum's value of the test metric
against the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if a is the integer count of the built-in test metric enum value and b is the
integer count of the total number of tests, then the percentage metric is computed as
(a / b)*100

For example, if
test.pass = 8
test.fail = 2
test = 10

then the value of test.percent.pass = 8/10 and is reported as 80%.
The following is the example for the usage of percent metrics:
feature f1;
test.percent.pass = test.percent.pass > 60%;
measure test, test.percent.pass m1;
source = "testname*";

Consider the following example,
feature parent:
test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:50.00%
feature block1
test:5[pass:3 fail:2 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:60.00%
feature block2
test:1[pass:0 fail:1 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass: 0.00%

In this example, the test.percent.pass score in feature parent is calculated from the test
score of:
feature parent test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0] 50%

which is equal to 3/6. The total test score of feature parent is the sum of the test scores of
feature block1 and feature block2.
The following figure shows the derived sub-metrics displayed by Verdi coverage:
Figure 128

Viewing Percent Metric in Verdi Coverage

Test.completion Metric
The test.completion metric allows you to measure the progress of tests being written
against the number of tests expected to be written.
The score of the test.completion metric is the ratio of total integer count of all sub-metrics
of the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and the
expected number of tests in a plan/feature. The expected number of tests should be set
using the test.expected attribute.
Where,test.completion=total_test_count/test.expected and
total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.as sert+test.unknown
Test.expected Attribute
You can use the test.expected built-in attribute assignment, as shown below, to set the
expected number of tests in feature/plan scope.
test.expected = <number>;
The expected number is like an annotation value kept in feature/plan node. The default
value of test.expected is 0.

Figure 129

Viewing test.expected in Verdi Coverage

The test.completion metric can be calculated only after setting the
test.expectedattribute.
The following example illustrates the usage of the test.completion metric:
feature Goal_pass;
test.expected = 2;
test.percent.pass = (test.percent.pass >= 0.5);
measure test, test.percent.pass, test.completion Measure_1;
source = "test3";

The following are examples that describe how sections containing images are handled
during spec-linking.
Consider the following two cases for a linked section containing images:
* A section contains images and text as well.
* A section contains image(s) only
These two cases are handled different ways during review and updating the section to a
new document during spec-linking.
Case 1: Section contains both images and text
In this case spec-linking follows the following process:
* Review and update the text to the new section in the new document.
* Find the images in the updated section in the new document.
* Generate a new section based on the text section and images, the decision table below
lists all the possibilities and review results.
Table 10

Review Results for Text and Image Selection
Image Text Matching

Missing

New

Matching

matching

Conflict

Missing

missing

New

The review result for an image depends on the updated text section in the new document.
There can be three results for image comparison: Matching, Missing, New. The result
conflict is not applicable for images.
* Matching: The image in the old document is found in the new document and it is
present by the updated text section.
In this case, image is found means that the image in the old and new documents are
the same.

* Missing: The image is not found in the new document, or it is found but it is NOT in the
updated text section.
* New: The image is in the updated text section but not in the old document. In Verdi
New is treated as a Conflict.
The image and text works as an entire link in the review process, so whatever actions
(accept, reject) that you choose to apply, the action is applied to both the image and the
text.
You may not be able to treat the text or the image as separate review-able objects.
Case 2: A section contains only image(s)
Without considering in the text in the review process, the search scope of an image is not
limited to the updated text section in the new document. The whole document is within the
search scope.
For example, if an image at page 10 was selected and linked as a section in the old
document, Verdi spec-linking feature searches the image at page 10 then around page 10,
that is page 11, page 9, page12, page 8 and so on, until the image is found.
If the image is found, then it is marked as matching, otherwise it is marked as missing.
The review result types new and conflict are not applicable in this case.

Difference Between Masks and Filters
As discussed, Verdi Planner supports two ways to customize the features displayed:
masks and filters. Though they appear to operate in a similar way, there is a distinct
difference in the way that they behave. Filters not only remove features from the displayed
plan view, they also disable the effect that those removed features' scores have on the
remainder of the plan. For example suppose a feature A with a score of 50% has 2 child
features A1 (0%) and A2 (100%). If you filter out feature A1 then its 0% score no longer
affects the parent feature A and A's score becomes 100%.
Masks are different because they simply hide rows based on the masking criteria. The
hidden rows' scores continue to affect scores. In the same example if A1 is masked, its
parent feature A's score remains at 50%.
In addition to this, the key differences between quick filters and masks are as follows:
* Any changes applied to a quick filter also affects scores; masks do not affect scores.
* Operations on quick filters can be saved as a modifier file that can be reloaded again;
masks cannot be saved as a modifier file.
* For quick filters, the filter icon
is displayed only when you click on the Quick Filter
icon; the mask icon
is always displayed on the right of Result columns.
* Quick filters are for attribute columns; masks are for Result columns.
Quick filters and masks can exist at the same time. However, quick filters have higher
priority than masks.

either click the Apply or OK to view the changes.

Transformation Rules of User Data to HVP Annotation
The following are the transform rules of User Data while annotating to HVP:
* Scientific notation with 'e' notation use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes
preference option is disabled):
For numbers with more than 5 decimal places.
Any number greater than or equal to 1,000,000 or less than or equal to -1,000,000.
All the other use cases are represented using normal notation with 5 decimal
places.
* SI Prefixes use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes preference option is enabled)
The following values are represented in SI Prefixes:
Numbers greater than or equal to 1000 and less than or equal to -1000.
Numbers in between -0.01 and 0.01, except 0.
* Floating point precision:
Scientific notation with 'e' notation: 6 decimal places
SI Prefixes: 6 decimal places
Normal Notation: 5 decimal places
* Display format for Scientific notation with 'e' notation:
Trailing zero: "." should be followed by "0" when there is no mantissa (for example,
1.0e+09).
Leading zero: A minimum of 2 digits are required for notation presentation. That is,
leading zero is displayed if the exponent is less than 3 digits.
* Display format for SI Prefixes:
Trailing zero: No trailing zero is used in the SI Prefixes. For example, 1M.

Following is the syntax when specified on the simulation UCLI command line:
fsdbDumpClassObject class_name_or_object_name [option]*

Where, class_name_or_object_name is the class name or object name in full hierarchy
format that is specified to dump.

Dumping Dynamic Class Objects

When you invoke VCS to compile the design, you must use the -debug_access
+class or -debug_access+ckbd options at the compile command line.
To dump the expandable class pointer signal, set the following environment variable:
setenv FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS 1

Following are the options supported for the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command:
+object_level=depth: Keyword to identify the number of levels of hierarchy to dump for
the subsequent objects. The default value of depth is 1.

Where, depth can have the following value:
N: N level sub-object under the current object or object instantiated from the current class
object.
0: All sub-objects under the current object or objects instantiated from the current class
object.
Note: It is recommended not to set +object_level to 0 as it costs more with a complex
testbench and limited resources.
+fsdbfile+<fil

> setenv FSDB_ENABLE_CLASS
> setenv FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS 1

Dumping Queue, Dynamic Array and Associative Array Inside
Class Object
Use the +fsdb+variant_size_array runtime option to dump non-static arrays
(queue, dynamic array, and associative array) inside class objects. Use the +fsdb
+max_variant_size_array runtime option to set the maximum array size for dumping.
To dump queues, dynamic arrays, and associative arrays inside class objects, use this
runtime option:
+fsdb+variant_size_array

Or set this environment variable:
setenv FSDB_VARIANT_SIZE_ARRAY 1

To set the maximum array size to dump, use this runtime option:
+fsdb+max_variant_size_array=<size>

Or set this environment variable:
setenv FSDB_MAX_VARIANT_SIZE_ARRAY <size>

The default max size is 10.
Specify +fsdb+variant_size_array before +fsdb
+max_variant_size_array=<size>.

Dumping Queue, Dynamic Array, and Associative Array in HDL
Instance
You can enable the dumping of non-static array (queue, dynamic array, and associative
array) in HDL instance using the following options.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option enables dumping for the non-static arrays in HDL instances, such as dynamic
array, queue, and associative array. As the array size can be big, FSDB dumper only
dumps several array elements in a non-static arrays. The default number is 10 and the
array element starts from index 0.
* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option specifies the different element numbers of non-static arrays. The number must
be 0 ~ 1023.
+fsdb+max_variant_size_array=20

* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.

The following are the limitations of this feature:
* For D, Q, and A array dumping, the following types are not supported:
Event
Hybrid array: For example, int [][0:1]

FSDB Dumping for SystemVerilog in VCS

Multi-dimension variant array: For example, int [][]
Struct non-static array: For example, struct {bit b1; reg r1;} s1[];
Array struct contain variant array or variant array struct contain array:
For example, struct { int a[] } s1[0:1] struct { int a[0:1] } s2[]
* Sequence and region are not supported on a variable that contains D,Q, and A arrays.
* For associative array, index type only supports the integral variables which can map to
a one-dimensional packed array.
* Wildcard index type and user-defined index type are not supported for dumping.
* Variant size array dumping does not support class and string. Both are not supported in

FSDB Dumping for SystemVerilog in VCS
Verdi supports the following dumping for SystemVerilog only:
* Built-in data type
* Fixed-size array, non-static struct, built-in data type and the combinations
* One-dimensional variant-size array with built-in data type in class, except an event
* Index of the associative array only supports built-in data types which can map to a onedimensional packed array

FSDB dumping has these limitations:
* Dumping does not support class objects that include encrypted code.
* Dumping does not support mailbox, semaphore, or unpacked union.
* Dumping does not support enum with dimension data type in class.
* Dumping does not support combinations of variant size array and/or struct.
* Dumping does not support struct used in module that has a class member.

* For normal class object dumping, if the class definition has protected information, the

Encrypted IP Waveform
This chapter describes the Encrypted IP Waveform feature, flow summary, and its
limitations.
It includes the following topics:
* Encrypted IP
* Debugging Standalone IP
* Encrypted IP Waveform Flow Summary
