Support for Verdi Machine Learning Library
Starting with this release, Verdi provides you an unified platform to collect data from EDA
tools and allows you to access data for machine learning applications. This platform
includes three abstract layers, such as table, model, and application.Each layer can read
and write from the database of APIs.
In the table layer, the tables are constructed using both C++ and Python. In this layer, you
can construct your own tables and extract specific data by any utility. You can also read
these tables using Python.
In the model layer, pre-defined types and properties can be selected to extract data from
the database by different utilities. These tables can be read using Python as well where
pre-defined relations between types are resolved. Currently, only 'waveform' model is
In the application layer, both the data collection and access methods are provided in the
'Database' class of the 'verdilearn' package in Python. You can take the tables as an input
to their machine learning applications.
These tables provide information about the C++ and Python APIs.

Required Data
For the block stimuli replay flow, a few additional files and settings must be prepared and
specified. After running the simulation, some additional files are generated. The complete
configuration is described below.
The following files must be prepared, if needed, depending on whether you use the twostep or three-step flow in VCS:
* The FSDB file dumping form block-level testbench (BL-TB) simulation, for example,
block.fsdb

* The run file of SoC testbench (SoC-TB) simulation (for VCS two-step flow), for
example, run_soc.f
* The configurations for replay simulation, for example, wi_config
* The simulation compile script, for example, wi_compile.rc
* The simulation run script, for example, wi_run.rc
* The VCS configuration (for VCS three-step flow), for example, synopsys_sim.setup
The following mapping files need to be manually prepared, or they are automatically
created by specific configurations:
* The mapping of input stimuli to apply to the Replay Simulation, for example,
stimuli.map

* The mapping of signals to apply waveform comparison, for example, compare.map

WISIM Replay Block Stimuli on SoC

The following resultant output files are generated.
* The FSDB file by Replay simulation on the SoC after applying the block stimuli, for
example, wi_result.fsdb
* The comparison error report between BL-TB and SoC-TB simulations, for example,
wi_cmp_error.nce

* The comparison summary between BL-TB and SoC-TB simulations in wi_flow.log
To use WISIM to replay block stimuli on SoC, perform the following steps:
* Preparation (for VCS three-step flow):
Analyze the SoC design using vlogan and vhdlan for SystemVerilog and VHDL design,
respectively, and prepare the corresponding script for the analyzed library. Prepare the
configuration file and the corresponding scripts.
* Extract:
Generate WISIM testbench using the -replay_extract option. With Auto_Map and
Auto_Compare_Map, the automatic mapping files are generated in this phase. When
the mapping files or configuration are modified, you can add the -remap option after
-replay_extract to run the remap flow. You can skip generating the design by setting
the environment variable WISIM_SKIP_CG to 1, if you use VCS three-step flow. Then,
load designs from library (analyzed with -kdb=common_elab) with -lib options with
-replay_extract.
* Compile:
Compile the SoC design and WISIM testbench, using the -replay_compile option.
If you compile in the SoC environment, add wi_test.sv during compilation (two-step
flow) or analyze wi_test.sv into witbLib and add WI_TB_TOP (three-step flow) during
elaboration in compile script.
* Simulate:
Run simulation for the SoC design by applying FSDB stimuli under WISIM
testbench, using the -replay_sim option. With Compare_Map or Auto_Compare_Map,
wi_result.fsdb is automatically compared with the block-level one. It is able to
re-compare the same FSDB files with different options (Compare_Option) or signal
mapping (Compare_Map and Auto_Compare_Map) by adding the -recompare option
after -replay_sim.

Configuration File Format
The Configuration file is divided into two parts. They are as follows:
* Common
* Record
The Common part has the following mandatory fields:
* MODE
* SIMV_DAIDIR
* CHECKER_SIM_FILELIST

Assertion Replay for Emulation/FPGA Prototyping

* CHECKERSIM_TOP_MODULE
In the Configuration file, the Common part must always be placed on the
top.
The Record part has the following mandatory field:
* WAVEFORM
Each Record part must be enclosed with parenthesis ({}).
Following is an example of a configuration file. The Mandatory fields and the parenthesis
in the Record part is in bold.
####################################################################
# Common fields
# The fields here will give impact on all FSDB files
####################################################################
//MODE. The same if you specify 1. ex: MODE = 1 [MUST HAVE]
MODE= CHECKER_SIM_WAVEFORM_REPLAY
//abs path. [MUST HAVE]
SIMV_DAIDIR = $PWD/simv.daidir
//optional. Necessary runtime options for running original simulation.
SIMV_OPT =
//optional. Necessary runtime options for running new simulation run.
CHECKER_SIM_OPT =
//optional. Necessary options for compiling new simulation binary.
CHECKER_SIM_COMPILE_OPT = -sverilog -timescale=1ns/1ns
//abs path. [MUST HAVE]
CHECKER_SIM_FILELIST = assert.v
//optional. If this was specified, skeleton is not extracted. The
file(s) here are used as skeleton.
CHECKER_SIM_DESIGN_FILELIST=
//top module names [MUST HAVE]
CHECKER_SIM_TOP_MODULE = top
//optional. Do waveform dumping. Use semicolon to separate tasks
#WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all
+fsdbfile+assertion_result.fsdb ; fsdbDumpSVA
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK =
#####################################################################
# Record fields (Wave dedicated fields)
# The files here will give impact to the WAVE file here only
#####################################################################
############## record 1 ##############
{
//golden file abs path. [MUST HAVE]
WAVEFORM = $PWD/src.fsdb
//optional. Assertion module ports are extracted automatically as the
MAP file to do the replay

Assertion Replay for Emulation/FPGA Prototyping

MAP=
//optional. Specify a file to do the force replay
FORCE_MAP=
//optional. Give a global delay time: impacts all replayed signal in
current record.
DELAY=
DELAY_MAP=
DELAY_EXCLUDE_MAP=
AUTO_MAP=
SCOPE_MAP=
COMPARE_MAP=
AUTO_COMPARE_MAP=
COMPARE_OPT=
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION=
//optional. You can give [+force|+deposit|+force +deposit] Default:
+force
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE=
BLACKBOX_MAP=
}
############## record 2 ##############
{
}

This feature has the following limitations:
* This utility supports only pure Verilog design.
* SVA essential signals must be checker module ports or driven by them.
Cross reference does not work if MAP is generated by filling the field AUTO_MAP.

Cross Log Probing
In some cases, you need to cross-reference multiple logs. The following are the two use
model examples:
* One simulation run generates two logs with time information. While checking these two
logs, many cross references are required.
In this scenario, you can use the log-probing by time feature.
* Open one log twice in two tabs as follows:
The first one is kept as full log without any filtering.
The second one is planned to be filtered.
While checking these two logs, many cross references are required between the
full-text-log and filtered-log.
In this scenario, you can use the log-probing by line feature.
To open the Log Probing dialog box, use the highlighted option on the toolbar.

The log-probing dialog box opens, as shown in the following figure:

Log Probing Dialog Box

The probing is mutual mapping. For example, if Log1 is set to probe Log2, then Log2 is
also set to probe to Log1.
The probe mapping is broken once any mapping log is changed to "none-probing" status.
The breaking is also in mutual way. The probing includes two factors: <Time>
and <Line>.
The usage is explained in the following examples:

Traverse Related Message Search Mechanism
PureLog traces 1000 blocks upward or downward from the starting block that you rightclick. A block is a group of messages with the first line matched by the partitioning rule, for
example, UVM header.
PureLog analyzes the first three lines of each block because:
* The key-value attributes are most likely to sit in the first few lines.
* It can speed up the searching.
Key and value are matched by the exact match mode by default.

Signal Type of Log-to-Wave
The following are the rules for log-to-wave to determine a signal type:
* Contains only a positive integer or a value string (for example, 0x123) : bit-vector
(digital)
* Contains a floating point number or a non-positive integer : analog
* Contains non-numerical data : enum

The PureLog DB enables you to keep the information of logs through the logCompile
script. Whenever you need to check a log for debugging, you can access it through APIs
or by using the simple UI query system. Some PureLog features also rely on the PureLog
DB. Generally, the PureLog DB can be written by the daily regression script at night and
can be accessed by you or PureLog in daytime.

Benefits of PureLog DB
The PureLog DB has the following benefits:
* Better performance: Most PureLog features can have better performance with the
PureLog DB.
* Less memory consumption: Most PureLog features can have less memory
consumption with the PureLog DB.
* AI technology: AI-related features of PureLog rely on the PureLog database.
* Customized application: You can access the PureLog DB through APIs or by using the
query system UI. Based on APIs and query systems, it is easy to develop a customized
application. It means that you can have your own debugging way.

Setting Up the PureLog DB Server
Before saving or reading logs from the PureLog DB, you need to launch the server.
PureLog provides the msgdbControl utility to start or stop the server.

Starting the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>

After starting the server, you can compile logs by logCompile and debug on DB debug
platform.

Stopping the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

Remember to stop server:
* When you finish debugging.
* Before you want to clean up the DB storage.

Restarting the Server
You can restart the server under the same DB storage path. The compiled logs are
preserved.
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> logCompile <opts> # compile/debug
%> msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path> #
restart server

Compiling Logs Into the PureLog DB
PureLog provides the logCompile utility to compile log information into the PureLog DB.
The utility supports CSV format and customized format.

CSV Format
(-log_type="csv")
logCompile
[-log_type="csv"]
-storage_path="<database_storage_path>"
-project_name="<project_name>"
-log_list="<log.ls>"
-separator=','
[-comment='#']
[-none_regexp='-+']
[-quotechar='"']
[-escapechar="\"]
[-hyper_rule="<hyper_rule_path>"]
[-date ="date"]

In case of CSV format, logCompile removes leading and trailing whitespace for each cell
and skips a blank line.
The CSV file list is specified in -log_list="<log.ls>".In this input file, each line includes
two sections. The left side is the input file path, and the right side is the database file path
to be saved.
Example log.ls file
./trace1.csv user_case/trace1.log
./trace2.csv user_case/trace2.log
./

ify the virtual path to be stored in the database.
Default: simWLogCompileDir/<TARGET_LOG>

<TARGET_LOG> is specified by -l or -incr_log option.

* -num_process <NUM_WORKS>: Number of logCompile worker processes for parallel
compilation.
Default: 1

Types of Simulation
The simWLogCompile wrapper consists of following types of simulation:
One Step Simulation
* %> simWLogCompile vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog

-ntb_opts uvm-1.1 -timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH
+incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD -R +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM
+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Two Step Simulation
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Compile with -incr_log option
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT"
-storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1 -virtual_path
"case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls" -incr_log "./simv.log"

Attributes in the PureLog DB
The attributes can be kept in the PureLog DB as string type or numeral type. You can
impose only numeral query on numeral attributes through APIs or the DB debug platform.
If you expect the attributes to be saved in numeral type, here is the summary of the
supported format:
* Number with decimal point (example, 1.6)
* Verilog integer literal constants (size <= 64)
* 0x (example, 0x1200)

A message within a log is supposed to follow certain rules. For example, users expect
that the message "B" shows up after message "A". This kind of a rule is like a message
protocol. In the simulation log, the message protocol can reflect the SoC system protocols.
For example, IP protocols, system power up sequence, system power down sequence,
and so on. During debugging, it is a good start to check message protocols first to narrow
down the debug scope. Message protocol debugging can be done using the GUI or batch
mode.

Message Protocol in GUI Mode
This section provides the flow to check the message protocols:
1. Specify the message protocol (a one-time effort).
Each message protocol may include one or more message events. In the following
case, we try to build the <DMA_RD> protocol that includes the following two events. The
first event is that RISC enables the DMA controller. The second event is that the DMA
controller returns the good status.

To specify the message protocol, perform the following steps:
a. Add the first event through RMB actions on related attributes.

protocolCheck -storage_path STORAGE_PATH -project_name PROJECT
[-dir DIR_LIST] [-date DATE] [-output_log OUTPUT_LOG]
[-protocol_file PROTOCOL_FILE_LIST]
[-protocol_list_file PROTOCOL_LIST_FILE]

Users can add the protocolCheck utility to their daily regression script.
When they debug message protocols, all violations are summarized in the database.
PureLogDB also provides a way to open logs based on message protocols.
Users who debug protocol violations may not know which logs to open.
In that case, use the From Protocol Report tab in the Open Database dialog box.
This tab opens logs based on protocols.
Pick certain protocols and all related logs open.
The Violation column shows protocols with protocol violations.
In most cases, open only the protocols with violations.

2. Specify the click function in the PureLog command option:
purelogDB -click_func_header "<header1> <header2> <headerN>"
-click_func_file "<file1> <file2> <fileN>"

In the command option, the click function of <header1> is described in <file1>,
the click function of <header2> is described in <file2>, and the click function of
<headerN> is specified in <fileN>.

Abnormal Analysis
When a log file includes enormous lines and messages, it becomes very difficult to find
the abnormal points. The Abnormal Analysis feature of PureLog sums up the abnormal
points in a log. You only need to feed PureLog with some golden logs that are related to
the current error log.

Launching Abnormal Analysis
To launch Abnormal Analysis, set the following environment variables:
setenv PYTHONPATH
setenv VL_VERSION TD
setenv PYTHONPATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python:$PYTHONPATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
module load cmlp/2021.06-py36

More Details of Time Check Enable
Some timing violations happen before the reset stage. You can ignore these violations.
In the TimeCheckEnable section, you can set the message after which timing violations for
the selected instance are captured.
If you do not specify a message, all timing violations are captured.

Open or Check Timing Violation Report
To open or check the Timing Violation Report, perform the following steps:
1. Under the Tools menu, click New Timing Violation Report to open the timing violation

2. Click Open database icon in the timing violation window. Follow the guidelines that
appears in the dialog box, to open reports within the database.

3. The summary reports for each component appears and sorted by the count of
violations.

4. Use check or uncheck to record the violations which are checked.

5. Use waive or unwaive violations to record the reason and username for the projectlevel review.

The waived violations are moved to the root node <Waived> in the bottom.

6. Click View Details to see raw messages in the SmartLog.

The action is only available in the node of simulation log.
7. Click the link of SmartLog to access related signals in nWave.

In the common active fan-in path report (refer to Check Common Active
Fan-in for Timing Violation), it helps to display the temporal flow view result.

Save or Load the Waived Result
Save or Load the Waived Result has the following sections:
Save or Load wavied result of current opened report

To save or restore waived results for current opened reports, use the actions listed below:
* Under File menu,
Click Load Timing Violation Waive Status to restore the waived result.
Click Save Timing Violation Waive Status to save the waived result.

Save or Load whole Database.
Use msgdbControl to export the waived result from the database.
msgdbControl export_data -storage_path $storagePath -type timingWaiveFile
-project_name $projName [-date yyyy-mm-dd] -output $outputFile

* -date: Is optional. If not specified, it exports waive file based on the latest date. -date
is in yyyy-mm-dd format.
For example, 2025-09-17.
* -output: Is the option to specify the destination path for the exported file.
Feed the overall waive file into logCompile in the next run.
logCompile timing_violation -waive $waiveFile

Regression Debug Automation (RDA)
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by RDA as a part of this
release:
* Static Bug Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA)
* RDA Integration With Verdi VMS

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects domain crossing and
glitch issues, such as reset domain crossing (RDC) or glitches. Static bug finding is a part
of RTL sign off and saves weeks of efforts in a project cycle.
Debugging violations found by static bug finding can be difficult, especially when RDC
bugs appear in large numbers, such as during MCP verification. RDA offers a Static Bug
Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA) solution that automatically organizes violations into
fewer groups. This solution connects violations to waveform, source code, and simulation
log for further debugging and uses Verdi for analysis.
* Technology Overview
* SBRCA Usage
* Smart Waiver

Technology Overview
SBRCA helps you to debug the static bug findings using Verdi. VCS complies with the
SDC commands containing RDC/Glitch property. After completing simulation with VCSSDC, SBRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and helps in finding out the violations.
SBRCA extracts details of a violation message and displays the information in a binstructured report.
RDA provides Verdi GUI to review SBRCA reports generated after analyzing violations
from the log file. Use the Verdi GUI to continue debugging in the source code, logs, and
waveform.

Grouping
The Grouping feature is a core part of SBRCA. It helps to review all the violations grouped
into bins with different information, which means that the same bin might have the same
bug.
You can group violations using the following grouping rules for RDC and Glitch:
RDC
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* reset: Group by the same reset signals name
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command

Glitch
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command
On Verdi GUI, you can select the Group by option to choose the grouping rule. Using the
Grouping feature, you can review the results of different grouping rules in the active report
window as shown in the following figure:

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS
You need to use RDA plugin to load RDA in Verdi VMS. To invoke the RDA plugin, perform
the following steps:
1. Add RDA plugin to synopsys_eman.setup.
plugins:
- rda:
<VERDI_HOME>/platform/linux64/bin/rcaIntgrFlow/python38/rca_plugin.so

where <VERDI_HOME> is the full path of Verdi.
2. Load the RDA plugin in your .emc file.
plugins:
- rda

3. Register a load RDA report template using the following command:
vms admin register_custom_template -t $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/
python38/etc/vms/web_template/load_rda_report.emd -a

The Open RDA report button is added to the Verdi VMS GUI.

When you run the vms -gui command, select a session. Click the Open RDA report
button to open the RCA Manager window, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 579

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS

Enabling RDA Binning
RDA binning is always enabled in the RDA plugin.

Enabling Debug Facilitator/RCA
Define the debug engines Debug Facilitator and DUTRCA. Enable these engines for the
error patterns that you want to analyze.
Debug facilitator is defined by default; you need to include DF.emc as shown in the
following command:
include:
- $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/python38/etc/vms/engine_template/DF.emc

However, you need to define DUTRCA as shown in the following commands:
debug_engines :
- name: DUTRCA
cmd: $current_dir/dutrca_debug_engine_cmd.sh
log_file: $${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_dutrca_debug_engine.log
run_dir: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH
custom_values:
REF_CL_WORK_DIR: $$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL_WORK_DIR
DUTRCA_CONFIG: $current_dir/dutrca.yaml

TARGET_SCOPE: minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0
REPORT_PATH: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH/dutrca_report.xml

After defining the debug engines, enable them for the specific error patterns. In the
following example, DF and DUTRCA are enabled for the uvm_error error pattern:
error_patterns:
- name: uvm_error
pattern:
(?P<Type>UVM_ERROR)\s+.*\s+\[(?P<Code>\S+)\]\s+(?P<Description>.*)
base_status: fail
custom_status: uvm_error
priority: 0
debug_rerun_count: 1
debug_engines: DF DUTRCA

the test fails in its custom failure category. Parallel debug provides the following benefits:
* Overlapping of the regular run and the debug run saves the overall turnaround time.
* Analyzing the RDA report and debugging before

DesignDiff
The DesignDiff feature introduces a GUI to compare the source code of two designs:
the reference design and the target design. You can analyze the comparison results.
DesignDiff shows differences between the two designs based on the semantics of the HDL
code, rather than the text of the HDL code. The DesignDiff feature includes the following
functions:
* Integrates the RTL difference (XML format) into DesignDiff.
* Adds the difference functionality.
* Displays the number of design changes in the nTrace hierarchy.
* Allows you to click each scope to view related design changes.
* Shows the target source code in Verdi.
The DesignDiff feature provides options to calculate and display the number of design
changes in the Instance View pane and ignore any module or source code file.
This section provides details on the following topics:
* DesignDiff Requirements
* Enabling DesignDiff
* Reviewing DesignDiff
* Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
* DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Requirements

DesignDiff Requirements
The following are the requirements for the DesignDiff feature:
* The RTL difference generates the DesignDiff report only when the VSO folder is
available; otherwise, it throws errors.
* You must provide the target and reference designs as two versions of the same
design. It allows DesignDiff to generate meaningful reports for review and analysis. To
generate the target and reference design directories, refer to the Generating Required
Directories section.

Generating Required Directories
The DesignDiff feature requires simv.daidir and ref.daidir directories for the current
and reference designs, respectively. To generate these directories, use the following
compile options for the respective simulator:
* VCS
When VCS is used for simulation, compile the design using the -kdb=designdiff
compile-time option, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -kdb=designdiff -lca [other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the other compile-time options.
* VCS with VSO.ai
When VCS is used with VSO.ai, compile the design using the -vso cso -kdb option
along with other compile-time options, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -vso cso -kdb -lca [other_options]

After compilation, the *.vso folder is generated along with *.daidir in the same
directory.
You must save these two files at the same directory level.
* Third-Party Simulators

Enabling DesignDiff

For third-party simulators, elaborate the design using the -useius=adv -designdiff
or -usemti=adv -designdiff option along with other compile-time options, as shown
in the following command:
For IUS flow,
% elabcom -useius=adv -designdiff [other_options]

For MTI flow,
% elabcom -usemti=adv -designdiff [other_options]

Enabling DesignDiff
After generating the target and reference design directories using the compile-time options
provided in the Generating Required Directories section, enable the DesignDiff feature
using the designdiff command.
Use the following syntax to compare the two simv.daidir design directories:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
[other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the DesignDiff runtime options. You can add the following
DesignDiff runtime options:
* -diffreport <filename>: Specify the file name for the report. By default, the file
name is designdiff_report.xml.
* -ignore_module <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of module
names to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_module <filename> option, refer
to the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -ignore_file <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of source code
files to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_file <filename> option, refer to
the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -with_score: Calculates the design change score for the report. For more details,
refer to the -with_score section.
For example, % designdiff -dbdir ./target/simv.daidir -refdir ./reference/
ref.daidir.
The designdiff command analyzes the design difference details and generates the
corresponding report in an XML format, designdiff_report.xml.

To view the generated report, designdiff_report.xml, in Verdi, run the following
command:
% verdi -load_trace_report <generated_xml_report>, or
% designdiff -load_report <generated_xml_report>

You must load Designdiff reports using the command line; the GUI Load RDA
Trace Report option is not supported for DesignDiff reports.
For example, % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml

The following figure displays the GUI overview of the DesignDiff report uploaded to Verdi
using the % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml command:
Figure 586

DesignDiff Report Overview in Verdi GUI

The GUI of the DesignDiff report consists of the following three main components:
* Instance View
* Source View
* Source Code Changes
You can debug a design in the following two ways:
* Instance: To check the design difference of an instance with a large number of designdifference changes, click the scope in the Instance View pane. This synchronizes the
Source View pane with the source code of the module and displays the design-change
entries in the Source Code Changes section.
* Source code changes: When you click an entry in the Source Code Changes section,
the Source View pane displays the corresponding difference between the two designs.

Instance View
The Instance View pane displays the hierarchy tree of the design. The instance table
provides the name of the module, and the inclusive and exclusive change for the selected
instance, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 587

Instance View

When you run the designdiff command with the -with_score option, the DesignDiff
feature calculates the design changes and displays the score in the Instance View
pane, as shown in Figure 588. The score indicates the summation of the design changes
(addition, deletion, and modification).
% designdiff -dbdir <target>.daidir -refdir <reference>.dbdir -with_score

The exclusive change indicates the number of current scope changes, and the inclusive
change indicates the number of current scope and the child scope changes. A higher
count for an instance means that the instance contains a higher number of design
changes.

Figure 588

Instance View With -with_score

When you run the designdiff command without the -with_score option, the scores for
the design changes are not displayed in the Instance View pane. However, the design

change scope and the modules with design changes are highlighted in yellow, as shown in
Figure 589

Instance View Without -with_score

Source View
When you click an entry in the Instance View or Source Code Changes pane, the
Source View pane displays the source code difference between the two designs. The
following figure displays the Source View pane:

The Source View pane is split into two vertical views, where the left view displays the
reference design view and the right view displays the target design view. The right-arrow
icon,

, in the Source View pane highlights the active difference.

The Source View pane consists of the following information:
* Status string
It displays the name of the module in the ignore list.
* Icons

everal elements, such as the File column, the Module

* The following priority is used for comparison:
File column = Module column > Source code difference (add, delete, edit) > begin line

> end line.

* The following priority is followed for sorting when Syntax is available:
1. Syntax
2. File
3. Edit mode
4. Begin line
5. End line
If two items match on one sorting element, use the next element to decide the order.
* You can sort entries alphabetically by file name or module name.
* If the file name or module name is the same, entries are sorted based on differences in
the source code. Entries that are not deleted appear before entries that are deleted.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files

* When comparing two deleted items, Verdi uses the following order of priority:
1. Target view begin line
2. Target view end line
3. Reference view begin line
4. Reference view end line
* When comparing two items that are not deleted, first compare the target view begin
line. If these lines match, compare the target view end line next.
* Sort keys are case-sensitive.
* The initial view sorts by the File column.
* The Line column does not support sorting.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
To ignore a module file and a source code file, use the -ignore_module
<ignore_module_file> and -ignore_file <ignore_source_code_file> options,
respectively, and run the following command:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
-ignore_module <ignore_module_file> -ignore_file <ignore_source code
file>

The -ignore_module <ignore_module_file> option reads modules listed in the userspecified module list and excludes them from comparison. The following is the format of

DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Limitations
The following are the limitations of the DesignDiff feature:
* Supported versions
The DesignDiff feature is supported for the following VCS release versions:
V-2023.12-SP2-8, W-2024.09-SP2-3, and later.
* File location requirements
The simv.vso folder must be saved in the same place as the simv.daidir.
* Unsupported languages and features
SystemC, Unified Power Format (UPF), Testbench, and VHDL languages are not
The scores of unnamed statements might not be accurate.
The Source View pane displays differences where a MACRO is used but not
defined.
DesignDiff cannot identify the exact changed line within an encrypted (protected)
block. It can only highlight the first line of that block as the changed location.
* Design reloading
To reload a design, you must run the srcDiffView -on Tcl command; otherwise,
Verdi cannot read the reference design.
* Scroll bar synchronization
When you select the SyncScrollBar check box, you can synchronize only from the
target view to the reference view, and not vice versa.
* Reference view limitations
Most of the reference view options, such as setting the active view, the right-click
options, and the drag option, are not available.
The reference view does not support the parameter annotation.
Non-manual scroll bar options, such as the srcGotoLine Tcl command, are not
When you jump to the target file line in the target design, the target line does not fall
in the range of a valid scope. The reference view does not get refreshed because of
the outdated data.
* Unsupported compilation flows

DesignDiff Limitations

VCS compilation is not supported with the -preserve_path option and in the
Scalene and PCH flows.
The -kdb=only and -kdb=common_elab:off flows are not supported.
The Verdi full-load mode is not supported when the design is compiled using the
-kdb=postelab flow.
* Design change detection
Any change in value format is treated as a design change. For example, if 3'b001
changes to 1'h1, the tool considers it as a design change.
A change in the order of the sensitive list is considered a design change.
A difference in the initial value in a declaration is not considered a design change.
Modules with different parameterizations cannot be combined for comparison.
DesignDiff does not detect modport changes within interfaces. Changes to modport
declarations, such as adding or removing signals fro

tments. You can also generate a new waveform based on
these changes.
* Generate Counter-Example Waveforms for Failing Properties: This feature
generates counter-example waveforms and shows how and why a SystemVerilog
Assertions (SVA) property fails.
In addition to the above-mentioned tasks, you can experiment with different verification
scenarios without changing the testbench and recompiling to run the simulation again,
thereby increasing productivity.
After you load the design into Verdi and launch Navigator, VC Formal runs in the
background automatically. When the VC Formal engine is ready, the Navigator window
opens in Verdi, allowing you to generate waveforms without a testbench.
You can edit the signal values in a waveform cycle-by-cycle, plot the waveform again, and
generate a new scenario, or extend the current waveform for additional cycles. If you write
SVA, you can also independently create SVA assert and cover properties. It allows you to
generate a waveform to verify whether assert properties fail or cover properties are met.
For more information about how to use the Navigator feature, refer to the VC Formal User
Guide.

Verdi Assistant
Verdi Assistant is an AI-powered feature that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM)
into the Verdi environment. It provides a chatbot interface for conversational debugging.
This feature allows you to interact with Verdi by using natural language. As a result, you
can find commands, execute them, obtain documentation or answers to usage questions
easily. Verdi Assistant automates command execution and provides instant support. It
reduces the learning curve for new users and increases productivity of experienced users.
Verdi Assistant provides the following benefits:
* Simplifies command discovery and execution through natural language prompts.
* Reduces the need to consult documentation or application engineers for common
tasks.
* Supports both new and experienced users by streamlining workflows.
* Executes multiple commands with a single prompt, saving time.
* Provides context-aware assistance based on the current GUI state.
* Offers feedback mechanisms to improve the responses generated by the assistant.

Understanding the Chat History Database
This section describes the chat history database, which stores all Verdi Assistant
promptresponse interactions in an SQLite3 file. This file also includes the configuration
of the Verdi Assistant directory, file name, data format, and the fields recorded for each
conversation turn.
This section contains the following topics:
* Database File Configuration and Format
* Data Stored Per Prompt

Database File Configuration and Format
This section explains how the Chat History Database file is configured, including how the
directory and file name are determined through environment variables. The database is
stored in SQLite3 format for easy access and compatibility.
* File Directory
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_DIR environment variable to specify the database
directory.
If you do not set this variable, the directory defaults to your home directory under
.verdi (for example, ~/.verdi).
* File Name
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_NAME environment variable to specify the
database file name.
If you do not set this variable, the file name defaults to chat_<username>.db, where
<username> is your operating system username.

* File Format
The database uses the SQLite3 format. Access the database by using SQLite3 scripts
or any SQLite3-compatible browser.

Data Stored Per Prompt
For every prompt and response, Verdi Assistant records one row in the sessions table of
the Chat History Database. Each row includes the following columns, with a composite
primary key on (chat_id, idx).
Column

Data Type

chat_id

Unique identifier of a chat session (UUID-style
string). All turns in the same conversation share
the same chat_id.

idx

INTEGER

Zero-based index of the turn within a session.
For example, 0 for the first turn, 1 for the
second and so on.
Together with chat_id, this identifies a single
row.

user

Operating system username associated with
the interaction.

prompt

User prompt text sent to Verdi Assistant.

response

model

LLM model used by Verdi Assistant for the
prompt.

prompt_tokens

INTEGER

Number of tokens in the prompt; where -1
indicates unknown or not recorded.

completion_tokens

INTEGER

Number of tokens in the model's completion;
where -1 indicates unknown or not recorded.

timestamp

INTEGER

Unix timestamp (seconds since epoch) when
the turn is recorded.

extra_content

JSON-formatted string containing any
additional metadata for the turn.

The Waveform Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses AI-driven
agentic techniques to enhance waveform analysis.

The new capabilities are specifically designed to streamline the analysis of complex user
waveform files with enhanced precision and efficiency. These capabilities help users
identify potential issues earlier and ensure faster, more reliable design verification.
You can submit natural-language queries to request detailed information about a waveform
file. The agent processes these requests and retrieves relevant data.
In GUI mode, you interact with both a chatbot and a waveform view. This mode is also
called Waveform-Viewer-Integrated mode.
It enables contextual queries and visual signal analysis. You can reference items in the
waveform view using phrases such as "the selected signals," "the cursor time," or "the
waveform".
The waveform view updates based on the chatbot's responses. This provides instant
visual confirmation.

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.

Set Default Debugging Target
Before querying signal debugging information, you can set the default debugging target,
such as FSDB file path and time unit. This eliminates the need to repeat the information in
every prompt.
Set Default FSDB
You can set the active FSDB for debugging once, eliminating the need to specify the full
FSDB path in each prompt. In GUI mode, the active FSDB is automatically synchronized
with the active FSDB in the waveform window.
In MCP mode, when an FSDB is not explicitly provided in the prompt, the most recently
mentioned FSDB is used. To change the default FSDB file path, enter the new FSDB file
path in a new prompt.

efault Waveform and Time Unit
Default settings for waveform and time unit can be configured to streamline repeated
prompts. These defaults are synchronized with the active waveform window and are
applied automatically unless new values are specified. Refer to the Set Default Debugging
Target section for more details.
Radix
To ensure consistent interpretation, always include the radix specifier when writing values.
* 'h for hexadecimal
* 'd for decimal
* 'b for binary
* 'o for octal
For example, to specify the decimal value 17, use 'h11, 'd17, or 'b10001.
You can also specify the width of the bit before the radix specifier. For example, 8'h3C
represents an 8-bit hexadecimal value.

When a number is written without a radix specifier, it is interpreted based on its value:
1. If the value contains only 0 and 1, it is treated as binary.
Example: 1010 Interpreted as binary.
2. If the value contains any digits from 2 to 9, it is treated as decimal.
Example: 123 Interpreted as decimal.
3. If the value contains any letters from A to F (case-insensitive), it is treated as
hexadecimal.
Example: 3C Interpreted as hexadecimal.
Simple and Full Hierarchical Name
Full hierarchical name is required unless the signal is already visible in the active window
within Verdi. For example, the following prompt uses full hierarchical signal name
'tb_CPU.system.m1':
Find the value of signal "tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD" at 0 ns.
Alternatively, you can add signal tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD to the waveform window then
the signal can be referenced using the simple name:
Find the value of signal "CARD" at 0ns.
Delimiter
Only the dot (.) character is supported as a delimiter for hierarchy. The slash (/) character
is not supported.
Bus Signals with Unknowns (Xs)
When searching for unknown values in a bus signal, any value that contains 'x' is identified
as unknown. For example, 'bxxxx, 'b010x, and 'b1x11 are all identified as unknown values.
Matching Value Including Unknowns
To search for a specific value that includes unknown (X) values, the value must be written
in binary format. Note that an unknown value needs to be specified by a lowercase 'x'. For
example, 8'b10x01100.
Complex Scenarios
When describing a complex scenario, break it down into clear steps. Avoid including
unnecessary expertise, for more effective outcomes.

Known Issues and Limitations of Waveform Agent
This section describes the known issues and limitations of Waveform Agent.
Assertion and Transaction Waveform
Waveform analysis for assertion signals and transaction waveform is not supported.
[Prompt] Find the first assertion failure timestamp for the signal system.i_cpu.INCPC2.
Phase Between Clock Signals
Phase measurement between clock signals is not supported.
[Prompt] Measure the phase between clock signals
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK1 and tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK2.
Gated Clock and Multiple Clock Frequency
Retrieving clock-related information is not supported for gated clocks.
This limitation also applies to clock signals with multiple clock frequencies. Examples
include clock frequency and cycle length.
[Prompt] Obtain the period of the system.gated_clock clock signal.
The system.gated_clock is assumed to be a gated clock signal in the waveform.
Member Signals
For composite objects such as SystemVerilog structs, unions, and interfaces, individual
member signals cannot be accessed; only the parent signal is supported.

Design Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses agentic AI to automate
and speed up HDL (Hardware Description Language) design analysis. You can submit
natural-language queries to explore RTL (Register-Transfer Level) codebases, extract
insights, and find structural patterns.
Design Agent is designed to streamline the analysis of complex hardware designs.
It enhances precision and helps engineers gain a deeper understanding of module

hierarchies, signal interactions, and potential design issues. By identifying issues earlier
in the development cycle, Design Agent reduces manual effort and accelerates design
verification.
This chapter covers the following topics:
* Getting Started
* Prompting Basics
* Advanced Prompting

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.
Import Design
Before using Design Agent, you need to import designs into the Verdi Assistant
environment. This ensures the agent has access to the full RTL codebase for accurate
analysis.
You can prompt the agent to load a design by providing the path to simv.daidir.

Import the design from /path/to/simv.daidir

The design has been successfully imported
from the directory path/to/simv.daidir

Design loading is currently supported only through the -dbdir option, which requires the
path to the compiled simulation database (for example, simv.daidir).
Reload Design
Reloading the design ensures that the Design Agent operates on the latest RTL code after
any modifications. This action re-imports the compiled simulation database and all existing
applications into Verdi.

Reload the design

The design has been successfully reloaded

Import FSDB
To change the default FSDB file path, enter a new FSDB path in a new prompt.
Certain Design Agent capabilities depend on FSDB files. If the required FSDB files are not
available, the system notifies you.
Waveform Agent handles FSDB file import. It loads and processes waveform data to
support analysis.

Import /path/to/my.fsdb

The FSDB file located at /path/to/my.fsdb has
been successfully imported and is now active.

The following example illustrates the scenario and response when the required FSDB file
has not been imported for Design Agent.

Trace the value of "system.En_A" at time 250
ns

To trace the value of system.En_A at 250ns, I
need the FSDB (waveform database) file name
associated with the design. Could you provide
this information?

Prompting Basics
Design Agent uses natural language prompts to analyze RTL design data, facilitating both
structural and functional exploration. This section introduces how to write clear, effective
prompts through simple examples.

Active Signal Tracing
Active signal tracing analyzes signal behavior using simulation data to identify active
drivers and trace unknown values.
Active signal tracing requires simulation data (FSDB) to analyze signal behavior at a
specific simulation time. This type of tracing focuses on the dynamic behavior of signals
during simulation.
In GUI mode, Temporal Flow View (TFV) is used to visualize active tracing results, and
relevant traced signals are recorded to a file during the tracing process.
Trace Active Driver
Trace active driver identifies which driver is actively driving a signal at a specific simulation
time. This is essential for debugging signal contention and understanding multiplexed

Glossary
This glossary defines important terms, signals, and concepts referenced in the Verdi
Assistant documentation.

Model Context Protocol

A communication protocol that defines how a client interacts with an AI model or
system. MCP ensures structured data exchange, command handling and process
control.
MCP can operate in different modes depending on the communication method. For
example, STDIO Mode and SSE Mode.

Glossary

Standard Input/Output Mode

A mode in which the MCP communicates with the AI model process through standard
input and output streams. This setup is commonly used for local or embedded
integrations where data is exchanged via terminal-like interfaces rather than network
sockets.

SSE Mode (Server-Sent Events Mode)

A mode in which the MCP communicates over HTTP using Server-Sent Events. This
allows the server to push real-time updates, such as progress messages or streaming
responses, to the client in a continuous connection.

API key

A unique authentication token used to identify and authorize a user or application when
accessing an API service or system API.
API keys help control access, track usage and enforce rate limits.

Endpoint

A specific URL or network address where a service or API can be accessed.
In the context of SCS (Service Control System), the endpoint defines the connection
target for structured requests. Examples include job creation, model queries, and
debug commands.

InstHdl includes two types: module instance and primitive instance.

A module reference in the design that serves as a container for sub instance, port,

npiNlBufCell.

Practice
The following practice example illustrates the following:
* How to generate the FSDB file that includes the Testbench Hierarchy Tree information,
and how to load this dynamic data into the Verdi platform for viewing the hierarchy and
the connection information.
* View the detailed call-stacks of this dynamic information.
* Correlate the dynamic recorded information with the source code.
* Understand the source of testbench objects generation from the source code.
The practice example uses the OVM UART example located in the $VERDI_HOME/share/
vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/examples/ uart16550 directory. It demonstrates the use of the
Testbench Hierarchy tree to debug the connection of a port.
1. Copy the case to your local directory.
%> cp -r $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/ .

2. Change directory to sv_latest.
%> cd lib/examples/uart16550/verif/testbench/sv_latest

3. Setup the environment variable for this practice.
%> setenv VERDI_HOME <Verdi_Install_Directory>
%> setenv OVM_HOME $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib

4. Generate an FSDB file with the TBH tree dumped.
a. Setup the variable for your simulation machine:
%> setenv MACHINE LINUX64

b. Open the run_vcs file, modify the SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE and VCS_HOME variables
to match your simulation path.

Chapter 5: Practice

./simv +sps_enable_hier_trace +fsdb+trans_begin_callstack

d. Run VCS to dump the FSDB:

1. npiPortType is one of the following three types: npiPort, npiInterfacePort, and
npiModportPort. Port type depends on the formal, not on the actual.
2. npiHighConn indicates the hierarchically higher (closer to the top module) port
connection.
3. npiLowConn indicates the lower (further from the top module) port connection.
4. npiLowConn of a npiInterfacePort is always be npiRefObj.
5. If a port is explicitly named, then the explicit name is returned. If not, and a name
exists, then that name is returned. Otherwise, NULL is returned.
6. npiPortIndex is used to determine the port order. The first port has a port index of zero.
7. npiLowConn returns NULL if the module or interface or program port is a null port (for
example, "module M();"). npiHighConn returns NULL if the instance of the module,
interface, or program does not have a connection to the port.
8. npiSize for a null port returns 0.
9. Ports and IO Declaration have the same behavior as npiDirection. That is, npiDirection
returns npiRef for pass by ref ports or arguments, and the npiDirection of the port is
undefined if the npiActual of the ref obj is an interface or modport declaration.
10. If a slice name (npiVhSliceName) or indexed name (npiVhIndexedName) comes from
a VHDL port, it can get its parent port by applying method npiParent. However, the
parent of sliced name of port could be a port or an indexed port, and the parent of
indexed name of a port must be a port.
11. The npiVhBaseType, npiVhInitExpr and npiVhType methods are only available for a
VHDL port. That is, a non-VHDL port returns NULL by applying these three methods.
Further information about VHDL port is shown in Object Declaration.
12. npiPortInstFile and npiPortInstLineNo are only for NPI SystemVerilog Model. They

Detail Mode Setting

There are a bunch of stop conditions for this system. You can specify the cell type of

also specify the module names that you want to stop tracing.
To prevent loop and complexity of the graph, it does not pass through flip-flops, and a

Further, a module ports mapping can be given to prevent tracing too deep into modules. It
simply jumps from input port to the corresponding output port while tracing.
The following section covers the map file mapping rules:
Basic Mapping Rules
Map file:
modName portA portB
1. If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
2. If trace to a bit portA[idx], it maps to portB[idx].
3. If trace to slice portA[lidx,ridx], it maps to slice portB[lidx:ridx]. (For example, portA [1:0]
maps to portB[1:0]).
4. If output port not existed, it stops tracing at input port and the port is listed in the result
5. If portB has size = 1, then any part of portA maps to portB. (for example, both portA[1]
and portA[1:0] maps to portB).

Extended Mapping Rules
Map file:
modName portA portB
modName portA[0] portB[2]
If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
If trace to portA[0], it maps to portB[2]. Since the map relation is specified.
If trace to portA[1], maps to portB[1] according to basic mapping rules.
Map file:
modName portA portB
modName portA[0] portB
If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
If trace to port portA[0], maps to portB. Since the map relation is specified.
If trace to port portA[1], maps to portB[1] according to basic mapping rules.
Map file:
modName portA portB[1]
If trace to portA, it maps to portB[1].
If trace to portA[idx], maps to portB[1].
If trace to portA[lidx:ridx], maps to portB[1].
The map is bidirectional. portB maps to portA, and the spec is also applicable.

Introduction
The Verdi system assigns an attribute to each token (including space) of the imported
design files. In the NPI Text model, you can use two APIs -- npi_text_property() and
npi_text_property_str() to query the attribute's integer value or string value.
All supported attribute types and the corresponding integer/string value are listed in the
following table.

The FSM Extraction Engine
The FSM recognition engine provides benefits such as accurate FSM extraction,
diagnostic messages, support for FSM reset filtering, and compile-time performance. The
engine improves the analysis of FSMs split across module boundaries. It also improves
the analysis of FSMs with code in functions.
The FSM engine identifies when there are multiple signals used to hold the next-state
value as it is being computed. There are some cases where signals are not considered to
be FSMs. If you see differences you do not understand, it is recommended that you use
the -diag fsm switch on the VCS command line at compile time. This produces messages
explaining why signals are or are not recognized as FSMs.
The FSM extraction engine finds some impossible state-to-state changes. Also, you can
see that the order, in which states and transitions is reported, helps in identifying the
source line numbers for states and transitions. Note that VCS uses a strict ordering for
both states and transitions.
The VHDL FSM extraction engine is enabled by default. This section discusses the
following features that are enabled by default in the VHDL FSM extraction engine to
enhance its quality, scalability, and performance:

The document briefly describes the compilation flows, such as incremental flow and

Introduction
Partition compile flow allows you to compile portions of the design and get significantly
faster turnaround time during the iterative process of compile and recompile. There are
two modes of using partition compile flow. They are as follows:
• Autopartitioning
• Manual Partitioning
Autopartitioning
Autopartitioning is the default mode in partition compile flow where partitioning is decided
by VCS by simply enabling the partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time
option. Autopartitioning automatically partitions the design and the testbench. You do not
need to specify yourself what parts of the design and testbench are in which partitions.
VCS creates optimal number of partitions to get better performance and the typical
compile time of each partition is 3-4 minutes. Further, the partitioning is regularly updated
based on the incremental changes done in the design to get optimal recompile time.
Autopartitioning automatically takes care of the cross-partition limitations across partitions
and re-adjusts the partitioning to avoid any cross-partition errors.
The use model for autopartitioning is easy to adopt partition compile flow.
To use partition compile flow with autopartitioning, use the following command in VCS two-
step flow:
% vcs -partcomp top <other vcs elaboration options>

Chapter 1: Overview
Managing Cross-Module References
You can change the autopartitioning threshold using the following option:
-partcomp=autopart_[low|medium|high]
The option applies autopartitioning to both modules and packages with a low, medium
and high threshold. By default, the option applies autopartitioning to both modules and
packages with a medium threshold.
Manual Partitioning
When you want to create a separate partition for a specific block that is under debugging
or development, then you can use the manual partition to create a separate partition along
with autopartitioning.
You can specify manual partition using the following command:
% vcs -partcomp top +optconfigfile+pc.cfg <other vcs elaboration options>
Here, +optconfigfile is a simple text file. You can specify a partition in the
+optconfigfile files with a line beginning with the partition keyword. The cell keyword
specifies that the partition is for all instances of the module name or the program block
name that follows.
For example:
// +optconfigfile configuration file cfg.txt
partition cell test;
partition cell dut;
This configuration file specifies:
• one partition for program block test.
• one partition for both instances of module dut.
VCS honors manual partitioning mentioned in the configuration file as well as enables
autopartitioning for the remaining portion of the design.
Managing Cross-Module References
When your design is partitioned, there is a chance that there are cross-module references
(XMRs) across partitions. That is, signals and variables from one partition are accessed
from another partition.

Chapter 1: Overview
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
You can manage XMRs using the partition compile flow as follows:
• If there is no change in XMRs, you do not need any extra option or any change in
configuration file for the partition compile flow.
• If the XMR changes, use the -partcomp=noxmrconfig option, so that only the
changed partition is recompiled or it might cause some runtime slowdown. If you do not
use any option, both the referrer and the referee partitions are recompiled.
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
The following scenarios causes recompilation of a partition:
• ◦ ▪ Changes in module definition.
▪ Changes in vcs command-line option or in the synopsys_sim.setup or
+optconfigfile configuration file.
▪ Changes to the global design property, such as adding $dumpvars to a partition.
This retriggers recompilation of all the partitions.
▪ Changes to the $unit scope: Any change (addition of new signal, type, module,
interface) to the $unit results in recompilation of all the partitions associated
with this $unit scope.
▪ Changes to an interface require the recompilation of all modules connected to
that interface.
▪ Changes to a shared package. In this case, recompilation is required for all the
partitions sharing this package.
Note:
Complete list of scenarios that triggers recompilation of a partition is available in
the Partition Compile section of the VCS/VCS MX LCA Features Guide.

Introduction
When you are debugging or developing a block in the design, then you end up spending
lot of time compiling the entire design for a small piece of change in the block in your
design.
To improve compile-time performance in VCS/VCS MX, you can use the default
incremental compilation method or enable the partition compilation method and save
on the overall compile turnaround time (TAT) during the process of debugging or
development.
Incremental compilation is the default method in VCS/VCS MX. During incremental
compilation, VCS/VCS MX analyzes and compiles only those design units that are
changed since last compilation.
However, when the design is complex and you want further optimized compile
performance, then you can use the partition compile flow. Partition compile flow allows you
to decide on how to partition your design so that you can fine tune the recompile behavior.
The partition compile can significantly reduce the compilation turnaround time by allowing
you to recompile only the changed partitions (portions of the design) and reuse the
partitions for the unchanged portions of the design that are already compiled earlier. You
can enable partition compile flow using the -partcomp compile-time option.

Incremental Compile Flow
Incremental compile flow works for both two-step and three-step flows and it recompiles
only the modified files. It is enabled by default to give optimized compile-time performance.

Stable Endpoint MCPs: When Protocol Meets Timing
Figure 2 shows the canonical stable MCP pattern. The dvalid signal strobes every three
cycles, creating a microarchitectural protocol that enforces the multi-cycle relationship.
Even in zero-delay simulation, the design functions correctly because dvalid controls
when FF2 samples.
Figure 2 MCP With Stable Endpoint
What the Figure Shows:
• FF1/Q changes data when dvalid pulses (every three cycles).
• FF2/D samples only when dvalid is high.
• The combinational logic between them has a three-cycle MCP declared in SDC.
• At zero delay, dvalid ensures correct operation, independent of SDC .

Figure 3 illustrates the critical failure case:
• RTL Reality: dvalid strobes every three clock cycles
• SDC Declaration: set_multicycle_path -setup 4 (timing team relaxed to ease
convergence)
• Zero-Delay Simulation: Passes completely—dvalid protocol ensures correct three-
cycle sampling
• Silicon Failure: Timing tools optimized assuming four-cycle capture. On cycle 4, FF2
samples while FF1 is transitioning → metastability
Why Traditional Simulation Misses This: The functional protocol dvalid is correct. The
timing assumption (four-cycle) is never tested because zero-delay simulation treats all
paths as instantaneous.

three cycles prior; SDC requires ≥4)

MCP Setup Violation: Source changed 3 cycles after destination
captured (expected ≥4)
• X-Injection (Purple Shaded Region): Shows where VCS SDC injected X-values at
the input of FF2
◦ Duration: Cycles 1–3 (modeling the uncertainty window)
◦ Purpose: Forces downstream logic to prove it does not depend on early data arrival
• Checker Firing Point (Red Arrow): Cycle where the violation was detected and
logged

-partcomp Enables partition compile. Applies autopartitioning to both modules
and SystemVerilog packages.
-partcomp=autopart_low Applies autopartitioning to both modules and packages with a low
threshold, which results in smaller and more numerous partitions.
-
partcomp=autopart_high
Applies autopartitioning to both modules and packages with a high
threshold, which results in larger and fewer partitions.
-
partcomp=autopart_re
lax
Applies autopartitioning in relax mode. Use
-partcomp=autopart_relax option when
-partcomp=autopart_high gives less balanced partitions. It
relaxes the partitioning with a high threshold to get maximum gain
in turnaround time.
-partcomp=autopartdbg Creates the vcs_partition_config.file file, which contains the
design partitioning information.. Note that this option can be used
along with any of the other autopartitioning options to create this
configuration file.

me>

r_name>

subsequent compile step, the -simcopy_opts=mv option

Enables the parallel compilation of partitions using N cores.
vcs <filename1> <filename2> <filename3> -partcomp -fastpartcomp=j<N>
[other options]
Examples\
vcs top.v test.v add_mult.v -partcomp -fastpartcomp=j4 [other options]
This command allows the compilation of a maximum of 4 partitions in parallel on a 4 core
(or above) machine.
-simcopy
When the -simcopy compile-time options are used along with -partcomp_sharedlib,
it enables VCS Turbo Compile flow (by reusing existing partitions) and also enables
relocatable compilation or relocatable simulation in a new directory. It helps to run the
simulation in parallel for multiple user environments.
This option moves the partitions from the partition library (default: partitionlib unless
specified with -partcomp_dir) into the simv.daidir/partitionlib directory. In the subsequent
compile step with -partcomp_sharedlib option is used, this option does not copy all
partitions, only the partitions shared from the partition library which is specified with
-partcomp_sharedlib are copied into the simv.daidir/partitionlib directory in your current
working area.

% vcs -partcomp -simcopy -fastpartcomp=j4

directory and ensures that the complete content is relocatable. Also, enables this directory
to be used in the relocatable compilation

-simprofile=mem This compile time option specifies compiling the design and

information. Then at runtime, specifies collecting machine memory

-simprofile
The unified simulation profiler reports the amount of CPU time and machine memory used
by the Verilog, SystemVerilog, SystemC, and VHDL parts of the design. Compile your
design using the -simprofile compile-time option.
%> vcs <file_name> -simprofile <=optional_argument>

%> vcs source.v -simprofile
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=time
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=mem
-simprofile=time
This compile time option specifies compiling the design and testbench for collecting both
CPU time and machine memory profile information. Then at runtime specifies collecting
CPU time profile information.
With the time argument, you can omit the -simprofile runtime option if you want to
collect the profile time information that you have specified at compile time.
If at runtime you want VCS to collect the profile memory information, you can specify the
mem argument with the runtime option.
%> vcs -simprofile=time
%> vcs -simprofile=time
In the following example, the mem argument is specified with the runtime option for the VCS
to collect the profile memory information:
%> vcs source.v -simprofile=time
%> simv -simprofile mem
-simprofile=mem
This compile time option specifies compiling the design and testbench for collecting both
CPU time and machine memory profile information. Then at runtime, specifies collecting
machine memory profile information.
With the mem argument, you can omit the -simprofile runtime option if you want to
collect the profile memory information that you have specified at compile time.
If at runtime you want VCS to collect the profile time information, you can specify the time
argument with the runtime option.

%> vcs -simprofile=mem

Enables monitoring toggle coverage for modport when specified along with the -cm_tgl
fullintf option. For each modport in an array, VCS reports toggle coverage for each of the
signal members of the modport.

+modportarr

% vcs <design_file> <other_compile_options> -cm tgl -cm_tgl signalsort
% vcs -sverilog -cm tgl -cm_tgl signalsort test.v
-cm_tgl portsonly
Instructs VCS to compile and monitor only the ports in your design for toggle coverage, so
that the coverage reports that URG writes contain information only about the ports. These
reports do not contain information about either the variables and nets that are not ports in
your Verilog modules or the variables and signals declared in your VHDL architectures.
% vcs <design_file> <other_compile_options> -cm tgl -cm_tgl portsonly
% vcs -sverilog -cm tgl -cm_tgl portsonly test.v

+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path>
Specifies the cdb database to be stored. If this option is not specified, the database is
stored in simv.cst/stimuliDb/record.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path>
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=./record
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<path>
If used in shared mode, path specifies the cdb database to be stored as a backup load
from the shared record. If this option is not specified, the database is stored in simv.cst/
stimuliDb/load_record.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<path>
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_load_record=./record
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record>
Specifies the cdb shared database stored/updated by all concurrent simv runs. If this
option is not specified, then distributed sharing is disabled.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<Shared_record>
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=./record

+ntb_solver_bias_diag=<0|1|2|3>
Enables solver bias diagnostics.
0: Disables diagnostics
1|2|3: Enables diagnostics with increasing levels of information
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_diag=<0|1|2|3>
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_store_record=1

Enables auto bias feature.
auto_bias_mode: 0 to 10 (default: 0).
0: Disable auto bias

10: Aggressive auto biasing
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=<auto_bias_mode>
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto=5

0: Disable auto bias for intra simv
1: Enables auto bias for intra simv

% simv +ntb_solver_bias_auto_intra_enable=<0|1>

+ntb_solver_bias_zip=<level>
Allows you to reduce the size of a cdb with lossless compression technique.
Compression level (level): 0 to 9 (default: 0).
0: No compression
1: Fastest compression

9: Best compression
Compression level greater than 0 compresses local store record (specified
with +ntb_solver_bias_store_record), local load record (specified with
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record), and shared record (specified with
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record).

and distribution information of the class instance variables and the bins that
are below the parent class by a given level are merged. To enable base class

merging, you must enable the collection of class hierarchy information by specifying
+ntb_solver_bias_class_info=1.

-assert enable_diag Enables further control of results reporting with runtime options.
The runtime assert options are enabled only if you compile the

enabled when -assert enable_diag option is used:

• -assert maxsuccess=N

-assert hier=file.txtassert hier=file.txt[-]
hier=file.txt, which allows turning assertions on or off.

enable_hier option is used:
• -assert hier
• -assert maxfail=N
• -assert finish_maxfail=N
-assert hier VCS recommends to use -assert enable_hier in place of
-assert enable_diag . The following runtime assertion options
can be enabled at runtime if -assert enable_hier is passed
because it does not have any performance overhead.

finish_maxfail=N

What’s New In This Release
This section describes the new features and improvements in VCS Intelligent Coverage
Optimization (ICO). The following points introduce the new and enhanced features of ICO
and provide pointers to additional information:
• ICO improves error detection by analyzing failure history-including unique signatures,
total failures, and failure rates to accelerate error detection through the following two
mechanisms:
◦ Predictive Bug Hunting: Learns from the past regression runs and applies that
knowledge to stress the observed failure spaces for adjacent failures and to explore
new failure spaces.
◦ Adaptive Bug Hunting: Uses the new bugs mode to automatically adjust bug
modes (such as bug, bug2, and so on) based on a prescribed methodology as
testing progresses and failure rates stabilize.
For more information, refer to Predictive and Adaptive Bug Hunting.
• Starting with this release, ICO can record Important Signal Predictor (ISP) data during
simulation as a compressed binary file named record.isp under the store record
directory. You can then use the crg command to translate this file into a readable form
(for example, CSV) and to generate an ID map that links each recorded value back to
its source location and variable name. The recorded data can be used for downstream
analysis, debug, and machine-learning flows.
For more information, refer to Identifying and Recording Important Signal Predictors
(ISP).
• Starting with this release, ICO can dump failure signatures during simulation when
you run it in bug-finding mode. A failure signature is a normalized form of an error
message in which dynamic content , such as simulation time and data values, has
been removed. As a result, multiple error messages that report the same underlying
problem collapse to a single signature.
For more information, refer to Dumping Failure Signatures.
• Starting with this release, ICO supports functional context aware class naming for
learning. Use +ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt to enable function or task context in
class instance names and +ntb_solver_bias_class_fcxt_depth to control context

depth. This helps ICO distinguish randomization calls that occur through different call
paths and improves learning precision.
For more information, refer to Functional Context for Class Naming.
• Starting with this release, you can run the bugs strategy without the -l <log_file>
option when you enable an internal log by setting a positive log chunk size. This feature
is enabled using the +ntb_solver_bias_log_chunk_size runtime option.
For more information, refer to Manage Log Files for Bug and Failure Prediction.

Performing Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
Figure 11 Detail Report
ICO supports Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of the uncoverable/illegal bins generated during
runtime. This feature reports the constraints responsible for the uncoverable bins, which
can be useful to improve the TB. Also, this feature allows you to go deep into the bin-level
information of particular variable and explore why the bin is illegal.
You can add the runtime option +ntb_solver_bias_rca_config=1 during simv to enable
the root cause analysis feature. Following is the syntax:

Mode Add-ons
+256 Enables biasing of variables

Option for Using Bias for Randomization
Mode Description
+512 Enables collect always (ignore ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit)
+1024 Enables alternating between bias/no bias
+2048 Enables bias after a threshold number (=32) of randomization
+4096 Enables Binary Decision Diagram (BDD) biasing
+8192 Enables bin biasing
+16384 Enables part-select. For more information, see Biasing of the Part-Select
Variables.
+32768 Enables edge biasing. For more information, see Edge Biasing to Improve
Coverage of Corner Values.
The following is an example for enabling multiple modes using the
+ntb_solver_bias_mode option:
+ntb_solver_bias_mode = 1289 (= 9 + 256 + 1024)
This option does the following:
• Enable both record and bias modes. The variable values are biased with varying
weights across randomization in both intra- and inter runs (9).
• Enable bias variables ( +256)
• Enables alternate biasing/no biasing ( +1024)
Option for Using Bias for Randomization
+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit
+ntb_solver_bias_rand_limit=N
Uses bias for randomization when count <=N. There is no randomization limit if N <= 0 .
Option to Specify Scope Variables
+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file
+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=<file>
Specifies a file with scope variables for record/bias. (Format of scope is discussed in
section Scoping Random Variables and Constraint Blocks for Biasing).

Option to Store Information
Option to Store Information
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record
+ntb_solver_bias_store_record=<path>
Specifies the cdb database to be stored. If this option is not specified, the database is
stored in simv.cst/stimuliDb/record.
Option to Load Records
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record=<path>
If used in shared mode, path specifies the cdb database to be stored as a backup load
from the shared record. If this option is not specified, the database is stored in simv.cst/
stimuliDb/load_record.
Backup load is required to debug simv failures.
If used for replaying simulation failures of the runs in shared mode, the
path should be pointing to the same cdb database that is specified with the
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record option during the shared mode.
If not used in shared mode, then the path specifies the cdb database to be loaded from
a previous run for chaining. If this option is not specified, then there is no chaining.
If used for replaying simulation failures of the runs in non-shared mode,
the path should be pointing to the same cdb database that is specified with the
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record option during non-shared mode.
Option to Specify Shared Database
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared>
Specifies the cdb shared database stored/updated by all concurrent simv runs. If this
option is not specified, then distributed sharing is disabled.
Option to Enable Solver Bias Diagnostics
+ntb_solver_bias_diag=<0|1|2|3>
Enables solver bias diagnostics.
0: Disable

10: Aggressive auto biasing
For more information, refer to ICO Auto Biasing.

+ntb_solver_bias_auto_intra_enable

Enables auto bias for intra simv. Default value is 0.
0: Disable auto bias for intra simv
1: Enables auto bias for intra simv
For more information, refer to Support for Changing Bias Mode During Simulation.

+ntb_solver_bias_test_type
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type=<uvm|ovm|vmm|cm_test|cm_name>

Tracks the test name in the crg reports. Id should be random seed (specified using

following default order specified in the command line:

• +vmm_test
