Incremental Recording and Merging
ICO supports incremental (non-accumulating) recording of each run in the cdb using the
+ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode simulation option. Incremental recording allows you to
bias the contribution of some tests differently than others during merging, which can also
improve the overall diversity.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode=<0|1|2>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<recordShared> …
+ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode=<0|1|2> (default: 0)
0: No incremental recording 1: Enables incremental recording 2: Enables incremental
recording and biased merging

Configuring Shared CDB for Congested Network
You can use the following command to generate runtime report:
% crg -dir <dir1> -dir <dir2> -incr -merge <mdir> -report <rpt>
-incr
Specifies to use incremental information for merging, report generation, and get the
difference between two coverage databases.
% crg -dir inc_store -incr -merge mergedCdb -report crgReport -diff
Figure 71 shows improved diversity scores with no change in the coverage score when the
+ntb_solver_bias_incr_mode=2 option is used at runtime.
Figure 71 Viewing Improved Diversity Scores
Configuring Shared CDB for Congested Network
Performance of ICO, measured in terms of diversification of stimulus, also diminishes
when huge test run data cannot be merged online as the subsequent test runs of the
regression cannot exploit the new information learned. Also, congestion is more severe
when the regression size is big.
To address this issue, ICO supports a mechanism to configure the shared cdb at the time
of its initialization using the -shared init_sfs crg runtime option. This feature helps you
to mitigate online merging failures and improves the performance of ICO.

Optimizing Load Record Directory Size
You can use the following command to configure shared coverage database to address
merging failures due to congestion:
% crg -dir <shared_record> -shared <init|init_sfs>
Specifies cdb database <dir1>.
-shared init
Initializes shared record <dir> for normal file server (nfs).
-shared init_sfs
Initializes shared record <dir> for slow file server (sfs).
Examples:
% crg -dir sh1 -shared init_sfs
The sh1 directory is initialized for shared recording and configured for slow file server.
% crg -dir sh2 -shared init
The sh2 directory is initialized for shared recording.
Optimizing Load Record Directory Size
The load record (load_cdb) file allows you to replay the failing tests at any given point
of time. Large file sizes of the load_cdb files require excessive memory to save them for
later use.
To create and store the optimized load record, you can use the following runtime options:
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable

ias_load_record_opt_enable=<0|1|2>
1: Enables creating optimized load record.
2: Enables 1 and enables overwriting the load record with the optimized load record in the
shared mode.
• The +ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=2 option only impacts
the shared mode with replay=0. It does not have any impact on non-shared
mode or replay=1|2.
• No change in the behavior of
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=1. The backward
compatibility is preserved.

Reporting Recommendation to Purge the Shared CDB or Use New DB
• The clean option does not delete the load record that was
overwritten by +ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt
with +ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=2.
In contrast, clean=2 removes load_record with
+ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=1.
• No change in the CNST-SBLROF error message.
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 +ntb_solver_bias_wdir=wdir
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=shared +ntb_solver_bias_test_name=test
+ntb_random_seed=100 +ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=2
This creates an optimized load_record under wdir/test_100.load_record.
In contrast,
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 +ntb_solver_bias_wdir=wdir
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=shared +ntb_solver_bias_test_name=test
+ntb_random_seed=100 +ntb_solver_bias_load_record_opt_enable=1
This creates an optimized load_record under wdir/test_100.load_record_opt and also
creates wdir/test_100.load_record.
For replaying, you must add the replay option as follows (no change in behavior):
% simv +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2 +ntb_solver_bias_wdir=wdir
+ntb_solver_bias_test_name=test +ntb_random_seed=100
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=1
Reporting Recommendation to Purge the Shared CDB or Use
New DB
The shared cdb can be reused across regressions and across changing models. To use
across models, it is generally recommended to purge the stale variables from the cdb. Too
many stale variables can increase the resident memory size of the cdb during the run. ICO
provides a measure that can be used to decide when to purge the shared cdb or when to
use a new DB.
You can use the -stat crg runtime option to report fraction of the resident memory that is
relevant (that is, in the scope). You can use that information to decide whether to purge or
use a new DB based on if the fraction is above a threshold or not respectively.

Reporting Recommendation to Purge the Shared CDB or Use New DB
% crg -dir <cdb_record> -stat -purge_untag <scope|reset> -purge <inFile>
-work <wdir> -purgeX <exFile>
Specifies cdb database <dir1>.
-stat
Prints cdb statistics in <work_dir>/stat.txt.
-purge_untag <scope|biased>
Purges variables that are not tagged as scope or biased.
-purge <inFile>
Purges variables in <inFile>.
-purgeX <exFile>
Purges variables excluding those in <exFile>.
• Options specified in syntax (other than -stat) are unaffected, but affect
-stat.
• Other options (not specified in syntax) are unaffected, and do not affect
-stat.
% crg -dir record -stat -work mywork

Categorizing and Grouping Illegal Bins
Illegal bins can be due to soft constraints, static parameters, state dependent values,
variables that are switched off for randomization, or variables that are unreachable due to
combination of hard constraints of one or more random variables.
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
• Categorizing Illegal Bins
• Grouping Illegal Bins
Categorizing Illegal Bins
Managing huge number of illegal bins can be difficult. It can also lead to oversight and
user may miss a real over-constraint. The categorization of illegal bins can help you
to prioritize and help manage large number of illegal bins for potential over-constraint
analysis. Without categorization, it is not easy to know the reason without individually
clicking the hyperlink and looking into the blocking constraints.
ICO supports categorization of illegal bins by tagging each illegal bin with attributes SOFT,
UNR, ROFF, and PARA, and prioritizing them. This feature can be enabled by using the
-illegal_attrruntime option in the post-simulation crg utility. Also, you must run the
simulation with RCA enabled, preferably with +ntb_solver_bias_rca=3.
You can use the post runtime option -illegal_attr to annotate CRG HTML and text
report with illegal bin attributes.
% crg -dir <record> -report crgReport -illegal_attr -format both

Categorizing and Grouping Illegal Bins
RCA Visualization
There is no change in the format of the HTML report when -illegal_attr is enabled.
However, each illegal bin with a hyper-link will have one of the following attributes:
ILLEGAL::SOFT - If the value is blocked by at least one soft constraint.
ILLEGAL::UNR - If the value is unreachable due to the combination of hard constraints of
one or more random variables.
ILLEGAL::ROFF - If the value is blocked by hard constraints with at least one random
variable whose rand mode is off.
ILLEGAL::PARA - If the value is blocked by hard constraints due to the presence of
parameter or state values, with no rand-mode-off variables.

Support for Exclusions in ICO Biasing Scope File and CRG Purge File
+ntb_solver_bias_scope_file=<scopeFile>
Restricts recording and biasing of variables to those specified in the scopeFile.
+ntb_solver_bias_scopeX_file=<scopeXFile>
Excludes variables specified in the scopeXFile from recording and biasing.
If both options are provided, then the recording and biasing variables are the
intersection of the variables specified by scopeFile and those NOT specified in
scopeXFile.
Excluding Variables from Purging
% crg -dir <cdb> -purge <scopeXFile> -purgeX <scopeFile>
-purge <scopeXFile>
Purge variables specified in the scopeXFile.
-purgeX <scopeFile>
Purge variables excluding those specified in the scopeFile.
If both options are provided, then the variables retained after purging are the
intersection of the variables specified by scopeFile and those NOT specified in
scopeXFile.

Improving Usability With Mnemonic Strategy Options
ICO improves the usability of the strategy options with mnemonics such as bug, cov, rca,
and so on. This feature helps to easily remember the options and avoids setting of the
combinations of runtime options for various strategies.
The following is the syntax:
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_strategy=<bug|bug2|bug3|cov|bal|nob|rca>
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=<shared_record>
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=<0|1>

Reporting Warning Messages When CDB is Empty or Not Created
Reporting Warning Messages When CDB is Empty or Not Created
When the testbench does not have any randomization call, or if the constraint random
variable to be recorded does not exist, then the store record is not generated. Similarly,
when the scope file excludes all constraint random variables, or rand mode is off for all the
constraint rand variables, the store record is created but is empty. In these scenarios, ICO
issues a warning message that provides information on why the CDB/prognosis report is
not generated.
The following scenarios describe this feature in detail:
• Scenario-1: No Valid Constraint Random Variable in the Testbench
• Scenario-2: Valid Constraint Random Variable is Not in Scope
• Scenario-3: No Valid Constraint Random Variable Enabled for Randomization
Scenario-1: No Valid Constraint Random Variable in the
Testbench

Please make sure to randomize and add constraints on random variables.
The CNST-ICO note message is not printed at the start. The [CNST-SBSRN]

Generating and Using CDB Across Different Platforms
ICO allows cdb to be generated and used across different platforms. That is, cdb
generated by a 32-bit binary can be used by a 64-b

ared cdb. If the value is 0, then this
option quits immediately after creating a backup.
The save option can run in a single process only, whereas the regression using the same
shared db can run concurrently with the process running the save option.
The restore option can run in a single process only, whereas the regression using the
same shared db must not run concurrently with the process running the restore option.
NFS Use Model
The following steps describe the NFS use model:
1. Initialize new regression run using the -shared init crg option. Following is the
example:
% $VCS_HOME/bin/crg -dir /tmp/ico/shared -shared init
% mkdir /tmp/ico/wdir
2. Launch the simulation. Following is the example:
% simv <run_opts> +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=/tmp/ico/shared
+ntb_solver_bias_wdir=/tmp/ico/wdir
+ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm

Non-NFS Use Model
Non-NFS Use Model
The following steps describe the non-NFS use model:
1. Start the CIOL server as follows:
$CIOL/ciolStartService -appname $regrId
2. Initialize new/Restore regression run. Following is the example:
$CIOL/ciolStartClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId <client.cfg>
$VCS_HOME/bin/crg -dir /tmp/$regrId/shared -shared init
mkdir /tmp/$regId/wdir
$CIOL/ciolStopClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId
Start the shared cdb backup client. Following is the example:
$CIOL/ciolStartClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId <client.cfg>
$VCS_HOME/bin/crg -dir /tmp/$regrId/shared -shared save
-shared_save_period 10
3. Launch each simulation with $simId (multiple clients per host). Following is the
example:
$CIOL/ciolStartClient -mntpoint /tmp/$simId <client.cfg>
%simv <run_opts> +ntb_solver_bias_mode_auto_config=2
+ntb_solver_bias_shared_record=/tmp/$simId/shared
+ntb_solver_bias_wdir=/tmp/$simId/wdir +ntb_solver_bias_test_type=uvm
$CIOL_HOME/ciolStopClient -mntpoint /tmp/$simId
4. Stop the shared cdb backup client. Following is the example:
$CIOL/ciolStopClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId
5. Stop the CIOL Server
• <client.cfg> is an easier-to-read format for the environment setting
printed out when the CIOL server is started.
• In step 3, you can also use a while loop to take a backup at your
convenience using shared_save_period 0 as follows:
while (true) {
Start the shared cdb backup client, take the backup and
quit
$CIOL/ciolStartClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId
<client.cfg>
$VCS_HOME/bin/crg -dir /tmp/$regrId/shared -shared
save -shared_save_period 0
$CIOL/ciolStopClient -mntpoint /tmp/$regrId
Sleep(<period>
}

LRM Non-Compliant Options
• For a variable with boundary conditions such as L <= var <= U , the distribution
may not be strictly uniform, there is some affinity to lower values to explore
corner areas when ICO is enabled. If you do not want this behavior, use
+ntb_enable_fast_solver=1.
• For a fraction of runs in regression, dist constraints are converted to inside to explore
more behaviors and expose more bugs. If you do not want this behavior, use the option
+ntb_solver_bias_auto_dist_to_inside_enable=0 to disable it when auto biasing
is enabled.

Limitations
Following are the known limitations:
• All dynamic objects of a class are collapsed into a single dynamic object of that class.
In the following example, each dynamic instance of class foo is not tracked separately.
class foo {}

repeat (100000) begin
foo obj = new;
obj.randomize();
end
• Objects of the same constraint class randomized at file and line locations are not
differentiated.
In the following example, obj1 and obj2 are not tracked separately as separate class
instances of foo.
class foo { }
foo obj1, obj2;

obj1. randomize(); obj2.randomize();

As a workaround, rewrite as follows:

obj1.randomize();
obj2.randomize();

Enhancements to the Result Metric
The enum-type result metric is enhanced to support the following features:
• Derived Percent
• Goal Expressions
• Metric Expressions
Derived Percent
When an enum-type result metric is created, a derived percent metric is created
automatically for each enum value.
For example, if you want to define a metric to track the status of features in a plan, you
could create a result metric definition feat_status with enum values fail and pass as
shown below:
result enum {fail, pass} feat_status;
value.pass = default;
value.fail = (test > 0) && (test.pass < test);

result bool GoalStatus;

Metric Expressions
When a metric has no score in a feature, the metric is set to NULL. If a NULL metric is
used in an expression, that expression is evaluated to true.
Planner supports <metric> ==/!= NULL expressions to set the expected behavior of the
NULL metric. For example, if a Line metric has no score in a feature, then Line == NULL
can be used and it is evaluated to true. However, if you want to specify that all features
should have a Line score, use Line != NULL.
Consider a plan top that contains multiple features as shown in the following figure:

Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric

In the example, a feature is “complete” if it meets the following conditions:
• A test is not NULL.
• All tests must be passed.
• Line and Group must not be NULL.
• Coverage scores must be greater than or equal to 90%.
Note that if a feature does not have test score or all its tests are unknown, then the feature
is not started.
In the figure, the completionSummary column is calculated as follows:
result completionSummary;
value.in_progress = default;
value.not_started = ((test == NULL) || (test == test.unknown));
value.complete = (((test != NULL) && (test == test.pass)) && (((Line !=
NULL) && (Line >= 90%)) || ((Group != NULL) && (Group >= 90%))));
In the top plan, f_complete, f_complete_line, and f_complete_group are complete
features, as their tests are not NULL, all tests are passed, Line and Group are not NULL,
and their coverage scores are 100%. However, the following features are not started:
• f_not_started as its tests are NULL.
• f_empty as its tests are unknown.
Note that the value in_progress is the default value.
Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric
The result metric is enhanced to support enum-type values. The result metric already
supports string-type values; this is explained in the "Defining Result Value for a Plan"
section in the Verdi and Siloti LCA Features Guide.

Supporting enum Values for the Result Metric
The syntax of the enum-type result metric is as follows:
result enum-type identifier;
{value-specification}

verification results of these features, consider the following result metric definition of a
metric status with enum values unknown, fail, and pass:
result enum {unknown, fail(default), pass} status;
value.unknown = default;
value.fail = (((Line < 0.8 || (cond < 0.5)) &&
(test.percent.pass < 0.7));
value.pass = (((Line >= 0.8 || (cond >= 0.5)) &&
(test.percent.pass >= 0.7));

Inferencing of the 1:1:1 Compression
You can conceal a measure in a report if a feature qualifies for the 1:1:1 compression.
VCS can infer from the structure of the feature whether it is qualified for the compression.
To qualify for the compression, the feature should meet the following criteria:
1. The feature is a leaf feature, that is, it does not contain any subfeature.
2. The feature contains exactly one measure.
3. The measure contains exactly one source.
4. The source name should not contain wildcard and regular expressions.
For example, the following feature is qualified for the 1:1:1 compression:
feature add;
owner = "a";
measure test m1;
source = "/dut/block/add";
The Verification Planner Doc annotator enables creation of verification plans using
Microsoft Office (.doc) documents, and back-annotation of coverage and other scores into
the .doc plan. You must properly format the .doc verification plan with predefined styles
and keywords built into the Verification Planner Doc annotator.
You can use MS-Word 2003 or later to create the .doc verification plan.
Unlike the Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator flow, the Word Doc flow
does not currently support OpenOffice input.
Back-annotation is an extension of the existing Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator
flow. The hvp annotate command and most of its switches are used for back-annotation
in the same way that they are used with the spreadsheet annotator.

The Verification Planner Doc annotator provides the following features:
• Simple hooks in MS Word-compliant documents to interface with Verification Planner-
enabled applications.
• Flexibility in formatting verification plan doc XML for nicely formatted coverage reports.
The same doc XML file is used by Verification Planner as a verification plan and as an
annotated report. Formatting features such as selectable fonts, text alignment, graphics,
charts, tables, and descriptions are applied in both the plan and the annotated output
report.

Doc Annotator Usage
MS Word has many auto-correction options that might cause problems in your Doc
verification plan. Before you start editing a Doc verification plan, it is recommended to turn
off auto-correction options as described below:
1. Click the Office button at the left-top corner, and then click Word Options in the pop-
up menu.
2. Select Proofing in the left menu and then click AutoCorrect Options in the right pane.
3. Select the AutoCorrect tab, and uncheck each of the Capitalize options.
4. Select the AutoFormat tab, and uncheck "Straight quotes" with "smart quotes".
5. Select the AutoFormat As You Type tab, and uncheck "Straight quotes" with
"smart quotes".
6. Turn off any other unnecessary options.
These instructions are for MS Word 2003. For other versions of MS Word, turn off the
equivalent options.
Process Flow
1. Capture your verification plan in the Doc XML format. This is typically done by starting
with a Synopsys-provided template file and marking-key paragraphs in the created doc
with Synopsys-defined styles, and copying and pasting Synopsys-defined tables.
You can access the template file from the following location:
$VCS_HOME/doc/examples/coverage/Verification_Planner/VerificationPlann
er_template/DocPlanTemplate.xml
2. Prepare Synopsys coverage database and HVP user data files.
3. Run hvp annotate with XML plan , covdb, userdata, and other required switches.
4. Fix any errors you see. You can find more error information in filename.dbg.xml.
Even if you do not see any errors, open the filename.dbg.xml file, and check to make
sure that Verification Planner processed your verification plan hierarchy and contents
as you intended. This debug check process only needs to be done on newly-created
or recently-edited plans. Once the plan becomes stable, you can skip this debug check
step when annotating with new coverage databases.
5. If there are no errors, open filename.ann.xml to see the annotated scores.

Compatibility With the Verification Planner Spreadsheet
Annotation Flow
The Verification Planner Spreadsheet annotator flow and Doc annotator flow share the hvp
annotate command and most of its switches. When an XML plan file is specified in -plan
xml-in-file, Verification Planner automatically detects the XML file format and invokes
the proper process depending on the format of the XML.
hvp annotate Command Arguments
hvp annotate -plan xml-in-file
[-h]
[-mod hvpfiles]
[-plan_out annfile]
[-feature " hierarchies"|-featurefile txtfile]
[-dir covdbpath|-f txtfile]
[-userdata vedata|-userdatafile txtfile]
[-userdata_out outvedata]
[-metric_prefix prefix]
[-group ratio|merge_across_scopes]
[-show_ratio]
[-show_incomplete]
[-v]
[-q]
Options
-plan xml-in-file: Specifies a Spreadsheet XML file or Word XML file containing your
verification plan. This option is mandatory.
For example: -plan myplan.xml

-h: Shows the help message.
-mod hvpfiles: Filters or overrides files in the HVP language format. You can specify
multiple files. They are applied in the order in which they are specified.
For example: -mod override.hvp filter.hvp
-plan_out annfile: Specifies the name for the output annotated spreadsheet or doc
XML file. If -plan_out is not entered, a file with the original filename and .ann.xml
extension is generated.
-feature " hierarchy [ hierarchy]": Specifies HVP scopes, which you want
to annotate with the covdb or HVP userdata database. You can use multiple scopes
and wildcards (*, **, ?), but you should enclose the string with the double quotes. Sub-
hierarchies of matched scope are automatically annotated. If the -feature option is not
given, covdb and HVP userdata are annotated to the entire plan.
Example 1:
% hvp annotate -feature "myplan.feat1.play*" -dir \
cov1.vdb -feature "myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan \
<myplan.xml>
where, myplan.feat1.play* expands to the following:
myplan.feat1.play1
myplan.feat1.play2
myplan.feat1.play3
The score of myplan.feat1.play1, mplan.feat1.play2, and myplan.feat1.play3 is
annotated with cov1.vdb.
Similarly, myplan.feat1.rec* expands to the following:
myplan.feat1.rec1
myplan.feat1.rec2
myplan.feat1.rec3
The score of myplan.feat1.rec, mplan.feat1.rec2,and myplan.feat1.rec3 is
annotated with cov2.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature \
"myplan.feat1.play*" -dir cov1.vdb -feature \
"myplan.feat1.rec*" cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
The scores of the matching regions of the play feature is the average aggregator of
cov1.vdb and global.vdb. Similarly, scores of the matching regions of the rec feature is
the average aggregator of cov2.vdb and global.vdb.

-featurefile feature-database mapping file : Specifies a text file that contains a
list of hierarchy feature paths. Verification Planner puts a feature path on separate lines of
feature-database mapping file . This file is used in conjunction with the -dir switch to
provide a list of feature paths inline without required to specify each feature.
For example, a feature-database mapping file with three feature paths is arranged as
shown in the following examples:
Example 1:
% hvp annotate -featurefile map1 -dir cov1.vdb -plan \
<myplan.xml>
where, map1 is the text feature database mapping file that contains previous feature
hierarchies. Following is the content of the text feature file with three feature hierarchies:
a.b.c
a.b.d
a.b.e
When you invoke the above hvp annotate command, it effectively expands to the
following:
% hvp annotate -feature "a.b.c a.b.d a.b.e" -dir \ cov1.vdb -plan
<myplan.xml>
Here, the scores of a.b.c, a.b.d, and a.b.e are annotated with cov1.vdb.
Example 2:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -featurefile map1 -dir \
cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
This command effectively expands to the following:
% hvp annotate -dir global.vdb -feature "a.b.c a.b.d \
a.b.e" -dir cov1.vdb -dir cov2.vdb -plan <myplan.xml>
Example

For example: -dir wishbone.cm wishbone.vdb
-f txtfile: Specifies a text file that contains a list of covdb coverage database paths.
-userdata vedata: Specifies the ve.data file path. You can specify multiple paths
separated by commas.
For example: -userdata result.txt bugcount.txt
-userdatafile txtfile: Specifies a text file that contains a list of user database file
paths.
-userdata_out outvedata: Dumps an annotated score of all measures into the specified
outvedata userdata file.
-metric_prefix prefix: Changes a metric name in the output user database file used
by -userdata_out.
-group ratio | merge_across_scopes :
-group ratio : Aggregates the group metric score as a ratio type (covered/coverable)
instead of as a percent.
-group merge_across_scopes : Merges the group score across scopes.
-show_ratio: Displays ratio type scores in a ratio form instead of a percent.
-show_incomplete: Indicates incomplete scores with [inc].
-v: Activates the Verbose mode, which shows progress status messages.
-q: Activates the Quiet mode, which turns off all warning messages.

Built-In Styles
In the Doc XML plan template, there are predefined styles that are prefixed with HVP.
Verification Planner extracts contents and their styles to establish the HVP hierarchy. A
template document containing predefined styles is provided with the Verification Planner
Doc annotator. Make a copy of that template and then use your copy as a basis to create a
new plan.

HVP Plan Style
Content with the HVP Plan style (see the figures below) is assigned as the name of the
HVP Plan. Use this style only once in the plan, typically at the very top of the document.

HVP Feature 1 to HVP Feature 9
There are nine levels of "HVP Feature" styles, which are used to represent the HVP
feature hierarchy. The index is seamless in terms of hierarchy, which means that HVP
Feature 1 is either followed by another HVP Feature 1 or by HVP Feature 2 , but not by
HVP Feature 3 or HVP Feature 4 , for example. If HVP Feature 2 is found, the feature
becomes a subfeature of the previous HVP Feature 1 . If HVP Feature 1 is found, the
feature becomes a sibling of the previous HVP Feature 1 , if one exists.
This limited number of styles also limits the number of levels of hierarchical depth in a
verification plan. You cannot create a plan with more than nine levels of features.

You can also use HVP Feature number for subplan declaration. To instantiate a subplan,
place the subplan keyword as the first word on the HVP Feature number line followed by
the name of the subplan. For example, subplan name-of-subplan.
You can also pass attributes to the subplan. Annotation value overrides using the #()
syntax, which is the same syntax as in the HVP language. For more information about
syntax for instantiating a parameterized subplan in the HVP language, see the Verification
Planner User Guide.

HVP Description
The paragraph with the HVP description style is extracted as the built-in description
attribute in the HVP feature. You can also use an HVP Assignment table to override
description values.
Table Keyword
When a table is found, Verification Planner looks at the contents in the first cell of the
table, and determines whether the table needs to be interpreted as part of the HVP
hierarchy. The following keywords are reserved:
• HVP Assignment
• HVP Measure name
• HVP Metric name
• HVP Attribute name, HVP Annotation name
• HVP Include File
HVP Assignment
A table with an HVP Assignment style is used to override attributes, annotations, and
goals for metrics. The keyword cell is followed by two-column rows. The left cell must have
the name of an attribute or annotation to override the value of the name or annotation, or
the name of a metric to override a goal expression. All names of attributes, annotations, or
metrics in this table must be defined in the plan. Otherwise, Verification Planner generates
warnings and ignores the undefined names.

HVP Include File
A table with the HVP Include file keyword in the first cell is used to declare other XML
plans to be included as subplans. The XML plans that are included in this table are used
as subplans. Add as many one-column rows containing XML filenames as you need.

Other Contents
Other content is text, images, and charts, which are neither in a predefined HVP style nor
in a table with a predefined keyword. All such content is ignored during the annotation
process and appears in the annotated plan exactly as it appears in the original plan
document. Formatting is limited to the formatting features that are allowed in Microsoft
Word 2003 XML .doc format.
Debugging the Doc Plan
When an error is detected in a .doc verification plan, it is difficult to find where the error
occurred. In addition, Verification Planner might interpret your verification plan in a different
way than what you intended or expected due to reasons such as typographic errors,
incorrect styles, and so on. This is because the paragraph styles are essentially invisible
in the normal WYSIWYG view of the document. You might, for example, select the wrong
style, not knowing that Verification Planner may not recognize the paragraph properly.

When you run hvp annotate , a filename.dbg.xml is created for each plan file, which
provides detailed debugging information.
This section contains the following topics:
• [Style|Table] Keyword Indicator
• Unique Error Code in Error Messages
[Style|Table] Keyword Indicator
In filename.dbg.xml, a blue term enclosed in square brackets, [Style|Table],
indicates that the section is either a predefined HVP style or a predefined HVP table.
Several examples are shown below. If you do not see [Style|Table] where you expect
to see it, there is an error in your HVP file such as a wrongly used style or a typographic
error.

Unique Error Code in Error Messages
The following error while running hvp annotate indicates that an invalid metric, Group 1 ,
is found at the location of ERR001:
Error:[DOC_060] memsys_wordplan.xml:ERR001: Invalid metric name(Group1)
was used in Measure(_m1) in Feature(1.2. cpu1)
To find where Group1 is used, you can open the file named memsys_wordplan.dbg.xml
and search for the ERR001 string. ERR001 is a unique string in the filename.dbg.xml file,
so you can easily find the location of the error. Then, you can open the original plan and
edit it to fix the error.

Sequential Distance Coverage for Assertions
This feature provides coverage of sequential elements for assertions by measuring the
sequential distance between an assertion and a sequential element (a latch, a register, or
a primary input).
This feature is supported for designs written in
• Verilog
• SystemVerilog
• OVA using bind statements to bind OVA units to the design. An OVA unit shall be
considered as an assertion, and the inputs of the OVA unit shall be considered the
inputs of that assertion.
This capability is part of VCS Design Checker, provided as a rule to be
checked during compile-time static checking. Other rules provided by
VCS Design Checker can also be invoked during this analysis. For more
information about how to use VCS Design Checker, see the VCS Design
Checker User Guide.
When you write assertions to check the behavior of a design, it is equally important to
know what portion of the logic is being tested by the assertions as it is to know what
behavior is being captured by those assertions.
For any complex design, it is not practical to write assertions such that all signals are
included in one or more assertions. The number of assertions required for such inclusion
of all signals is neither productive nor provides effective use of resources to test a design.
Given these consideration, an effective measure is needed that can be an indicator of how
well logic is being addressed by the assertions.
One such measure is the notion of sequential distance between an assertion and a
sequential element. You can call this sequential distance coverage of sequential elements
by assertions. A sequential element is a latch, a register or a primary input.

Sequential Distance Analysis
Sequential Distance Analysis
Consider the case of typical logic as conceptualized by a series of sequential elements
with combinational logic between the sequential elements. This is shown in the following
figure.
Figure 9 Structural view of a digital circuit
An input to an assertion is a signal included in any expression that is evaluated to
determine the truth of the assertion. This excludes clocking event expressions and
expressions used in task/function calls of sequence match items.
Sequential distance from a sequential element to an assertion is the minimum number of
sequential elements in any path from an input of the assertion to that sequential element,
excluding the assertion input. The sequential element itself is counted in the dis

rt directive.

Calculates the sequential depth from a given sequential element to all assertions. Specify
the sequential element(s) with full hierarchical path(s).
ELEMENT: Defines one or more sequential elements, using the full hierarchical path(s), in a
comma-separated list.

You can specify this parameter with multiple commands. The parameters are appended

specify multiple sequential elements with the wildcard notation (*).

Calculates the number of assertions from which a sequential element can be reached
within the specified sequential depth. The sequential elements that are within the hierarchy
of the specified design_top are analyzed.
DEPTH: Specifies the sequential depth that needs to be reached from an assertion.
Default: Any depth up to the primary inputs
MAXASSERTS: Reports only violations of sequential elements that can be reached from
more than the specified number of assertions.

Force/Release Functionality for Mixed HDL Cross-Module
References
VCS allows you to force or release any VHDL signal, or a Verilog wire/reg in a mixed
HDL design. You can use the following VHDL procedures or Verilog system tasks to
achieve the same:
• hdl_xmr_force() and hdl_xmr_release()
• $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release()
Synopsys recommends to call these procedures and system tasks from the
testbench.
Important:
With hdl_xmr_force for mixed language design, force (freeze) value
propagates across the language boundary, however, force property does not
propagate.
Instead, you can use the UCLI force to propagate both force freeze and
force property values across the language boundary.

Data Types Supported
hdl_xmr_force(), hdl_xmr_release(), $hdl_xmr_force() and $hdl_xmr_release
supports the following data types:
• The following data types of VHDL signals are supported:
◦ Integer
◦ Bit
◦ Boolean
◦ UX01, UX01, X01, X01Z
◦ std_logic/std_ulogic/std_logic_vector/std_ulogic_vector
• On the Verilog side, the following data types are supported:
◦ Scalars and Vectors
◦ Signed and Unsigned
hdl_xmr_force() Procedure and $hdl_xmr_force System Task
Using the hdl_xmr_force() procedure or the $hdl_xmr_force system task you can force
a value on any existing VHDL or Verilog node at any level of the design hierarchy. You
can also invoke hdl_xmr_force() from a VHDL procedure to control force enabling by an
event.
All these following delimiters are supported - /, ., : except for a pure VHDL
design where you cannot use . as a delimiter.

hdl_xmr_force("destination_object", " value",

verbose|open]);

Using the $hdl_xmr_force System Task
$hdl_xmr_force("destination_object", " value",
[" rel_time"], ["force_type"], [" cancel_time"], [verbose]);
destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS issues a warning message if
the destination_object does not exist or is not specified.
Verilog nets are read-only by default. Therefore Verilog nets cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on the write capability on these nets using a tab file.
value: Specify the value to which the destination_object is to be forced. The specified
value must be appropriate for the type and can be specified in any valid syntax for any
radix as supported by the language.
rel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS forces the specified
value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format as follows:
rel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
$hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns", "freeze", "5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the force happens at the
end of the current time step.

force_type: force_type must be one of the following:
• freeze - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any drivers later in time have no impact on the destination_object.
• deposit - forces the specified value on the specified destination_object at the
specified time. Any driver later in time can override the forced value.
• default - The default is freeze.
cancel_time: Specify a time relative to the current simulation time. VCS cancels the
forced value on the specified destination object at the specified time plus the current time.
Specify the relative time in the format as follows:
cancel_time [fs | ps | ns | us | ms ]
$hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns","freeze", "5 ns");
If the specified time is less than the simulation precision, then the forced value is canceled
at the end of the current time step.
The default behavior is to never cancel the forced value and is specified by leaving this
field blank.
$hdl_xmr_force("top.dut.reset", "0", "4 ns", "freeze");
cancel_time is irrelevant to the ‘deposit’ force_type. If specified, the cancel
time is ignored.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise, possible
integer values are 0 or 1. The value 0 indicates no verbosity and the value 1 enables
verbosity.

Example 3
In this example, the first initial block has $hdl_xmr call to bind top.dut1.pin1
and top.dut2.pin2. The second initial block has $hdl_xmr_force call to force
top.dut2.pin2 to the value 1. In this case, the order of execution is indeterministic, and is
one of the two following scenarios:
Scenario 1:
If $hdl_xmr_force is executed first, the destination node is forced to the value 1. Later,
when the $hdl_xmr () task is called, VCS binds the source and destination nodes.
However, it generates a warning message stating that an existing force of 1 continues to
override the connection until the $hdl_xmr_force is released or canceled.
Scenario 2:
If the $hdl_xmr() task is executed first, then the source and the destination nodes are
bound together and the source continually drives the destination node. However, when
$hdl_xmr_force() is executed, a warning message is generated stating that the force
overrides the $hdl_xmr() connection and the forced value drives the destination node.
Therefore, the source node have no effect on the destination node.

Multiple $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls
You can have multiple $hdl_xmr_force system tasks or hdl_xmr_force procedure
calls in your code. In such cases, if multiple calls are executed at the same time step,
but if each call has different relative time, then each force command executes at the
corresponding future time. However, at the same time-step, if there are more than one call
to the same node and have the same relative time, then the force command executed last
prevails. Note that VCS does not generate warning message in such situations.
The last force command can be UCLI force,
$hdl_xmr_force/hdl_xmr_force() or the force command in your code.

The hdl_xmr_release() Procedure and the $hdl_xmr_release
System Task
Use the hdl_xmr_release() procedure or $hdl_xmr_release() system task
to release the force applied to an existing VHDL or Verilog destination. You can
use hdl_xmr_release() or $hdl_xmr_release() to any objects forced using
hdl_xmr_force() or $hdl_xmr_release(), UI or the force commands in the design.
hdl_xmr_release works the same as the Verilog release command. These signal release
functions can be called concurrently or sequentially from a VHDL architecture (For
example: a testbench), a process or from any Verilog scope where a system call can be
made. Once the signal is released using hdl_xmr_release, the expected behavior of the
released node is as follows:
• If the destination node is of type VHDL signal and if there is no driver on the destination
n

hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/data", 1);
hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/reset", 1);

end process stim_design;

In this example, the hdl_xmr_release() procedure calls are used to release the forced
signals data and reset when the release_flag signal is set to 1. The verbose is turned off
by specifying open for the first hdl_xmr_release procedure call. Therefore, this call does
not generate any message. However, the second hdl_xmr_release() call has verbose
option enabled, therefore, this call sends a message to the transcript stating the signal
name and the time it was released.
use work.sigdecl.all;
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
library synopsys;
use synopsys.hdl_xmr_pkg.all;

entity testbench is

architecture only of testbench is
signal release_flag : std_logic;
stim_design : process

wait until release_flag = '1';
hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/data", open);
hdl_xmr_release("top/dut/reset", 1);

end process stim_design;

Using the $hdl_xmr_release() System Task
$hdl_xmr_release ( destination_object, [ verbose]);
destination_object: destination_object could be a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
Specify an absolute path or a relative path to the object. VCS generates a warning
message if the destination_object does not exist or is not specified.
Verilog nets are read-only by default. Therefore, Verilog nets cannot be used as
destination objects. To specify Verilog nets as destination objects, you should
turn on write capability on these nets using a tab file.
verbose: If the argument is not specified then the default value is 0, otherwise, possible
integer values are 0 or 1. The value 0 indicates no verbosity and value 1 enables
verbosity.

Using $hdl_xmr_force (Verilog) and hdl_xmr_force (VHDL)
The $hdl_xmr_force() or hdl_xmr_force() calls can be used to force a value on an
existing Verilog or SPICE or VHDL node. It allows you to force signals, from and at any
level of the design hierarchy from within the VHDL architecture or the Verilog module and
from any scope from where the standard defined system functions can be called. The
hdl_xmr_force() procedure works similar to the Verilog force command. A status is
returned from this function, which can be used to control the flow of the code.
$hdl_xmr_force(destination_object, value, rel_time,
force_type, cancel_period, verbose);
The following table provides the description of these arguments
Argument Details
destination_object The destination_object is a hierarchical path specified as
a string. A full hierarchical path (or relative path with reference
to the calling block) to an existing VHDL signal or Verilog
register/net or SV nettype or a SPICE node can be specified.
The path can contain any hierarchy including SPICE hierarchy.
value The actual value is the value to which the destination_object
is to be forced. The value should be specified within quotes.
The specified value must be appropriate for the type and can be
specified in any valid syntax for any radix as supported by the
language.

Argument Details
rel_time The rel_time argument can of type string and must be

hdl_xmr_release does not require hdl_xmr_force to have been called. However, it
affects only if the node or the object is forced through hdl_xmr_force. At the end of
hdl_xmr_release, the behavior of the released node is as follows:
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes Z if it is of type
wire in the Verilog scope.
• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node retains its current value
until future evaluations if it is of type reg in the Verilog scope.

• If there is no other driver on the destination node, the node becomes U if it is of type
signal in the VHDL scope.
• If there is a UCLI force or a $hdl_xmr_force or a code force on the destination node,
hdl_xmr_release removes any force attached to that node and the behavior is as
mentioned previously.
• If there is no force and if there is a direct connection, hdl_xmr_release removes any
hdl_xmr_force on that node and the node is scheduled for a re-evaluation, so that the
driver's value may get resolved to drive this destination node.
A2D or D2A Fidelity and Delta
In an HDL testbench and UCLI run scripts, hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force and UCLI force are
required on an analog target.
When a cell view is switched from a digital HDL view to an analog view the same hdl_xmr,
hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force must be applied to the analog target.
Correct digital to analog conversion must take place for a digital 0,1,X,Z force on what was
a digital target that has now changed to an analog target.
An auto vdd detection mechanism similar to that used for traditional interface element
thresholds and voltage swings must be used to automatically select voltage thresholds
and voltage swings for analog2digital conversions and digital2analog conversions required
for the hdl_xmr, hdl_xmr_force or UCLI force.
If the auto vdd methodology breaks down or fails, the voltage thresholds and swings
can be manually changed with the mixed signal control commands and the vcsAD.init

generated voltage swings, thresholds and options are recorded in the report file.

used, copied and pasted to use in the mixed signal control file (vcsAD.init) to change or

Fast Compilation
The VCS compile-time performance optimizations called
compilationfastfast compilation
fast compilation that you can use
to reduce compile-time for your design (and therefore overall turnaround time). You can
enable fast compilation using the -fastcomp compile-time option.
There are two levels of fast compilation, specified by the -fastcomp=0 and -fastcomp=1
compile-time options.
• -fastcomp=0 is same as the -fastcomp option (without the argument). This is the
recommended fast compilation mode. This option accelerates the compile time by
suppressing internal optimizations in VCS front end with moderate simulation time
degradation.
• -fastcomp=1 is same as the -fastcomp=all option. This option applies more
aggressive compile-time performance than the default mode. However, the simulation
time degradation is high compared to the default mode.
The above options are a trade-off between the compile time and the simulation time. You
can choose the option based on which performance is more important to you.

Guard Check Utility
Guard Check Utility
The Guard Check utility checks all source files parsed by VCS (design files, header files,
testbench files, library files, and so on.) for the presence of Guard statements and the
characteristics of the guard directives. It reports the characteristics of the guards in the
parsed file.
A guard directive is a combination of an `ifndef compiler directive a

guardCheck [-all-guards]
-sources <source_files>
-includes <include_files>
-defines <cmd_defines>
Each of these files contain one item (filename or macro name) per line.

Guard Check Utility
The output of the utility is a set of errors or warnings and the error count. In the case of a
non-unique guard, the utility lists all the files that share the same guard name, if not, only
the corresponding erroneous file name is listed.
When the -gather_guard compile-time option is specified, the following three files are
generated in a directory called Guards:
• source_files: The name of each file processed during compilation (one per line).
• include_files: The name of each file read by a `include directive.
• cmd_defines: The name of all +define command line directives specified.
% cmd_defines include_files source_files
For example, the above three files can be directly included in the Guard Check utility as
guardCheck -sources ./Guards/source_files -includes ./Guards/
include_files -defines ./Guards/cmd_defines
The name of the Guards directory can be changed by specifying the option as
-gather_guard=<dir>, where <dir> is the name of the directory. If the directory name is
not specified, the default directory name Guards is used. This option allows different sets
of files to be gathered separately in the same directory. Note that in order to perform the
global checks (for example, unique guard names), all the files must be collected together
prior to running the guard utility.

module s2();

`else
`ifndef GUARD `define GUARD 100

Relaxed Time Scale and Time Precision
You can use the -xlrm timescale_relaxed compile option to enable relaxed (or flexible)
delay adjustments for delays and time literals for the entire module. If a timeunit or
timeprecision keyword is specified, this feature is applied consistently to the entire
module. This option also provides relaxed constraint on time scopes like modules,
programs, packages, or interfaces.
This feature is enabled using -xlrm timescale_relaxed compile-time option as follows:
%vcs -xlrm timescale_relaxed -full64 -sverilog <filename>

Relaxed Time Scale and Time Precision
The following are the examples of this feature.

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
VCS allows you to set black box by module-based and instance-based with value of the
output ports of black boxes.
VCS ignores and removes the following contexts:
• Bind directive failed to apply
• Assertions crossing black box boundary
This feature is supported using +optconfigfile option.
The following are the use models of this feature:
• Module-level black-box:
module {comma_separated_module_list} {blackbox} [{0|1}];
comma_separated_module_list ::=
[library_name.]module_name {,[library_na

Bricking Instances of User Specified Modules
assign w2 = m1.local_w1; // Error due to unable to resolved.
assign w3 = m1.s1.o1; // Error due to unable to resolve.

module mid(o1, in1, in2);

Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test1.sv +optconfigfile+bb1.cfg
bb1.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
module {mid} {blackbox};
Example 2: Tie Value To Output Ports
Example 10 test2.sv
mid m1();

module mid(o1, in1, in2);
modC c1_inst(); // tie 0 to the output port
modC c1_dummy(); // tie 1 to the output port
modC c2_inst(); // leave undriven

Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test2.sv +optconfigfile+bb2.cfg
bb2.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
module {modC} {blackbox};
instance {top.m1.c1_*} {blackbox} {1};
instance {top.m1.c1_inst} {blackbox} {0};
Example 3: Remove Assertions Crossing Black Box Boundary
Example 11 test3.sv
wire mclk, data_phase;

sub s1();
assert(s1.r1); // this assertion will be removed
end
module sub;
reg r1;
Use the following command to run the above example:
vcs -sverilog test3.sv +optconfigfile+bb3.cfg
bb3.cfg configuration file specifies the following:
instance {top.s1} {blackbox};
• This feature cannot be used at the same time with -Xpartialdesign or -bboxModule
options.
The target module and instance can only be Verilog. This feature can use when design
have other languages but if target is not Verilog, the black box does not happen and
does not apply to the black box module.

Enabling and Using SystemVerilog 2023 Method Specifiers in
VCS
Starting with this release, SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) introduces the following new
method specifiers such as :initial, :extends, and :final. These specifiers give you
more control over class method declarations, helping you define how methods can be
overridden in class hierarchies. VCS now supports these specifiers when you enable the

SystemVerilog 2023 standard. This feature helps you write clearer, more robust object-
oriented code and catch errors related to method overriding at compile time.
Usage
To use the new method specifiers, you must enable the SystemVerilog 2023 standard
in VCS. Use -std=1800-2023 VCS compile-time option to enable SystemVerilog 2023
standard in VCS.
To write class methods with specifiers, you can use the following method specifiers:
• :initial
Marks a method as the initial implementation in the class hierarchy.
• :extends
Marks a method as an extension (override) of a virtual method in a base class.
• :final
Prevents further overriding of the method in derived classes.
The LRM does not allow the following:
• Using both :initial and :extends on the same method.
• Marking a pure virtual method as :final.
The SV'23 LRM supports the following syntax for the method specifiers:
function_declaration ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
function_body_declaration

function_prototype ::=
function [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 data_type_or_void
function_identifier [ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

task_declaration ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 [ lifetime ]
task_body_declaration

task_prototype ::=
task [ dynamic_override_specifiers ]25 task_identifier
[ ( [ tf_port_list ] ) ]

dynamic_override_specifiers ::= [ initial_or_extends_specifier ]
[ final_spec

end

Enabling SystemVerilog 2023 Static type(this) Support in VCS
Starting with this release, VCS allows you to use the type(this) operator inside class
static functions in SystemVerilog, as defined by the SystemVerilog 2023 (SV'23) standard.
Previously, type(this) was only available in non-static functions. With this enhancement,
VCS now parses and displays error if type(this) is used incorrectly in static functions.
Usage
Use the following option to enable SV'23 static type(this) support:
-std=1800-2023
The type(this) points to the type of the enclosing class of the static method.
Example 22 Usage of type(this) in Functions
//lrm.v

class registry #(type T=int);
static function type(this) get(); // calls to get() return a
registry #(T)
static type(this) m_inst;
if (m_inst == null) m_inst = new();
return m_inst;

registry #(int) obj = new();

$display("return type of function get is: %p",
$typename(obj.get()));
end
Behavior With SV'23 Standard

Enabling SystemVerilog 2023 Static type(this) Support in VCS
%vcs -full64 -sverilog lrm.v -std=1800-2023
No error message is displayed during compilation.
Run the following simulation command:
%simv
The following is the output:

Static Bug Finding in VCS
Static defects like the following can be functional hazards:
• Glitches: glitches on asynchronous paths, Multicycle Paths (MCP), and DFT Logic and
P2P.
• Reset Domain Crossing (RDC): metastability caused by asynchronous reset assertions
VCS leverages the results of the structural analysis from VC SpyGlass to perform dynamic
SDC verification. Using this feature, you can inject Delay/X at RTL to improve confidence
for RDC/Glitch sign off and verify the correctness of RTL level by providing SDC dumped
by VC Spyglass to VCS.
VCS uses the database generated by VC SpyGlass and determines whether a glitch or
RDC property can fail. The database is in the SDC format that contains both user written
constraints for example, MCP/FP/GC, and so on. and the property data.
This feature helps you with the following:
• Identify unsafe RDC using dynamic simulation.
• Report simulation failure in the downstream circuit caused by an RDC.
• Accurate classification of rising and falling glitches (010, 101 type).
• Checking RDC, Flop-to-Flop glitches, and Point-to-Point glitches.

Calculation of Glitch Delay and Pulse Width:
By default, the glitch delay and pulse width are supported as a fraction of the clock cycle.
VCS-SBF Glitch Delay and Pulse Width by Clock Period
The following switch defines the fraction of clock cycle after which a glitch check should be
performed:
-sdc= glcapdel:<N(in float)>
-sdc=glcapdel:.3
clk_period = 10 ns
The glitch check is performed at the destination after 3 ns of the source change.

The following switch defines the fraction of clock period for which a glitch is inserted in the
destination:
-sdc= glxdelta:<N(in float)>
Ex: -sdc=glxdelta:.3
Clk_period = 10ns
Glitch is inserted for 3ns.
Virtual clocks are also supported in VCS-SBF, Glitch violation is as per the time
period of a virtual clock.
The VCS-SBF Clock Glitch identifies all potential post-simulation clock glitches during
the RTL-level phase. The goal is to inject glitches in RTL simulation to cause simulation
failures, enabling designers to detect and address clock glitch circuits earlier in the design
process.
• Detects all possible post-simulation clock glitches during RTL simulation.
• Ensures glitches are injected and cause simulation failures, so issues are not missed.
• Avoids injecting false glitches that could cause incorrect simulation failures.
Clock glitch check in VC Static
The following scenario explains how to detect glitches in a clock path when the select pin
of a multiplexer (MUX) changes, such as during clock mode selection.

Figure 15 Example 1
VC Static generates the following glitch command for all clock merging cases:
SETUP_SYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*,
SETUP_ASYNC_CLOCK_OVERLAP*
set_glitch_path -from <sig_list> -to <gate_output> -type clock
Here,
sig_list: All first-level RTL signals in the fan-in of the MUX select pin.
gate_output: Output of the MUX. If the MUX output is an internal net, the first RTL net in
the fanout is reported.
• If async or sync clock overlap occurs on a combinational gate other than a
MUX, VC Static does not generate a set_glitch_path command for that
overlap.
Generated SDC Example:
Glitch paths are generated at the VC Static stage, and the SDC includes an
extra field to mark it as a clock path glitch:
set_glitch_path -from {d} -to {clk_mux1/O} -to_clock {clk} -type
clock

Glitch Identification in VCS SBF
When the select pin toggles, X propagates to the MUX output following the X-propagation
mechanism. A glitch violation is reported at the MUX output. The gli

• A new runtime switch -sdc=glclkdel:<N> is added, where N is the fraction
of the clock period for which the glitch needs to be injected at mux output.
• The use of -sdc=glxdelta:<N> for clock glitches has been eliminated, as
long-duration delay injection is not needed for propagation to flops.
• X propagation from select to mux output and from mux output to downward
hierarchy follows the Xprop mechanism.
• Verdi marking on mux output is done for the entire -sdc=glclkdel:<N>
duration, regardless of input changes to the mux.
• Clock mux output should not be given as a P2P glitch destination; an error is
reported if the input clocks to this mux, are defined in SDC.
• Only Boolean changes ( 0→1, 1→0) in mux select line are considered for clock
glitch.
• If select changes while mux output is already X, no violation or glitch
injection is reported.
• For UDPs, penultimate module pins going into the UDP instance are
dumped from VC Static.
• Multiplexer outputs have multiple drivers.
• The -sdc=no_x runtime option has no impact on clock glitch paths.
• MDANETs and MDAs as select or mux output are not currently supported.
• For UDP muxes, the X injection time at mux output is for -sdc=glclkdel
value, regardless of any input/select changes.
• Both destination and source of set_glitch_path command should be
present in the same module.

To limit glitch detection to specific clock paths going to a particular clock pin, use the

clock

Support for -sdc=glmaxdel Option in P2P Glitch Multi-Clock
Scenarios
In VCS, when a point-to-point (p2p) glitch command references multiple clocks, the tool
must select a clock period to compute the glitch delay for checking and injection. By
default, VCS selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock, ensuring conservative glitch
detection. However, for certain validation scenarios—such as worst-case or maximum-
delay analysis—it is desirable to use the largest-period (slowest) clock instead.
The -sdc=glmaxdel simulation-time option changes the clock selection rule for p2p
glitch commands referencing multiple clocks.
When a p2p glitch command uses more than one clock, the tool must choose one clock
period to calculate the glitch delay for checking and injection.
Clock Selection Behavior
• Default Behavior:
◦ The tool selects the smallest-period (fastest) clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this period.
◦ No user action required.
• Behavior with -sdc=glmaxdel option:
◦ The tool selects the largest-period clock among those specified.
◦ Glitch delay is computed using this maximum period.
◦ Enable this behavior by passing -sdc=glmaxdel at simulation time.

The corruption mechanism follows a sticky approach. In sticky corruption,
each P2P glitch node receives its own independent, deterministic corruption
lifetime. As a result, a fault injected at a node remains visible for its designated
duration, rather than being prematurely cleared or overwritten when logic
paths reconverge or when other nodes are evaluated later in the same time
slice. Corruption is cleared only by a genuine design-driven value change after
injection or when the glxdelta timeout expires.

Top Down Flow in SOC Verification
The top-down flow in SoC verification is a hierarchical approach that improves
performance by excluding paths fully contained within validated IPs during SoC-level
verification. This method prevents redundant validation of IP constraints, saving time and
effort.
In the following example, path5 is entirely within an IP: therefore, it can be excluded from
top-level validation.
Use a configuration file to define IPs as a glassbox, which removes self-contained paths
from SoC-level validation. You can enable the top-down flow for excluding IP-contained
paths during SoC verification. This ensures that all the IP paths, including additional SoC-
level paths, are verified.

• Use the +optconfigfile option to specify such IPs during compilation to include the
file.
Example command: +optconfigfile+<filename>.cfg [Compile Phase]
• When you glassbox an IP by using {sdcGlassboxIp} in the sdc_module.cfg
configuration file, all timing paths that are fully contained within the IP are excluded
from SoC-level validation.
The following is a sample command line:
vcs -sverilog -full64 test.v tb.v -sdc=test.sdc,current_design:top -l
comp.log +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
Both module and instance level exclusions are supported.
• Example configuration File for module-level exclusion:
% +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
sdc_module.cfg
instance {Top.IP1} {sdcGlassboxIp}
• Example configuration File for instance-level exclusion:
% +optconfigfile+sdc_module.cfg
sdc_module.cfg
module {IP1} {sdcGlassboxIp}
All excluded points are dumped in the mcpLogs/sdc_config_diag.txt log file. All paths
inside the IPs are excluded for the IPs specified in the sdc_module.cfg file.
1. The -sdc=only_excluded_path option considers and reports only the paths that
are fully contained within the IPs specified in the configuration file. It is used to report
excluded paths.
2. The -sdc=report_excluded_cmds option reports, in the SDC summary file, both
partially excluded and fully excluded SDC commands.
Comparing IP and SoC Equivalence Check
Occasionally, few constraints are incorporated at the SoC level to account for additional IP
paths that were not present during the IP level verification. This flow helps to compare self-
contained IP paths between IP-level verification and SoC-level verification.
This Unified Report Generator (URG) is a coverage-based solution.

Chapter 7: Top Down Flow in SOC Verification

Follow these steps to perform the equivalence check:
1. Validate IP constraints: Run IP-level verification and generate coverage databases
(simv.vdb) for each IP.
2. Merge Coverage Databases: Use the URG tool to merge coverage databases for all
IPs.
Example command: urg -dir ip1.vdb ip2.vdb -dbname merged.vdb -format
text -dump full_exclusions -show sdcpath
3. Generate Excluded Paths at SoC Level: Mark the IPs as glassboxes during the
SoC-level verification and generate soc_ex.vdb SoC coverage database using the
-sdc=only_excluded_path option.
4. Create Mapping File: Generate map.txt file to map IP paths to the respective SoC
paths.
5. Perform Coverage Analysis: Use the URG tool to compare IP and SoC paths, including
additional paths at the SoC level.
Example command: urg -dir soc_ex.vdb merged.vdb -mapfile map.txt -log
urg.log -format text -sdc level 3 -show sdcpath

Error Handling
VCS skips modtreefile merging and reports syntax errors if the following scenarios are
encountered:
• Keywords other than MODULE and INSTANCES are used in the modtreefile.
• The keyword INSTANCES is used without the keyword MODULE.
• Module name is not specified after the keyword MODULE.
VCS skips modtreefile merging and reports warnings if the following scenarios are
encountered:
• Module name specified with MODULE is not found in the VDB.
• Instance name specified with INSTANCES is not found in the VDB.

INSTANCES: T.Y.M1, T.Y.M2

Coverage Computation for Glitch
VCS computes coverage per glitch assertion. For an n-source glitch, multiple (n) glitch
paths are generated.
For each glitch assertion, VCS monitors the following coverage metrics for each source:
• Count of toggle for each source
• Count of toggle of each source when any other source is also toggled
• Status (Inactive, Active, Violating)

• Count of Glitch 010 and Glitch 101
Coverage computation is performed only for the probable glitch cases
(multiple sources change, destination does not change.)

Coverage Computation for SDC
Use the VCS
-sdc
-cm sdc switch at compile time to enable coverage computation for SDC. Its
syntax is as follows:
% vcs
-cm sdc
-cm sdc -sdc=<sdc_file>, current_design:<top_design>
-cm sdc is used to enable coverage for SDC.
-sdc=current_design:<top_design> : This option can be specified at the command line
or in an SDC file.
<sdc_file> is the name of an SDC file.
Consider the following code snippet that shows signal connections from ff1-->ff3:
Example 28 SDC Coverage
module mult2x(input[3:0] in, input clk, input clk2, output[3:0] out,
input rst);
reg[3:0] ff1,ff2,ff3;
wire[3:0] mout;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff1 <= 0;
else ff1 <= in;
assign mout = ff1*ff1;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff3 <= 0;
else ff3 <= mout;
always @(posedge clk2 or negedge rst)
if (!rst) ff2 <= 0;
else ff2 <= ff3;
assign out = ff2;
The sample content of the .sdc file is shown in Example 29:
Example 29 test.sdc
create_clock -period 20 -name sys_clk [get_ports clk]
create_clock -period 60 -name sys_clk2 [get_ports clk2]
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from ff1* -to ff3*
set_clock_group -asynchronous -group sys_clk -group sys_clk2
In the example, create_clock, set_multicycle_path, and set_clock_group are SDC
commands. SDC commands are the set of rules defined inside the .sdc file.

The compile time and runtime commands for Example 28 are as follows:
%vcs -lca -sverilog -kdb +vcs+fsdbon -full64 tb.v dut.v -cm
sdc -sdc=test.sdc, current_design:mult2x, print_violation,
verify_clock_group
%simv -sdc=max_destination_violation:10000 -cm sdc
The URG report of this example is shown in Figure 42.
Merging
VCS enables you to create a report by merging the paths from multiple simulation runs.
The simulation data can be merged whether it was produced from the same compilation or
from different compilations. Here is the reporting command for SDC:
%urg -show sdcpath -dir simv1.vdb [simv2.vdb] -format text
It is possible to give one or more VDB arguments to the -dir option.
Example 30 demo.v
module mult2x(input[1:0] in, input clk, output[1:0] out, input
rst);

assign out = ff2;
Here is the .sdc file for Example 30:
current_design mult2x
create_clock -period 20 -name sys_clk [get_ports clk]
set_multicycle_path 3 -from ff1* -to ff2*
In the example, current_design, create_clock, and set_multicycle_path are SDC
commands.

The URG report for SDC coverage report covers the following:
• Total paths relevant for an SDC command
• Categorization of the paths per “Violating”, “Inactive”, “Active”
• Details of the paths (start and end point)
Figure 42 shows the URG Report of Example 28 using the following command:
urg -show sdcpath -dir simv.vdb -format text

Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
This feature has the following limitation:
• The urg -dbname command of union merge is not supported for SDC.
Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
VCS supports monitoring Finite-State Machine (FSM) coverage for FSMs modeled in
multi-dimensional arrays (MDAs), that is, an array of arrays or an array of arrays of arrays.
• URG Report
• Support for Arrays With Constant Index Value
• Support for Arrays With Unknown Index Values
To monitor FSM coverage for MDAs, use the -cm_fsmopt mda switch at compile time as
vcs
-cm fsm
-cm fsm
-cm_fsmopt
-cm_fsmopt mda
By default, VCS extracts 1000 FSMs from a multi-dimensional array for coverage
computation. To raise this limit, use the -cm_fsm_limit switch at compile time as follows:
vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsmopt mda -cm_fsm_limit 2000
VCS skips the FSMs that are over the limit and displays the following warning message:
Warning-[VCM-FSMMDAMAX] Array of FSMs is too large
file.v, 100
The array 'mybigmda' may be a collection of finite-state
machines, but it contains 6400 elements, which is above the
maximum number 1000 that VCS will create for a single array.
To avoid significant compile-time and runtime overhead, no
FSMs based on this 'mybigmda' will be monitored for coverage.

Monitoring FSM Coverage for Multi-Dimensional Arrays
Consider the following example of an array of arrays of FSMs:
Example 31 An Array of Arrays of FSMs:
typedef enum logic [1:0] {STATE_0 = 2'd0,
STATE_1 = 2'd1,
STATE_2 = 2'd2,
STATE_3 = 2'd3
} fsm_enum_e;

fsm_enum_e [1:0][7:0] cur_st, nxt_st;

for (genvar ii=0;ii<2;ii++) begin
for (genvar jj=0;jj<8;jj++) begin
always_comb begin
case(cur_st[ii][jj])
STATE_0: nxt_st[ii][jj] = sel? STATE_2 : STATE_1;
STATE_1: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_2;
STATE_2: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_3;
STATE_3: nxt_st[ii][jj] = STATE_0;
endcase
end
always @ (posedge clk or negedge rstb) begin
if (!rstb) begin
cur_st[ii][jj] <= STATE_0;
end else begin
cur_st[ii][jj] <= nxt_st[ii][jj];
end
end
end
end
In this example, nested generate loops are used to specify the FSM logic that applies to
all FSMs in the array of arrays of type fsm_enum_e. When the -cm_fsmopt mda switch is
given at compile time, VCS recognizes that this is an array of arrays of FSMs, one each
for cur_st[0][0], cur_st[0][1],, cur_st[0][7]. All of the FSMs have the same list

can be used to generate a merged VDB with a report using the
following command:
urg -dir comp.vdb run*.vdb -modtreefile mod.txt -dbname merged
If a merged VDB is created with the -modtreefile option, the merged VDB saves the
merged coverage scores.
Merged VDBs created with -modtreefile cannot be merged with VDBs that are not
created with -modtreefile. Merged VDBs created with -modtreefile can be combined
if the modtreefile.txt file contains the same list of modules in the same order.

Consider the following figure that shows M1, M2, and M3 are instances of Module M, and B1
and B2 are instances of Module B:
Figure 43 Module M and Module B
If the modtreefile.txt file contains the following content, then the coverage data for all
instances of the module M is merged together, and the coverage data of the B1 and B2

The instances that belong to the same parameterized versions are merged along with their

If T1.M1 has a different parameterized shape than T2.M1, then T1.M1 is not merged with

If the metric shape of an instance of a module is not same to another instance

If exclusions are applied to an object in one instance of a module, its exclusions propagate
to all of its sibling instances. For example, consider three objects, T.M1.P1, T.M2.P1, and
T.X.M1.P1. If T.M2.P1 is excluded, then the exclusion is automatically applied to T.M1.P1
and T.X.M1.P1, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 46 Exclusion Propagation
When an exclusion in a moduletree-merged region is applied, the exclusion is copied
as a separate exclusion object for each instance. A single exclusion is saved that is
automatically propagated to the matching instances when the exclude file is loaded.

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
VCS enables you to define a single hierarchical configuration file to control monitoring of
coverage for both code and assertion coverage. To use this feature, specify your hier file
to the -cm_hier switch (compile time) or the -hier switch (URG) as normal, and add the
-cm_common_hier switch to enable the common hier mode.
For more details on this switch, see the following sections:
• Related Features

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
To specify hierarchical exclusions at compile time, use the following command:
vcs -cm_hier <config_file> -cm_common_hier
-cm line+cond+tgl+fsm+branch+assert
To specify hierarchical exclusions at report time, use the following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -hier <config_file> -cm_common_hier
Consider the following configuration file, config.txt that excludes a module, kp_fsm:
-module kp_fsm
When no hierarchical switch is used at compile time, both code coverage and assertion
coverage are reported for kp_fsm, as shown in the following figure:
When -cm_common_hier is used with -cm_hier at compile time, both code coverage
and assertion coverage are excluded for kp_fsm, therefore, kp_fsm is not shown in the
following URG report:

Unifying Hierarchical Configuration Files
Related Features
Few important points for consideration:
1. If -cm_hier, -cm_assert_hier, and -cm_common_hier are used at compile time,
-cm_common_hier discards -cm_assert_hier but excludes assertion coverage, as
-cm_hier with -cm_common_hier exclude both code and assertion coverage.
2. There is no change in the existing behavior of -cm_hier or -cm_assert_hier when
they are used separately at compile time.
3. In the unified -cm_common_hier flow, a -tree directive accepts only a hierarchy name
for excluding all assertions of the hierarchy. In the -cm_assert_hier flow, a -tree
directive accepts both a hierarchy name and an assert name. Such assertions cannot
be excluded using the -tree directive in the -cm_common_hier flow. For example, the
following assertion exclusion is not valid in the -cm_common_hier flow:
-tree top.m1.A1
where, A1 is an assertion under the instance, m1.
Alternatively, use an -assert directive to exclude a specific assertion by specifying its
hierarchy and assert name. For example, the following assertion exclusion is valid if
used with -assert:
-assert top.m1.A1
For more details on -assert, see -assert <assertion_name> or
-assert <assertion_hierarchical_name> in the Coverage Technology Reference
4. All directives, such as -module and -moduletree, in the unified hierarchical file are
supported for assertion coverage.
5. Assertions can be excluded or including at report time.
6. Metric-specific rules with begin-end can be applied to assertion coverage.

Excluding Generic Values for Coverage
Excluding Generic Values for Coverage
When generic values are used in conditional expressions, some combinations of values
tracked by VCS for condition coverage may not be possible to cover. You can direct VCS
to try to automatically exclude such condition vectors from coverage monitoring using the
-cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch, as follows:
vcs -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics
Note that the VDBs generated with the -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch are
not merge-compatible with the VDBs generated without this switch.
• URG Report
Consider the following code snippet from a module, mod:
OUT1 <= '1' when (((IN1 = tmp_sig0) and (data_width = 64)) or ((IN1 =
tmp_sig1) and (data_width = 32))) else '0';
end behave;
Now consider that mod is instantiated in two places in the design, as inst1 and inst2,
with the two different generic maps as shown in Table 2.
Table 2 Generic map of inst1 and inst2
inst1: mod inst2: mod
generic map ( data_width => 64,
addr_width => 20 )
generic map ( data_width => 32,
addr_width => 20 )
In inst1, the following condition becomes constant, as data_width is always 64 and
therefore, the condition is determined to be 0 at compile time:
(IN1 = tmp_sig1) and (data_width = 32)
When the -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch is used at compile time, the
condition above is not monitored for inst1.

Excluding Generic Values for Coverage
In inst2, the following condition becomes constant, as data_width is always 32 and
therefore, the condition is determined to be 0 at compile time:
(IN1 = tmp_sig0) and (data_width = 64)
When the -cm_cond vhdl_noconst_generics switch is used at compile time, the
condition above is not monitored for inst2.

feature:
◦ Only generic values of scalar types ( integer, enum, std_logic, std_ulogic,
boolean, bit, and char) are supported.
◦ Concatenation of multiple generics as part of a conditional expression is not
