Reducing Compile Time for FGP Analysis
You can use the -fgp=hier option to reduce the compile time and compile memory. This
option is particularly useful for gate-level simulation (GLS) designs.
Use the -fgp=hier option at compile time. For example,
% vcs -fgp=hier <other compile options>
• Dynamic reconfiguration is not supported.
• The -fgp=multisocket option is not supported.

VCS Performance Tuning Using Dynamic
Performance Optimizer (DPO)
VCS performance is an important aspect that impacts the verification and project time
lines. Traditionally, simulation performance has been a function of CPU performance,
memory efficiency, and serial algorithm. VCS has multiple options to improve the simulator
performance depending on certain characteristics of the design environment that is being
compiled and simulated. These options allow you to identify performance bottlenecks
and tune the command-line arguments and/or coding styles to extract best possible
performance.
Dynamic Performance Optimizer (DPO) is an intelligent automated approach that
enables necessary diagnostics during VCS compile and simulation and leverages AI to
recommend the appropriate set of options for enabling maximum performance without
manual intervention.
DPO supports performance analysis of the full regression or multiple tests per simv.
Enabling DPO With VCS
DPO is enabled by adding the -dpo option to the vcs compile command line. DPO specific
options are enabled using the -dpo_opts <option=value> option. For the complete list
of DPO options, see DPO Options.
-dpo is ignored when specified inside arguments passed to -f/-F/-file. This
option should explicitly be passed on the vcs command line.
DPO Flow
Typical DPO flow involves the following two steps:
Step-1: Learn and Merge
Learn — This step performs analysis and stores learnings/recommendations in the
database. The -dpo_opts mode=learn option at the compile time enables Learn mode.

DPO Options
Merge — This step merges the learnings across the designs/tests. This step is mandatory
for applying the learnings. For more information, refer to Merging Learn Databases.
Step-2: Apply
Apply — Learnings/Recommendations are fetched from the merged database and applied
automatically. This step is enabled by default when the -dpo_opts mode option is not
specified or when the -dpo_opts mode=apply option is explicitly specified.
The Apply mode is valid only when a merged learn database is available.
The recommended usage is to run all designs/tests in Learn mode once and then merge
the learnings. You can switch to Apply mode for all subsequent runs.

You can use the test_type dpo option to override the default priority order of picking

-dpo_opts test_type=<dpo|uvm|ovm|cm_test|cm_name>
dpo – Selects the test name from +DPO_TESTNAME if it is specified, otherwise default order
of priority is used.
uvm – Selects the test name from +UVM_TESTNAME if it is specified, otherwise default order
of priority is used.
ovm – Selects the test name from +OVM_TESTNAME if it is specified, otherwise default order
of priority is used.
cm_test – Selects the test name from -cm_test if it is specified, otherwise default order of
priority is used.
cm_name – Selects the test name from -cm_name if it is specified, otherwise default order of
priority is used.
• If test_type is specified and if the relevant argument is missing, the default order is
considered.
• If test_type is not specified, the default order is considered.
• Specifying -dpo_opts test_name in simulation command line overrides all above,
omitting test_type.

Sample Content of the dpo_reco_detail.csv File
Detail recommendation file is useful to review the recommendation per test. The
_AT_LEAST_ONE_ entry in the testname or test_variant column of the dpo_reco.csv
file indicates that not ALL simulation tests or variants of the tests have the same
recommendation.
Enabling the recommendation in such scenarios might potentially lead to errors during the
apply phase compile or simulation. You must review the detail recommendation file that
captures the recommendations per test and decide if a particular recommendation should
be enabled. Sample content of the dpo_reco_detail.csv file is as follows:
## DPO RECOMMENDATION FILE HEADER
## Created at 18:52:42 on Monday 26-July-2021
## VCS Version S-2021.09

## PLEASE NOTE ##
##,#1,Purpose of this file is only to provide detailed information on the
recommendations for user review.
##,#2,"To enable or disable a recommendation, please make the changes to
'enable (Y/N)' column entry in 'dpo_reco.csv' file."

app,action,options,design_tag,testname,test_variant,recommendation,stage,
benefit,cost,category,reason

lint,REMOVE,"[['-assert','enable_diag']]",dpo_design,
test2,1,No,vcs,"['RT', 'CT']",None,Assertion,Remove heavy assertion
debug flag for regressions

Reviewing and Enabling Recommendations
lint,REMOVE,"[['-assert','enable_diag']]",dpo_design,
test1,1,Yes,vcs,"['RT', 'CT']",None,Assertion,Remove heavy assertion
debug flag for regressions
lint,REMOVE,"[['-assert','success']]",dpo_design,
test2,1,Yes,simv,['RT'],None,Assertion,Stop reporting assertion success
to improve sim performance
Enable/Disable Recommendations in Apply Mode
You must review the dumped CSV file after the learn phase and modify the value
of column enable (Y/N) to have either Y or N. If you want to enable a particular
recommendation, then the value of the field enable (Y/N) must be set to Y. If it is set to N,
then the App considers it as a disabled recommendation.
These feedbacks can be passed to App using either of the following:
• Through the DPO configuration file using the -dpo_opts cfg option. Specify the
recommendations CSV file pointer with App configuration parameter reco_file.
• Through the following DPO option reco_file:
-dpo_opts reco_file=<path_to_reco_csv_file>
◦ Priority is given to the -dpo_opts reco_file option.
◦ If no -dpo_opts reco_file or config options are passed in the Apply phase,
recommendations that are ON by default are applied.
Following is the sample content of DPO configuration file. You can specify reco_file
either at app_configs (applies reco_file globally) or at app as follows:
app_configs:
reco_file : <dpo_reco.csv>
lint:
reco_file : <dpo_reco.csv>
upfopt:
reco_file : <dpo_reco.csv>
The reco_file entry under the app section gets higher priority over the entry under the
app_configs section. For an entry under the app section, only the recommendations
specific to the App are picked from the CSV file.
Dumping recommendations for user review and update is currently enabled for
the lint and upfopt Apps only.

Configuration File
Configuration File
Optional configuration file can be specified by using the -dpo_opts cfg=<config file
path> option to set the necessary DPO specific logging modes, and App parameters to
override any default values for Apps.
The following sections describe this feature in detail:
• Configuration File Syntax
• Supported Message Logging Modes
• Supported App Configuration Variables
Configuration File Syntax
Following is the configuration file syntax (YAML format ^^):
app_configs:
<Message Logger variables>
< app1_name>:
<app specific config variables>
<config>: <path to app specific config file with
config variables> **
<app2_name>:
<app specific config variables>
<config>: <path to app specific config file with
config variables> **
All variables are specified in the key: value format.
^^ YAML mandates four white spaces for every indentation. Do not use <tab>.
** You can also choose to specify the variable values in an App-specific configuration file
(YAML format).
Sample Configuration File
Following is the sample configuration file:
Example 133 Sample Configuration File
log_output: file
log_level: error
plilearn:
ELAPSED_TIME_THRESHOLD: 600
fgp:
config: /home/cfg_files/fgp_config.yaml

Configuration File
Following is the sample fgp_config.yaml file:
MAX_NUM_THREADS: 6
Supported Message Logging Modes
Messaging is primarily configurable using log_level to choose the severity and
log_output to choose the target for logging. Specify logging related variables in the
app_configs: section of the configuration file. Following is the syntax:
log_level: <info/warning/error> (info is default)
• info: Report messages with info, warning, error severity
• warning: Report messages with warning and error severity
• error: Report messages with error severity
log_output: <stdout/file/quiet> (file is default)
Table 56 Supported Message Logging Modes
Mode Target
file (default) info/warning/error to stdout and dpo_workdir log files
stdout info/warning/error to stdout only
quiet info/warning/error to dpo_workdir log files only
Messages logged to stdout are also captured in the user-specified vcs/simv
log files.

DB Migration Utility
The DB migration utility (dpo_db_migrate) allows you to update the existing learn db
(from older version) to the current version without the need to re-learn.
Following is the use model:
dpo_db_migrate [-h] [-d DB_DIR] [-f filelist] [-l logfile]
-d - Specifies the comma separated list of DB directories
-f - Specifies the list of DB directories in a file
-l - Specifies the log file

Plilearn App
• By default, the migrated databases are available in the original directory. DPO saves
the old databases at the database directory level in a new directory <basename>.old/.
All the old .db files are renamed with an extension .db.old.
• If DB migration tool ran on a DB, which has already migrated to the supported version,
DPO issues an info message and will not run any migration.
• When the existing DB version is older than the currently supported tool version, the tool
automatically migrates up.
Plilearn App
The plilearn app supports the following four modes or types of PLI Learn supported by
VCS:
+vcs+learn+pli Enables the module level PLI learn.
+vcs+learn+pli+instpli Enables the instance level PLI learn.
+vcs+learn+pli+sigpli Enables signal PLI learn at the module level.
+vcs+learn+pli+sigpli
+vcs+learn+pli+instpli
Enables signal PLI learn at the instance level.
You can configure the required PLI Learn mode for a design run using the following dpo
option:
-dpo_opts cfg=dpo_plilearn.cfg
PLI_LEARN_MODE is the configuration variable that decides the type of PLI Learn mode for
a design run. It accepts the following valid values:
MODULE_PLI [Default mode] Generates module PLI tab file.
INSTANCE_PLI Generates instance PLI tab file.
MODULE_SIGNAL_PLI Generates module signal PLI tab file.
INSTANCE_SIGNAL_PLI Generates instance signal PLI tab file.
The dpo_plilearn.cfg file contains the following content:
app_configs:
log_level: info

Automg App
log_output: stdout
plilearn:
PLI_LEARN_MODE: MODULE_SIGNAL_PLI
The default PLI_LEARN_MODE is MODULE_PLI. When the PLI Learn mode is not specified in
the cfg file, then the DPO plilearn app generates the module pli tab file.

Automg App
Sample run_script:
#!/bin/csh
rm -rf csrc simv simv.daidir ucli.key vcs.cfg

vcs test.sv -sverilog -dpo -dpo_opts apps=automg -lca
-l vcs.log
simv -l simv.log
grep 000abcd88000000a simv.log
if ($status == 0) then
set MY_STATUS="PASS"
set MY_STATUS="FAIL"
endif
echo $MY_STATUS
$VCS_HOME/bin/dpo_automg --update $DPO_REGID --status $MY_STATUS
--workdir <automg workdir path>
2. Initialize DPO automg app
% dpo_automg --reference_version <passing stream> --run_script <path
to script that launches the run and passes the status of the run back
to DPO> --init
Following is the sample command:
% dpo_automg --reference_version 2020.12 --run_script ./bm_run.csh --
init
It generates a wrapper script that launches run_script with different BCID and MHID
setups.
3. Launch the wrapper script
% sh $PWD/automg_workdir/automg_wrapper.sh
It calls run_script automatically for every iteration.

Migration Helper App
Migration Helper App
You can use the Migration Helper (mg_help)app during release migration when you
encounter compile errors in the current VCS release, but passing in the older VCS
release. The DPO mg_help app allows you to quickly identify the necessary BCIDs during
release migration and migrate with ease.
Following is the use model:
% vcs -dpo -dpo_opts apps=mg_help <other vcs options>
If the mg_help app finds any applicable BCIDs, it lists the BCID, provides
recommendation, and generates a BCID file, for example:
[DPO][MG_HELP] [INFO] Recommended BCIDs: 'ASSOC_ARRAY_DELETE_METHOD'
[DPO][MG_HELP] [INFO] RECOMMENDATION: Applicable BCIDs are listed in
'//mg_help_test/mg_help_synopsys_bc.setup' file. Please point the
environment variable SNPS_SIM_BC_CONFIG_FILE to the file and re-compile.
[DPO][MG_HELP] [INFO] Please refer to '//mg_help_test/mg_help_bc.log'
for more information regarding BCIDs.
Once recommendation is manually applied and compile is successful, the mg_help app
issues the following message:
[DPO][MG_HELP] [INFO] NO RECOMMENDATION: VCS compile is successful.
Once the compilation is successful, the subsequent compiles need not enable the
mg_help app.
• DPO is not supported with the following:
◦ Verdi interactive mode
◦ VHDL-top environment
◦ Save/Restore flow
◦ Reverse debug/Checkpoint
• The ctopt App is not supported with Partition Compile (PC)

• Every unique simulation executable (simv) built represents a unique design tag from
DPO perspective. For example, a regression environment with 'N' compiles require 'N'
unique

Next Generation Parallel Compiler
To improve compile time for a large RTL or GLS design in VCS, use the Next Generation
Parallel Compiler feature with the -parallelcomp option. This method provides significant
compile time reduction through advanced parallelization techniques. Parallel Compile,
• Creates balanced partitions for maximum parallel efficiency.
• Uses lightweight elaboration engines for faster incremental builds.
• Scales automatically as design size increases.
As parallel compile (-parallelcomp) extends partition compile (-partcomp), designs that
use -parallelcomp also inherit the following partition-compile benefits:
• Supports incremental compilation (only modified partitions recompiled).
• Enables shared partition libraries using -partcomp_sharedlib.
• Enables autopartitioning of the design.
• Supports cross-module references (XMRs).
• Supports relocatable databases for sharing compiled partitions.
Parallel Compile enables faster scratch compilation, reduced incremental compile time,
and better memory scalability for large RTL or GLS designs.
Use the -parallelcomp compile option to enable the parallel compiler. Following is the
usage:
vcs -parallelcomp <other_options>
The -parallelcomp option compiles 4 partitions in parallel by default. In larger designs
where the number of partitions is high, the user can override the default 4 parallel
processes by using -parallelcomp=jN, where, N is the required number of parallel
compilations. You can choose N number based on the cores available in the grid. In
addition to this, parallel compile has improved global analysis time and faster elaboration
during the subsequent compilation stages.

Dynamic Test Loading
Dynamic Test Loading (DTL) is an approach to load and run any test dynamically at any
time during simulation. The test loaded at runtime can include different UVM tests or
sequences.
For detailed information on DTL, refer to Dynamic Test Loading chapter in VCS User
VCS introduces a simplified use model of DTL (2-step) flow, referred to as DTL single-step
flow. This can be enabled using -dtl option. See Use Model section for details on how to
enable DTL single step flow.
Following are the steps to use DTL using simplified single-step flow:
1. Encapsulate all test classes derived from UVM classes in SystemVerilog packages.
2. Compile the test packages using DTL Single-Step Flow. Note that this step is simplified
and fastest way to enable DTL by using -dtl option. Add the -dtl option to the
existing partition compile setup and convert into DTL flow.
◦ Use -dtl=<package_name> at the compile step.
◦ At the compile step, use the -dtl option and the package name that corresponds
to the dynamic test package along with other partition compile options, top module,
and static test package.

-dtl=test1_pkg,test2_pkg

Enabling Congruent Mode to Improve Parallelization
The event-driven simulation of Verilog can cause race conditions at the RTL level. This
happens when several parallel processes update signals at the same simulation time,
without a set order. This can lead to results that do not match real hardware behavior.
To avoid this, design teams use nonblocking assignments for sequential logic and blocking
assignments for combinational logic. They also add timing offsets or use structured
clocking to separate data and clock events. These methods ensure predictable simulation
and easier debugging.
Sometimes, adding delays between clock and data to prevent races can slow down
parallel performance. This is because extra time steps are needed to transfer data.
VCS HyperSim congruent mode solves this by removing delays from inferred flip-flops and
latches. It keeps the simulation race-free by sampling the old data value when clock and
data change together. This increases events at clock edges and improves parallelization.
To enable congruent mode for more constructs such as continuous assignment, use the
-hypersim compile-time option.
Remove the -hypersim=bringup_mode option, as it overrides congruent mode.
To disable congruent mode on specific modules, you can use the following configuration
file syntax:
module {<module_name_or_comma_separated_list_of_module_names>}
{noJagCongruency}
Then, add the configuration file with the following compile-time option:
+optconfigfile+<cfg_file_name>
Enabling Passive Mode
Passive elements are parts of your design that only read the simulation state. They do not
change or write to the simulation state.

A module that has only input ports and does not have any output ports is called a passive
element. If the module does not change any value during simulation, either through cross-
module references, or by using a PLI application, it is also considered passive.
The following is an example of a passive module:
module (input a);
always @(a) $display(a);
HyperSim can detect and automatically mark passive modules based on how they are
used.
By default, all DPI functions are considered non-passive. This is because their behavior
in C code is unknown. If you have a DPI function which is passive, you must mark it as
passive in the configuration file.
Use Model to Apply Auto-Inferred Passive Elements
When you use the -hypersim or -hypersim=bringup_mode compile-t

end

Deviation From Regular Simulation
The passive thread uses a separate scheduler that is not linked to the main simulation.
The simulation time for the passive thread is different and is always at least one timestamp

behind the main simulation time. This can cause the following differences from a regular
simulation:
• Order of Simulation Log
The simulation logs from the passive thread and the main thread can overlap and are
not sorted by simulation time. For example, a display at time t in the passive thread
might appear after a display at time t+5 in the main thread.
• Difference in Finish Time
If the passive thread stops because of an error, the main thread might continue running
past the error time. As a result, the simulation finish time and the error time might not
be the same.
Enabling Testbench Mode
Modern testbench methods, such as UVM, are widely used. UVM gives design and
verification teams a strong and standard way to work. It supports projects from small IP
blocks to large SoCs. UVM helps teams reuse code by using modular components. It also
makes it easier to create test stimulus with constrained random methods. This leads to
better coverage and higher-quality silicon.
In the default HyperSim flow, UVM-based testbench activities run on the main thread. The
main thread waits until all testbench actions are complete.
With HyperSim testbench mode, testbench activities can run on a separate thread.
DUT activities can run on other threads at the same time. This can improve simulation
performance, especially if the testbench workload is less than 20 percent of the total.
To enable the testbench mode, use the following compile-time option:
-hypersim=tb
HyperSim testbench mode uses one CPU core. For example, if you set
-hypersim=num_threads:3, HyperSim uses 4 cores in total. One core is for
the main thread, one for the testbench thread, and the other two for parallel

For example, in the following always block, HyperSim sees q as the output of a sequential

When you run the % vcs -hypersim -debug_acc+f -hypersim=debug_perf test.v

Limitations of HyperSim
HyperSim has the following limitations:
• HyperSim does not support the dynamic reconfiguration feature.
• HyperSim does not support SDC.
• The HyperSim testbench flow does not support the save-restore feature.
• HyperSim does not support the reverse debug feature.
• The HyperSim passive flow is disabled in the DTL flow.
• The +vcs+loopreport option disables the HyperSim passive flow.
• HyperSim does not support analog or mixed-signal (AMS) flows.
• Remove the -hypersim=num_threads* option from the runtime options to use
simprofile for simulation profiling.
• Expect the compile time to increase by up to 1.5 times during a scratch compile.
• HyperSim does not support the +allmtm option.
• HyperSim and FGP are both multi‑core technologies. However, HyperSim offers a
wider set of features compared to FGP, as described in the HyperSim: Hyper-Scaling
Simulation Performance section.

variable that does not infer a sequential element is not changed by this command.

Support for a Single-Step Flow in DTL
VCS supports Dynamic Test Loading or DTL, an approach to load and run any test
dynamically at any time during simulation. The test loaded at runtime can include various
UVM tests or sequences. You can run these tests without repeating the compilation
process for regenerating the simulator executable (simv) for each test. Also, you do not
have to run common routines like reset and initialization in each test, thus saving runtime.

single-step flow of DTL and can be enabled using the -dtl option.

configuration, it should be bound to the same module under all configurations, and

In the analysis phase, VCS checks the design for the syntax errors. In this phase, VCS
generates the intermediate files required for elaboration and saves these files in the
design or work library pointed to by your default logical library. For information on library
mapping, see “The Concept of a Library in VCS” . You can instruct VCS to save these
intermediate files in a different library using the -work option with the vhdlan or vlogan
executables.
Before you analyze your design using vhdlan or vlogan, ensure that the library mappings
are defined in the synopsys_sim.setup file, and that the specified physical library for
the logical library exists. If the physical directory does not exist, VCS exits with an error
message.

Optimizing Testbenches for Debugging
Improve VCS simulation performance by selectively enabling or disabling testbench
debugging features such as VCD and FSDB file writing, using conditional compilation,
runtime plusarg control, or a combination of both techniques.
Debugging operations like $monitor, $display, $dumpvars, and $fsdbDumpvars
significantly degrade simulation speed, particularly file-writing operations that generate
VCD or FSDB simulation history files. Use conditional compilation with `ifdef and +define
+macro to exclude debugging system tasks at compile time for maximum simulation
performance. Alternatively, use the $test$plusargs system function for runtime control
without recompilation, at the cost of reduced optimization since VCS must prepare for
worst-case runtime scenarios. Combine both techniques for granular control over when
simulation history files are written during different stages of the design development cycle.
Testbenches typically execute debugging features, for example, displaying text in certain
situations as specified with the $monitor or $display system tasks. Another debugging
feature, which is typically enabled in testbenches, is writing simulation history files during
simulation so that you can view the results after simulation.
Among other things, these simulation history files record the simulation times at which the
signals in your design change value. These simulation history files can be either ASCII
Value-Change-Dump (VCD) files that you can input into a number of third-party viewers, or
binary FSDB files that you can input into Verdi.

The vcdiff Utilityvcdiff utility
The vcdiff utility compares two dump files and reports any differences it finds. The dump
file can be of type VCD, EVCD, or VPD.
The vcdiff utility cannot compare dump files of different types.
Dump files consist of two sections:
• A header section that reflects the hierarchy (or some subset) of the design that was
used to create the dump file.
• A value change section, which contains all of the value changes (and times when those
value changes occurred) for all of the signals referenced in the header.
The vcdiff utility first compares the header sections and reports any signals/scopes that
are present in one dump file, but absent in other. Then, the vcdiff utility compares the
value change sections of the dump files for signals that appear in both dump files. This
utility determines value change differences based on the final value of the signal in a time
step.
Syntaxvcdiff utilitysyntax
The syntax of the vcdiff utility is as follows:
vcdiff first_dump_file second_dump_file
[-noabsentsig] [-absentsigscope scope] [-absentsigiserror]
[-allabsentsig][-absentfile filename][-matchtypes] [-ignorecase]
[-min time] [-max time] [-scope instance] [-level level_number]

[-include filename] [-ignore filename] [-strobe time1 time2]
[-prestrobe] [-synch signal] [-synch0 signal] [-synch1 signal]
[-when expression] [-xzmatch] [-noxzmatchat0]
[-compare01xz] [-xumatch] [-xdmatch] [-zdmatch] [-zwmatch]
[-showmasters] [-allsigdiffs] [-wrapsize size]
[-limitdiffs number] [-ignorewires] [-ignoreregs] [ignorereals]
[-ignorefunctaskvars][-ignoretiming units] [-ignorestrength]
[-geninclude [filename]] [-spikes]
The vcdiff Utility Output Example
The following is an example of the vcdiff output:
--- top.sig1 --- 200 ---
< 200 0
---
> 100 1

--- top.sig2 --- 200 ---
< 100 1
---
> 200 0
In this example, there are two differences between the two compared dump files. The
format of a difference is as follows:
--- signal_hierarchical_name --- time_of_mismatch ---
< time_of_last_change change_to_this_value
---
> time_of_last_change change_to_this_value
< (line beginning with <)
Contains the time of the last value change of the signal (at or before the time of the
mismatch) in the first dump file on the vcdiff command line.
> (line beginning with >)
Contains the corresponding information in the second dump file on the vcdiff command

Auto-partitioning
You enable auto-partitioning when you use the
-partcomp compile-time option. This
is the default and recommended mode of partitioning. Auto-partitioning automatically
partitions the design and the testbench. To specify the partitions yourself apart from the
auto-partitioning see section Specifying Partitions Manually.
Use the following compile-time options to control auto-partitioning:
•
Applies auto-partitioning to both modules and SystemVerilog packages.
•
-partcomp=autopart_low-partcomp=autopart_low[partcomp=autopart_low]
-partcomp=autopart_low
Applies auto-partitioning to both modules and packages with a low threshold, which
results in smaller and more numerous partitions.
•
-partcomp=autopart_high-partcomp=autopart_high[partcomp=autopart_high]
-partcomp=autopart_high
Applies auto-partitioning to both modules and packages with a high threshold, which
results in larger and fewer partitions. Larger and fewer partitions take more time to
compile or elaborate than smaller and more numerous partitions.
•
-partcomp=autopart_high-partcomp=autopart_high[partcomp=autopart_high]
-partcomp=autopart_huge
Applies auto-partitioning to both modules and packages with threshold higher than
-partcomp=autopart_high, which results in much larger and very fewer partitions.
•
-partcomp=autopart_relaxh-partcomp=autopart_relax[partcomp=autopart_relax]
-partcomp=autopart_relax
Applies auto-partitioning in relax mode. Use -partcomp=autopart_relax option when
-partcomp=autopart_high gives less balanced partitions. It relaxes the partitioning
with a high threshold to get maximum gain in turnaround time.

Specifying Partitions in an +optconfigfile File
You specify a partition in this file with a line beginning with the keyword partition.
The keyword cell specifies that the partition is for all instances of the module name or
program block name that follows.
Example 46 Partition Compile +optconfigfile Configuration File
// +optconfigfile configuration file cfg.txt
partition cell test;
partition cell multiplier;
This configuration file specifies:
• one partition for program block test
• one partition for both instances of module multiplier
The default and unspecified partition contains the top-level module top and module adder.
Compile the design and testbench with the -partcomp option and specifying the
configuration file with the +optconfigfile option, for example:
% vcs
-partcomp top.v test.v add_mult.v \ +optconfigfile+config.txt
[other options]

Specifying Partitions in a VHDL Configuration File
VHDL and VHDL-on-top, mixed-HDL designs require a VHDL configuration file to specify
the partitions (see Example 47). The syntax and semantics of the configuration file are
the same as for a regular VHDL configuration file, with the addition of the new keyword partition
partition.
partition compileVHDL configuration

library work;
USE STD.textio.all;
USE IEEE.STD_LOGIC_TEXTIO.all;
use IEEE.STD_LOGIC_1164.all;
use work.all;
configuration topcfg of top is
for top_arch
for partition i1: child use entity work.child(module);
end for;
end for;

Turbo Compile Flow
Verification engineers change only the verification environment (testbench or tests) and
the DUT remains constant. Many engineers are involved in the design and verification of
small to large designs. Some of the common scenarios are:
• Changes are local to the testbench or the verification environment, but not in the
• Changes are local to a design, but not in the testbench or the verification environment.
Each change can lead to huge compile time. Partition compile creates partitions of the
design and the testbench that are compiled separately and enables faster compilation of
design and verification environment during incremental compile.
The incremental compile flow with partition compile does not trigger the compilation of
unused or unchanged common portions of the design or tests. Incremental compilation
is faster because it shares the compiled data from other portions of the design. Hence it
reduces compile-time and disk space consumption across multiple tests.
Also, incremental compilations can be done in parallel to further speed up the compile
turnaround time across multiple tests or multiple users in SOC designs.
At the same time, the compile areas need to be relocatable, as anything can be moved
anywhere to reduce NFS access for users.
All these can be achieved using Turbo Compile Flow with Partition Compile. It helps to
create a relocatable database along with the benefits of incremental compile with partition
compile flow.

The Partition Compile Two-Step Flow
1. Synopsys recommends using autopartitioning using the -partcomp option. This is

2. You can create a partition configuration file to generate different partitions than

Commonly Used Partition-Compile Options
You can use the following options for partition compile flow:-dir=<dir_name>
-dir/-partcomp_dir=<dir_name>

-sharedlib/-partcomp_sharedlib=<dir_name>

Limiting Partitions
You can use the following options to limit the module and package partitions in partition
compile flow:
-partcomp=modpart_limit:N
Limits the module partitions to the specified number.
-partcomp=pkgpart_limit:N
Limits the package partitions to the specified number.
The modpart_limit and pkgpart_limit are considered as guidelines by the
VCS partitioner. The tool can still create slightly more or slightly less partitions
based on the module or package sizes and inter-dependencies.

Relocation Methods with Partition Compile
VCS allows you to move the simulation executable to the location of your choice. With the
relocated database, you can get the benefit of a faster compile turnaround time by reusing
the existing partitions and compiling (relocatable compilation) or running the simulation
(relocatable simulation) in a new directory.
The following are the two methods to relocate the database in partition compile - turbo
compile flow:

By default, VCS allows calling non-blocking tasks such as tasks without delay, event
control or wait statements, from within a function. For blocking task calls, an error
message is issued.
In the partition compile flow, the blocking and non-blocking nature of a task call may not
always be determined at compile-time. Compilation may complete without errors when
calling a blocking task from within a function.
You can use the -partcomp=LRM_1800_2012 compile-time option to enable checking of
stricter SystemVerilog compliant rule. When the option is specified, an error message is
issued in the partition compile flow for calling any tasks, blocking or non-blocking, from
within a function.
Scenarios Causing a Recompilation of a Partition
The following cases cause a recompilation of a partition:
• Change of a module definition in a partition, either instance- or cell-based.
• Change in VCS command-line option (addition, deletion, or sub-argument value
change).
• Change in the synopsys_sim.setup or
+optconfigfile
+optconfigfile file.
• Global design property changes like adding
$dumpvars
$dumpvars to a partition, in which case all
partitions need to be recompiled.
• Changes to the ports or parameters that affect the ports of a partition. If there is a
parent and child partition, and this change is only to the child partition, the parent need
not be recompiled.
• Changes to
$unit
$unit scope. Any change (addition of a new signal, type, module, or
interface) to a $unit causes recompilation of all the partitions associated with the
$unit.
• Changes to an interface require the recompilation of all modules connected to that
interface.
• Changes to a shared package. In this case, all the partitions sharing this package
require recompilation.
• Reanalysis of source code ( vlogan or vhdlan) with different command-line options
causes recompilation of the source code and all partitions that share the logical library.

configuration files.
• The change in a package partition leads to recompilation of its dependent partitions.
• When two or more modules/packages/interfaces are grouped into one partition,
then even if only one module/package/interface is changed, the whole partition is

Achieving the Best Turnaround Time with Partition Compile
To get the maximum gain in turnaround time from the partition compile flow, note the
• Do not create too many partitions
◦ Start with autopartitioning and then tune for performance, if needed.
• Avoid code in $unit
◦ Code changes in the $unit may affect many partitions.
◦ $unit is not sharable across multiple tests.
• Create separate partitions for each top-level design in hierarchy, if more than one top-
level change in subsequent compilation.
◦ All parallel top-level are a single partitions, by default.
◦ Create a separate partition for the top-level that changes frequently compared to
the other parallel top-level that are idle.
• Create separate partitions for each test (program) and only test partition gets
recompiled in this case.
• Make external IP/VIP modules as separate partitions.
• Partitions for mixed HDL designs
◦ Create separate partition for a VHDL entity if it is going to change frequently.
◦ If it is not a separate partition then it is compiled as part of default VHDL top
partition.
• Create one or more partitions for SV packages that are going to change frequently.
• Import packages only where required.
◦ Package changes can cause recompile of multiple partitions (if all packages are
imported in a file and that file is included in many partitions).

The -pcmakeprof compile-time option enables profiling of time spent in each step of a

Partition Compile Limitations
The following are the limitations with partition compile:
• Delayed or conditional SDF annotation is not supported.
• The -race option is not supported.
• Utilities like -metadump, -Xrawtokens can be used in regular compile to generate the
• Dynamic Reconfiguration
◦ Dynamic configuration with SDF is not supported.
◦ Dynamic configuration with VHDL
VHDL instance inside dynamic configuration enabled module
Dynamic configuration enabled instance in VHDL
• Interface instances with reference ports inside dynamic configuration enabled module.
• XMR across PE is not supported in partition compile flow.
• XMR referrer in PE module connected as module reference port is not supported in
partition compile flow.

• Cross-partition SDF (VHDL) is not supported.
• Only designs with SystemC on top are supported.
• When using VMC/SWIFT models then the VMC model cannot be a top-level module of
the design.
• Verilog-AMS Mixed Signal Simulation:
◦ Verilog-AMS amsd ie and setd commands are supported.
◦ GenBlock in Verilog-AMS flow is supported.
◦ Mixed Signal Simulation with FINESIM. (No HSIM and Nanosim compatibility with
VCS).
◦ Partition of top-level cell in the Mixed-Signal setup file is not supported in partition
compile flow.
◦ Multiple drivers for wreal net are not supported in partition compile flow.
• Coverage; Constant analysis ( -cm_noconst/-cm_seqnoconst) is more conservative in
partition compile, so some objects which are marked "unreachable" in single compile
are not marked in partcomp.
• The stop -thread <thread_no> command is expected to be different in partition
compile flow due to different thread ID between single compile and partition compile
flow.
• For mixed designs, processing of assertion configuration file (through compile-time
option -assert_hier) occurs at runtime in partition compile flow. This can have some
impact on runtime performance or may capture assertion related errors during runtime
instead of compile-time.
• Cross-partition DPI routine declaration mismatch error is generated at compile-time in
single compile flow for inconsistent declarations of DPI and DPI-C. You can use the
-error=noDPI-DRWIDT compile-time option to workaround this error in single compile
flow.
• Partition Compile does not support the interface port when it is a multi-dimensional
array.
• A compilation error Error-[SV-DOSIF] Delay or synchronization in function
is generated when a time-consuming task is invoked from within a function. For cross-
partition tasks, however, the error is deferred until runtime.

Restored DTL simulations can inherit the simulation log file from the saved base
simulation and continue it. This means that after the restored simulation has ended,
its log file contains the following:
▪ command-line of the base simulation
▪ log output of the base simulation up to the point of the snapshot save
▪ message that indicates that the log file has been inherited by the restored
simulation
▪ command-line of the restored simulation
▪ full log output of the restored simulation
This functionality is supported for DTL flows with $save/-r, native UCLI
(-ucli), and -ucliProc for both Verilog-only and MX designs. The option
-save_options=inherit_log is used for this purpose.
For more information, refer to “-l filename -save_options=inherit_log” in the VCS
Command Reference Guide.
◦ In case of only one UVM run phase in the test and there are no sub-phases:
The test is saved in the middle of the UVM run_phase of base_test, then at
restore it resumes execution and completes the run_phase of base_test. Once
the current phase execution is completed, UVM switches to the next phase of
dyn_test.
◦ For DTL $save and $restore, the UVM run phase must have at least two sub-
phases so that you can save the simulation in one sub-phas

This section describes the programming language interface (PLI) between the C/C++
functions and VCS. It helps link applications containing C/C++ functions with VCS, so that
they execute concurrently. The C/C++ functions in the application use the PLI to read and
write delay and simulation values in the VCS executable. Later during simulation VCS can
call these functions.
VCS supports PLI 1.0 and PLI 2.0 routines for the PLI. Therefore, you can use VPI, ACC,
or TF routines to write the PLI application. See Appendix , .
This chapter covers the following topics:
• Writing a PLI Application

Writing a PLI Application
When writing a PLI application, you need to perform the following tasks:
1. Write the C/C++ functions of the application calling the VPI, ACC, or TF routines to
access data inside VCS.
2. Associate user-defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions in
your application. VCS calls these functions when it compiles or executes these system
tasks or system functions in the Verilog source code. In VCS, associate the user-
defined system tasks and system functions with the C/C++ functions in your application
using a PLI table file (see PLI Table File). In this file, you can also limit the scope and
operations of the ACC routines for faster performance.
3. Enter the user-defined system tasks and functions in the Verilog source code.
4. Compile/Analyze, elaborate, and simulate your design, specifying the table file and
including the C/C++ source files (or compiled object files or libraries) so that the
application is linked with VCS in the simv ex

Reducing Compilation Time in Native Certitude With VCS Partition Compile Flow

Reducing Compilation Time in Native Certitude With VCS
Partition Compile Flow
This feature is Limited Customer Availability (LCA). Limited Customer Availability (LCA)
features are features available with select functionality. These features will be ready for a
general release based on customer feedback and meeting the required feature completion
criteria. LCA features do not need any additional license keys.
With the integration of Native Certitude with VCS Partition Compile flow, you can improve
the turnaround time for successive compilations in Native Certitude.
Partition Compile is used primarily to improve the turnaround time in successive
compilations. In Native Certitude, you have various phases of compilation. Therefore,
when you integrate Native Certitude along with the Partition Compile flow, you are able
to reduce the compilation time at each step. This results in improved performance during
compilation time.
The Native Certitude use model remains the same as that of the previous use model. For
information about the use model, see the Native Integration of Certitude and VCS section
in the Certitude User Manual.
Native Certitude consists of three phases in the following order:
• Model
• Activation
• Detection
The three different phases always run in the same order.
The model phase and the activation phase occur in a single compilation. The model phase
analyzes the DUT and creates a list of faults. The activation phase generates the simv
executable, which is used to determine the activated faults. The detection phase performs
the new compilation that generates the simv executable to determine the propagation and
the detection status of the faults. All the phases target the DUT part of the design and they
do not affect the testbench.

Reducing Compilation Time in Native Certitude With VCS Partition Compile Flow
If you want to fine-tune the testbench and recompile the design at activation or detection
phase, you must recompile the entire design including the DUT.
Similarly, after you are completed with the model and activation phases compilation and
you want to perform compilation in the detection phase, you must recompile the entire
design including the testbench that has not changed.
By integrating with Partition Compile, you can avoid the recompilation of unchanged
testbench part of the design. The compilation of testbench partition takes place only when
the testbench is changed.
Consider the following test cases:
//topcfg.v
design top;
partition instance top.dut use dut;

Coverage Directed Solver
Coverage Directed Solver helps you to speed up functional coverage convergence,
identify over-constraints affecting coverage closure, and provide Root Cause Analysis
(RCA) for SystemVerilog Constraint-based Random Verification (CRV) testbenches.
The features of Coverage Directed Solver are as follows:
• Automated Coverage Convergence: Reduces the number of runs required to get to
coverage closure or eliminates manual tests.
• Stimulus and Coverage Diversification: Finds more bugs in the testbench or design
due to a more diverse exploration of the coverage and stimulus space.
• Coverage Hole and Over-Constraint Identification and Root Cause Analysis:
Reduces the debug time to triage coverage holes or to identify over constraints, which
cause coverage holes and can improve testbench quality and reduce the potential for
subtle bugs hidden by testbench over-constraints.
• Improved Coverage Visualization:
◦ Provides URG and Verdi coverage integration of the guided constraint solving
results and analysis when availa

les and options that
are not related to Coverage Directed Solver.
To run Coverage Directed Solver in a three-step (or UUM) flow, use the following
commands:
• % vlogan [vlogan_options] file_list
• % vcs -vso ccex [elab_options] [libname].design_unit
• % simv -vso ccex <run_options>
The <vlogan_options>, <elab_options>, and <run_options> represent files
and options that are not related to Coverage Directed Solver.
Compile Commands
The first step in Coverage Directed Solver is to identify the connections between
covergroups and random variables. Identification of a connection at compile time is
referred to as compile-time connectivity generation.
To generate Coverage Directed Solver compile-time connectivity report, use the following
command:
%vcs -vso ccex -ccex_opts connect_report <compile_options>
• -vso ccex : Enables Coverage Directed Solver in compile-time connectivity mode if
connected covergroups are detected.
-ccex_opts connect_report : Generates the compile-time connectivity report of
Coverage Directed Solver.
User can specify path for connectivity report by specifying an additional argument to the
connect_report option as follows:
-ccex_opts connect_report=<report_path>
To visualize the connections between the coverpoint and crosses in covergroups to
random variables generated by Coverage Directed Solver at compile time, a covergroup-
level summary report of connectivity is available in ccex_summary.json under the same
directory where the compilation is done. This connectivity information is also annotated in
the URG report.

Runtime Commands
By default, Coverage Directed Solver biases the constraint solutions in the direction of
coverage inside a single simulation. This is referred to as intra-simulation biasing.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with intra-simulation biasing, use the following
command:
% simv -vso ccex <other runtime_options>
To enable Coverage Directed Solver to bias the constraint solutions across multiple
parallel simulation jobs running on the simulations, each Coverage Directed Solver-
enabled simulation needs to know the merged coverage state of the simulations which
have completed.
To enable Coverage Directed Solver with inter-simulation learning by reading from the
previous VDB, use the following command:
% simv -vso ccex -ccex_opts auto_merge_dir=<inter-sim shared directory>
The <inter-sim shared directory> is the commonly accessible path by all
simulation jobs and has a different path than the one specified with -cm_dir.
The command above performs automated distributed merging of covergroup metrics and
deposits the merged coverage results into the specified directory. Coverage Directed
Solver uses the merged directory as an input to identify covered targets and therefore,
focus efforts on targeting and diversifying over uncovered or rarely covered coverage bins.
Alternatively, if you already have an external method to merge the VDB directories

Reports
Coverage Directed Solver reporting brings together the information from the existing
constraint and the coverage reports or information into a URG report, which contains the
linked coverage to the connected constraints and random variables.
To generate the URG report for Coverage Directed Solver, use the following command:
% urg -ccex -dir simv.vdb <URG options>

Verdi Coverage CCEX Difference
The “Diff Databases” feature in Verdi Coverage is enhanced with CCEX information.
% verdi -cov -ccex
From the Tools menu, choose “Diff Databases…” to open the configuration dialog box
named Database Diff. You can load two different VDBs using this dialog box.
In the “Database” scope, you can specify the VDB databases and tests to differentiate.

Verdi Coverage CCEX Difference
In the diff view, you can see the difference data, based on the value of Database 1.
Click the
button on the Database Diff dialog box to exchange the databases
automatically. After the exchange, the diff view shows the difference data, based on
Database 2 instead.
The diff view divided into two parts. The left part is the view to show the difference of
covergroups and coverpoints. The right part is used to show the difference of bins.
In the diff table cell, the number before the brackets is the value of the first database.
The number in the brackets is the diff value, which equals (vdb1- vdb2). If there is no
corresponding value of one database, “NA” is displayed; however, 0 is considered to
calculate the diff data. If the two values are equal, the text is marked in black; otherwise, it
is marked in red.
An RCA column is added to the bin diff view. If the RCA Type is marked in black, it means
that both the RCA type and the detailed RCA information are same.

Verdi Coverage CCEX Difference
Click the RCA cell to open the RCA Info dialog box, which displays the RCA information in
detail. Click the hyperlink to navigate to the specific line in the source file.
In the RMB menu, two options are added. You can change the sorting rules by the
option “Sort By Diff”. If it is enabled, the table gets sorted by the diff data (the value in the
brackets) when you click the table header. Otherwise, the table gets sorted by the value of
Database 1 (the value before the brackets).

Exclusion Support in CCEX
Exclusion supports excluding cover item objects from Coverage Directed Solver targeting
at runtime.
For dumping exclusions, use the following command:
urg -dir simv.vdb -ccex -dump full_exclusions ccex_illegal
The new files are dumped in the directory where you are running. These files contain
excluded objects for the group coverage in the commented form. You can copy this file
to a new file, uncomment the objects you want to exclude and pass the new file as an
argument with the Coverage Directed Solver exclusion option -elfile in runtime.

Change-Based Verification
Change-Based Verification (CBV) is a key component of the VSO.ai smart stress phase,
leveraging its ability to identify changes in the design and its associated Cone of Influence
(COI). CBV optimizes test selection with the goal of catching all the unique failure
signatures around identified area of code changes.
When global ICO phase configuration is used, the recommended tests for
failure recall are impacted.
Installation and Setup
Separate installation or license is not required to enable CBV flow in VSO.ai.
The following are the minimum VCS version requirements to enable this functionality:
• VCS 2023.12-SP2-9
• VCS 2024.09-SP2-3
• VCS 2025.06
• VCS 2026.03
CBV Workflow
The CBV functionality is seamlessly woven into various stages of the VSO.ai workflow.
After design changes are identified, they are mapped to the coverage targets that exist in
the VSO.ai ML model.
Initialization Stage
To use the CBV flow, it is mandatory to enable the line or tgl portonly metric during
the Day0 run of generating the VSO.ai ML model. This is essential because identified
design changes are mapped back to line or tgl portonly coverage targets, allowing
you to stress coverage around those mapped targets in the VSO.ai stress phase.

CBV Workflow
1. Compile Step:
The CBV flow is tightly integrated with VCS compile. Enabling VSO.ai options is
mandatory during the compile step to allow the CBV flow to identify design changes
during the VSO.ai init step.
$VCS_HOME/bin/vcs \
-vso cso \
-vso_opts buildname=<buildname> \
-vso_opts workdir=<workdir> \
[other VCS options]
If multiple builds are used in the project, ensure that a buildname is
associated with each compile, as the CBV flow identifies design changes on
a per-build basis.
2. Init Step:
In the init step, the CBV flow identifies design changes and applies them to the
VSO.ai ML model. This left-shifts coverage closure for code changes and targets
unique failures around the modified areas during the Smart Stress phase. By default,
VSO.ai enables all the following three phases:
◦ Smart Stress
◦ Acceleration
◦ Exploration
If you need to target only the design changes and exit, you can specify --phase
stress[:<N>]. Where, N is an optional value used to specify the number of times the
identified design changes are to be stressed around coverage. By default the value of N
is 1.
On Day0, there are no design changes; therefore, the init step tags only the design-
level information to the vso_workdir.
You must specify the simv location to tag the design information generated during VCS
compile to vso_workdir.
The simv path can be specified to the init step using the simv_location variable for
each build in the configuration file. Alternatively, the simv path can also be specified
using one of the following options:
◦ simv_paths: Comma-separated paths to all the build simvs being targeted by the
regression run.
◦ simv_path_list: File containing simv paths to all the build simvs to be targeted by
re

V-
specific handling during the finalize and merge steps.
Additionally, CBV flow also offers the capability to generate exclusion file for all unchanged
targets identified for current regression run. The generated .el file (exclusion file, typically
with .el extension) can then be used to create an urgReport for the modified portions of
the design, ensuring only the original changed targets are unexcluded. The .el file can
also be consumed by Verdi for interactive exclusion analysis.
$VSO_HOME/bin/driver \
--dump_exclusions_for_changes
--workdir <workdir> \
--vdbdir <vdb_path> \
--target_metric <metrics> \
--elfile_outdir <outdir> \

Analytics and Reporting
where,
• --dump_exclusions_for_changes is a Boolean option that enables the generation of
an exclusion file for unchanged design targets.
• --vdbdir specifies an input vdb to generate an exclusion file compatible with that vdb.
The vdb can be as follows:
◦ vdb for any single build and test
◦ Merged vdb across all tests of a particular build
◦ Merged vdb across all builds
◦ Merged vdb with different flex_merge options
The VDBs generated with flex_merge modules or using –
merge_across_libs as an input may not contain the complete information
on the changes identified.
• --target_metric: If specified, allows to selectively dump the exclusions for the
required metric.
• If specified, --elfile_outdir defines the output directory for generated .el files. If
not specified, these files are generated within the workdir by default. The resulting file
is named excl_for_changes.el.
Analytics and Reporting
For information related to CBV analytics for Smart Stress phase, refer to Visualization in
VSO.ai chapter in the VSO.ai User Guide.
The CBV flow dumps the detailed change report, change_detail_report.txt, for each
build during the init step. This report includes detailed information about the identified
changed elements in the design. The detailed report is saved under workdir/online/
info/builds/<buildname>/change_detail_report.txt.

Limitations
The following are the limitations of the CBV feature:
• Identification of design changes is supported only for Verilog, SystemVerilog, and
VHDL portions of the RTL.
• CBV support for testbench and VHDL is currently a beta feature, which requires
additional options to be specified during the initialization phase of VSO.ai. For more
information, refer to the VSO.ai Beta Features Guide.

This command opens the Interface Browser form.
Figure 79

Interface Browser Form

The Interface Browser form includes the following panes, options, buttons and field.
* Interface Tree: This pane (on the left) lists the interface definitions, interface instances,
modports, and HDL instances in a tree node format. Each interface definition is shown
as a top node with the associated instances listed as underlying nodes. The modports
and HDL instances are listed under the interface instance. The interface instance,
modport and HDL instance nodes may be dragged to the source code frame to show
the associated code, the nSchema window to show the schematic, or the nWave
window to show the waveform.

* Interface Summary: This pane (on the right) lists the ports, variables, and subroutines
of the interface. The contents in this pane are automatically updated when a node in
the Interface Tree pane is double-clicked. Signal node types can be dragged to other
windows.
* Show Active Annotation: This option is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded. When
this option is turned on, the simulation values is displayed in the right-most column for
the variables or ports in the Interface Summary pane. The default value of this option
* Sync Selection to nTrace: When this option is turned on, double-clicking an interface
instance, or HDL instance in the Interface Tree pane displays the associated code
in the source code frame. When this option is turned off, double-clicking an interface
instance, or HDL instance in the Interface Tree pane only updates the Interface
Summary pane. The default value of this option is off.
* By: Click this selection button to specify the search criteria for the value change of a
signal. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Search Backward: Click this button to search backward in time and locate the
previous value change. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Search Forward: Click this button to search forward in time and locate the next value
change. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.
* Cursor Time: This text field displays the current cursor time and also sets the cursor
time. This button is enabled when an FSDB file is loaded.

Verdi 2023.12
Starting from this release, you can migrate to NPI Waveform Model/Writer, which is
the latest FSDB Reader/Writer to seamlessly read FSDB. The following data types are
supported only with NPI Waveform Model/Writer:
1. Modport/interface port
2. Virtual file
3. The FSDB which includes power signals
4. Packed mode dumping

Verdi 2019.06
* Starting from this release, by default, Verdi filters the Value Change (VC) of
Value Change Dump (VCD) real signal. To revert the previous behavior, that
is, keeping two duplicates VC in real signal, set the environment variable
FSDB_KEEP_TWO_DUPLICATE_REAL_VC.
* Add ffrGetAPIVersion to get the FSDB Reader API version.
* FSDB is upgraded from version 5.7 to version 5.8.

Verdi 2017.12
* Starting from this release, the FSDB is upgraded from version 5.5 to version 5.6.
* The fsdbVarIdcode is enlarged from int to int64 so that larger designs (over 2G
idcode) can be handled with ease in the future.

Verdi 2023.12
Starting from this release, you can migrate to NPI Waveform Model/Writer, which is
the latest FSDB Reader/Writer to seamlessly read FSDB. The following data types are
supported only with NPI Waveform Model/Writer:
1. Modport/interface port
2. Virtual file
3. The FSDB which includes power signals
4. Packed mode dumping

Verdi 2017.12
* Starting from this release, the FSDB is upgraded from version 5.5 to version 5.6.
* The fsdbVarIdcode is enlarged from int to int64 so that larger designs (over 2G
idcode) can be handled with ease in the future.

Verdi 2016.06
Starting from this release, functions and tasks can be dumped to FSDB. By default, they
are not dumped for performance consideration. You can use one of following methods to
dump them to FSDB during runtime (simulation)
1. Using the FSDB_FUNCTIONS environment variable:
For example: setenv FSDB_FUNCTIONS 1
2. Using the +fsdb+functions runtime option:
For example: simv +fsdb+functions

Safety Specification Format
The Safety Specification Format (SSF) is a file format used in Synopsys functional safety
flows.
It defines safety mechanisms for a design.
An SSF file specifies the safety mechanisms to implement in the design.
This file helps ensure that required safety features are inserted and tracked during the
design process.
After implementation, the tool uses the SSF file to compare the RTL and the physically
implemented netlist.
It performs functional safety (FuSa) equivalence checks. These checks confirm that safety
mechanisms are correctly realized in the final design.

nTrace enables showing or hiding safety virtual cells in the hierarchy tree by using the
Safety Core Cell filter option. This option makes it easy to focus on safety-instrumented
logic as needed. The default status is toggle off.

Figure 3

Safety Core Cell Option

All general features that apply to an RTL instance also apply to a safety virtual cell.
Synchronizing a Safety Virtual Cell with RTL
Double-clicking a safety virtual cell in a hierarchy tree synchronizes the RTL source code
view in nTrace automatically to its module definition. As a result, you can quickly locate
and review the underlying RTL even though the RTL itself is unchanged.

Locating the SSF Source View
The Locate Core Rule Command context menu enables you to locate the SSF source
view for a related safety core rule command.
Figure 4

Context menu of the Locate Core Rule Command

Dragging a Virtual Cell to the RTL Source View
Dragging and dropping a virtual safety cell to the RTL source view changes the active
scope to the scope related to the virtual safety cell. The Data pane and Source view are
updated accordingly.

Safety Instrumental Signal in nTrace
Safety instrumented signals are automatically generated signals that implement or support
safety mechanisms defined by SSF rules. Verdi displays safety instrumented signals by
scope in the Signal pane.
Figure 5

Instrumental Signal in Signal Pane

These signals can be filtered or searched for by using the Safety Inserted option. The
default status is toggle on.

Figure 6

Safety Inserted Filter Option

Synchronizing a Safety Instrumented Signal with RTL
Double-clicking a safety instrumental signal automatically synchronizes the RTL source
code view in nTrace to the original signal declaration. This allows users to quickly locate
and review the underlying RTL, which remains unchanged.
Adding Instrumentation Signals to the Waveform
* To add low-power-related instrumental signals to a waveform by type, choose Add
Instrumented Signals to Waveform > Power.
* To add safety-related signals to a waveform by type, choose Add Instrumented
Signals to Waveform > Safety.
Other than the Add Instrumented Signals to Waveform feature, all general features that
apply to a normal RTL signal also apply to a safety instrumental signal.
If an RTL signal is impacted by a safety rule, the context menus corresponding
to that rule are enabled when you add an instrumented signal to the waveform.
For example, if an RTL signal is impacted by a register rule, the Register
Signals context menu is enabled. If the RTL signal is not impacted by any
safety rule, the Safety submenus remain disabled.

Configuring the Source View of the RTL Signals Impacted by Safety Rules
The Safety Aware page in the Preferences window enables you to specify a color for the
safety aware objects in the source view.
Figure 16

Safety Aware page in the Preference Window

The following is the default color table for safety aware objects:
Figure 17

Default Color Table for safety aware objects

If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple types of rule, the colorize priority as follows:
* A safety register object is higher than a safety-fsm object.
* A safety-fsm object is higher than a safety core object.
* A safety core object is higher than an error correction object.
* An error correction object is higher than the compare error object.
The preference option Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) highlights the safety
aware objects in the source view. The default status is toggle on.
The preference option Annotate Safety Aware Design Object(s) enables users to show/
hide the upper annotation for safety aware objects in the RTL source view. The default
status is toggle on. The option status aligns with the top menu command Source > Upper
Annotation > Safety Aware Annotation.

You can view the applied target right after the safety model name in the <name> (<target>)

Figure 24

Rules Displayed as Children Nodes

The rule type is displayed in the <name> (<type>) format right after the rule name. The
binding target (HDL signal/instance) lists are available as the child nodes of the rule node
as shown in the following figure:
Figure 25

Binding Target Under the Rule Node

The unused safety-models are available as sibling nodes of the default safety model in the
tree.
Double-clicking a policy node syncs the source view to its declaration and highlights the
policy name in the source view. The Data pane is updated based on the active safety
policy.
Double-clicking the attribute node syncs the source view to its related safety policy
declaration and highlights the attribute in source view.
Double-clicking the nodes that belong to the unused safety models makes the source view
jump to the related command line. However, the related line is inactivated and no actions
are available in the source view. The Data pane does not show any signal for such nodes.
Safety Manager supports search and filter features and unified find search in the safety
tree.

The Safety Specification Format support in nSchema helps users identify, analyze, and
debug safety-related logic in their designs. This is done through safety virtual cells and
safety instrumented signals. These features visually mark cells and signals that are
instrumented for safety. This makes it easier to trace safety mechanisms, understand their
impact, and ensure compliance with safety requirements. By leveraging these features,
users can quickly locate safety-critical elements, view related properties, and add relevant
signals to waveforms for further analysis.

The following topics describe the SSF support available in nSchema:
* Safety Virtual Cells in nSchema
* Safety Instrumental Signals

Safety Virtual Cells in nSchema
Safety virtual cells are instrumented by the set_safety_core_rule command. nSchema
adds the DC label to identify them.
Viewing a Virtual Cell in a Full Window
You can identify a virtual cell in a full window highlighted with the DC symbol. The symbol
is positioned on the right top inside the body of the cell in the same color as the color of
the instance name.

Configuring the Source View of the RTL Signals Impacted by Safety Rules
You can use the preference option Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) to color the
safety-aware objects in the source view. The default status is toggle on.

Highlight Safety Aware Design Object(s) Option in View Menu

If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple types of rule, the colorize priority as follows:
* A safety register object is higher than a safety-fsm object.
* A safety-fsm object is higher than a safety core object.
* A safety core object is higher than an error correction object.
* An error correction object is higher than the compare error object.

Configuring the Display of Signals in the Get Signals Form
You can highlight the signal name in the Get Signals form signal list by using the
Preference->Safety Aware->Annotate Safety Aware Design Object(s) option. The
colors can be configured through Preference->Safety Aware.
If the RTL signal is impacted by multiple types of rule, the colorize priority as follows:
* A Safety Register object is higher than a Safe-FSM object.
* A Safe-FSM object is higher than a Safety Core object.
* A Safety Core object is higher than an Error Correction object.
* An Error Correction object is higher than a Compare Error object.

The Safety menus in the source view enable users to debug for safety purposes.

If an RTL signal is impacted by a safety rule, the context menu corresponding to the

-dut

Checks if the root cause is in the DUT or testbench so that
tracediff utility can annotate a root cause with the accurate
reason. It is optional and need not be specified.

-gen_list

It is provided for running auto mode and stop once the
signal list is dumped. You can revise the file and then reboot
tracediff manual mode with the revised signal list.

-ignore_signal
<signal_list_file_name>

Specifies the location of the file which contains the list of
signals to ignore tracing. Each line contains a signal pattern
and the pattern can be one of the following:
- signal#time: ignore tracing the signal at specified time.
- signal: ignore tracing the signal at any time.
This option can be used if any signal causes tracediff utility
to not function in the auto mode and it is ignored for auto
mode to work. It can also be used in manual mode.
Default is NULL and no signal is ignored.

-jmp_to_earliest

Jumps to the earliest point in time while tracing in the batch
mode.

Specifies the hierarchy level limit for the module to be
compared. For example, /top/a is compared but /top/a/b is
not compared if -compare_scope is /top and -max_level is
1 because /top/ais 1 level but /top/a/bis 2 levels from /top.
When n is 0, all signals in the hierarchy starting from the
specified module are compared.
Default value is 0 if not specified.

-auto_max_
sample_per_signal <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches for each
pair of signals, starting from the earliest mismatch until
the maximum number is reached. When the maximum is
reached, the remaining pairs of signals are not compared.
When n is 0, there is still a limit of 2097152 mismatches for
each pair of signals due to the limitation of nCompare.
Default value is 1 if not specified.

-auto_max_
err_cnt_number <n>

Specifies the maximum number of mismatches in a
comparison. When n is 0, there is no limitation on the number
of mismatches.
Default value is 1000 if it is not specified.

-ncompare_opts

Specifies nCompare input options. The format is tracediff
[tracediff options] -ncompare_opts "[nComapre
options]. When -ncompare_opts is used, nCompare

options that are originally supported in tracediff auto mode
are unavailable.Waveform files set up in -ncompare_opts
is ignored. You have to specify what are the target and
reference waveforms for tracediff.
-out_file reportFile.txt Sets the name of the output report file.
-out_format
[plain|smlog]

Sets the format of the output file.If this option is not specified,
the default format of the output file is smlog. If the smlog
option is specified, you can open the output file with Smart
Log to analyze it.

-ref_waveform

The secondary waveform file used to compare signals. This is
a mandatory option in both manual and automatic mode.

-signal_list

Specifies signals that need to be added to the signal list.

-target_waveform

Specifies the target waveform. This option imports the
design of the target waveform as the fundamental design for
comparison.
-auto_type <signal_type> Specifies the type of signals to be compared. Type can be (in,

out, inout, boundary, local, all, buffer, linkage, net, register) or
the union of some of them, such as boundary+register or
out+inout. Default value is boundary.

Input Format
The following figure provides information about the format that you must follow to provide
the input.
The format of the signal can be signalName#time and signalName#timeWithUnit with
hierarchy delimiter either "/" or ".", for example, /tb/fout1#800, in one signal list. The
target waveform and the reference waveform must be specified in the command line with
-target_waveformand -ref_waveform options, respectively.
Following is an example for the input format:

Input Example
Examples
You must import the design with appropriate Verdi options.
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt -f srcFileList.f
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt -lib work

If you have a design source file named as design.v and list input signals with the
prescribed input format in the signalList.txt signal list, and if you need to save the
output file as reportFile.txt in the parent directory of the current directory, execute the
following command:
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v -out_file ../
reportFile.txt

If you need to trace mismatch fan-ins of each signal listed in the signalList.txt file from
their first mismatch time, execute the following command:
tracediff -signal_list signalList.txt design.v -out_file ../
reportFile.txt -jmp_to_earliest

generated in tracediffLog/ under the current directory by default.

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression
Starting with this release, if there are any failed tests during regression, Verdi finds the bug
and fixes it before allowing any new changes.
Verdi first takes the file to determine the debug entries. Debug entries are monitored
signals in the DUT that have mismatches between the failing and passed waveform. Then
it traces back to find the root causes, and summarizes it in a text file report. This report is
then loaded into Verdi to see the detail trace path from debug entry to root cause.

The following sub-sections provide the details of the use model:
Determining the Bug Entry
The debug entries are read from a .rc file. There are three types of tags in the .rc file:
* Signal: If the tag is Signal, each line must include the full hierarchical name and
a timestamp. These signals are scanned and they become the debug entries if the
values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two waveform files. For
example,
top.memory.nROutstanding#123
top.mySig1#1000
top.mySig2#50

* Scope: If the tag is Scope, each line must include a list of scope names and a
timestamp. Boundary signals within these scopes are scanned and those signals
become the debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different
within the two waveform files. For example,
top,top.myScope1#200
top.myScope2#300
top#100-200

Enhancement to Support Design Changes During Regression

* Assertion: If the tag is Assertion, each line must include an Assertion name and a
timestamp. Signals that are associated to that assertion are scanned and become the
debug entries if the values of this signal at the specified time is different within the two
waveform files. For example,
top.memory.eos#160390000

The follow error message is an example on how to specify an assertion failure as debug
entry:
Error: "token.v", 144439:top.memory.eos : at time 160390000
ALL_DONE_EOS: All write transaction addresses must have been
matched with corresponding write response.
nb_cycles: 16040
Executing Axi End Of Simulation checks

here, ALL_DONE_EOS is the name of the assertion and 160390000 is the time.
Analyzing Root Cause
The root cause is analyzed by running the TraceDiff utility in Verdi. The following are the
enhancements to TraceDiff for root cause:
Trace Multiple Root Cause
For root cause, TraceDiff searches all fanins with mismatch on every level.
Trace Database
For root cause, TraceDiff saves the trace results in a trace result database that can be
efficiently and accurately replayed.
Ignore Mismatches on Waveform Time Boundaries
For root cause, TraceDiff does not trace signals with mismatches on the time boundary
only, because the mismatch may be due to inconsistency in the simulation evaluation
order. This helps to filter out false alarms.
Ignore Shifted Sequence
