Utilities for Performance Improvement

Utilities for Performance Improvement
Verdi supports the following two features or utilities for performance improvement:
* Prerequisites
* Trace Cache Utility
* Scan Utility

Prerequisites
To use these functionalities,
1. Set the VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE environment variable as follows:
setenv VERDI_TRACEX_ENABLE

2. Specify the -lca option while invoking Verdi.

Trace Cache Utility
Verdi supports the trace cache feature that saves tracing time on the traceX utility. If a
signal is already traced, the trace engine stops at the cached signal and uses cached
traced results. The trace cache feature is enabled by default.You can disable/enable this
feature using the TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE environment variable.
To disable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 0

To enable this feature, use the following command:
setenv TFV_ENABLE_ROOT_CAUSE_CACHE 3

Here, the default value is 3.
The trace cache feature is only supported for -cause_count 1. If you set this option with
number greater than 1, trace cache is turned off.

Scan Utility
Verdi provides the scan functionality or utility to scan signals with an X value. The following
options are available to help you to get the X signal list:
[-max_x_per_signal number] [-max_total_x number]
[-max_analysis_level number]

Specifies the maximum number of analysis X levels. If no analysis scope is specified, it
counts from the root scope. When the number is 0, all signals are analyzed. Its default
value is 0.
-max_total_x number

Specifies the maximum number of X for tracing. If the number is 0, it is unlimited. Its
default value is 1000.
-max_x_per_signal number

Specifies the maximum number of X for each signal. When the maximum is reached, the
remaining value changes of the signals are no longer analyzed. Here, 0 signifies no limit.
Its default value is 1.

Verdi supports the following utilities for FSDB:
* Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File Without Gate
* Support for Waveform Utility

Support for Converting an FSDB File With Gate to an FSDB File
Without Gate
In previous releases, the FSDB Reader takes more memory and CPU time to read an
FSDB file with gate when compared to reading an FSDB file without gate.
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the use of a utility, parallelWaveExpand, to
convert an FSDB file with gate to an FSDB file without gate. You can use this utility to
perform a one-time process to retrieve an equivalent FSDB from an FSDB with gate
enabled. Also, the FSDB Gate in the converted FSDB file is disabled. The FSDB contains
all the value changes so that an FSDB reader does not need to perform any reconstruction
of values.

You can also use the converted FSDB file to replace the original file in the remaining
debug flow. Therefore, you can reduce the consumption of memory and time. You need
to enable the environment variable VERDI_PARALLEL_WAVE_EXPAND for this feature along
with the -lca command line option.
parallelWaveExpand <input fsdb file> -t <number of threads> -o <output
fsdb file name>

<input fsdb file name> - represents an FSDB file with FSDB Gate enabled to be

converted.

<number of threads> - represents the number of threads to be used in this conversion.
<output FSDB name> - represents the output FSDB file name.

When using 8 threads to convert novas.fsdb to full_dump.fsdb, use the following
command:
parallelWaveExpand novas.fsdb -t 8 -o full_dump.fsdb

The waveutils utility has the following limitations:
* Supports only input file version equal or greater than 2.0.
* Supports only fully array/struct/record.
* Does not support formbus.
* Does not filter user interested scope without any signals.
* Does not support information with sequence.
* Does not support "?" in -scope, -exclude_scopeand -sig.
* The unmatched scope/sig/exclude_scope message is printed only on console.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is signal based waveform
file.
* The output waveform file from waveutils --tool=extract is dumped by cheetah
technique.
* The thread number cannot be one when a multi-process is opened.
The memory limit flow cannot work with the multi-process flow.

Strict Exclusions Mode
In strict exclusions mode, excluding a covered object is not allowed. If you load an exclude
file in strict exclusions mode, only the uncovered objects in the exclude file are excluded.
Objects that are covered are not excluded even if they are listed in the exclude file.
When a region such as a module, module instance, or covergroup was excluded in
previous releases and had only uncovered objects in it, the region was excluded and an
exclusion for it could be saved to an exclude file. If a region contained both covered and
uncovered child objects, exclusions for uncovered child objects were not created and
they could not be saved. Starting with this release, when a region is excluded in strict
exclusions mode and it contains both covered and uncovered objects then its uncovered
child objects are excluded properly and those exclusions can be saved to an exclude file.
Note that if annotations are set on the region's exclusion, then those annotations are
automatically propagated to these uncovered child objects when the parent object is
excluded in strict mode.
This feature is now supported for the following exclusions:
* Module/Instance-level exclusions
* Covergroup definitions/instance-level exclusions

Two-Dimensional Visualization of Covergroup Crosses
Verdi enables you to select any two coverpoints from an n-dimensional cross and project
the cross coverage data into a two-dimensional projection table with those two coverpoints
as the X and Y axis.
This feature helps in identifying coverage holes in the cross, such as when no bins are
covered, when a given coverpoint has a specific value.
For each cross, Verdi provides a list of projection tables and arranges the tables using the
following ranking criteria:
* Rows or columns that are completely uncovered
* Cells that are uncovered in table cells
* Low-coverage cells in table cells
Note that a low-coverage cell is a cell whose score is less than a tenth of the overall score
of a cross.
Also, projections with the same coverage for every cell are considered as least interesting
projections.

To generate two-dimensional projection tables for an n-dimensional cross, click the Cross
2D Proj button in the CovDetail pane in the Verdi GUI.

In previous releases, Verdi provided a unique feature ID for each plan and feature. This
feature ID is globally unique and supports concurrent edits in the same .hvp file. However,
its length makes it cumbersome for people to read and use in other documents.
Starting with this release, Verdi provides a new built-in string attribute, HVP_FEAT_ID,
which is short, user-friendly, and easy-to-manage ID. Note that this new HVP_FEAT_ID
is not globally unique and is only unique within the HVP file. Moreover, it enables only a
single user to edit any .hvp file at a time to avoid conflicts.

Generating HVP_FEAT_ID for a Top-Level Plan
To generate HVP_FEAT_ID from the Verdi GUI, perform the following steps:
1. Click Tools ->Preferences to display the Application Preferences dialog box.
2. In the Application Preferences dialog box, select Plan View>Enable HVP_FEAT_ID

Once the Enable HVP_FEAT_ID option is selected, Verdi generates unique

ively. The features inside a subplan consist of two parts:
<parent_subplan_id>.<HVP_FEAT_ID>.
* <parent_subplan_id>: is stored in the HVP top-level plan for each subplan with the

Creating a Custom Compound ID Attribute
As HVP_FEAT_ID conveys information only about feature ID, you can create a custom
compound ID attribute that may convey additional information about a feature, such as
its project number and block number along with HVP_FEAT_ID. This custom attribute, say

FULL_ID, can be created using the HVP file and the Verdi GUI. In the HVP file, use the
following syntax to construct FULL_ID:
attribute string PRJ_ID = "P1";
attribute string BLK_ID = "B1";
attribute string FULL_ID =
"${PRJ_ID}_${BLK_ID}_${HVP_FEAT_ID}";

In the Verdi GUI, perform the following steps to create the FULL_ID attribute:
1. In the HvpDetail pane, click the Create an attribute
Attribute dialog box.

icon to display the New

2. In the New Attribute dialog box, specify identifier, type, and default value of FULL_ID

3. Click OK.

Verdi enables you to save the current configuration of the panes in the GUI using
bookmarks. Bookmarks provide quick access to these saved views and enable you to
easily toggle between them.
Bookmarks are useful when you need to analyze multiple sections of a design or views of
different coverage results. Consider a scenario in which you perform several operations to
select a particular scope, configure Verdi panes, apply a Plan filter, and so on.
The bookmark feature allows you to save such setups and return to them in the future by
selecting the saved bookmark.
Bookmarks enable you to save pane configurations, pane dock and undock status, scroll
bar locations, expand/collapse status, column configurations, sorting, filtering, and so on.
However, it does not save information such as which database, user data, HVP files,
exclusions/elfiles, specifications, and modifiers files are loaded, so that you can use the
same bookmark for different data sets.
This section discusses the following topics:
* Creating Bookmarks
* Editing Bookmarks
* Saving and Loading Bookmarks

Saving and Loading Bookmarks
You can save bookmarks using File-->Save Bookmarks(see the figure below). A saved
bookmark file has .bk as its default suffix. Bookmarks are independent of the specific
coverage database or design that is loaded when they are created.
Thus, you can create a bookmark while viewing one design and reload that bookmark to
return to the same view/configuration but with different data.
To load a bookmark, use File --> Load Bookmarks(see the figure below).

Consider a scenario in which you load version1 of simv_v1.vdb, navigate to the packet
covergroup, view the bins of a coverpoint z, and scroll both Summary and covDetail
panes.

Then, you notice that certain bins, such that no[0e:0f], are not hit and you decide to
improve the test. Now, you can create a bookmark for this view and save it for future use
(see the figure below).

After improving the test, you collect coverage in simv_v2.vdb, which has the same shape
as that of simv_v1.vdb.
Now, loading the saved bookmark instantly takes you to the bins that were previously not
hit and should be hit with the improved test. For example, the no[0e:0f] bin is now hit
with the improved test (see the figure below):

To load a bookmark file on the Verdi command line, use the -bookmark
<bookmark_file.bk> option as follows:
verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb -bookmark <bookmark_file.bk> &

Bookmarks may not restore the following information correctly:
* Toggle signal vector compressed and expanded bits are not preserved.
* Covergroup expanded bins and the bins shown by "Show More" in crossbin tables are
not preserved.

In Verdi Planner, various functional coverage objects such as covergroups, covergroup
instances, coverpoints, crosses, and bins may be used as sources for data in a plan
feature.
These are connected to plan features by name. As these functional coverage objects were
explicitly created to collect coverage, it is helpful to know if any object was created but left
out of the plan.
Starting with this release, Verdi Coverage provides a new feature that enables you to
find functional coverage objects that are not referenced by any feature in the plan "unmapped" objects - and report them in an .hvp file.

To find unmapped objects in a plan, invoke the Report Unmapped Objects form using the
Plan -> Report Unmapped Objects command.

The following figure shows the Report Unmapped Objects form:
Figure 79

The Report Unmapped Objects Form

In the Report Unmapped Objects form, you can specify the plan to report from the list of
plans.
Also, you can specify the type of unmapped objects that you need to map. The types of
objects are as follows:
* Definition/Variant, Instance
* Point/Cross
* Bins
To generate the report for covergroup instances, for example, select the Cover Group
Instance check box in the Report Unmapped Objects form.
In the form, you can select the following different strategies that determine the number of
objects to be reported:
* High
This strategy considers a definition/variant and an instance as separate entities. If a
definition/variant is mapped but its one or more instances are not mapped, then the
instances are considered as unmapped.
For example, consider cg_var as a variant having coverpoints, cp1 and cp2, cross
cr1, and instance cg_inst. If cg_var is mapped, cg_inst is not mapped, and High
is selected as a strategy to determine the number of reported objects, cg_inst is
reported as unmapped.

* Medium

As the unmapped objects are reported as a complete HVP plan, you can include the
unmapped_objs plan into your main top plan as a subplan to ensure that you do not miss

One useful technique is to periodically generate unmapped_objs and use Verdi copy-paste

the main verification plan by collating unmapped and newly-created coverage into their
proper meaningful places in the main plan.

Specification Coverage Merge
Verdi Coverage provides the specification coverage for each PDF in a plan. Previously, if
the same PDF was linked to different plans, you needed to select each plan separately.
You could view the specification coverage for the PDF in each plan. There was no way to
see the total coverage for a PDF from all linked plans.
The specification coverage feature now provides an overall summary of the specification
coverage for the PDF with the specification coverage from different plans.

To calculate the specification coverage for both main plan and subplan, Verdi Coverage

The algorithm provides priority to calculate each plan, which is categorized as Linked,
Ignored, and Todo. The priority sequence of these categories is as follows:
Linked > Ignored > Todo

This section explains how VC Formal coverage is integrated with the Verdi coverage
reporting flow.
The two primary links between Verdi and VC Formal are displaying VCS Formal results in
Verdi, and linking VC Formal results into your verification plan using Verdi Planner.

The section describes how Verdi coverage is used to display and link to VC Formal
results. This sectio

The properties are categorized according to usage fields in VC Formal as:
* assert: The property specifies an assertion to be solved. Its values are proven,
inconclusive, vacuous, and falsified.
* assume: The property specifies as a constraint.
* cover: The property specifies as a cover property. Its values are covered, inconclusive,
and uncoverable.
* unused: The property is disabled.
VC Formal Coverage in Verdi
To load the coverage database generated with VC Formal in Verdi, use the following
command:
verdi -cov -covdir my_covdb.vdb

-cov: Starts Verdi in the coverage mode
-covdir: Opens the coverage database
my_covdb.vdb: The name of the coverage database that gets opened. This is specified in
the test.tcl script with the save_covdb command.

The command generates the following pane:
Figure 83

The Verdi Coverage Assert Pane

The VC Formal information is displayed in the Assert tab in the columns: FVtype,
FVstatus, and FVdepth.
This information should be same as the VC Formal results. The green color represents
Proven or Covered, the red color represents Falsified, Uncoverable, or Vacuous, and the
yellow color represents Inconclusive.
FVtype indicates the usage field. The value in this column can be either Assert, Cover, or

Assume.

FVstatus indicates the run status of VC Formal. Its possible values depend on FVtype:

* If FVtype is Assert, the value of FVstatus can be Proven, Inconclusive, Falsified, or
Vacuous.
* If FVtype is Cover, the value of FVstatus can be Covered, Inconclusive, or
Uncoverable.
The FVdepth column is interpreted as follows:
* If FVstatus is Proven, Vacuous, or Uncoverable and its value is -1, it represents
infinite depth.
* For other FVstatus, N>=0 represents the depth of the trace.

Measuring VC Formal Assert Status in HVP
VC Formal results can be annotated automatically onto features in your verification plan.
Using these results, you can measure your expectations with FVstatus.
The figure below shows VC Formal results in a verification plan with attributes and metrics.
Figure 84

VC Formal Results in HVP

To measure the VC Formal Assert status in HVP, perform the following steps:
1. Set the expected FV Assert status with FV attribute values using
fvassert_expected_status.
feature f_default;
//These values are same as default value, no need
//assignments again here.
//
fvassert_expected_status = proven;
//
fvassert_expected_mindepth = -1;
//
fvcover_expected_status = covered;
//
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 0;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.*";
feature f_expected_assigned;
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive;
fvassert_expected_mindepth = 50;
fvcover_expected_maxdepth = 50;
measure Assert, FVAssert m1;
source = "property: fsm.a2", "property:
fsm.a_loop_break", "property: fsm.c2";

2. Add measures with property type sources and reference the FV Assert metric.
The new FV Assert built-in metric is added to keep the score of the FV Assert status
against users' expectation.
If FVstatus is same as fv

For example, the matching property top.a11: FVtype=assert and
FVstatus=Proven. If the expectation is fvassert_expected_sthe tatus
= Proven, the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1. If the expectation is
fvassert_expected_status = inconclusive and fvassert_expected_depth =
60, the FVAssert metric score becomes 0/1.
For example, consider the following figure that shows six cases to measure the VC
Formal Assert status in your verification plan:

Case1: fsm.a2: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is falsified, FVdepth is 6 and it is
excluded. In the top.f_default.m1 feature, the property: fsm.* source matches
the excluded property, therefore, no score is added.
Case2: fsm.a_loop_break: FVtype is assert, FVstatus is inconclusive, and FVdepth
is 70. In the top.f_expected_assigned feature, fvassert_expected_status is
inconclusive and fvassert_expected_mindepth is 50 which are set by users. It is met
with users' expectations and the FVAssert metric score becomes 1/1.
Case3: fsm.a_trans: FVtype is assume. In the top.f_assume feature,
fvassume_status is reviewed which is set by users. The FVAssert metric score

becomes 1/1.

Case4: fsm.c_blk_cnt: FVtype is cover, FVstatus is covered, and FVdepth is 1. In
the top.f_default feature, with default attribute values, fvcover_expected_status
is covered and fvcover_expected_maxdepth is 0. Compare FVstatus to expected
attributes values and if the expectation does not meet, the FVAssert metric score
becomes 0/1.
Case5: fsm.c_trans, no FV annotation. In the top.f_default.m_no_fv_ann
measure, matching fsm.c_trans without FV annotation, the FVAssert metric
becomes 0/1 because the FVAssert metric is referred explicated in measure.
Case6: dummy source. In the top.f_default.m_dummy measure, for all metrics for no
matching region, the score becomes all 0.

Deleting a Server
You can delete a server using the
icon. When you delete a server, Verdi asks for
confirmation of the operation as follows:
Figure 116

Deleting a Server

Once you click OK to confirm, the related server pane is closed automatically, if currently
open. The plans linked to the server also loose connection to the server and are not able
to link, unlink and sync issues.
Deleting a server breaks the existing association between the server and the plans linked
to it.

Managing Issues in Verdi HVP
Once you have configured and connected to the Redmine servers, you can access the
issue data using the Issue Management pane.
The Issue Management pane is a web page based flexible pane that hosts the third web
page. It provides following extending features besides the capability of hosting the third
party tool:
* List Issues - Shows issues matching a given criterion in the pane.
* Filter Issues - Filters issues based on the filters provided by the third part tool.
* Show Issue Details - Shows the issue details in the Issue Details page.
* Link Issues - Link selected/checked issues to the currently selected feature in the HVP
plan.
* Create an issue and link it to a feature.
This functionality is described in detail in the following sections:
* Finding, Creating, and Filtering Issues
* Displaying Linked Features of an Issue
* Creating Bug Metric and Adding Source Regions From Issues
* Linking a Feature to an Issue
* Unlinking a Feature from an Issue
* Linking the Plan to Projects in Server
* Linking to a Third-Party Issue Server
* Syncing With Issue Server
* Displaying Bug Details
* Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature

Finding, Creating, and Filtering Issues
You can use all the capabilities of the third party tool including finding, creating and filtering
issues in the Issue Management tool.
Displaying Linked Features of an Issue
Verdi planner provides a convenient way to know if the current issue in the Issue
Management plan is linked to any feature. To do that, click the button Show Feature to
find the linked feature in the HVP Plan pane.
Those features linked to the issue are annotated with a small icon <Provide icon>. If you
leave the Issue Details page, the small i

er URL are saved to the
.hvp.bug file.
The server Id is also a part of issue_id whose format is <server_id>:<third party

issue id>.

The server URL in the .bug file is the only key that lets the HVP planner find the correct
server to link in Verdi.
* If you link a plan to an issue server, the server Id and server URL is saved to the .bug
file.
* If open a plan created by another user and if server_URL in plan is not found in the
existing Verdi server list, Verdi prompts you to configure a new server with the server Id
and server URL in the plan.
The new created server configuration is saved in <user.home>/.vedi/
server.config and is listed in the Server pane.
* If server_URL is found in the existing server list, Verdi uses the existing server to
connect to the third party tool. Verdi internally creates a mapping from the server Id of
the existing server to the server Id defined in the .bug file.

However, if you want to replace server_id in the bug file with the one of the existing
server, you can save it as another plan using the Save as option.
In the Save as dialog box, select the Override Server Id option to replace the server Ids
in the .bug file.
Figure 125

Linking to a Third Party Issue Server

It is suggested that you define a server with the same Server Id for a project or
a team.
Syncing With Issue Server
The HVP planner provides a way to automatically link a feature in plan with issues,
provided that these issues have a field named verdi_plan_feature_id and its value
matched feature_id.
If an issue satisfies this above condition, a bug source region is added to the measure
source list of the feature.
You can use the CSM item Sync Issues to refresh these bug source regions once you
add or delete some related issues in the third party issue management tool.
Select the feature(s) for which you want to create bug source regions. If no feature is
selected in the plan, all features in the plan are affected.

Each bug status belongs to one of the two categories Open or Closed. If the category is
not given it is set to Open by default.
Displaying Bug Details
The HVP pane provides the CSM Show Bug Details that shows the issues related to the
current feature or bug measure source in the plan correspondingly.

Creating a New Issue From the Selected Feature
Once a plan is connected to the issue servers, you can select a feature in the HVP plan
and use CSM Create an Issue to open the New Issue page in the Issue Management
tool.
If there is more than one server connected to the plan, a sub level menu is available to list
all servers.

Figure 127

Creating a New Issue

After the New Issue page is loaded, you can drag the feature to the desired text field. The
full path of the feature and the feature Id in the plan is appended to the text fields.

Verdi Verification Planner: Derived Test Metrics
Verification Planner for Verdi supports the following additional built-in derived test metrics
to track verification progress:
* Percent Metric for Test Metric
* Test.completion Metric
Using these derived metrics, you can gather the percentage of tests with different status
and test completion percentage in a verification plan.

Percent Metric for Test Metric
In previous releases, the built-in test metric of enum type reports integer count for submetrics test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.unknown, and test.assert. For example,
test = 6;
test.pass = 3;
test.fail = 3;

In previous releases, the test metric reports the basic number of tests with status pass,
fail, warn, unknown, and assert in the HVP annotated report. It does not display the
percentage of these scores.

Verification Planner for Verdi reports percentage score for each enum value of the test
metric. This enables you to get the percentage of tests with status pass, fail, warning,
unknown, or assert. The following is the list of the derived percent sub-metrics:
* test.percent.pass
* test.percent.fail
* test.percent.warn
* test.percent.unknown
* test.percent.assert
The score of a percent metric is the percentage of each enum's value of the test metric
against the total number of tests in that feature.
For example, if a is the integer count of the built-in test metric enum value and b is the
integer count of the total number of tests, then the percentage metric is computed as
(a / b)*100

then the value of test.percent.pass = 8/10 and is reported as 80%.
The following is the example for the usage of percent metrics:
feature f1;
test.percent.pass = test.percent.pass > 60%;
measure test, test.percent.pass m1;
source = "testname*";

Consider the following example,
feature parent:
test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:50.00%
feature block1
test:5[pass:3 fail:2 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass:60.00%
feature block2
test:1[pass:0 fail:1 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0 ]
test.percent.pass: 0.00%

In this example, the test.percent.pass score in feature parent is calculated from the test
score of:
feature parent test:6[pass:3 fail:3 warn:0 assert:0 unknown:0] 50%

which is equal to 3/6. The total test score of feature parent is the sum of the test scores of
feature block1 and feature block2.
The following figure shows the derived sub-metrics displayed by Verdi coverage:
Figure 128

Viewing Percent Metric in Verdi Coverage

Test.completion Metric
The test.completion metric allows you to measure the progress of tests being written
against the number of tests expected to be written.
The score of the test.completion metric is the ratio of total integer count of all sub-metrics
of the test metric (test.pass, test.fail, test.warn, test.assert, test.unknown) and the
expected number of tests in a plan/feature. The expected number of tests should be set
using the test.expected attribute.
Where,test.completion=total_test_count/test.expected and
total_test_count=test.pass+test.fail+test.warn+test.as sert+test.unknown
Test.expected Attribute
You can use the test.expected built-in attribute assignment, as shown below, to set the
expected number of tests in feature/plan scope.
test.expected = <number>;
The expected number is like an annotation value kept in feature/plan node. The default
value of test.expected is 0.

Figure 129

Viewing test.expected in Verdi Coverage

The test.completion metric can be calculated only after setting the
test.expectedattribute.
The following example illustrates the usage of the test.completion metric:
feature Goal_pass;
test.expected = 2;
test.percent.pass = (test.percent.pass >= 0.5);
measure test, test.percent.pass, test.completion Measure_1;
source = "test3";

Figure 130

The following are examples that describe how sections containing images are handled
during spec-linking.
Consider the following two cases for a linked section containing images:
* A section contains images and text as well.
* A section contains image(s) only
These two cases are handled different ways during review and updating the section to a
new document during spec-linking.
Case 1: Section contains both images and text
In this case spec-linking follows the following process:
* Review and update the text to the new section in the new document.
* Find the images in the updated section in the new document.
* Generate a new section based on the text section and images, the decision table below
lists all the possibilities and review results.
Table 10

Review Results for Text and Image Selection
Image Text Matching

Missing

New

Matching

matching

Conflict

Missing

missing

New

The review result for an image depends on the updated text section in the new document.
There can be three results for image comparison: Matching, Missing, New. The result
conflict is not applicable for images.
* Matching: The image in the old document is found in the new document and it is
present by the updated text section.
In this case, image is found means that the image in the old and new documents are
the same.

* Missing: The image is not found in the new document, or it is found but it is NOT in the
updated text section.
* New: The image is in the updated text section but not in the old document. In Verdi
New is treated as a Conflict.
The image and text works as an entire link in the review process, so whatever actions
(accept, reject) that you choose to apply, the action is applied to both the image and the
text.
You may not be able to treat the text or the image as separate review-able objects.
Case 2: A section contains only image(s)
Without considering in the text in the review process, the search scope of an image is not
limited to the updated text section in the new document. The whole document is within the
search scope.
For example, if an image at page 10 was selected and linked as a section in the old
document, Verdi spec-linking feature searches the image at page 10 then around page 10,
that is page 11, page 9, page12, page 8 and so on, until the image is found.
If the image is found, then it is marked as matching, otherwise it is marked as missing.
The review result types new and conflict are not applicable in this case.

Verdi Coverage provides a new block named Result language that defines the overall
status of a feature. The value of the result field is derived from various metric scores
present in an annotated plan. This helps you perform further analysis on the plan/feature
and improve on it if required.

The following sections describe how you can define the result value for a plan, edit and
display it in the HVP page:
* Defining the Result Value in the CovDetail Pane
* Adding or Editing a Result Value
* Displaying the Result Value in the HVP Hierarchy Pane
* Error Handling
* Masking the Result Column

Defining the Result Value in the CovDetail Pane
When you select a plan, you can see additional area (sub-tab) below the Metrics sub-tab,
named Result in the CovDetail pane. When you click on the Result button, an additional
tab is shown displaying with a two column list view. The Name column displays the result
identifier and Value column displays all the values of this result. Both of the columns are
non-editable.
When you move mouse to this column, the ToolTip shows the detailed expression for this
result item as shown in the following figure:
Figure 162

Result Sub-Tab in CovDetail Pane

You can use the icons available at the top-right corner to perform the following actions:
*

: Add a new result at the end of list view

*

: Delete the current result item.

*

: Edit the current result item.

If the result created/updated has warnings, the color of the Name or Value is displayed in
orange as shown in figure Figure 163. To see the detailed warning, move the cursor to the
column.
If you switch the view mode, the result information is shown in the HvpDetail pane as
shown in figure Figure 164.

Difference Between Masks and Filters
As discussed, Verdi Planner supports two ways to customize the features displayed:
masks and filters. Though they appear to operate in a similar way, there is a distinct
difference in the way that they behave. Filters not only remove features from the displayed
plan view, they also disable the effect that those removed features' scores have on the
remainder of the plan. For example suppose a feature A with a score of 50% has 2 child
features A1 (0%) and A2 (100%). If you filter out feature A1 then its 0% score no longer
affects the parent feature A and A's score becomes 100%.
Masks are different because they simply hide rows based on the masking criteria. The
hidden rows' scores continue to affect scores. In the same example if A1 is masked, its
parent feature A's score remains at 50%.
In addition to this, the key differences between quick filters and masks are as follows:
* Any changes applied to a quick filter also affects scores; masks do not affect scores.
* Operations on quick filters can be saved as a modifier file that can be reloaded again;
masks cannot be saved as a modifier file.
* For quick filters, the filter icon
is displayed only when you click on the Quick Filter
icon; the mask icon
is always displayed on the right of Result columns.
* Quick filters are for attribute columns; masks are for Result columns.
Quick filters and masks can exist at the same time. However, quick filters have higher
priority than masks.

Transformation Rules of User Data to HVP Annotation
The following are the transform rules of User Data while annotating to HVP:
* Scientific notation with 'e' notation use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes
preference option is disabled):
For numbers with more than 5 decimal places.
Any number greater than or equal to 1,000,000 or less than or equal to -1,000,000.
All the other use cases are represented using normal notation with 5 decimal
places.
* SI Prefixes use cases (when the Format in SI Prefixes preference option is enabled)
The following values are represented in SI Prefixes:
Numbers greater than or equal to 1000 and less than or equal to -1000.
Numbers in between -0.01 and 0.01, except 0.
* Floating point precision:
Scientific notation with 'e' notation: 6 decimal places
SI Prefixes: 6 decimal places
Normal Notation: 5 decimal places
* Display format for Scientific notation with 'e' notation:
Trailing zero: "." should be followed by "0" when there is no mantissa (for example,
1.0e+09).
Leading zero: A minimum of 2 digits are required for notation presentation. That is,
leading zero is displayed if the exponent is less than 3 digits.
* Display format for SI Prefixes:
Trailing zero: No trailing zero is used in the SI Prefixes. For example, 1M.

Dumping Class Objects by Level
You can use the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command to dump the value change in
object to the FSDB file.
Following is the syntax when specified in the design:
$fsdbDumpClassObject( class_name_or_object_name [, option]*)

Following is the syntax when specified on the simulation UCLI command line:
fsdbDumpClassObject class_name_or_object_name [option]*

Where, class_name_or_object_name is the class name or object name in full hierarchy
format that is specified to dump.

Dumping Dynamic Class Objects

When you invoke VCS to compile the design, you must use the -debug_access
+class or -debug_access+ckbd options at the compile command line.
To dump the expandable class pointer signal, set the following environment variable:
setenv FSDB_ENABLE_EXPAND_CLASS 1

Following are the options supported for the $fsdbDumpClassObject dumping command:
+object_level=depth: Keyword to identify the number of levels of hierarchy to dump for
the subsequent objects. The default value of depth is 1.

Where, depth can have the following value:
N: N level sub-object under the current object or object instantiated from the current class
object.
0: All sub-objects under the current object or objects instantiated from the current class
object.
Note: It is recommended not to set +object_level to 0 as it costs more with a complex
testbench and limited resources.
+fsdbfile+<fil

Dumping Queue, Dynamic Array and Associative Array Inside
Class Object
Use the +fsdb+variant_size_array runtime option to dump non-static arrays
(queue, dynamic array, and associative array) inside class objects. Use the +fsdb
+max_variant_size_array runtime option to set the maximum array size for dumping.
To dump queues, dynamic arrays, and associative arrays inside class objects, use this
runtime option:
+fsdb+variant_size_array

Or set this environment variable:
setenv FSDB_VARIANT_SIZE_ARRAY 1

To set the maximum array size to dump, use this runtime option:
+fsdb+max_variant_size_array=<size>

Or set this environment variable:
setenv FSDB_MAX_VARIANT_SIZE_ARRAY <size>

The default max size is 10.
Specify +fsdb+variant_size_array before +fsdb
+max_variant_size_array=<size>.

Dumping Queue, Dynamic Array, and Associative Array in HDL
Instance
You can enable the dumping of non-static array (queue, dynamic array, and associative
array) in HDL instance using the following options.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option enables dumping for the non-static arrays in HDL instances, such as dynamic
array, queue, and associative array. As the array size can be big, FSDB dumper only
dumps several array elements in a non-static arrays. The default number is 10 and the
array element starts from index 0.
* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.
+fsdb+variant_size_array

This option specifies the different element numbers of non-static arrays. The number must
be 0 ~ 1023.
+fsdb+max_variant_size_array=20

* This option only works for $fsdbDumpvars or $fsdbDumpvarsByFile
* The -debug_access+vararray option must be specified for the VCS
compile option.

The following are the limitations of this feature:
* For D, Q, and A array dumping, the following types are not supported:
Event
Hybrid array: For example, int [][0:1]

Multi-dimension variant array: For example, int [][]

For example, struct { int a[] } s1[0:1] struct { int a[0:1] } s2[]

* For associative array, index type only supports the integral variables which can map to

Verdi supports the following dumping for SystemVerilog only:

Encrypted IP Waveform
This chapter describes the Encrypted IP Waveform feature, flow summary, and its
limitations.
It includes the following topics:
* Encrypted IP

Encrypted IP
Debugging is complicated when dealing with encrypted IPs due to limited knowledge and
visibility. This leads to time-consuming back-and-forths between SoC and IP teams. To
tackle these challenges, new verification, debug capabilities, and robust methodologies
are required.
An encrypted IP block is a secured version of the RTL source code or its gate-level netlist,
processed through an encryption algorithm. This encryption allows certain tools to operate
on the code, but prevents users from viewing the source. The most versatile encryption
scheme is the IEEE-P1735 standard, widely adopted for interoperability among IP and
EDA vendors.
The objective is to serve IP suppliers and the design teams in the following ways:
* IP Supplier: Protects the security of the IP in the design flow across different EDA
tools.
* IP Users: Ensures the interoperability of the IP across different EDA tools and vendors.

Encrypted IP

The IEEE-P1735 uses the following two levels of encryption to generate an encrypted IP:
1. The first level of encryption creates a random session key that is used to encrypt the
source code into a data_block using a symmetric encryption algorithm such as AES.
2. The second level of encryption uses the public keys of the EDA tool vendor to encrypt
the session key into a key_block using an asymmetric encryption algorithm such as
RSA.
The decryption flow that resides in the EDA tools applies the same process in the reverse
order as follows:
1. The tool scans the key-block searching for its own key; once located, the tool uses its
own private key to decrypt the key-block thus obtaining the symmetric session key.
2. The session key is then used to decrypt the data-block allowing the tool to compile
the original source code.

IEEE-P1735 Encryption and Decryption Flows

An encryption envelope is the preamble to the IP block in the source code. An IP supplier
must prepare an encryption envelope containing the public keys for each EDA tool that
is to be given access to the IP block. The encryption envelope consists of pragmas that
provide information such as encryption scheme, encoding type, key owner, key name, and
key method.
The following figure illustrates an encrypted IP containing multiple key-blocks, each
corresponding to a tool or vendor to be given access to the IP. One of the advantages
of the P1735 scheme is that the data block is common to all tools. Therefore, the same

flows. The session keys are automatically generated, therefore, they are not known to

Although the simulator does allow IP users to manipulate the behavior of a
signal internal to an encrypted IP block by specifying its hierarchical name,
this type of external manipulation of the behavior of the IP block is highly
discouraged and should be used rarely and in extreme cases. Instead, all
interactions between the design and an encrypted IP component should occur
through the IP's hardware interface, that is, top-level ports. Forcing signals in
lieu of a proper hardware reset or an initialization or configuration sequence can
cause the IP to malfunction and create problem that is difficult to debug.

Debugging Standalone IP
Debugging a potential IP problem while running a full chip test is challenging not just
due to lack of IP visibility; SoC or system-level simulations are large and compile and
run much slower than standalone IP tests. This situation is exacerbated when IP owners
incrementally request additional data from IP users to analyze a problem; the IP user must
typically recompile and rerun a lengthy simulation to generate the additional information.
To enable effective IP reuse, the debug problems associated with encrypted IP need to be
addressed.
Encrypted FSDB, is a proposal enabled by an asymmetric encryption scheme to protect
not just the source code (as enabled by P1735) but also the simulated waveforms.

Encrypted IP Waveform
When an encrypted IP includes unpredictable constructs or its internals are manipulated
beyond its I/O ports, IDX may not replicate a system level issue at the IP level. For
debugging, the IP supplier requires waveforms of all signals, which can be done using
Verdi alone. However, due to encrypted IP policies, an IP user cannot dump the internal
waveforms unless the IP supplier discloses all internal names, which is impractical. To

Debugging Standalone IP

solve this, the IP supplier can allow the dumping of waveforms during system level testing,
which are then encrypted for confidentiality. The IP user can generate the encrypted FSDB
but can't view the waveforms unless given the decryption key.
The Encrypted IP Waveform is a mechanism for securely exporting encrypted FSDB
files that can only be decrypted by IP suppliers using their private decryption key. The
Encrypted IP Waveform feature changes several aspects of the IP creation as well as the
simulation and debug flows. The Encrypted IP Waveform feature proceeds in the following

1. Obtains an asymmetric RSA key pair.
2. Adds the public key to the IP and encrypts the IP.
IP User
1. Compiles the design with the new IP, which contain the public key.

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow

Although the Encrypted IP Waveform capability introduces changes to the IP preparation
and encryption flow, these changes are required to safeguard the IP. Other options such
as a post-encryption option to add the public key would give someone other than the IP
owner the ability to tamper with the IP. Encrypting the public key with the rest of the source
code ensures that no one other than the simulation tool use the key. It thus provides the
same security as the encrypted IP flow itself.
IP users are responsible for safeguarding their own data. VCS honors a request by an IP
user to dump the waveforms of nonencrypted design blocks - albeit all the waveforms
are encrypted using the IP owner's public key. Therefore, the IP owner can view all the
waveforms in the encrypted FSDB, even those that are not part of the IP. To avoid this, IP

Debugging Standalone IP

users must be careful to only dump non-proprietary data or limit the waveform dump to
only the IP of interest.
VCS protects the encrypted IPs that have different public keys. If instructed to dump
the waveforms of IP blocks with different public keys, VCS issues an error and does not
generate the FSDB. This means that if different IP owners need to debug a failure, multiple
simulation runs are needed; one run for each IP owner - or one for each public key.
1. Obtaining RSA Keys
There are many ways to obtain an RSA private/public key pair. You can use
fsdbEncKeyGen to generate RSA key pair or use official RSA website to generate it.
2. Adding the Public Key and Encrypting the IP
IP owners can use the new option -fsdb_public_key to have the -ipprotect
option of the VCS compiler to automatically add the public key attribute as part of the
encryption. The fsdb_key attribute is only relevant for the top-level module of the IP,
VCS automatically extends it to encompass the full hierarchy of the IP. The fsdb_key is
disregarded if specified anywhere else in the hierarchy of the IP block. In addition, only
one fsdb_key attribute should be specified in the IP.
vcs -full64 -sverilog -ipopt=noincludeprotect -ipprotect
encryption_header -fsdb_public_key public.pem ip.v

Specifying the fsdb_key to all the files causes VCS to add the fsdb_key
attribute to every module, which, as stated above is functionally immaterial
and increases the size of the encrypted data.
3. Compiling the Design
To enable the waveform dumping capabilities, the IP user must specify the
-debug_access and -debug_region=encrypt options to the VCS compile command
vcs top.v ip.vp -debug_access -debug_region=encrypt

This command generates a simv executable that is capable of generating an encrypted
FSDB.
4. Running the Simulation
To enable Encrypted IP Waveform for a simulation run, IP users need to add the +fsdb

+public_key_ip simv option when running the executable, as follows:
simv +fsdb+public_key_ip

5. Specifying Instances to be Dumped

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow Summary

IP users designate the design instances to be dumped using the $fsdbdumpvar task.
If any of the design instances specified to $fsdbdumpvars is an encrypted block that
includes a fsdb public key then the entire FSDB is encrypted using the public key.
As noted earlier, attempting to dump waveforms for encrypted IPs with different fsdb
keys result in an error and the dump is aborted. Similarly, adding instances in multiple
$fsdbdumpvars commands and any of the instances have a different public key results
in an error and the dump is aborted, even if a dump has already started.
6. Loading an Encrypted FSDB
The IP owner can load an encrypted FSDB into Verdi by specifying the private key
through the environment variable FSDB_DECRYPT before running Verdi.
setenv FSDB_DECRYPT private.pem
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb

If the private key is incorrect or it is not specified the FSDB fails to load. An encrypted
FSDB is rendered useless to anyone without the private decryption key. One of the
advantages of the Encrypted IP Waveform flow is that the IP owner does not need to
run the simulation. The encrypted FSDB contains all the simulation data as it executed
in the system level test.

Encrypted IP Waveform Flow Summary
This appendix provides the Encrypted IP Waveform flow summary as follows:

* Adds the public key to the IP and encrypts the IP.

Encrypted IP Waveform Limitations
Encrypted IP Waveform feature has the following limitations:
* Top-level scope of the system-level test must be non-encrypted.
* Only works with P1735 encryption. The protect or protect128 flows are not supported
(No support for +/-autoprotect, +auto2protect, auto3protect129, )
* Encrypted module with public key inside, the following hierarchy is not dumped.
Non-Verilog scope : under VHDL, SystemC, Spice, AMS and so on.
Protected Verilog without public key.
Protected Verilog with different public key.
* The following items are not dumped inside encrypted module with public key:
Encrypted module without public key or with different public key
Non-encrypted module
Other language
SVA
Interface port
Global parameter
Class object
* Supports only $fsdbdumpvars, and all the options inside the task are ignored for the
dumping of encrypted IP part, that is, it is treated as full dump. Note that the options
still take effect for normal part.
* Selecting dumping individual items inside encrypted blocks is disallowed. Only a full
instance of an encrypted hierarchies is supported.
* Only one public key per encrypted IP is supported.
* Partial protection/encryption is not supported. that is, a whole module must be in the
envelope.
* Addition of the public key attribute changes the number of lines in the IP.

PyVerdi Python Package
Verdi provides a Python package PyVerdi, which supports the following two APIs:
* callCommand
* addCallback
Before you execute Python inside Verdi, Verdi automatically imports both APIs, letting you
to directly write callCommand and addCallback inside your Python script without the need
for from PyVerdi import *.
PyVerdi.callCommand
The callCommand API is used to run Tcl commands. This API returns both Tcl return value
(integer) and the result (string) as a tuple.
Syntax: callCommand(tclString: str) -> tuple[int, str]
PyVerdi.addCallback
The addCallback API is used to register the Python function as an event callback
function, like addEventCallback in Tcl. This API returns true if the callback is registered
successfully; otherwise, it returns false. If you register both the Python callback and the Tcl
callback for the same event reason, only the Python callback gets triggered.
Syntax: addCallback(callbackReason: str, callbackFunc: callable[[str],
any]) -> bool

EDR (Electronic Debug Record) is a feature that allows you to create, save, and load a
Verdi session, which may contain texts, screenshots, Tcl scripts that are used to reproduce
or solve an issue in Verdi. A common usage scenario would be that an R&D wants
to share his Verdi debug session with another R&D. He can create and save an EDR
session that contains the necessary steps to reproduce an issue. Then the other R&D can
reproduce the Verdi debug session quickly with a single click.

* CPU: A modern processor with at least 1 GHz clock speed
* RAM: Minimum of 8GB
* Disk: Minimum of 20GB

EDR Server Management
This section covers common server management tasks such as starting, stopping,
restarting, and monitoring the EDR Server.

Starting the Server
First-time Installation (Recommended):
setenv VERDI_HOME /path/to/verdi
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/install.csh --use_template_config

Interactive Mode:
setenv VERDI_HOME /path/to/verdi
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/install.csh

Checking the Server Status
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/install.csh --check_server

Output examples:
* EDR server is running at <hostname>:<port>/edr.
* EDR server is not running at <hostname>:<port>/edr.
Restarting the Server
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/install.csh --restart_serve

* Category: A predefined list of error characteristics. The default value is Unknown
Issue.
* Tags: You may add one or more Tags (separate by comma) to the record.
* Permission: The permission drop-down list contains Public and all Linux groups
of the current users. The default value is public. Once permission is set to group,
enable_case_extration is disabled. If an EDR has public permission, all users can
access it. If an EDR has group permission, only users who have the corresponding
Linux group permission can access it.
* Description: You may add the description of the debug record to capture the main
purpose of the session.
* Other Setting:
Environment Setting: The environment setting does not add all user environments
to the record; however, only the important ones are added. The users can add other
environment settings to the record as needed.
Data Preparation: This tab enables you to set the batch mode commands to
prepare the data for Verdi debug. Default Commands are the pre-defined batch
mode commands by EDR. You may change it if needed. Once you write your own
data preparation commands, Enable Case Extraction check box is disabled.

Figure 214

Save EDR - Data Preparation

Data Path: FSDB or KDB or simulation logs are collected by default. You can also
add customized data paths.
Figure 215

Data Path

For simulation logs, EDR automatically gathers files that are opened with the
viaLogViewerOpenLog SmartLog Tcl command.
For FSDB, EDR automatically gathers files that are opened with the wvOpenFile or
debLoadSimResult nWave Tcl commands.
* Advanced: This field shows the advanced features that enables you to set multiple
checkpoints in the record, and Case Extraction. You may click "+" to add the
checkpoint. A checkpoint contains the command history executed so far (from last
saved checkpoint or from beginning) with a snapshot and checkpoint notes. You may
also use Update Snapshot to update from the current active window. If multiple views
are selectable, you may choose which individual view to save. (The feature is based

on standard Capture Window feature of Verdi.) If there is no new command between
the new checkpoint and last one, a warning message is issued to let you know that the
current checkpoint is discarded.
Figure 216

Save EDR - Advanced Setup

* Enable Case Extraction: If this field is enabled, EDR tries to collect the data needed
to run the session. For Verdi run (post process and interactive debug), KDB/FSDB is
collected. The collected data is saved in a centralized location to avoid dependency
data being overwritten by users, so that the EDR replay can work independently.
* Enable Debug Telemetry: If this field is enabled, EDR tries to run Debug Telemetry
Analysis after the EDR is saved. Then the telemetry results get uploaded to the
database as part of EDR.
After the record is ready, click Save to upload the EDR record to Web Server. Clic

on) needs to be run before
invoking Verdi.
* Maximum EDR number: If the work dir has more replayed EDR sessions than the
maximum EDR number, older ones are deleted.
* Auto save: If it is checked, EDRs are automatically saved. You do not need to open
the EDR Save dialog to save it. (Checkpoint is added on a hourly basis if Verdi is idle.)
* Group: Displays user's linux group (this field cannot be edited.)
* Lsf Command: You can enter the lsf command here and it is applied when invoking
Verdi.

Analytics Dashboard
You can view the aggregation metrics and chartings in terms of data collected from EDR
and Debug Telemetry flows using the Dashboard available on the EDR main page.
Figure 223

EDR Dashboard

You can select the begin and end dates, and query aggregation metrics, chartings, and
signature list based on given criteria.
Figure 224

Debug Analysis

In the Failure Signature tab, you can see aggregation metrics: (a) number of EDRs
(b) number of signature categories, chartings: (c) count of EDRs per date (d) distribution
of failure signatures, and detailed information of signature list (name, description, count,
more is a hyperlink can navigate to main page with filtering parameters, such as dates
and signature type).
In the Design Hotspot tab, you can view similar chartings based on data of Debug
Telemetry: (e) count of modules / signals per date (f) heatmap to show frequent (top 10)
accessing modules or signals (switching by drop-down menu and click refresh icon).
Similar to field more shown in the Failure Signature tab, clicking on each block of
heatmap takes you to the EDR main page with filtering parameters (only display records
including related modules or signals).

Run Status of EDR Replay
Click the Status tab to navigate to EDR Session Status View.

You can check the run status of an EDR replay through the status list view:
Figure 225

EDR Session Status

You can filter the session status by user name, run status, and running machine.

EDR Replay From Verdi EDR Browser
You can also replay an EDR session through Verdi EDR Browser.
Client setup is not needed.
You can open this browser through Tools->Browser EDR.

Searching in Verdi EDR Browser
You can use the search pane to search the EDRs using the JQL Style Query.

After you press Enter, EDR view gets refreshed with the latest 50 search results from the
EDR server.

When you enter a search query and press Enter, the latest 50 EDRs from the web server
are listed.
Applying Filters in Verdi EDR Browser
The filters that you have saved from the EDR web page can be synchronized with Verdi.
You can apply the filter using the drop-down menu on the Verdi EDR Browser.

The Verdi EDR browser does not have a filter if you do not save any EDR on the EDR web
page.

Customized Setup in Verdi EDR Browser
You can check the Enable Customized Setup checkbox to enable the Settings button.
After clicking Settings, you can enter the customized environment settings in the EDR
replay Setup dialog box.

edrSearch
The edrSearch utility allows you to search through EDRs.
Input
A search string that follows the rules below.
Supported Search key:
"session_name"
"session_description"
"session_sig_catg"
"session_creator"
"session_id"
"session_workmode"
"session_group"
"time_range"
"path.KDB"
"path.FSDB"
"path.simulation_log"

Supported Logical Operators
"AND"
"OR"

Supported Match Operators
"="
"~"

For example, the following string queries the EDRs whose session_name contains verdi
and session_creator is jack.
edrSearch "session_name ~ verdi AND session_creator = jack"

Note that time_range is a special key and it only supports three value: week, month,
quarter.
For example, the following string queries the EDRs that are created in last seven days and
session_description contains debug.
edrSearch "time_range = week AND session_description ~ debug"

Output:
One or more matched EDR session IDs, if not found, the output is "No matched records in
database."
edrReplay
The edrReplay utility allows you to replay the EDRs.
Input
* EDR session ID
* Work directory (optional)
Replay Verdi is invoked if session ID is valid. Else, print an error message.
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrReplay -session_id
6c47cb1b3a2d483ab408f0171211ee90 -work_dir /remote/vgemanits/yuesenlu/edr

edrUtil
The edrUtil utility allows you to configure your personal EDR setup.
Input
One or more combination of the options supported by the script.
Successful configuration of the EDR.
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrUtil -display abcodcvde0xxx7:1
-replay_dir /u/abc/my03/edr
abc's display is set to abcodcvde0xxx7:1.
abc's replay dir is set to /u/abc/my03/edr.

EDR Replay Dialog
The EDR Replay dialog can be opened using Tools -> EDR Replay.

After a session is replayed either from the web server or directly from Record URL, Verdi
launches with an EDR Replay dialog.
The EDR Replay dialog lists the checkpoint list of the record, and a snapshot of each
checkpoint. By default, checkpoint 1 is executed. And you can select other checkpoints
by clicking on "Go to Checkpoint". (For example, go to checkpoint 3 from checkpoint 1).
The checkpoints in between are executed in the order if it is a TCL-based checkpoint;
otherwise, it restores the session for the selected checkpoint directly.

Debug Telemetry
Debug Telemetry is a utility integrated with EDR. It collects information about user
activities during the debugging process.
Examples include modules, scopes, and signals.
The VERDI_ENABLE_ELECTRONIC_DEBUG_RECORD environment variable must be
set to 1 to use the Debug Telemetry feature.
You need to click Advanced<< to view the Enable Debug Telemetry field.

summarizes the number of modules and signals accessed during debugging.

details.
The summary page provides basic EDR information. This includes session ID, name,
description, and date.
It also shows aggregation metrics, such as the number of modules, scopes, and signals.

Additional content includes charting of the top 10 modules by signal count, plus module

0x12345)
edrSmartDebug --app_type "selective_dumping" --query_type "edr_id" -edr_session_id "0x12345"

* Generate the configuration of a preloaded design based on the time range (from
2024-04-01 to 2024-04-30)
edrSmartDebug --app_type "preload_design" --query_type "time_range" -date_range_from "2024-04-01" --date_range_to "2024-04-30"

* Generate the configuration of selective dumping based on the signature type:
mismatch_dut
edrSmartDebug --app_type "selective_dumping" --query_type "signature"
--signature_type "mismatch_dut"

* Generate the configuration of a preloaded design based on the signature type and time
range
edrSmartDebug --app_type "preload_design" --query_type "signature"
--signature_type "mismatch_dut" --date_range_from "2024-04-01" -date_range_to "2024-04-30"

* Generate the configuration of a preloaded design based on the time range and launch
Verdi
edrSmartDebug --app_type "preload_design" --query_type "time_range"
--date_range_from "2024-04-01" --date_range_to "2024-04-30" -launch_verdi -dbdir /path/demo/case/cpu/simv.daidir &

For the application type selective_dumping, the utility only generates the
dump.config configuration file and the example selective.ucli. You need
to modify and integrate them into dumping flow of FSDB on your own. As for
the preload_design application type, you can check the preload.config
configuration file before launching Verdi with the design source.

EDR Serverless Mode
EDR Serverless Mode lets you save and replay Electronic Debug Record (EDR) sessions
locally without connecting to a server. Use this mode to keep debug data on your own
machine or when server access is limited.
* Saving EDR in Serverless Mode
* Replaying EDR in Serverless Mode
EDR runs in serverless mode if the environment variable

SNPS_VERDI_INTERNAL_ELECTRONIC_DEBUG_RECORD_WEB_SERVER_URI is not set.

Saving EDR in Serverless Mode
When saving an EDR session, Verdi displays a warning indicating serverless mode is
active.

* The Save EDR dialog box shows the storage path and lets you choose where to save
the EDR session.
* After saving, Verdi displays the local path of the saved EDR session.

Replaying EDR in Serverless Mode
Using the Command Line Utility
1. Run the following command to replay a saved EDR session:
$VERDI_HOME/share/edrServer/edrReplay -session_dir <path_of_saved_EDR>

2. Replace <path_of_saved_EDR> with the actual path where your EDR session is
saved.
Using Verdi EDR Browser
1. Open the EDR Browser in Verdi.
2. Enter the local path to search for EDR records on your disk.
The search is recursive with a default maximum depth of 3.
If the search takes too long, click Stop to end the search.

3. After the search finishes, results are displayed in the EDR Browser.
4. Click Replay to replay the selected EDR session.

Upgrading Server
Upgrading the server means updating the server software to a newer version, typically
to match changes in Verdi or its database schema. This upgrade is important when the
Verdi version changes, as the underlying database (such as MongoDB) schema may also
change, requiring the server to be updated so you can continue to save, share, and replay
debug sessions without issues.
To upgrade the server, use the following command:
vms server upgrade -app <app_name>

If you do not set -app, the tool works as before. This command does not support all
option for -app. The available apps are edr and verdi_vms.

Overview
Synopsys Memory VIPs are based on Synopsys SystemVerilog Technology (SVT)
infrastructure. The infrastructure includes SystemVerilog classes and Memory Server.
The Memory Server is one of the key elements of SVT Memory VIP infrastructure. Actual
memory values are stored in the Memory Server, rather than in a SystemVerilog array.
The primary advantage of this approach is performance independence. The Memory
VIP does not rely on each simulator's sparse array server implementation. For multi-GB
memories, the simulation typically accesses only a small portion of the overall address
space. In addition, this approach supports virtual patterns. These patterns enable memory
initialization without significant memory or performance overhead.
In a Memory VIP, protocol-level transactions and memory actions are stored in an FSDB
file. The Memory Server can be configured to record all memory actions to the same
FSDB file. You can then view the memory-related data in the Verdi Memory Protocol

Viewing Cache Related Data in Verdi
Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzerdisplays data related to cache memory to help you
to analyze and debug the design efficiently, as it provides visualization and analysis of one
or more cache memories at a specific simulation time.
You can invoke the Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer window using any of the
following methods:
* In the Verdi main window, click the Tools -> Transaction Debug -> Cache and Memory
Protocol Analyzer command.
* In the Protocol Analyzerwindow, click the Tools ->New Cache and Memory Protocol
Analyzer command.
* In the Protocol Analyzerwindow, select a coherent/snoop transaction and click the
Show Cache Operations right-click option to open either a filtered (single address) or
an unfiltered view. This view occupies the bottom half portion of the available area, but
can be rearranged or moved (if required).

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview
The cache debug view window comprises of the following panes:
* Hierarchy Tree pane
* Cache pane
* History pane
* Details pane
The following figure illustrates the cache debug view window:
Figure 231

Cache Debug View

Hierarchy Tree Pane
The Hierarchy Tree pane displays scopes and streams that have associated cache or
memory data and each scope/stream has a corresponding check box. You can select a
stream/scope check box to view its associated cache or memory data.
If you select a cache scope or stream, the cache data is opened with the cache view.
If you select a memory scope or stream, the cache data is opened with the memory view.
The check box is mutually exclusive. In a given memory browser at a given
time, you can view either memory data or cache data, but not memory and
cache data together. To view both memory data and cache data simultaneously,
you need to open two memory browser windows.

Cache and Memory Protocol Analyzer Window Overview

Hierarchy Tree Pane

All the possible actions and the resultant behaviors are as follows:
* If no items are checked in the Hierarchy Tree pane,
Checking a memory instance loads the memory data.
Checking a cache instance loads the cache data.
* If a memory instance is already loaded,
Checking a memory instance loads new memory data in the current view (only one
memory instance can be selected at a time).
Checking a cache instance loads the cache data in the current view.
* If a cache instance is already loaded,
Checking a memory instance loads the memory data in the current view (replacing
the cache data).
Checking/unchecking a cache instance adds/removes the cache data in the current
view.
The memory data can now be opened using the Hierarchy Tree, instead of the
Select Memory option used in previous releases. You can open and view the
memory data by checking the associated check box for a scope or stream.

Support for Color Themes in the nSchema Window

You can change the color theme of the nSchema window by selecting one of the following
themes in the Color Theme section, as illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 243

Color Themes

* Classic Theme:Applies the color theme selected for the schematic area in the
nSchema window. By default, the option is on.
* Black Theme: Applies the background color as black. The signal, instance port, and so
on are changed accordingly for clarity.
* White Theme: Applies the background color as white. The signal, instance port, and
so on are changed accordingly for clarity.
* Customized Theme: By default, this option is disabled. It is enabled when the line
style or color is changed and applied.
Tcl Commands and Options
Starting with this release, following are the new Tcl options to change the color theme in
the schematic area:
schSetDisplayAttr
The schSetDisplayAttr Tcl command sets the display attributes for the type.
A new argument -qtColor QColor_name is added to the command.
schSetDisplayAttr Background -style line_solid -qtColor #ff0000 -color
ID_BLACK

schResetDisplayAttr -customized | -black | -white | [-default]

Support Hierarchy Tree in fastGate Mode
Starting with this release, Verdi supports hierarchy tree based on ShellDB in fastGate
mode.

The following command is used to invoke this feature:
setenv VERDI_FASTGATE_HIERARCHY_TREE
verdi -lca -fastGate -dbdir simv.daidir

If it is disabled, you can invoke Verdi using Find Instances widget.
There are two columns supported Hierarchy and Module as shown in the following
figure. The Module column can be customized to 'show' or 'hide' by the RMB Menu or
Preferences window. When you import the design, the default view is the top view. It
supports multi-selection and selects the whole row by default.

nWave Enhancement
The following section describes the nWave LCA features supported by Verdi as part of this
release:
* Unified Transaction and Signal Waveform Debugging in nWave
* Dynamic Object Signal Enhancements in nWave
* Improved Waveform Drawing Performance for FSDB-GATE Signals

This feature enables you to add both transactions and signals into nWave. Thus, the
integrated nWave window helps you get the maximum benefit of the screen size and other
features to debug an error using both transactions and waveforms on a single application
For more information about this feature, refer to the Transaction Debug chapter.

After loading a waveform file into Verdi which stores the dumped dynamic objects, you can
review the waveforms in the nWave with following enhancements:
* Support for UVM Component and Register Objects
* Viewing UVM Hierarchy Name for Class Object Signal in nWave Signal Pane
* Support to Expand Class Object
* Support Filtering of Internal Attributes for Expanded Class Object/Pointer
* Support for Queue, Dynamic Array, Associative Array in Class Object

Support for UVM Component and Register Objects
To enable the following enhancements,
perform the following:
* Set the environment variable VERDI_ENHANCE_DYNAMIC_OBJECT.
* To dump UVM component object, you must specify +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE
option at simulation runtime.
* To dump UVM register object, you must specify +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE option at
simulation runtime.
* To specify dumping level for UVM component object, you must specify
+UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N option at simulation runtime. The default value of N is 1. If N
is specified as 0, all level of objects are dumped.
Or,
* You can also use the Object Level preference option (Tools -> Preferences ->
Interactive Debug->Dynamical Dumping page) in Verdi interactive mode, as shown in
the following figure, to specify dumping level for UVM component object. The default
value is "1".
Figure 246

New Object Level Option in Preferences Dialog

If +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE or +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE is not specified, the
object dumping level is determined by the Object Level preference option.
If +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE or +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE is specified, the object
dumping level is determined by the largest number between +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N
and Object Level Options. For example, if +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N is specified and

Object Level is set to M, the object dumping level is determined by the largest number
between N and M.

Perform the simulation for the demanded debugging features using the corresponding
runtime options:
./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+UVM_AWARE+COMPWAVE +UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=2

Set the environment variables for nWave features introduced in this section, using the
following command:
setenv VERDI_ENHANCE_DYNAMIC_OBJECT

Invoke Verdi using the following command:
verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -lca &

Improved Waveform Drawing Performance for FSDB-GATE
Signals
Describes nWave performance enhancements for FSDB-GATE signals: pixel-based
drawing (SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER), multitasking dense drawing, optional
red X highlighting (Waveform > View Options > Waveform Pane > Show X Color in
Multitasking Dense Drawing), docked/undocked progress display, default vs NeedX mode,
and limitations (unfinished files, auto-update, virtual files, anyall/real signal).
This feature improves the speed of drawing waveforms in nWave when working with
FSDB-GATE signals. FSDB files can contain many signals that are marked as secondary,
meaning their value changes are not dumped directly but reconstructed during reading.

This reconstruction can slow down nWave operations, especially for gate-level FSDBs with
many value changes. The new solution speeds up waveform drawing and makes the user
interface more responsive.
* Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
* Enabling and Using X Color Display in nWave Multitasking Dense Drawing
* Limitations of Multitasking Dense Drawing and Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave

Enabling Pixel-Based Drawer for nWave
The pixel-based drawing feature in nWave improves how waveform data is displayed,
especially when handling large datasets. This feature changes how dense pixels and
'X' (unknown) values appear in the waveform view.
Setting Environment Variables
To activate the pixel-based drawer feature, set the following environment variable before
launching Verdi and nWave:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_PIXEL_BASED_DRAWER 1

Using the Feature
* Open nWave as usual after setting the environment variables.
* nWave polls the FSDB reader and update the waveform incrementally.

* The interface remains responsive; you can scroll, click, and view signal tips even while
data is loading.
* Unfinished waveform data appears as blue pixels. These pixels update as more data
loads.

Configuring RTVS in AMS Designs

The following are the columns in the Time Based configuration table:
start: Defines the start time of the RTVS window for the new configuration.
end: Defines the end time of the RTVS window.
control: Points to a local control file that specifies which blocks use use_spice,
use_verilog, and the related commands.
label: Specifies a label for the new configuration.
sim_opt: Specifies simulation options applied during this time window. The options
must be specified between start = <start_time> and end = <end_time>. This
is optional.
ic_file: The options must be specified between start = <start_time> and end =
<end_time>. This is optional.
The following are the columns in the Event Based configuration table:
sel_val: Defines the signal value or integer value associated with the mixed-signal
configuration defined in the command.
control: Defines the new configuration for specific blocks using use_spice,
use_verilog, and the related commands.
label: Specifies a label for the new configuration.
sim_opt: Specifies simulation options applied during this time window. The options
must be specified between start = <start_time> and end = <end_time>. This
is optional.
ic_file: The options must be specified between start = <start_time> and end =
<end_time>. This is optional.
* Config File: Displays the RTVS configuration file name linked to the selected row.
* Preview: View the configuration in a text browser. The colors indicate changes: green
is new, gray is deleted, blue is updated, and black is unchanged.
* Save: Click to save settings to a file (for example, vcsAD.init).
* Apply: Click to save the init file to $logDir/vcsAD_Verdi.init and reload the design.
* OK: Click to save and close the dialog box.

* Add Successor Stream(s) by Relation
This option loads the successor streams of the selected transactions, if not already

This option marks the selected transaction in purple. You can choose multiple
transactions as marked transactions. Even after the transaction selection changes, all
marked transactions continue to show in purple. This option is enabled by default for all
types of transactions.
* Clear All Marked Transactions
This option clears all marked transactions back to their default color.
* View Marked Transactions
On selecting this option, the Waveform pane area displays only the marked
transactions, and all other transactions are hidden. If none of the marked transactions
are available, it generates a warning message.
This is a toggle option. On selecting this option again, you can view all the transactions.
* View Source
This option loads the source code responsible for recording the transaction into the
nTrace window.

Save and Restore Support
Save and restore feature is supported in line with the nWave feature. You can save
and restore the displayed signals and transactions and their attributes such as color,
height, and other information to a file. You can easily restore the same waveforms later by
restoring this file. For more information, refer to the Verdi User Guide and Tutorial.
