Support for New Instrumentation Methodology for SystemVerilog
Interfaces
VCS supports a new instrumentation methodology for SystemVerilog interfaces using the
-power=upfim compile option. For example:
% vcs test.v -upf demo.upf -kdb -lca -power=upfim
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidr

Starting with this release, Verdi supports this methodology by default. It supports all
existing low power debugging features based on this new instrumentation methodology.

The following are the limitations of this feature:
* This feature supports only the modport port name same as the signal name. That is,
this feature only works based on the signal names inside modport/interface.
* Nested modport is not supported.
* All instrumented signals in interface are not supported in FSDB.

Support Verdi Low Power XML Functionality for VHDL
VCS Plato supports the UPF Information Model (UPFIM). The UPFIM flow preserves all
existing Verdi GUI behavior. That is, there is no behavior change between the Verdi low

Chapter 17: Power-Aware Debug
Verdi Low Power Import Performance Improvement

power XML (lp_xml) flow and the Verdi UPFIM flow. You must use the -power=upfim
compile option on the vcs command line to enable UPFIM flow. For example:
% vcs test.v -upf demo.upf -kdb -lca -power=upfim
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidr

Starting with this release, UPFIM flow supports VHDL.

Verdi Low Power Import Performance Improvement
Profiling shows that Verdi low power import takes a long time to traverse all UPF
commands from the power database. To resolve this issue, run a batch mode executable,
lpcom, in parallel with VCS compilation.
lpcom processes the power database and serializes it into an archive. During Verdi bring

up, Verdi automatically picks up the archive and transforms it into the Verdi database.
This support is now enabled at compilation using the -kdb=lpcom compile option.
Following is the usage example:
% vcs design.v -sverilog -upf file.upf -lca -kdb=lpcom
% verdi -dbdir simv.daidir

When you use this option, Verdi imports resolved power KDB (PW-KDB) directly instead of
building Verdi Power Model.
You can use the following environment variable to disable -kdb=lpcom:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_DISABLE_LPCOM 1

UVM Aware Debug
The following section describe the UVM-Aware Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as
part of this release:
* Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug
* Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features
* Native UVM Dumping Support

Instant Recall Flow for UVM Debug
When you debug a UVM error or fatal event in Verdi interactive mode, you need to rerun
the simulation to reach the error point after starting Verdi.
The Verdi Instant Recall feature lets you save the error point as a debug session during
batch-mode simulation. The UVM error message report helps you find error types, group
them, and plan your next steps for debugging with Instant Recall.
After you save the simulation session for a UVM error or fatal event, you can use Verdi to
restore the session in interactive mode. This saves time because you do not need to rerun
the simulation.
To enable the Instant Recall flow, use the -instantRecall VCS runtime option. The
Instant Recall flow enables the following:
* Record the simulation session at the first UVM error or fatal, and then use Verdi to start
debugging from the point where the simulation session was recorded.
* Stop the simulation at the first UVM error or fatal, print out the error message, create
checkpoint information of debug point, save the session, and then exit the simulation.
You can know at which UVM_ERROR is the checkpoint saved and identify that the test failed
with UVM_ERROR.
UVM error message report helps you to identify error types, group them, and perform the
next step for debugging with Instant Recall.
You can continue to perform debugging by using the -i -cprestore [saved_session]
Verdi command line option to restore the simulation session to Verdi in interactive mode.

The following sections describe this feature in detail:
* Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
Enabling Instant Recall Flow in VCS and UCLI
* You can enable Instant Recall flow in VCS using the -instantRecall runtime option.
For example, simv -instantRecall.
For compilation, you must specify the -kdb and -debug_acc+reverse options to
enable this feature.
* The -instantRecall option auto-generates a default instant recall script named
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl under the run directory. The following are the
key points to note:
The instant recall script enables reverse debug (config reversedebug on), saves
debug point on the first UVM error or fatal, and then saves the session.
The saved session is the simulation session, not the Verdi session.
Simulation sources this Tcl script before sourcing your -do/-i script.
By default, .synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl is overwritten for every instant
recall run.
To modify this script, you can add a header in this Tcl file to keep the current Tcl
version by adding/removing comment, so that your modification can take effect in
later instant recall runs.
The session can be overwritten if it exists.
Provide default session name. You can also define session names in the
.synopsys_ucli_instant_recall.tcl file.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits.
Debugging in Verdi With Instant Recall Flow
* The session is saved under the run directory. You can execute from the Verdi
command line as follows to restore the session from the time point where the first UVM
error or fatal happened.
% verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore [checkpoint_session]

You can specify the simulation session name to restore. If no file is specified, the
default session file is restored.
* If the restore session fails, UCLI exits and Verdi closes the interactive debug mode.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features

* From the Verdi command line, the restore session should not be used with -do/-i.
Example: verdi -dbdir ./simv.daidir -i -cprestore sess -do myScript
Verdi issues a warning message and skips -do/-i.
The following is the limitation of this feature:
* When Verdi is invoked with the -i -cprestore option, it may not consider some
runtime options of the Restart simulation command. This can happen as the Verdi
behavior is the same as the restore mechanism. That is, Verdi may not extract some of
the runtime options applied to simv.
You can use one of the following workarounds to avoid this limitation:
1. If an FSDB file is dumped for the simulation with the -instantRecall option, you
can invoke Verdi using both the -i -cprestore option and the FSDB file together.
The simulation options are saved in the FSDB file and can be reused while invoking
Verdi.
Example:%> verdi -ssf novas.fsdb -i -cprestore
2. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options manually in the Verdi
command line as follows:
Example:%> verdi -dbdir simv.daidir -i cprestore -simDelim
+UVM_TEST_NAME=test_2m_4s // runtime options are used in the simulation
3. If no FSDB is dumped, you can add the runtime options after invoking Verdi and
before performing Restart.

Specifying FSDB File Name for UVM Enabled Features
By default, UVM data is dumped into the default FSDB file. You can use the
+uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> runtime option to specify the FSDB

file for the UVM debug features enabled by the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE runtime options.

The following options can be specified with the +UVM_TR_RECORD and
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE:
UVM_AWARE, HIER, TLM, TLM2, IMP, RAL, FAC, COMPWAVE, RALWAVE, or MSG.

If filename.fsdb is not specified, then the file name is set to uvm.fsdb

file name automatically.
When the +uvm_fsdbfile=<filename.fsdb> option is specified, the +UVM_VERDI_TRACE

The following section describe the HW/SW Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as part
of this release:
* HW/SW Debug Support for Adaptive Exclusions

Adaptive Exclusion allows you to load and review exclusions when the source code or
ELF file is updated. Verdi HW/SW Debug exclusion manager provides a way to generate
exclusions through GUI operation. It can also save/load exclude files. If the loaded exclude
file mismatches with the current source code, HW/SW Debug exclusion manager detects it
for user review.
Verdi HW/SW Debug supports exclusion management and adaptive exclusion. You must
use the following environment variable to enable this feature:
HWSW_DEBUG_COV_PLUGIN_EXCLUSION=2

Reviewing Loaded Exclusions
Reviewing loaded exclusions is required when there is any change in the coverable lines
when loading exclude files. When review is required, Coverage view is updated with the
following changes:

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format

Generating Coverage Reports in HTML Format
Verdi HW/SW debug supports generating coverage reports in HTML format using
the -lcov_capture FILE option (where FILE specifies the filename) of the
hwsw_debug_coverage tool. This option generates coverage information in a format
compatible with the LTP GCOV extension (LCOV) .info file. The default name is based
on the name of the gmon.out file. This information is input to the genhtml tool to generate
an HTML report. LCOV is an open-sourced GNU toolset, and genhtml is one of its tools.
LCOV can consolidate multiple .info files and generate the merged HTML report.

Interactive Simulation Debug
The following section describe the Interactive Simulation Debug LCA features supported
by Verdi as part of this release:
* New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
* Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages
* Adding a Variable Name to the Watch Window Manually
* Selectively Adding Class or Members From the Source View to the Watch View

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug
You can use the VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL environment variable as follows to enable the
new unified Tcl mode LCA feature in Verdi interactive debug:
setenv VERDI_NEW_UNIFIED_TCL 1

The new unified Tcl mode is applied in the following usages:
Launch Verdi with interactive debug mode together:
* simv -verdi
* verdi -I
* verdi -ssr [interactive_session_file]
* In simv UCLI mode, launch start_verdi
If interactive debug with new unified Tcl mode is exited to post-simulation mode, Verdi
switches to original unified Tcl flow.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

The following figure shows the process flow of Tcl commands:
Figure 299

Process Flow of Tcl Commands

The following points describe the process flow:
* Verdi interactive debug is launched using the simv -verdi or verdi -simBin simv
-i commands.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter is used as default interpreter. Initially, all Tcl commands and
procedures are sent to UCLI Tcl interpreter for processing.
* UCLI Tcl interpreter sends all Verdi commands to Verdi for execution.
* After enabling new unified Tcl mode, Verdi updates views once after script execution
is completed. Verdi does not update the views after executing each command in the
scripts.

New Unified Tcl Mode Support in Verdi Interactive Debug

Pausing Script Execution During Simulation
In the new unified Tcl mode, Verdi allows you to pause script execution during simulation.
Verdi displays the following Stop dialog box when you click the Stop button during script
execution:
Figure 300

Stop Dialog Box

* Abort: Aborts script execution.
* Pause: Pauses script execution. If the script is paused, you can use the resume
command on console to continue script execution, or you can use the abort command
to abort script execution. Verdi displays the Busy dialog if the script is not paused.
When the Busy dialog is displayed, you can click the Abort button to cancel th

Controlling the Display of Console Command Output Messages

You can also control the display of the console command output messages when
executing the scripts using the View -> Enable Script Echoing option in the Console
menu bar, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 301

Enabling Script Echoing From Console Pane

By default, theEnable Script Echoing option is enabled. This option is valid for both
source and do commands, and the behavior is same as adding -echo on for the do
command.

Displaying the Result of Multiple Commands Inline on the
Console
When multiple commands are present on the same line in the script file, Verdi displays
the result of all the commands if you use the VERDI_TBV_ECHO_DISPLAY 1 environment
variable. By default, Verdi displays only the result of the last command.
set a [get b]

In this case, Verdi displays the result of all the commands present on the same line, for
example as follows:
Verdi> set a [get m_pkt.is_dir]
'b1 // value of a
Verdi> get m_pkt.is_dir; stop -relative 1

Following are the limitations of this feature:
* The source <filename> command does not support -echo [on/off] option.
However, you can control the echo message display using the View -> Enable Script
Echoing option in the Console menu bar.
* Running the script files using command line options to invoke Verdi (for example,
-play, -do/-i) do not support echo message control.

Adding a Variable Name to the Watch Window Manually
Verdi allows you to add a variable name manually to the watch window. To enable this
feature, you must first set the VERDI_DISPLAY_STL_ELEMENTS environment variable as
follows and then use the -debug_access+all option during compilation.
setenv VERDI_DISPLAY_STL_ELEMENTS 1

This feature helps you to locate the variables in the local or member list easily. The
following variables are supported:
* this (current class scope)
* this.mem_name (current class scope member, mem_name is member name)
* Local variable
* Global variable
* HDL signal with full hierarchy (for example, top.a.b.c)
* Class object id and the member (for example, classA@1)
* SystemC local variable
You must use the -lca option while invoking Verdi to use this feature.

the Watch View
Verdi allows you to selectively add a class or the members of the selected signal in the
Source view to the Watch view manually. For example, if the Source view contains a signal
with format class.member (for example, c1.mem1), you can add either class c1 or member
mem1, or both, to the Watch view.

enable this feature:
setenv TBV_ADD_MEMBER_TO_WATCH_DIALOG 1

be added to the Watch view, Verdi enables the Add to Watchesright-click option.

The ICO Class/Instance View displays the total P-score/O-score and the test list which

Display Mode Switching button to switch between Class Table and Instance Table.
Figure 318

ICO Instance Table

The Coverage Pessimistic Score (COV-P), Coverage Optimistic Score (COV-O), Diversity
Pessimistic Score (DIVERSITY-P), and Diversity Optimistic Score (DIVERSITY-O) can
be listed by each randomized call or by each class. They can be colored based on their
score. Also, you can click the header to sort the table. You can double-click a class

Column Name Description
Expected

Variable bin value that is determined by variable precision
and signedness. It can be Coverable, Illegal, or Excluded bin.

Covered

Variable bin value that is hit, that is, bin value is picked as a
part of some solution.

Uncovered

Variable bin value that is coverable, but has not been hit yet,
that is, a bin value was not picked as part of some solution.

Excluded

Variable bin value that is recommended by the user to
exclude/ignore for O-score computation.

COV-P

Pessimistic coverage score of a given class computed by

Intelligent Constraint Debugger
Finding the root cause of test failures such as UVM_ERROR, SVA failures, and checker
failures is laborious. It requires several trial-and-error cycles.
These cycles slow the verification process and make it harder to achieve verification
closure on time.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) feature allows you to automate the localization
of the failure-inducing randomization constraints and reduces the manual debugging effort.
The architecture of ICD is shown in the following figure:
Figure 362

ICD Architecture

The ICD module is part of the VCS framework. The Constraint Solver solves
randomization problems generated by the Problem Generator based on the given
Constraint Random Testbench (CRT).
ICD uses AI/ML technology to identify minimal stimulus trigger conditions. These
conditions let the constraint solver reproduce the simulation failure. The Monitor checks
whether the current set of reduced stimulus trigger conditions triggered the simulation
failure.

ICD Use Model
ICD provides a unified executable with an intuitive interface that automatically runs the
process and generates comprehensive reports. The following is the use model:
% icd icd_config.json

The icd utility is available under the VCS installation at $VCS_HOME/bin/icd. It takes a
configuration file icd_config.json as input. It invokes ICD and generates reports.
.

Compilation:
vcs [compile-time options]

Debug with ICD:
% icd icd_config.json
% cat icd_config.json
{
"SIMV_CMD" : "simv <run_opt>",
"ICD_REGEX" : "<failure_regular_expression>",
"ICD_RECORD" : "ICD_DBG",
"ICD_REPORT" : "ICD_RPT"
}

SIMV_CMD: Specify the simulation command or a JSON list of commands with runtime

options that expose the failure.

ICD_REGEX: Specify regular expression of the failure message. For example, "ASSERT
FAILED. *ReqHighUntilAck_A".
ICD_RECORD: Specify the record directory to store intermediate results.
ICD_REPORT: Specify the report directory to store RCA reports.

The ICD flow iteratively minimizes stimulus trigger conditions required to reproduce the
simulation failure. It produces a failing test and a passing test with minimal differences in
constraint random variable values.
The report is dumped in the <ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.json file.

ICD requires VCS APEX and VT_VCS_VERDI_ICD license keys.

LLM Prompt to Leverage ICD Analysis
To enhance ICD usability and enable agent-based debug workflows, ICD generates a
text-based prompt. You can use this prompt directly with Large Language Model (LLM)-
enabled tools such as Cursor, Copilot, and similar environments.
This prompt aggregates relevant context and debug information from the ICD flow. It helps
you perform root cause analysis (RCA) and identify potential fixes for simulation failures.
This feature does not alter the existing ICD usage model or execution flow. ICD continues
to identify the closest passing and failing simulations. It also produces standard RCA
reports and artifacts.

chapter: 1 // return breakpoint ID after add breakpoint
text:
ICD is invoked in the usual manner:
% icd icd_config.json

chapter: 1 // return breakpoint ID after add breakpoint
text:
As in the existing flow, ICD generates analysis outputs under the directory specified by
the ICD_REPORT parameter. These outputs include failure-inducing stimulus differences,
randomization context, and trace information.
With this feature, ICD additionally generates the following file:
<ICD_REPORT>/icd_rca.prompt

This file is automatically produced as part of the standard ICD report generation process.

LLM Prompt File Description
The icd_rca.prompt file contains structured instructions intended for direct use within
the chat interfaces of agent-enabled IDEs. The prompt is not a static template. It is
automatically populated with data specific to the detected simulation failure.
The prompt includes the following information:
* Failure message, matching regular expression, log file, and failure location.
* Reference passing iteration and reduced failing iteration identified by ICD.
* Minimal set of stimulus and randomization variables required to reproduce the failure.
* Pass and fail values for each failure-inducing variable.
* Randomization sequence and hierarchical context
* References to ICD-generated trace and RCA artifacts

Intended Use
The generated prompt guides an LLM agent to perform the following tasks:
* Interpret the failure scenario using the embedded simulation and debug context.
* Analyze ICD-derived RCA findings.
* Identify likely failure sources, such as testbench stimulus, design logic, or checkers.
* Propose potential fixes or debugging actions based on failure-specific data.
The file can be copied and pasted directly into an LLM chat interface. ICD does not
execute or validate the responses generated by the agent.

* The prompt is informational and advisory.
* Fix recommendations must be reviewed and validated by the user.
* The effectiveness of the analysis depends on the LLM and its access to the
relevant codebase.

Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation
A multi-stage simulation consists of multiple sequential simulation runs. Each stage
consumes data generated by the previous stage.
Failures in later stages may depend on conditions or data from earlier stages. Debugging
these failures requires identifying failure-inducing conditions in preceding stages.
The Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) supports this capability through its multi-stage
simulation flow. Set the SIMV_CMD parameter in the ICD configuration file to a JSON list of
simulation commands (one for each stage).

text:
Debugging Multi-Staged Simulation

Include the runtime options that expose the failure. The following example illustrates this
setup.

Multi-Staged Simulation Debug Example
Consider the following simulation executables:
simv_write: Writes randomly generated configurations in a config.txt file.
simv_read: Reads configurations from config.txt and generates random stimulus. The
error Bad Stimulus is issued for a certain stimulus value.

Figure 363

2-Stage Simulation - simv_read Consumes `config.txt' Generated by simv_write

To debug the "Bad Stimulus" error in simv_read, configure the SIMV_CMD parameter as
a JSON list of simulation commands for each stage, as shown in the following example:
Example 1
{

}

icd_config.json

"SIMV_CMD" : [
"simv_write +ntb_random_seed=123",
"simv_read +ntb_random_seed=200"
],
"ICD_REGEX" : "Bad stimulus",
"ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "0"

In the following JSON configuration file, setting "REGEX_MLINE": "1" enables the regular
expression check to span multiple lines instead of being limited to a single line:
Example 2
{

}

icd_config.json

"SIMV_CMD" : [
"simv_write +ntb_random_seed=123",
"simv_read +ntb_random_seed=200"
],
"ICD_REGEX" : "Bad.*Bad.*stimulus",
"ICD_ICO_FAIL" : "0"
"REGEX_MLINE" : "1"

* The REGEX check is done on the simulation log file for the last stage only.

Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning
Debugging CRT test failures caused by complex randomization constraints is difficult and
time-consuming. It slows verification.
Intelligent Constraint Debugger (ICD) can use the hierarchical structure of randomization
components to reduce debug time. Set the parameter "ICD_HIER" : "1" and parameter
"ICD_PART" : "1".
The following example configuration file shows enabling the Hierarchical Layering and
Sequence Partitioning features:
Figure 364

Enabling Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning

Hierarchical Layering and Sequence Partitioning

In the following example, the highlighted randomization components are failure-inducing:
Figure 365

Failure-Inducing Randomization Components

The hierarchical ICD enables faster localization of the failure-inducing hierarchical
components. That is, class foo (blue arrow) at iter:2, class instance test.sv:10 (yellow
arrow) at iter:3, and randomization serial randomize_3 (red arrow) at iter:4.
* Convergence order is CLASS, INST, SERIAL, and DONE.
* If multiple layers converge at the same iteration, only the highest layer is
shown.

Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR)
In a Constraint Random Verification environment, reproducibility of runs is not guaranteed
even with the same seed. Other variables include command line options, testbench (TB)
changes, DUT changes, and version or patch changes.
The Intelligent Simulation Replayer (ISR) helps replay a simulation in a best-effort manner.
It accounts for design and testbench changes.
Resimulation lets you match generated stimulus values modulo testbench changes. This
feature helps reproduce rare observations, such as failures in a modified testbench.
The following sections describe ISR in detail:
* Simv Runtime Option
* Example
* Error/Warning/Note Messages
* Recommended Use Model

The following is the use model of ISR support for Non-ICO and ICO enabled runs:
Compilation
% vcs [compile-time options]

This feature does not require any change in the compilation.
Simulation
Enables ISR in the record mode.
% simv [vcs_runtime_options] [ico_runtime_options]
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=1 +ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record> -lca

Intelligent Simulation Replay

text:
You can recompile due to design/testbench change.
Simulation: Enables ISR in replay mode
% simv [vcs_runtime_options] [ico_runtime_options]
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=<2|3|4>
+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record> -lca

* The following are the requirements of ISR support for ICO-enabled and non
ICO-enabled runs:
You must specify same VCS and patch version
You must specify same runtime options
* You can make a broad range of TB changes, classified as 'Changed
Severity' as follows:
Table 29

Testbench Changes

Severity

Trivial

Change in the name, class name, line, class
rearrangement, and adding comments.

Easy

Reorder variable/constraints and reorder new().

Medium

Add, remove, or modify class, variable, constraint
(+with), and reorder randomization.

Hard

Add or remove randomization, change repeat count of
randomization, and add new randomize() of an existing
object.

Complex

Combination of Trivial, Easy, Medium, and Hard.

License Requirements for ISR
ISR requires VCS APEX and VT_VCS_VERDI_ISR license keys.

Simv Runtime Option
The following is the syntax of ISR support for non-ICO and ICO enabled runs:
%simv <vcs_runtime_options> <ico_runtime_options>
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=<0|1|2|3|4>
+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record> -lca

+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=<0|1|2|3|4>

Table 30

Enabling ISR

Value

Default

Enables the ISR save feature.

Enables the ISR restore feature.

Enables the ISR restore feature with save.

Enables the ISR restore feature using cache to speed up the
subsequent replays.

+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=<isr_record>

Specifies the ISR record where the simulation run information is stored and restored from.
It consists of the following files:
Table 31

ISR Record Files

Value

saved.rdb

Saves the simulation information (binary file) with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=1.

restored.rdb

Saves the simulation information after
restoring from saved.rdb (binary file) with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=3. This file is required
with +ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=4.

report.txt

Reports the confidence score of matching values with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=2|3.

replayed.map

Maps the serial numbers of replayed to original with
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=3.

text:
* By default, +ntb_solver_bias_replay=1 is enabled automatically when
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=2|3|4. However, you can change it to
+ntb_solver_bias_replay=2, but not to +ntb_solver_bias_replay=0.
* The <isr_record>/saved.rdb file is generated with mode_isr=1,
and <isr_record>/restored.rdb is generated with mode_isr=3.
Both saved.rdb and restored.rdb files are required for
+ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=4.
* The scope, focus, soft ignore, and sbin files should be passed in replay
modes without any change. The replayer automatically maps these old
variables specified in the file to the new variables internally.
* The *.rdb files are not backward compatible across internal versions. You
may have same internal versions across various VCS streams. If the internal
version is different between different VCS streams used to save and restore,
VCS issues the ISR-RRF (incompatible versions) error message. However,
if the internal version is same between different VCS streams used to save
and restore, the ISR-RVM (version mismatch) warning message is issued.

+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=isr_record -l simv.log -lca

% simv2 +ntb_solver_bias_mode_isr=4
+ntb_solver_bias_isr_record=isr_record -l simv_isr_cache.log -lca

SystemC Debug
The following section describe the SystemC Debug LCA feature supported by Verdi as
part of this release:
* Simulator Support for OSCI

Simulator Support for OSCI
SystemC Debug supports post-processing features such as viewing the SC Design
Hierarchy, Extended SC Dumping, and so on. Only the post-processing flow (FSDB and
RIDB) is supported and interactive debug features are not supported in this release. All the
feature support that is available for IUS, VCS, and ModelSim is also available for OSCI:
* Full FSDB Dumping: SC ports, signals, plain vars (Source code must be compiled
with debug info (gcc -g)), sc_fifo

OSCI support for the following are not supported: Other SystemC versions from
OSCI for example, 2.2.0, 2.3.0 User-modified SystemC versions Interactive
debug with SystemC.

Configuring the Simulator
Ensure that a working installation of Verdi is available and execute the following
commands:
Set the following environment variables:
% setenv VERDI_HOME <path to Verdi Installation>

It is necessary to set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH such that libfsdb_osci.so can be found:
% setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/OSCI/$PLATFORM

Activating the FSDB Dumper
You need to add a single statement to the SystemC source code which activates the Verdi
dumper and defines how much to dump. The statement must be called after the SystemC
elaboration is complete. For example, within sc_main after an sc_start(0) call.
#include <fsdb_osci.h>

int sc_main(int,char*[])
{

sc_start(SC_ZERO_TIME);
ridbDump("default.ridb");

Simulator Support for OSCI

}

fsdbDumpvars(0, NULL);
sc_start();

The fsdbDumpvars and related functions are declared in the C++ header file fsdb_osci.h
that is shipped in the Verdi image at $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/OSCI/$PLATFORM

DUT IP-XACT
The DUT IP-XACT file defines an IP-XACT component definition. The IP-XACT
specification defines an IPXACT component as follows:
An IP-XACT component is used to describe the meta-data associated with any IP that can
be instantiated in a design.
For determining the overall structure of the testbench, the DUT IP-XACT defines a
collection of bus interfaces to which other blocks can be connected. In the case of VC
AutoTestbench, these DUT bus interfaces are connected to one or more VIPs.

IP-XACT Overview

The DUT IP-XACT component describes all the bus interfaces that can be connected to
VIP instances. For the tool to enable connections between the DUT and one or more VIPs,
the bus interfaces that are referenced by the DUT IP-XACT must be standard protocol bus
interfaces that are known to be compatible with the VIPs that are available to the user.
Further, VLNV for each of the DUT-specified bus interfaces must exactly match VLNV of
at least one VIP to make a legal connection between the DUT and a VIP. The IP-XACT
standard specifies this strict matching requirement.
You must generate the DUT IP-XACT while generating the RTL/Verilog files for the DUT.
If you are using ARM tools, or Synopsys Core tools or Arteris tools and so on to generate
the RTL, you must also generate the IP-XACT file for that DUT from the tool.

VIP IP-XACT
The VIP IP-XACT files describe VIPs with bus interfaces. The following are the two types
of Port-Level VIP IP-XACT definitions:
* Port-level IP-XACT descriptions correspond to single port VIPs. Examples include AHB
master, AXI slave, and CSI2.
* System-level IP-XACT descriptions correspond to system VIPs. Examples include AHB
system and AMBA system. These VIPs consist of port-level VIPs and other systemlevel VIPs.
System-level VIPs can include port-level VIPs and other system-level VIPs. The systemlevel IP-XACT descriptions reference the port-level IP-XACT descriptions. They also
reference other system-level IP-XACT descriptions.
Port-level and system-level VIPs are building blocks for system-level VIPs. Likewise, portlevel and system-level IP-XACT descriptions are building blocks for other system-level IPXACT descriptions.
To summarize, port-level VIP IP-XACT definitions describe stand-alone VIPs or VIP
building blocks. These blocks specify bus interfaces that can connect to DUT bus
interfaces. They can also connect to other testbench components in theory. The section on
Port-Level VIP IP-XACT definitions describes how this connection is determined.
You must set the DESIGNWARE_HOME variable to the VIP installation to get the VIP IP-XACT
files.

Support for DUT Parameters
VC AutoTestbench enables you to perform the following actions:

wrapper for the DUT top component in a parameterized module.

values for the IP-XACT flow.
The Parameters section in the DUT Connections tab displays all parameters of an
instance. The parameter value is displayed in the Connection column of the DUT
Connections tab. You can double-click the Connection column to change the value of the
selected parameter.

Creating a Bus Interface for a Project
To create a bus interface for a project, perform the following steps:
1. In the DUT Connections tab, select an instance (a top module or a lower-level
instance). Click the Create Bus right-click option. The Create Bus form opens as
shown in the following figure:
Figure 373

Create Bus Form

2. In the Create Bus form, perform the following steps:
a. In the Name field, enter the name of the bus.
b. In the Mode field, enter the mode of the bus whose value can be Master, Slave,
MirroredMaster, or MirroredSlave.
c. In the Definition field, specify the VLNV information of the bus definition. Select its
value from the available VLNV information loaded from protocol IP-XACT files.
d. If there are multiple bus abstractions available for the specified bus definition, the
Abstraction field is enabled to specify the required abstraction, if not, it is disabled.
e. The Dut Port Signals field displays all port signals of the selected instance.
f. The Bus Signals field displays a signal list of the selected bus. For the selected
bus, the logical signals of the bus are listed in the table view. For each of the logical
signals, you must assign a physical signal. When you click a bus logical signal, the

DUT Port Signals list is ordered by the possibility of matching; the most possible
matched DUT port signal is highlighted.
g. Select Auto Connect to automatically connect all logical signals to the most
possible matches from DUT port signals.
h. Select Connect to connect the selected bus signal to the selected DUT port signal.
i. Select Disconnect to disconnect a connected bus signal.
j. Select Reset to clear all connections.
k. After all connections are assigned, click OK button to create the bus.

* Mask
At Initiator, Target: The Mask information is usually Range -1 from the IP-XACT
perspective. The Mask is more useful when you add a new row and want to specify
interleaving between two slave devices. Each Mask bit represents one addressable
bit (A0, A1, A2 An).
A Master CPU0 can access 1GB DDR0 and 1GB DDR1 interleaved at 4K starting
at address 0x0. This would need addressable space of 2GB in total at CPU0. This
would need Interleaved 4K up to 1GB for DDR0 and DDR1

configured link for unused rows cannot be used by memory map rows read from the IPXACT file.

This section describes the steps to use VC AutoTesbench for automatic testbench
generation. Make sure to refer to the Prerequisites section before performing the following
1. Invoke Verdi. Click the Tools -> VC AutoTestbench menu command in the Verdi GUI
to invoke VC AutoTestbench as illustrated in the following figure:

2. In the VC AutoTestbench window, click the File -> New Project menu command.
3. In the Create Project form,
Enter a name in the Project Name field.
You can utilize the Knowledge Database (KDB) library of the DUT to
create a project by selecting the from KDB checkbox. For details on
creating a DUT KDB library project, see Support for the KDB Flow.
Load the DUT IP-XACT file of your design by clicking the Browser button for DUT
IP-XACT field. For details on how to load internal DUT IP-XACT instances, see the
Internal DUT Instance section.
Load the catalog file by clicking the Browser button for the Catalog File field.
Load the Protocol IP-XACT directories by clicking the Add button for Protocol IPXACT field. The pre-added files in DESIGNWARE_HOME are used by default.
Enter the DESIGNWARE HOME path in the DESIGNWARE_HOME field. If the
DESIGNWARE_HOME environment variable is set, the value is used by default.

Enter the Design Directory path in the VCATB_DESIGN_DIR field. If the
VCATB_DESIGN_DIR environment variable is set, the value is used by default. If this
field is not set, you cannot perform configuration validation.
Enter the name of the output directory in the Output Directory field where you want
the tool to generate the testbench.
To specify your own testbench top, select the Testbench Top check-box. You can
specify your module name, DUT path and Instance name in the Module, DUT Path,
and Instance fields.
If the Testbench Top field is enabled, then the DUT top name in both DUT
Connections and IP-XACT tabs is changed to the DUT path name.

Support to Read the VCATB VIP Related Files
The environment variable VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE is supported to read the VCATB
VIP related files. The following command is used:
setenv VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE <Directory Path>

Only one path is allowed in the new environment variable. Therefore, it assumes the
environment variable value as one directory path.
/dir1/dir2/dir3//verdi_vcatb_vip_files

Multiple paths for VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE are not supported. In such cases, the tool
logs an error message in the vcatb.log file. The following command is used:
setenv VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE <path1>:<path2>:<path3>

The following types of error messages are logged into vcatb.log file based on the issue
while reading the path:
Examples of error messages:
Error. `VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE' referred path <{<Value>} is not valid. Multiple
paths are not allowed.
Error. `VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE' referred path <{<Value>} is not found
Error. `VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE' referred path <{<Value>} is not a valid directory
path. It's a file path
Error. `VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE' referred path <{<Value>} does not have read
permissions. Hence cannot read VCATB related files

Folder Structure
Structure of the VCATB VIP files in VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE locations as shown below:
$VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE/$vip_name/$version
$VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE/$vip_name/latest ./ $version

<path1>/amba_svt/R-2020.12/ipxact
<path1>/amba_svt/R-2020.12/vcatb

Multiple VCATB VIP related files can also be added into the VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE
location as shown in the following examples:
<path1>/lpddr_svt
<path1>/spi_svt
<path1>/amba_svt

You can override custom/third-party `VIP' details also using VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE
variable.
Referring Using the Latest Version
Tool updates the VIP details including version number in the Tcl variables. Therefore,
you should use the right version for VIP referred in VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE location.
Following are the examples:
vcatb_vip_suites.0.is_fixed = 0
vcatb_vip_suites.0.name = amba_svt
vcatb_vip_suites.0.version = R-2020.12

Tool always considers the `latest' version referred in VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE location
while updating the vcatb_vip_suites Tcl variables. Therefore, it is recommended to use
the right VIP version.
If VIP `latest' version in VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE location is different from
DESIGNWARE_HOME, then you should unset the VCATB_VIP_PATH_OVERRIDE location.

Creating a Bus Interface for a Project
To create a bus interface for a project, perform the following steps:
1. In the DUT Connections tab, select an instance (a top module or a lower-level
instance), and click the Create Bus right-click option. The Create Bus form opens as
illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 401

Create Bus Form

2. In the Create Bus form,
a. In the Name field, enter the name of the bus.
b. In the Mode field, enter the mode of the bus whose value could be Master, Slave,
MirroredMaster, or MirroredSlave.
c. In the Definition field, specify the VLNV information of the bus definition. Select its
value from the available VLNV information loaded from protocol IP-XACT files.
d. If there are multiple bus abstractions available for the specified bus definition, the
Abstraction field is enabled to specify the required abstraction, otherwise it is
disabled.
e. The Dut Port Signals field displays all port signals of the selected instance.

f. The Bus Signals field displays a signal list of the selected bus. For the selected
bus, the logical signals of the bus are listed in the table view. For each of the logical
signals, you must assign a physical signal.
When you click a bus logical signal, the DUT Port Signals list is ordered by the
possibility of matching; the most possible matched DUT port signal is highlighted.
The following rules are used to calculate the possibility of matching and locate the
most possible physical signals for the selected bus logical signal:
If the direction of the physical signal matches the direction of the logical signal
If the width of the physical signal is the same as the width of the logical signal
If the physical signal name includes the bus name or includes a substring that is
similar to the bus name
If the physical name includes the logical name or includes a substring that is
similar to the logical name
g. In some cases where the DUT port signals names are not related to the bus and the
logical signal name, the rules may not work as expected.
h. Use the Auto Connect button to automatically connect all logical signals to the
most possible matches from DUT port signals.
i. Use the Connect button to connect the selected bus signal to the selected DUT
port signal.
j. Use the Disconnect button to disconnect a connected bus signal.
k. Use the Reset button to clear all connections.
l. After all connections are assigned, click the OK button to create the bus.
After you create a bus, the created bus is listed directly under the instance, as
illustrated in the following figure:

If any of the port signals are used by the created bus, then these signals are removed from
the AdHoc Signals section. If any port signals are used by multiple created buses, then
these signals are listed in the Share Signal section.
After a bus is created for the selected instance,
* The same bus is applied to all other instances from the same module, if all the signals
of the bus are available and have the same definition (type, width, direction, and so
on) for a parameterized module; the parameter value may affect the signature of the
module, for example the existence, the width or the direction of some signals.
* The same bus is created for the outer instance, if the bus is exported to the outer
instance. For example, if a bus is created for the top.cpu0 instance and all signals of
the bus are connected to the port signals of top, then the same bus is created for the
top instance.
After all buses are created for the imported DUT, use the Save IP-XACT right-click option
to save an IP-XACT file for the entire DUT system, including the created bus interfaces.
Next time, when you work on the same DUT, you can use the saved IP-XACT instead of

Support for PHY Integration
Point-to-point controller IP requires the use of a PHY to drive the physical signaling. The
controller IP provides a parallel bus interface, which is connected to the PHY simulation
model. The PHY model is typically provided separately from the IP model, and you must
connect the IP controller to the PHY model.
The VC AutoTestbench flow identifies situations where a PHY is required and generates
a testbench with a PHY Shell module that is connected to the DUT and to the VIP. To
complete the testbench integration, you must replace the PHY shell module with a module
that wraps your PHY simulation model.

Prerequisite
PHY integration requires a protocol IP-XACT description for both bus interfaces. You
need one for the parallel PHY bus interface and one for the serial PHY bus interface. If a
standard protocol IP-XACT is not available, develop it and ship it with the appropriate VIP.
If DUT IP-XACT does not support the required protocol IP-XACT, then an adjunct file
must be developed that exposes these bus interfaces and allows them to be connected to
testbench elements.

Serial Interface From DUT Side
If DUT IP-XACT exposes a serial PHY bus interface, this implies that a PHY model
is integrated into the DUT and is connected to the IP Controller. In this situation, the
testbench element is connected directly to the exposed PHY serial bus interface in the
DUT.

Parallel Interface From DUT Side
If DUT IP-XACT exposes a parallel PHY bus interface, this implies that a p

Support for PHY Integration

In GUI mode, you can select whether you want to directly connect to the VIP provided
parallel PHY interface or use the PHY Shell module at the VIP selection step. If the
PHY shell module is selected, then VC AutoTestbench shows this in the testbench
hierarchy. The PHY shell module is presented like any other testbench element. It allows
for signal connection overrides in both the GUI and the config.ini file. After the testbench is
generated, you must replace the PHY Shell module with your simulation model.
Connecting to VIP
For a DUT PHY bus, you need to select not only the VIP to connect, but also how to
connect to the VIP. You can use PHY shell connection (serial) or direct connection
(parallel). For the PHY shell connection, you need to select which serial interface must be
used.
The Add New VIP right-click option lists all combinations of the possible selections. For
example, for the PCIE bus, the matched VIP is svt_pcie_device_agent. It supports both
parallel and serial connections. For serial connection, two different versions of serial
interfaces are available. Therefore, there are total of 3 different kinds of connections
supported. For each of them, the connection type and VLNV are displayed in the menu
title.

If you choose to connect a PHY bus through serial connection, the tool generates a PHY
shell module that is connected to the DUT and to the VIP. The PHY module is listed in the
TB Connections tab as a new section - PHY Module. For each module instance, all the
port signals are listed.

User Extensions
User extensions allow you to develop and maintain your own extended codes. You can
modify the testbench and can keep the modified files under the user created user_env
and user_tests directories. By default, the extensions use the term 'user' in their file
names, variable names, object names, and so on.
The following sub-sections explain the available extensions.

Name and Location Alternatives
* Naming
You can optionally specify a prefix value to be used for file names, variable
names, object names, code elements and so on. This can be done either in the
GUI or in the [USER EXTENSIONS] section of config.ini. The specified prefix
replaces the default prefix - user in all the code references. However, this does not
apply to the "Makefile Only" controls, such as, USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR and
USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR. For example, if you specify proj1 as the prefix,
then every user in the name is proj1 instead, such as, proj1_vcatb_base_test.sv,
proj1_vcatb_env.sv, and so on.
If no prefix is specified, the default prefix - "user" is used.

Support for Additional Tests
To provide additional tests using the user extension flow, the additional tests must
be placed in the $USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR directory. You must also create a
user_test_package.sv file located in the $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR directory. This
file should be modeled after the vcatb_test.pkg file and contain include directives for
all the additional tests. The actual file names (such as, ts.my_test.sv) can be used here,
without any directory prefix, as the $USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR directory is added as
an incdir by the Makefile.
The generated Makefile provides additional support for this capability by including
$USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR in the list of directories it searches to identify valid test
names.
The generated testbench includes these additional tests by including
$USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/user_test_package.sv in vcatb_test.pkg
automatically, if available. This automatically includes all of the test files included in the
user_test_package.sv file.
User tests must also adhere to the basic testcase design criteria so that they work properly
in this flow:
* Test classes must extend from vcatb_base_test
* Test files must follow 'ts.*.sv' test file naming convention

Examples of correctly specified testcases can be found in the list of generated test files
located in the tests_dir directory.

Support for Additional Files
In addition to the user test management and user test files , you might have other files
which they need to include into the system. These files are included automatically if they
are specified in a file list stored as $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/user_file_list.f.
This file list can include VLOG or SV files, packages or programs, other file lists (file lists
prefaced with the -f option), and so on. The only requirement is that the paths which are
specified in the file list are hard paths. For example, if additional files are stored locally
in $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR, you need the $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/ prefix. If
stored elsewhere on the network, you must specify the files with a relative path or a hard
path.

Extending Build Management
As indicated in the previous sections, there are some build extensions which are built
into the Makefile. In addition, you can also add your own Makefile extension. Create
$USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/Makefile containing any additional settings you want
to add. The $USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR/Makefile file is included by the top level
Makefile after all of its variables are specified and before any rules are defined.
This can be used to modify any of the top level Makefile variables that are referenced in
the subsequent rules.

Initial User Extension Development
It is recommended to use the GUI or the config.ini process to enable your extensions.
Create user environment and/or test directories, set the appropriate prefix, env_dir, and
tests_dir values in GUI or config.ini, and generate the testbench with this information.
The benefit of following this process is that every regeneration includes all the user
extensions added previously.
During the initial user extension development, however, it might be necessary to forego
some of these steps. For example, you might want to take an existing testbench area,
incorporate some extensions, get them working, and then go back and make them official.
Set env_dir and test values in the original testbench description. You can accomplish
this by modifying the Makefile.cfg file in the generated testbench. You can specify
USER_EXTENSIONS_ENV_DIR and/or USER_EXTENSIONS_TESTS_DIR values. Specifying
either of these values results in enabling the user extensions features and incorporating
the user extensions in the testbench.

User Extensions Flow

tests_dir settings. It is not supported for the prefix setting. Implementing this support
manually, that is, by modifying Makefile.cfg, also implies that these changes are not
picked up on subsequent testbench generation. That is, env_dir and tests_dir settings

Support for Execution Manager Integration
The generated testbench that the VCATB application creates includes a basic
configuration file at <output>/eman/eman/vcatb_eman.emc, which can be used with
Execution Manager. This provides basic rules for compiling the generated testbench and
running tests. The generated configuration file can be included by another user-created
configuration file, and the build rules and test execution rules can be reused.

To simplify batch-mode operation, a basic "wrapper" is created to encapsulate the required
Verdi VC AutoTestbench capabilities into an easy-to-use batch mode tool.
Use the following command to invoke the wrapper:
vcatb -dut_ipxact/-d <dut_ipxact_file_to_be_processed>
-config/-c <ini_files_to_be_processed>
-protocol_ipxact_dir/-p
<protocol_ipxact_file_directories_to_be_processed>
-output_dir/-o <output_directory>

The following are the user-specified parameters for the wrapper:
* The -dut_ipxact or the -d option specifies the location of the DUT IP-XACT file to be
processed.
If the specified DUT IP-XACT (XML) file does not exist or cannot be read by the tool,
the tool issues an error.
* The -config or the -c option specifies the user input files to be processed.
Multiple user input files can be specified, separated by a space. If any of the specified
input files do not exist or cannot be read by the tool, the tool issues an error.
* The -protocol_ipxact_dir or the -p option specifies one or more directories where
Protocol IP-XACT files can be found.
Multiple directories can be specified, separated by a space.
* The -output_dir or the -o option specifies the directory to which output files and
directories should be written.
If the specified directory does not exist, the tool creates the directory. If the specified
directory already exists, the tool overwrites the files in that directory.
In addition to the DUT IP-XACT file, the templates require access to other IP-XACT
files that specify information about the various VIPs that are involved in the testbench
generation process. A template file can include Tcl code to open and read a VIP IPXACT (XML) file (that is located in the $DESIGNWARE_HOME directory structure).
Since the DUT IP-XACT file is specified on the command line, that file is automatically
read by the tool (as an XML file).

* VIP Topology
The VIP topology generated automatically by the tool can be overridden by entering

; VIP topology overrides
[VIP_DUT_MAPPING]
PATH = amba_system_env_0.axi_system[0].master[0]
GROUP = M0,M0_AXI_VN,M0_VN0,M0_VN1,M0_VN2,M0_VN3

* VIP Configuration
Configuration values for a VIP can be set by specifying a hierarchical configuration
name and a value. When the VC AutoTestbench tool is first run, a temporary INI file is
generated. In this file, the [VIP_CONFIGURATION] section is populated with a list of every
configurable VIP component. The path to these VIP components must be constructed from
the following vendor extensions in the VIP IP-XACT:
component.busInterfaces.busInterface.vendorExtensions.configurationGeneratedName

In addition, the temporary INI file also includes the VIP properties which are set by the
tool, or the list of minimum required VIP configuration properties if that is returned instead.
For example, the following shows the content present in this temporary INI file. Note that
all of the lines are written as comments, which can later be uncommented and completed
by the users:
; Set VIP configuration values

* Compile Directives

as-is on the compile command. This section is not name/value pairs like the other
sections. No checking is performed on these values.

as-is on the elaboration command. This section is not name/value pairs like the other
sections. Checking is not performed on these values.

* Ad Hoc Signal Declaration
There may be a need to declare ad hoc signals in the DUT wrapper. The following INI
section can be used to declare a single signal.
[SIGNALS]
name = ad_hoc_signal0
type = bit
value = 1'b0

The name and type entries are required. The value entry is optional, if it is not provided
then the signal is declared and not initialized to any value. For example, the entry
above results in the following signal declaration in the dut_wrapper:
bit ad_hoc_signal0 = 1'b0;

The following is the entry:
[SIGNALS]
name = ad_hoc_signal1
type = logic [3:0]

This results in the following signal being declared:
logic [3:0] ad_hoc_signal1;

* VIP Signal Connection Override
The tool attempts to automatically connect VIP signals to DUT signals. There may be
some situations where you want to override the automated connections. The following
INI section can be used to achieve overrides for VIP signal connections:
[VIP_SIGNAL_CONNECTION_OVERRIDE]
name = ahb_if_0.slave_if[0].hsel
value = ad_hoc_signal0

The value provided to the 'name' entry should be the hierarchical path to the VIP
interface signal to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the VIP
interface instance. Since the instance name of this interface is not known when the tool
is first invoked, these connections likely need to be declared in the INI file used by a
second invocation of the tool.
The value provided to the 'value' entry could be an ad hoc signal that was previously
declared, or it could be a constant value. The tool uses the value that is provided as a
string.
* DUT Signal Connection Override
The tool attempts to automatically connect VIP signals to DUT signals. There may be
some situations where you want to override the automated connections. The following
INI section can be used to achieve overrides of DUT signal connections:
[DUT_SIGNAL_CONNECTION_OVERRIDE]

ew. This INI section provides a method to change
the root and the view of the file set.
[SET_FILESET]
instance = top_inst
view = RTL
root = ./src

* User Extensions
User extensions allow you to add additional capabilities to the generated testbench.
This INI section provides a method to describe the prefix used and the location of these
extensions.
[USER_EXTENSIONS]
prefix = project_prefix
env_dir = /remote/project/tb_env_ext
tests_dir = /remote/project/tb_test_ext

* PHY_CONNECTION
If the DUT exposes the parallel interface of a PHY, then the DUT Connection section
allows you to select whether the generated testbench should include a PHY Shell
Module or if the testbench should instead connect the VIP directly to the parallel
interface (if the VIP supports this). The busdefs are identified using the VLNV, and if
any of the settings are not specified, then it is treated as a wildcard situation for that
setting.
To set up for a specific bus type identified by VLNV:
[PHY_CONNECTION]
parallel_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
parallel_busdef_library = busdef.phy
parallel_busdef_name = pipeV4
parallel_busdef_version = 4.1
serial_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
serial_busdef_library = busdef.phy
serial_busdef_name = pcie-txrx-phy
serial_busdef_version = 2.0
direct_connect = [0|1]

To set up for a specific bus instance:
[PHY_CONNECTION]
dut_bus_name = ddr4_dfi_if_inst.DWC_ddr_umctl2_dfi

serial_busdef_vendor = synopsys.com
serial_busdef_library = busdef.phy
serial_busdef_name = pcie-txrx-phy
serial_busdef_version = 2.0
direct_connect = [0|1]

* COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS
You can select the control options in this section. Each section instance defines
settings that are to be applied to an individual component or component view. To
differentiate controls associated with different component versions, the component is
represented by its VLNV value. If any of the VLNV settings is not specified, then it is
treated as a wildcard situation for that setting. If the view value is not specified, then the
settings are applied to all of the component's views.
[COMPONENT_CONTROL_OPTIONS]
vendor = arm.com
library = Cores
name = CORTEX15
version = r4p1_0
view = verilog
use_file_list = [0|1]
use_y = [0|1]
add_file_based_incdir = [0|1]
add_includes_to_file_list = [0|1]
add_synopsys_sim_ver = [0|1]
add_v2k = [0|1]
add_vhdl87 = [0|1]

* DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE
VC AutoTestbench attempts to populate DUT parameters with the default value from
DUT IP-XACT file. However, the default value in the DUT IP-XACT file may not match
the actual value in the DUT file.
The following INI section can be used to specify overrides for the DUT parameter
value:
[DUT_PARAMETER_OVERRIDE]
name = cci400_inst.AWUSER_WIDTH
value = 2

The value provided to the name entry should be the hierarchical path to the DUT
parameter to be assigned. The hierarchical path should begin with the DUT instance.
Since the instance name of this instance is not known when the tool is first invoked,
these connections likely need

_list = [0|1]
add_synopsys_sim_ver = [0|1]
add_v2k = [0|1]
add_vhdl87 = [0|1]

You can specify additional -y, +incdir, general options, and files for use with a specific
component or component view in the [COMPONENT_COMPILE_DIRECTIVES] section. Each
value is applied to the per view file lists that are generated. If view value is not specified,
the settings are applied to all component views. No checking is performed on these
values.
[COMPONENT_COMPILE_DIRECTIVES]
vendor = arm.com
library = Cores
name = CORTEX15
version = r4p1_0
component = CORTEX15
view = verilog
-sverilog
-y /remote/vip/apps/arm_ip/cci500/cci_500_large_cfg/verilog
+incdir+/remote/vip/apps/arm_ip/cci500/cci_500_large_cfg/verilog
/remote/vip/apps/arm_ip/cci500/cci_500_large_cfg/verilog/cci500_large.v

Overriding the Testbench Top (Batch Mode)
If you want to use your own DUT wrapper instead of using the one generated by the tool,
you need to specify the module name of the provided wrapper and the full path of the DUT
inside the wrapper module.
You can specify your own module and the DUT path in the [TESTBENCH_TOP] section in
the config.ini file as follows:
[TESTBENCH_TOP]
module = testbench_top
dut_path = user_dut_inst

The following sections describe the LCA features supported by VC Apps as part of this
release:
* Support for Verdi Machine Learning Library

Support for Verdi Machine Learning Library
Starting with this release, Verdi provides you an unified platform to collect data from EDA
tools and allows you to access data for machine learning applications. This platform
includes three abstract layers, such as table, model, and application.Each layer can read
and write from the database of APIs.
In the table layer, the tables are constructed using both C++ and Python. In this layer, you
can construct your own tables and extract specific data by any utility. You can also read
these tables using Python.
In the model layer, pre-defined types and properties can be selected to extract data from
the database by different utilities. These tables can be read using Python as well where
pre-defined relations between types are resolved. Currently, only 'waveform' model is
In the application layer, both the data collection and access methods are provided in the
'Database' class of the 'verdilearn' package in Python. You can take the tables as an input
to their machine learning applications.
These tables provide information about the C++ and Python APIs.

Required Data
For the block stimuli replay flow, a few additional files and settings must be prepared and
specified. After running the simulation, some additional files are generated. The complete
configuration is described below.
The following files must be prepared, if needed, depending on whether you use the twostep or three-step flow in VCS:
* The FSDB file dumping form block-level testbench (BL-TB) simulation, for example,
block.fsdb

* The run file of SoC testbench (SoC-TB) simulation (for VCS two-step flow), for
example, run_soc.f
* The configurations for replay simulation, for example, wi_config
* The simulation compile script, for example, wi_compile.rc
* The simulation run script, for example, wi_run.rc
* The VCS configuration (for VCS three-step flow), for example, synopsys_sim.setup
The following mapping files need to be manually prepared, or they are automatically
created by specific configurations:
* The mapping of input stimuli to apply to the Replay Simulation, for example,
stimuli.map

* The mapping of signals to apply waveform comparison, for example, compare.map

WISIM Replay Block Stimuli on SoC

The following resultant output files are generated.
* The FSDB file by Replay simulation on the SoC after applying the block stimuli, for
example, wi_result.fsdb
* The comparison error report between BL-TB and SoC-TB simulations, for example,
wi_cmp_error.nce

* The comparison summary between BL-TB and SoC-TB simulations in wi_flow.log
To use WISIM to replay block stimuli on SoC, perform the following steps:
* Preparation (for VCS three-step flow):
Analyze the SoC design using vlogan and vhdlan for SystemVerilog and VHDL design,
respectively, and prepare the corresponding script for the analyzed library. Prepare the
configuration file and the corresponding scripts.
* Extract:
Generate WISIM testbench using the -replay_extract option. With Auto_Map and
Auto_Compare_Map, the automatic mapping files are generated in this phase. When
the mapping files or configuration are modified, you can add the -remap option after
-replay_extract to run the remap flow. You can skip generating the design by setting
the environment variable WISIM_SKIP_CG to 1, if you use VCS three-step flow. Then,
load designs from library (analyzed with -kdb=common_elab) with -lib options with
-replay_extract.
* Compile:
Compile the SoC design and WISIM testbench, using the -replay_compile option.
If you compile in the SoC environment, add wi_test.sv during compilation (two-step
flow) or analyze wi_test.sv into witbLib and add WI_TB_TOP (three-step flow) during
elaboration in compile script.
* Simulate:
Run simulation for the SoC design by applying FSDB stimuli under WISIM
testbench, using the -replay_sim option. With Compare_Map or Auto_Compare_Map,
wi_result.fsdb is automatically compared with the block-level one. It is able to
re-compare the same FSDB files with different options (Compare_Option) or signal
mapping (Compare_Map and Auto_Compare_Map) by adding the -recompare option
after -replay_sim.

Configuration File Format
The Configuration file is divided into two parts. They are as follows:
* Common
* Record
The Common part has the following mandatory fields:
* MODE
* SIMV_DAIDIR
* CHECKER_SIM_FILELIST

Assertion Replay for Emulation/FPGA Prototyping

* CHECKERSIM_TOP_MODULE
In the Configuration file, the Common part must always be placed on the
top.
The Record part has the following mandatory field:
* WAVEFORM
Each Record part must be enclosed with parenthesis ({}).
Following is an example of a configuration file. The Mandatory fields and the parenthesis
in the Record part is in bold.
####################################################################
# Common fields
# The fields here will give impact on all FSDB files
####################################################################
//MODE. The same if you specify 1. ex: MODE = 1 [MUST HAVE]
MODE= CHECKER_SIM_WAVEFORM_REPLAY
//abs path. [MUST HAVE]
SIMV_DAIDIR = $PWD/simv.daidir
//optional. Necessary runtime options for running original simulation.
SIMV_OPT =
//optional. Necessary runtime options for running new simulation run.
CHECKER_SIM_OPT =
//optional. Necessary options for compiling new simulation binary.
CHECKER_SIM_COMPILE_OPT = -sverilog -timescale=1ns/1ns
//abs path. [MUST HAVE]
CHECKER_SIM_FILELIST = assert.v
//optional. If this was specified, skeleton is not extracted. The
file(s) here are used as skeleton.
CHECKER_SIM_DESIGN_FILELIST=
//top module names [MUST HAVE]
CHECKER_SIM_TOP_MODULE = top
//optional. Do waveform dumping. Use semicolon to separate tasks
#WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK = fsdbDumpvars +all
+fsdbfile+assertion_result.fsdb ; fsdbDumpSVA
WAVEFORM_DUMPING_TASK =
#####################################################################
# Record fields (Wave dedicated fields)
# The files here will give impact to the WAVE file here only
#####################################################################
############## record 1 ##############
{
//golden file abs path. [MUST HAVE]
WAVEFORM = $PWD/src.fsdb
//optional. Assertion module ports are extracted automatically as the
MAP file to do the replay

Assertion Replay for Emulation/FPGA Prototyping

MAP=
//optional. Specify a file to do the force replay
FORCE_MAP=
//optional. Give a global delay time: impacts all replayed signal in
current record.
DELAY=
DELAY_MAP=
DELAY_EXCLUDE_MAP=
AUTO_MAP=
SCOPE_MAP=
COMPARE_MAP=
AUTO_COMPARE_MAP=
COMPARE_OPT=
REPLAY_TIME_DURATION=
//optional. You can give [+force|+deposit|+force +deposit] Default:
+force
MAP_REPLAY_TYPE=
BLACKBOX_MAP=
}
############## record 2 ##############
{
}

Traverse Related Message Search Mechanism
PureLog traces 1000 blocks upward or downward from the starting block that you rightclick. A block is a group of messages with the first line matched by the partitioning rule, for
example, UVM header.
PureLog analyzes the first three lines of each block because:
* The key-value attributes are most likely to sit in the first few lines.
* It can speed up the searching.

The PureLog DB enables you to keep the information of logs through the logCompile
script. Whenever you need to check a log for debugging, you can access it through APIs
or by using the simple UI query system. Some PureLog features also rely on the PureLog
DB. Generally, the PureLog DB can be written by the daily regression script at night and
can be accessed by you or PureLog in daytime.

Benefits of PureLog DB
The PureLog DB has the following benefits:
* Better performance: Most PureLog features can have better performance with the
PureLog DB.
* Less memory consumption: Most PureLog features can have less memory
consumption with the PureLog DB.
* AI technology: AI-related features of PureLog rely on the PureLog database.
* Customized application: You can access the PureLog DB through APIs or by using the
query system UI. Based on APIs and query systems, it is easy to develop a customized
application. It means that you can have your own debugging way.

Setting Up the PureLog DB Server
Before saving or reading logs from the PureLog DB, you need to launch the server.
PureLog provides the msgdbControl utility to start or stop the server.

Starting the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>

After starting the server, you can compile logs by logCompile and debug on DB debug
platform.

Stopping the Server
Run the following command:
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

Remember to stop server:
* When you finish debugging.
* Before you want to clean up the DB storage.

Restarting the Server
You can restart the server under the same DB storage path. The compiled logs are
preserved.
msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>

%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> logCompile <opts> # compile/debug
%> msgdbControl -stop_server -storage_path <database storage path>
%> msgdbControl -start_server -storage_path <database storage path> #
restart server

Compiling Logs Into the PureLog DB
PureLog provides the logCompile utility to compile log information into the PureLog DB.
The utility supports CSV format and customized format.

CSV Format
(-log_type="csv")
logCompile
[-log_type="csv"]
-storage_path="<database_storage_path>"
-project_name="<project_name>"
-log_list="<log.ls>"
-separator=','
[-comment='#']
[-none_regexp='-+']
[-quotechar='"']
[-escapechar="\"]
[-hyper_rule="<hyper_rule_path>"]
[-date ="date"]

In case of CSV format, logCompile removes leading and trailing whitespace for each cell
and skips a blank line.
The CSV file list is specified in -log_list="<log.ls>".In this input file, each line includes
two sections. The left side is the input file path, and the right side is the database file path
to be saved.
Example log.ls file
./trace1.csv user_case/trace1.log
./trace2.csv user_case/trace2.log
./

ify the virtual path to be stored in the database.
Default: simWLogCompileDir/<TARGET_LOG>

<TARGET_LOG> is specified by -l or -incr_log option.

* -num_process <NUM_WORKS>: Number of logCompile worker processes for parallel
compilation.
Default: 1

Types of Simulation
The simWLogCompile wrapper consists of following types of simulation:
One Step Simulation
* %> simWLogCompile vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog

-ntb_opts uvm-1.1 -timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH
+incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD -R +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM
+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Two Step Simulation
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT" -l
simv_verdi_i.log -storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1
-virtual_path "case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls"

Compile with -incr_log option
* %> vcs -debug_access+all -lca -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm-1.1

-timescale=1ns/100ps +incdir+$SVTB_PATH +incdir+$RTL_PATH $DUT_LOAD

* %> simWLogCompile ./simv +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM

+UVM_TESTNAME=test_r8_w8_r4_w4 +ntb_random_seed=1 +UVM_NO_RELNOTES
+FSDB_ON +UVM_TR_RECORD +UVM_LOG_RECORD +fsdbfile+verdi_i.fsdb
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE="UVM_AWARE|RAL|TLM|MSG|HIER|PRINT"
-storage_path ./db_storage -project_name project1 -virtual_path
"case1/sim.log" -attr_rule_list "./rule.ls" -incr_log "./simv.log"

Attributes in the PureLog DB
The attributes can be kept in the PureLog DB as string type or numeral type. You can
impose only numeral query on numeral attributes through APIs or the DB debug platform.
If you expect the attributes to be saved in numeral type, here is the summary of the
supported format:
* Number with decimal point (example, 1.6)
* Verilog integer literal constants (size <= 64)
* 0x (example, 0x1200)

A message within a log is supposed to follow certain rules. For example, users expect
that the message "B" shows up after message "A". This kind of a rule is like a message
protocol. In the simulation log, the message protocol can reflect the SoC system protocols.
For example, IP protocols, system power up sequence, system power down sequence,
and so on. During debugging, it is a good start to check message protocols first to narrow
down the debug scope. Message protocol debugging can be done using the GUI or batch
mode.

Each message protocol may include one or more message events. In the following
case, we try to build the <DMA_RD> protocol that includes the following two events. The
first event is that RISC enables the DMA controller. The second event is that the DMA
controller returns the good status.

Binding Related Signals to Message Protocol in Batch Mode
For experienced users or users who just want to refine the existing binding signals, for
example, change the hierarchy of each signal, using the GUI is less efficient. In this
case, you can edit the protocol .rc files directly. The file users can import these .rc files
as needed. The PureLog DB users can apply the protocolCompile utility with the
protocol .rc files to save the binding information in the PureLog DB. Then you can export
protocols with the binding signals from the PureLog DB as needed.

Abnormal Analysis
When a log file includes enormous lines and messages, it becomes very difficult to find
the abnormal points. The Abnormal Analysis feature of PureLog sums up the abnormal
points in a log. You only need to feed PureLog with some golden logs that are related to
the current error log.

Launching Abnormal Analysis
To launch Abnormal Analysis, set the following environment variables:
setenv PYTHONPATH
setenv VL_VERSION TD
setenv PYTHONPATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python:$PYTHONPATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
module load cmlp/2021.06-py36

Abnormal Analysis

Using Abnormal Analysis
1. Keep daily record in the database.
For example, if you have case1, case2, and case3 in your daily regression, you can
use PureLog every day to save the record of each testcase in the database through
the PureLog TCL process. The high-level features extracted by partition rules are also
saved in the database for abnormal analysis.
The database used by abnormal analysis is not integrated into the PureLog
database. In other words, abnormal analysis uses its own database that is
different from the PureLog database.
2. Apply abnormal analysis when there is a failure.
For example, there is a failure of case1. You can use PureLog to analyze the abnormal
points as follows:
Open the error log with PureLog.
Launch the abnormal engine, as shown in the following figure.
Figure 523

Launching Abnormal Engine

In the Input Case Name dialog box, specify the DB Path and Case Name.
Figure 524

Input Case Name Dialog Box

Abnormal Analysis

Click OK to apply the changes.

The SmartSheet feature available with PureLog allows you to view data in a spreadsheet
format, analyze it, and link it to the HDL design. You can choose to either open a new
sheet in SmartSheet or import an existing .csv file. Furthermore, in case you use
SmartLog to open the log with partition rules, you can save the partition results into the
CSV format and then open the file in SmartSheet. To save the file in CSV format, use the
File > Save Contents menu option in SmartLog.
SmartSheet offers the following features for viewing the data:
* Sorting the data entries based on number
Sort Smallest to Largest
Sort Largest to Smallest
* Filtering the data entries based on number
* Filtering the data entries based on text
* Finding data by column

Launching SmartSheet
To launch SmartSheet without design information, you can type PureLogDB. In case you
need design information, you can open Verdi with the design as usual and then click the
Tools > SmartSheet menu option in the Verdi GUI.

Toolbar and Menu Options
SmartSheet provides a toolbar with frequently used options to navigate the files, as
illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 529

SmartSheet Toolbar

The SmartSheet window provides the following menu options:
File Menu Options
* Open File
Menu Bar: File -> Open File
This option opens the Open CSV form to help you open an existing .csv file.

* New Sheet
Menu Bar: File -> New Sheet
This option opens a new sheet in the SmartSheet pane.
* Save
Menu Bar: File -> Save
This option saves the currently open sheet.
* Save As
Menu Bar: File -> Save As
This option saves the currently open sheet as a different sheet.
Edit Menu Options
* Copy
Menu Bar: Edit -> Copy
This option copies the selected data/entries.
* Paste
Menu Bar: Edit -> Paste
This option pastes the copied data/entries.
* Undo
Menu Bar: Edit -> Undo
