More Details of Time Check Enable
Some timing violations happen before the reset stage. You can ignore these violations.
In the TimeCheckEnable section, you can set the message after which timing violations for
the selected instance are captured.
If you do not specify a message, all timing violations are captured.

Open or Check Timing Violation Report
To open or check the Timing Violation Report, perform the following steps:
1. Under the Tools menu, click New Timing Violation Report to open the timing violation

2. Click Open database icon in the timing violation window. Follow the guidelines that
appears in the dialog box, to open reports within the database.

3. The summary reports for each component appears and sorted by the count of
violations.

4. Use check or uncheck to record the violations which are checked.

5. Use waive or unwaive violations to record the reason and username for the projectlevel review.

The waived violations are moved to the root node <Waived> in the bottom.

6. Click View Details to see raw messages in the SmartLog.

The action is only available in the node of simulation log.
7. Click the link of SmartLog to access related signals in nWave.

In the common active fan-in path report (refer to Check Common Active
Fan-in for Timing Violation), it helps to display the temporal flow view result.

Save or Load the Waived Result
Save or Load the Waived Result has the following sections:
Save or Load wavied result of current opened report

To save or restore waived results for current opened reports, use the actions listed below:
* Under File menu,
Click Load Timing Violation Waive Status to restore the waived result.
Click Save Timing Violation Waive Status to save the waived result.

Save or Load whole Database.
Use msgdbControl to export the waived result from the database.
msgdbControl export_data -storage_path $storagePath -type timingWaiveFile
-project_name $projName [-date yyyy-mm-dd] -output $outputFile

* -date: Is optional. If not specified, it exports waive file based on the latest date. -date
is in yyyy-mm-dd format.
For example, 2025-09-17.
* -output: Is the option to specify the destination path for the exported file.
Feed the overall waive file into logCompile in the next run.
logCompile timing_violation -waive $waiveFile

Regression Debug Automation (RDA)
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by RDA as a part of this
release:
* Static Bug Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA)
* RDA Integration With Verdi VMS

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects domain crossing and
glitch issues, such as reset domain crossing (RDC) or glitches. Static bug finding is a part
of RTL sign off and saves weeks of efforts in a project cycle.
Debugging violations found by static bug finding can be difficult, especially when RDC
bugs appear in large numbers, such as during MCP verification. RDA offers a Static Bug
Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA) solution that automatically organizes violations into
fewer groups. This solution connects violations to waveform, source code, and simulation
log for further debugging and uses Verdi for analysis.
* Technology Overview
* SBRCA Usage
* Smart Waiver

Technology Overview
SBRCA helps you to debug the static bug findings using Verdi. VCS complies with the
SDC commands containing RDC/Glitch property. After completing simulation with VCSSDC, SBRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and helps in finding out the violations.
SBRCA extracts details of a violation message and displays the information in a binstructured report.
RDA provides Verdi GUI to review SBRCA reports generated after analyzing violations
from the log file. Use the Verdi GUI to continue debugging in the source code, logs, and
waveform.

Verdi GUI Features
You can perform the following actions in Verdi GUI:
* Grouping

Grouping
The Grouping feature is a core part of SBRCA. It helps to review all the violations grouped
into bins with different information, which means that the same bin might have the same
bug.
You can group violations using the following grouping rules for RDC and Glitch:
RDC
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* reset: Group by the same reset signals name
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command

Glitch
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command
On Verdi GUI, you can select the Group by option to choose the grouping rule. Using the
Grouping feature, you can review the results of different grouping rules in the active report
window as shown in the following figure:

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS
You need to use RDA plugin to load RDA in Verdi VMS. To invoke the RDA plugin, perform
the following steps:
1. Add RDA plugin to synopsys_eman.setup.
plugins:
- rda:
<VERDI_HOME>/platform/linux64/bin/rcaIntgrFlow/python38/rca_plugin.so

where <VERDI_HOME> is the full path of Verdi.
2. Load the RDA plugin in your .emc file.
plugins:
- rda

3. Register a load RDA report template using the following command:
vms admin register_custom_template -t $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/
python38/etc/vms/web_template/load_rda_report.emd -a

The Open RDA report button is added to the Verdi VMS GUI.

When you run the vms -gui command, select a session. Click the Open RDA report
button to open the RCA Manager window, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 579

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS

Enabling RDA Binning
RDA binning is always enabled in the RDA plugin.

Enabling Debug Facilitator/RCA
Define the debug engines Debug Facilitator and DUTRCA. Enable these engines for the
error patterns that you want to analyze.
Debug facilitator is defined by default; you need to include DF.emc as shown in the
following command:
include:
- $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/python38/etc/vms/engine_template/DF.emc

However, you need to define DUTRCA as shown in the following commands:
debug_engines :
- name: DUTRCA
cmd: $current_dir/dutrca_debug_engine_cmd.sh
log_file: $${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_dutrca_debug_engine.log
run_dir: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH
custom_values:
REF_CL_WORK_DIR: $$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL_WORK_DIR
DUTRCA_CONFIG: $current_dir/dutrca.yaml

TARGET_SCOPE: minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0
REPORT_PATH: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH/dutrca_report.xml

After defining the debug engines, enable them for the specific error patterns. In the
following example, DF and DUTRCA are enabled for the uvm_error error pattern:
error_patterns:
- name: uvm_error
pattern:
(?P<Type>UVM_ERROR)\s+.*\s+\[(?P<Code>\S+)\]\s+(?P<Description>.*)
base_status: fail
custom_status: uvm_error
priority: 0
debug_rerun_count: 1
debug_engines: DF DUTRCA

p4_load_cl.sh
#!/bin/sh
ROOT_DIR=$(realpath "${BASH_SOURCE%/*}")
if [ -z $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR ]; then
echo "EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR is empty. Skip loading cl"
exit 1
fi
if [ -z $EMAN_REF_FIND_CL ]; then
echo "EMAN_REF_FIND_CL is empty. Skip loading cl"
exit 1
fi
mkdir -p $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR/${EMAN_REF_FIND_CL}
find_cl_dir=realpath $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR/${EMAN_REF_FIND_CL}
echo "find_cl_dir:$find_cl_dir"

cd $find_cl_dir
P4CLIENT_SUFFIX=echo $find_cl_dir | md5sum | awk '{print $1}'
export P4CLIENT="labRDA_${USER}_${P4CLIENT_SUFFIX}"
echo "P4CLIENT:$P4CLIENT"
rm -rf $P4CONFIG
echo "P4PORT=$P4PORT"
> $P4CONFIG
echo "P4CLIENT=$P4CLIENT" >> $P4CONFIG
source $ROOT_DIR/create_template
p4 client -i < p4_client_templete
p4 sync -f @$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL

Applying Incremental Binning on Verdi VMS Parallel Debug
The Verdi VMS feature, Parallel Debug, allows you to run debug tests immediately after
the test fails in its custom failure category. Parallel debug provides the following benefits:
* Overlapping of the regular run and the debug run saves the overall turnaround time.
* Analyzing the RDA report and debugging before

DesignDiff
The DesignDiff feature introduces a GUI to compare the source code of two designs:
the reference design and the target design. You can analyze the comparison results.
DesignDiff shows differences between the two designs based on the semantics of the HDL
code, rather than the text of the HDL code. The DesignDiff feature includes the following
functions:
* Integrates the RTL difference (XML format) into DesignDiff.
* Adds the difference functionality.
* Displays the number of design changes in the nTrace hierarchy.
* Allows you to click each scope to view related design changes.
* Shows the target source code in Verdi.
The DesignDiff feature provides options to calculate and display the number of design
changes in the Instance View pane and ignore any module or source code file.
This section provides details on the following topics:
* DesignDiff Requirements
* Enabling DesignDiff
* Reviewing DesignDiff
* Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
* DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Requirements

DesignDiff Requirements
The following are the requirements for the DesignDiff feature:
* The RTL difference generates the DesignDiff report only when the VSO folder is
available; otherwise, it throws errors.
* You must provide the target and reference designs as two versions of the same
design. It allows DesignDiff to generate meaningful reports for review and analysis. To
generate the target and reference design directories, refer to the Generating Required
Directories section.

Generating Required Directories
The DesignDiff feature requires simv.daidir and ref.daidir directories for the current
and reference designs, respectively. To generate these directories, use the following
compile options for the respective simulator:
* VCS
When VCS is used for simulation, compile the design using the -kdb=designdiff
compile-time option, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -kdb=designdiff -lca [other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the other compile-time options.
* VCS with VSO.ai
When VCS is used with VSO.ai, compile the design using the -vso cso -kdb option
along with other compile-time options, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -vso cso -kdb -lca [other_options]

After compilation, the *.vso folder is generated along with *.daidir in the same
directory.
You must save these two files at the same directory level.
* Third-Party Simulators

Enabling DesignDiff

For third-party simulators, elaborate the design using the -useius=adv -designdiff
or -usemti=adv -designdiff option along with other compile-time options, as shown
in the following command:
For IUS flow,
% elabcom -useius=adv -designdiff [other_options]

Enabling DesignDiff
After generating the target and reference design directories using the compile-time options
provided in the Generating Required Directories section, enable the DesignDiff feature
using the designdiff command.
Use the following syntax to compare the two simv.daidir design directories:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
[other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the DesignDiff runtime options. You can add the following
DesignDiff runtime options:
* -diffreport <filename>: Specify the file name for the report. By default, the file
name is designdiff_report.xml.
* -ignore_module <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of module
names to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_module <filename> option, refer
to the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -ignore_file <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of source code
files to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_file <filename> option, refer to
the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -with_score: Calculates the design change score for the report. For more details,
refer to the -with_score section.
For example, % designdiff -dbdir ./target/simv.daidir -refdir ./reference/
ref.daidir.
The designdiff command analyzes the design difference details and generates the
corresponding report in an XML format, designdiff_report.xml.

To view the generated report, designdiff_report.xml, in Verdi, run the following
command:
% verdi -load_trace_report <generated_xml_report>, or
% designdiff -load_report <generated_xml_report>

You must load Designdiff reports using the command line; the GUI Load RDA
Trace Report option is not supported for DesignDiff reports.
For example, % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml

The following figure displays the GUI overview of the DesignDiff report uploaded to Verdi
using the % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml command:
Figure 586

DesignDiff Report Overview in Verdi GUI

The GUI of the DesignDiff report consists of the following three main components:
* Instance View
* Source View
* Source Code Changes
You can debug a design in the following two ways:
* Instance: To check the design difference of an instance with a large number of designdifference changes, click the scope in the Instance View pane. This synchronizes the
Source View pane with the source code of the module and displays the design-change
entries in the Source Code Changes section.
* Source code changes: When you click an entry in the Source Code Changes section,
the Source View pane displays the corresponding difference between the two designs.

Instance View
The Instance View pane displays the hierarchy tree of the design. The instance table
provides the name of the module, and the inclusive and exclusive change for the selected
instance, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 587

Instance View

When you run the designdiff command with the -with_score option, the DesignDiff
feature calculates the design changes and displays the score in the Instance View
pane, as shown in Figure 588. The score indicates the summation of the design changes
(addition, deletion, and modification).
% designdiff -dbdir <target>.daidir -refdir <reference>.dbdir -with_score

The exclusive change indicates the number of current scope changes, and the inclusive
change indicates the number of current scope and the child scope changes. A higher
count for an instance means that the instance contains a higher number of design
changes.

Figure 588

Instance View With -with_score

When you run the designdiff command without the -with_score option, the scores for
the design changes are not displayed in the Instance View pane. However, the design

change scope and the modules with design changes are highlighted in yellow, as shown in
Figure 589

Instance View Without -with_score

Source View
When you click an entry in the Instance View or Source Code Changes pane, the
Source View pane displays the source code difference between the two designs. The
following figure displays the Source View pane:

Source View Pane

The Source View pane is split into two vertical views, where the left view displays the
reference design view and the right view displays the target design view. The right-arrow
icon,

, in the Source View pane highlights the active difference.

The Source View pane consists of the following information:
* Status string
It displays the name of the module in the ignore list.
* Icons

everal elements, such as the File column, the Module
column, and the source code changes (add, delete, or edit). It also displays the target
begin and end lines, and the reference begin and end lines.
* The following priority is used for comparison:
File column = Module column > Source code difference (add, delete, edit) > begin line

> end line.

* The following priority is followed for sorting when Syntax is available:
1. Syntax
2. File
3. Edit mode
4. Begin line
5. End line
If two items match on one sorting element, use the next element to decide the order.
* You can sort entries alphabetically by file name or module name.
* If the file name or module name is the same, entries are sorted based on differences in
the source code. Entries that are not deleted appear before entries that are deleted.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files

* When comparing two deleted items, Verdi uses the following order of priority:
1. Target view begin line
2. Target view end line
3. Reference view begin line
4. Reference view end line
* When comparing two items that are not deleted, first compare the target view begin
line. If these lines match, compare the target view end line next.
* Sort keys are case-sensitive.
* The initial view sorts by the File column.
* The Line column does not support sorting.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
To ignore a module file and a source code file, use the -ignore_module
<ignore_module_file> and -ignore_file <ignore_source_code_file> options,
respectively, and run the following command:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
-ignore_module <ignore_module_file> -ignore_file <ignore_source code
file>

The -ignore_module <ignore_module_file> option reads modules listed in the userspecified module list and excludes them from comparison. The following is the format of

module list name

DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Limitations
The following are the limitations of the DesignDiff feature:
* Supported versions
The DesignDiff feature is supported for the following VCS release versions:
V-2023.12-SP2-8, W-2024.09-SP2-3, and later.
* File location requirements
The simv.vso folder must be saved in the same place as the simv.daidir.
* Unsupported languages and features
SystemC, Unified Power Format (UPF), Testbench, and VHDL languages are not
The scores of unnamed statements might not be accurate.
The Source View pane displays differences where a MACRO is used but not
defined.
DesignDiff cannot identify the exact changed line within an encrypted (protected)
block. It can only highlight the first line of that block as the changed location.
* Design reloading
To reload a design, you must run the srcDiffView -on Tcl command; otherwise,
Verdi cannot read the reference design.
* Scroll bar synchronization
When you select the SyncScrollBar check box, you can synchronize only from the
target view to the reference view, and not vice versa.
* Reference view limitations
Most of the reference view options, such as setting the active view, the right-click
options, and the drag option, are not available.
The reference view does not support the parameter annotation.
Non-manual scroll bar options, such as the srcGotoLine Tcl command, are not
When you jump to the target file line in the target design, the target line does not fall
in the range of a valid scope. The reference view does not get refreshed because of
the outdated data.
* Unsupported compilation flows

DesignDiff Limitations

VCS compilation is not supported with the -preserve_path option and in the
Scalene and PCH flows.
The -kdb=only and -kdb=common_elab:off flows are not supported.
The Verdi full-load mode is not supported when the design is compiled using the
-kdb=postelab flow.
* Design change detection
Any change in value format is treated as a design change. For example, if 3'b001
changes to 1'h1, the tool considers it as a design change.
A change in the order of the sensitive list is considered a design change.
A difference in the initial value in a declaration is not considered a design change.
Modules with different parameterizations cannot be combined for comparison.
DesignDiff does not detect modport changes within interfaces. Changes to modport
declarations, such as adding or removing signals fro

tments. You can also generate a new waveform based on
these changes.
* Generate Counter-Example Waveforms for Failing Properties: This feature
generates counter-example waveforms and shows how and why a SystemVerilog
Assertions (SVA) property fails.
In addition to the above-mentioned tasks, you can experiment with different verification
scenarios without changing the testbench and recompiling to run the simulation again,
thereby increasing productivity.
After you load the design into Verdi and launch Navigator, VC Formal runs in the
background automatically. When the VC Formal engine is ready, the Navigator window
opens in Verdi, allowing you to generate waveforms without a testbench.
You can edit the signal values in a waveform cycle-by-cycle, plot the waveform again, and
generate a new scenario, or extend the current waveform for additional cycles. If you write
SVA, you can also independently create SVA assert and cover properties. It allows you to
generate a waveform to verify whether assert properties fail or cover properties are met.
For more information about how to use the Navigator feature, refer to the VC Formal User
Guide.

Using the Verdi Flow
To launch Verdi Formal Navigator from Verdi, do the following:
* Import the design by running the following command:
% verdi -lca -sverilog -f <filelist>

Using the VCS Flow
To launch Verdi Formal Navigator from VCS, do the following:
1. Set the following environment variable:
setenv SNPS_VERDI_NAVIGATOR 1

The Knowledge Database (KDB) is generated in the simv.daidir directory.
3. Import the design by passing the simv.daidir directory to the -dbdir option of Verdi.
% verdi -lca -dbdir simv.daidir

After you import the design in Verdi, right-click the signal in the Source View window and
click New Navigator, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 595

Open Navigator From Source View

Alternatively, click Tools > New Navigator, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 596

Open Navigator From Tools Menu

The Navigator Setup dialog box opens.

Figure 597

Navigator Setup Dialog Box

To set up Verdi Formal Navigator, perform the following steps:
1. Select a value from the Top list.
By default, Top is set automatically if you specify the Top in the VCS compilation step.
2. Specify values in the Clock(s) and Reset(s) fields.

3. Expand the Advanced Settings section and select a value from the Formal License
list.
4. Click OK.
After VC Formal compiles the design successfully, the Navigator window opens and
displays the waveform, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 598

Verdi Assistant
Verdi Assistant is an AI-powered feature that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM)
into the Verdi environment. It provides a chatbot interface for conversational debugging.
This feature allows you to interact with Verdi by using natural language. As a result, you
can find commands, execute them, obtain documentation or answers to usage questions
easily. Verdi Assistant automates command execution and provides instant support. It
reduces the learning curve for new users and increases productivity of experienced users.
Verdi Assistant provides the following benefits:
* Simplifies command discovery and execution through natural language prompts.
* Reduces the need to consult documentation or application engineers for common
tasks.
* Supports both new and experienced users by streamlining workflows.
* Executes multiple commands with a single prompt, saving time.
* Provides context-aware assistance based on the current GUI state.
* Offers feedback mechanisms to improve the responses generated by the assistant.

Understanding the Chat History Database
This section describes the chat history database, which stores all Verdi Assistant
promptresponse interactions in an SQLite3 file. This file also includes the configuration
of the Verdi Assistant directory, file name, data format, and the fields recorded for each
conversation turn.
This section contains the following topics:
* Database File Configuration and Format
* Data Stored Per Prompt

Database File Configuration and Format
This section explains how the Chat History Database file is configured, including how the
directory and file name are determined through environment variables. The database is
stored in SQLite3 format for easy access and compatibility.
* File Directory
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_DIR environment variable to specify the database
directory.
If you do not set this variable, the directory defaults to your home directory under
.verdi (for example, ~/.verdi).
* File Name
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_NAME environment variable to specify the
database file name.
If you do not set this variable, the file name defaults to chat_<username>.db, where
<username> is your operating system username.

* File Format
The database uses the SQLite3 format. Access the database by using SQLite3 scripts
or any SQLite3-compatible browser.

Data Stored Per Prompt
For every prompt and response, Verdi Assistant records one row in the sessions table of
the Chat History Database. Each row includes the following columns, with a composite
primary key on (chat_id, idx).
Column

Data Type

chat_id

Unique identifier of a chat session (UUID-style
string). All turns in the same conversation share
the same chat_id.

idx

INTEGER

Zero-based index of the turn within a session.
For example, 0 for the first turn, 1 for the
second and so on.
Together with chat_id, this identifies a single
row.

user

Operating system username associated with
the interaction.

prompt

User prompt text sent to Verdi Assistant.

response

model

LLM model used by Verdi Assistant for the
prompt.

prompt_tokens

INTEGER

Number of tokens in the prompt; where -1
indicates unknown or not recorded.

completion_tokens

INTEGER

Number of tokens in the model's completion;
where -1 indicates unknown or not recorded.

timestamp

INTEGER

Unix timestamp (seconds since epoch) when
the turn is recorded.

extra_content

JSON-formatted string containing any
additional metadata for the turn.

The Waveform Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses AI-driven
agentic techniques to enhance waveform analysis.

The new capabilities are specifically designed to streamline the analysis of complex user
waveform files with enhanced precision and efficiency. These capabilities help users
identify potential issues earlier and ensure faster, more reliable design verification.
You can submit natural-language queries to request detailed information about a waveform
file. The agent processes these requests and retrieves relevant data.
In GUI mode, you interact with both a chatbot and a waveform view. This mode is also
called Waveform-Viewer-Integrated mode.
It enables contextual queries and visual signal analysis. You can reference items in the
waveform view using phrases such as "the selected signals," "the cursor time," or "the
waveform".
The waveform view updates based on the chatbot's responses. This provides instant
visual confirmation.

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.

Set Default Debugging Target
Before querying signal debugging information, you can set the default debugging target,
such as FSDB file path and time unit. This eliminates the need to repeat the information in
every prompt.
Set Default FSDB
You can set the active FSDB for debugging once, eliminating the need to specify the full
FSDB path in each prompt. In GUI mode, the active FSDB is automatically synchronized
with the active FSDB in the waveform window.
In MCP mode, when an FSDB is not explicitly provided in the prompt, the most recently
mentioned FSDB is used. To change the default FSDB file path, enter the new FSDB file

efault Waveform and Time Unit
Default settings for waveform and time unit can be configured to streamline repeated
prompts. These defaults are synchronized with the active waveform window and are
applied automatically unless new values are specified. Refer to the Set Default Debugging
Target section for more details.
Radix
To ensure consistent interpretation, always include the radix specifier when writing values.
* 'h for hexadecimal
* 'd for decimal
* 'b for binary
* 'o for octal
For example, to specify the decimal value 17, use 'h11, 'd17, or 'b10001.
You can also specify the width of the bit before the radix specifier. For example, 8'h3C
represents an 8-bit hexadecimal value.

When a number is written without a radix specifier, it is interpreted based on its value:
1. If the value contains only 0 and 1, it is treated as binary.
Example: 1010 Interpreted as binary.
2. If the value contains any digits from 2 to 9, it is treated as decimal.
Example: 123 Interpreted as decimal.
3. If the value contains any letters from A to F (case-insensitive), it is treated as
hexadecimal.
Example: 3C Interpreted as hexadecimal.
Simple and Full Hierarchical Name
Full hierarchical name is required unless the signal is already visible in the active window
within Verdi. For example, the following prompt uses full hierarchical signal name
'tb_CPU.system.m1':
Find the value of signal "tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD" at 0 ns.
Alternatively, you can add signal tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD to the waveform window then
the signal can be referenced using the simple name:
Find the value of signal "CARD" at 0ns.
Delimiter
Only the dot (.) character is supported as a delimiter for hierarchy. The slash (/) character
is not supported.
Bus Signals with Unknowns (Xs)
When searching for unknown values in a bus signal, any value that contains 'x' is identified
as unknown. For example, 'bxxxx, 'b010x, and 'b1x11 are all identified as unknown values.
Matching Value Including Unknowns
To search for a specific value that includes unknown (X) values, the value must be written
in binary format. Note that an unknown value needs to be specified by a lowercase 'x'. For
example, 8'b10x01100.
Complex Scenarios
When describing a complex scenario, break it down into clear steps. Avoid including
unnecessary expertise, for more effective outcomes.

Known Issues and Limitations of Waveform Agent
This section describes the known issues and limitations of Waveform Agent.
Assertion and Transaction Waveform
Waveform analysis for assertion signals and transaction waveform is not supported.
[Prompt] Find the first assertion failure timestamp for the signal system.i_cpu.INCPC2.
Phase Between Clock Signals
Phase measurement between clock signals is not supported.
[Prompt] Measure the phase between clock signals
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK1 and tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK2.
Gated Clock and Multiple Clock Frequency
Retrieving clock-related information is not supported for gated clocks.
This limitation also applies to clock signals with multiple clock frequencies. Examples
include clock frequency and cycle length.
[Prompt] Obtain the period of the system.gated_clock clock signal.
The system.gated_clock is assumed to be a gated clock signal in the waveform.
Member Signals
For composite objects such as SystemVerilog structs, unions, and interfaces, individual
member signals cannot be accessed; only the parent signal is supported.

Design Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses agentic AI to automate
and speed up HDL (Hardware Description Language) design analysis. You can submit
natural-language queries to explore RTL (Register-Transfer Level) codebases, extract
insights, and find structural patterns.
Design Agent is designed to streamline the analysis of complex hardware designs.
It enhances precision and helps engineers gain a deeper understanding of module

hierarchies, signal interactions, and potential design issues. By identifying issues earlier
in the development cycle, Design Agent reduces manual effort and accelerates design
verification.
This chapter covers the following topics:
* Getting Started
* Prompting Basics
* Advanced Prompting

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.
Import Design
Before using Design Agent, you need to import designs into the Verdi Assistant
environment. This ensures the agent has access to the full RTL codebase for accurate
analysis.
You can prompt the agent to load a design by providing the path to simv.daidir.

Import the design from /path/to/simv.daidir

The design has been successfully imported
from the directory path/to/simv.daidir

Design loading is currently supported only through the -dbdir option, which requires the
path to the compiled simulation database (for example, simv.daidir).
Reload Design
Reloading the design ensures that the Design Agent operates on the latest RTL code after
any modifications. This action re-imports the compiled simulation database and all existing
applications into Verdi.

Reload the design

The design has been successfully reloaded

Import FSDB
To change the default FSDB file path, enter a new FSDB path in a new prompt.
Certain Design Agent capabilities depend on FSDB files. If the required FSDB files are not
available, the system notifies you.
Waveform Agent handles FSDB file import. It loads and processes waveform data to
support analysis.

Import /path/to/my.fsdb

The FSDB file located at /path/to/my.fsdb has
been successfully imported and is now active.

The following example illustrates the scenario and response when the required FSDB file
has not been imported for Design Agent.

Trace the value of "system.En_A" at time 250
ns

To trace the value of system.En_A at 250ns, I
need the FSDB (waveform database) file name
associated with the design. Could you provide
this information?

Prompting Basics
Design Agent uses natural language prompts to analyze RTL design data, facilitating both
structural and functional exploration. This section introduces how to write clear, effective
prompts through simple examples.
Design Agent offers two primary functionalities: Design Exploration and Signal Tracing.

Active Signal Tracing
Active signal tracing analyzes signal behavior using simulation data to identify active
drivers and trace unknown values.
Active signal tracing requires simulation data (FSDB) to analyze signal behavior at a
specific simulation time. This type of tracing focuses on the dynamic behavior of signals
during simulation.
In GUI mode, Temporal Flow View (TFV) is used to visualize active tracing results, and
relevant traced signals are recorded to a file during the tracing process.
Trace Active Driver
Trace active driver identifies which driver is actively driving a signal at a specific simulation
time. This is essential for debugging signal contention and understanding multiplexed
signal paths.
Tracing active drivers or value-change causes can be time-consuming. By default, the
agent traces only direct drivers. If you request a value-change cause, the trace continues
deeper. When a one-time tracing limit is reached, the agent prompts for confirmation
before continuing, and then resumes from the previous stop point.

Describes the example lab, including required files, environment setup, script execution,
and result verification for testing Verdi Assistant.
This lab provides an end-to-end workflow to verify that Verdi Assistant is installed and
functioning correctly in the local environment.

Example Lab Overview for Verdi Assistant

Prerequisite

customer_example_lab folder for the following files:
* README: Explains the usage instructions.

"<MCP_TOOL_NAME> <prompt>".

* run_vcs: VCS related file.

reference for creating custom MCP client configurations.

the example lab.

VERDI_MODEL_CONFIG to /path/to/your/<model>.yaml.
If VERDI_MODEL_CONFIG is not set, demo_script.sh automatically detects
available models and guides you through required inputs.

Glossary
This glossary defines important terms, signals, and concepts referenced in the Verdi
Assistant documentation.

Model Context Protocol

A communication protocol that defines how a client interacts with an AI model or
system. MCP ensures structured data exchange, command handling and process
control.
MCP can operate in different modes depending on the communication method. For
example, STDIO Mode and SSE Mode.

Glossary

Standard Input/Output Mode

A mode in which the MCP communicates with the AI model process through standard
input and output streams. This setup is commonly used for local or embedded
integrations where data is exchanged via terminal-like interfaces rather than network
sockets.

SSE Mode (Server-Sent Events Mode)

A mode in which the MCP communicates over HTTP using Server-Sent Events. This
allows the server to push real-time updates, such as progress messages or streaming
responses, to the client in a continuous connection.

API key

A unique authentication token used to identify and authorize a user or application when
accessing an API service or system API.
API keys help control access, track usage and enforce rate limits.

Endpoint

A specific URL or network address where a service or API can be accessed.
In the context of SCS (Service Control System), the endpoint defines the connection
target for structured requests. Examples include job creation, model queries, and
debug commands.

InstHdl includes two types: module instance and primitive instance.
* Module Instance:
A module reference in the design that serves as a container for sub instance, port,
instance port, and net objects.
* Primitive Instance:
Denotes the minimum design unit. It is used to represent low-level logic gates and
switches with specific cell functions. For example, npiNlAndCell, npiNlFSMCell, and
npiNlBufCell.
You can query a InstHdl by public functions, either by get_inst(), or traverse by
get_top_inst_list()get_top_inst_list(), and InstHdl.inst_list().

Practice
The following practice example illustrates the following:
* How to generate the FSDB file that includes the Testbench Hierarchy Tree information,
and how to load this dynamic data into the Verdi platform for viewing the hierarchy and
the connection information.
* View the detailed call-stacks of this dynamic information.
* Correlate the dynamic recorded information with the source code.
* Understand the source of testbench objects generation from the source code.
The practice example uses the OVM UART example located in the $VERDI_HOME/share/
vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/examples/ uart16550 directory. It demonstrates the use of the
Testbench Hierarchy tree to debug the connection of a port.
1. Copy the case to your local directory.
%> cp -r $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/ .

2. Change directory to sv_latest.
%> cd lib/examples/uart16550/verif/testbench/sv_latest

3. Setup the environment variable for this practice.
%> setenv VERDI_HOME <Verdi_Install_Directory>
%> setenv OVM_HOME $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib

4. Generate an FSDB file with the TBH tree dumped.
a. Setup the variable for your simulation machine:
%> setenv MACHINE LINUX64

b. Open the run_vcs file, modify the SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE and VCS_HOME variables
to match your simulation path.

Chapter 5: Practice

c. Add the +sps_enable_hier_trace option to simv:
./simv +sps_enable_hier_trace +fsdb+trans_begin_callstack
+OVM_TESTNAME=uart_testcase_modem_status_test -l vcssim.log

d. Run VCS to dump the FSDB:
%> source run_vcs

5. Import the design with OVM/UVM and load the generated FSDB file.
%> verdi +OVM_TESTNAME=uart_testcase_modem_status_test
-sv +incdir+$OVM_HOME/src $OVM_HOME/src/ovm_pkg.sv
+incdir+../../../rtl/verilog_lastest
-f ../../../rtl/verilog_lastest/compile.f uart_duv_if.sv
uart_duv_top.sv -ssf novas.fsdb &

2. npiHighConn indicates the hierarchically higher (closer to the top module) port
connection.
3. npiLowConn indicates the lower (further from the top module) port connection.
4. npiLowConn of a npiInterfacePort is always be npiRefObj.
5. If a port is explicitly named, then the explicit name is returned. If not, and a name
exists, then that name is returned. Otherwise, NULL is returned.
6. npiPortIndex is used to determine the port order. The first port has a port index of zero.
7. npiLowConn returns NULL if the module or interface or program port is a null port (for
example, "module M();"). npiHighConn returns NULL if the instance of the module,
interface, or program does not have a connection to the port.
8. npiSize for a null port returns 0.
9. Ports and IO Declaration have the same behavior as npiDirection. That is, npiDirection
returns npiRef for pass by ref ports or arguments, and the npiDirection of the port is
undefined if the npiActual of the ref obj is an interface or modport declaration.
10. If a slice name (npiVhSliceName) or indexed name (npiVhIndexedName) comes from
a VHDL port, it can get its parent port by applying method npiParent. However, the
parent of sliced name of port could be a port or an indexed port, and the parent of
indexed name of a port must be a port.
11. The npiVhBaseType, npiVhInitExpr and npiVhType methods are only available for a
VHDL port. That is, a non-VHDL port returns NULL by applying these three methods.
Further information about VHDL port is shown in Object Declaration.
12. npiPortInstFile and npiPortInstLineNo are only for NPI SystemVerilog Model. They
show the file name and line number of the port's port instance (high-connection object).

simply jumps from input port to the corresponding output port while tracing.
The following section covers the map file mapping rules:
Basic Mapping Rules
Map file:
modName portA portB
1. If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
2. If trace to a bit portA[idx], it maps to portB[idx].
3. If trace to slice portA[lidx,ridx], it maps to slice portB[lidx:ridx]. (For example, portA [1:0]
maps to portB[1:0]).
4. If output port not existed, it stops tracing at input port and the port is listed in the result
5. If portB has size = 1, then any part of portA maps to portB. (for example, both portA[1]
and portA[1:0] maps to portB).

Extended Mapping Rules
Map file:
modName portA portB
modName portA[0] portB[2]
If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
If trace to portA[0], it maps to portB[2]. Since the map relation is specified.
If trace to portA[1], maps to portB[1] according to basic mapping rules.
Map file:
modName portA portB
modName portA[0] portB
If trace to portA, it maps to portB.
If trace to port portA[0], maps to portB. Since the map relation is specified.
If trace to port portA[1], maps to portB[1] according to basic mapping rules.
Map file:
modName portA portB[1]
If trace to portA, it maps to portB[1].
If trace to portA[idx], maps to portB[1].
If trace to portA[lidx:ridx], maps to portB[1].
The map is bidirectional. portB maps to portA, and the spec is also applicable.

design files. In the NPI Text model, you can use two APIs -- npi_text_property() and
